contraindications/abs-01/text.text: Unstable vital signs (HR, RR, BP, temperature)

contraindications/rel-20/text.text: Ingestion of foreign bodies or caustics

contraindications/rel-24/text.text: Acid–base disorders without compromised vital signs

contraindications/rel-39/text.text: Envenomation by venomous animal bite or sting

entities/aborto/description.text: This pair prevents miscarriage. Abortion is the premature interruption and termination of pregnancy, whether natural or voluntary. In a broader sense, it can refer to the failure, through interruption or miscarrying, of any process or activity. Spontaneous abortion or natural miscarriage is one that is not intentionally induced. The most frequent cause is fetal death, due to congenital anomalies of the fetus, frequently genetic. In other cases it is due to abnormalities of the reproductive tract, or to systemic diseases of the mother or infectious diseases. When the gestational age is greater than 22 weeks or the weight of the fetus exceeds 500 grams, it is referred to as fetal death. Signs and symptoms include transvaginal bleeding.

entities/abraham/description.text: Pair related to Ménière's disease. It is named after the biblical figure Abraham. The place where the magnets should be placed (pole) corresponds to the place where Moses has horns (Michelangelo's work). It is at the hairline on the forehead.

entities/absceso-hepatico/contagion.text: Amoeba. Entamoeba histolytica. Amoebic liver abscess is caused by Entamoeba histolytica, the same parasite that causes amebiasis, an intestinal infection also called amoebic dysentery. After an infection has occurred, the parasite can be carried through the blood from the intestines to the liver. The disease spreads through consumption of water or food contaminated with fecal matter (sometimes due to the use of human excrement as fertilizer) and through direct contact between people.

entities/absceso-hepatico/description.text: Amoebic liver abscess occurs when the amoeba passes from the pylorus to the liver, causing an abscess. It is a collection of pus in the liver in response to an intestinal parasite: Entamoeba histolytica. This parasite causes amebiasis, an intestinal infection also called amoebic dysentery. After an infection has occurred, the parasite can be transported through the blood from the intestines to the liver. People with an amoebic liver abscess may have the following symptoms: abdominal pain, cough, fever and chills, diarrhea (in only one-third of patients), malaise, general discomfort or indisposition, hiccups that do not stop (uncommon), jaundice (yellowish discoloration of the skin and mucous membranes), lack of appetite, sweating, weight loss.

entities/absceso-medular/contagion.text: The infection is generally due to bacteria and is often caused by a staphylococcal infection that spreads through the spinal column. It can be caused by tuberculosis. In some rare cases, the infection may be due to a fungus.

entities/absceso-medular/description.text: A spinal abscess is a swelling and irritation (inflammation) and accumulation of infected material (pus) in or around the spinal cord. A spinal cord abscess is caused by an infection within the spinal column. This type of abscess in itself is very uncommon. Pus forms as an accumulation of destroyed tissue cells, fluid, white blood cells, bacteria and other dead and living microorganisms. The pus is usually covered by a lining or membrane that forms around the edges. The accumulation of pus exerts pressure on the spinal cord. The most common symptoms are chills, fever, loss of sphincter control, loss of movement of an area of the body below the abscess, loss of sensation in an area of the body below the abscess, lumbago (often mild, but slowly worsening), and severe back pain.

entities/absceso/description.text: An abscess is an infection and inflammation of the body's tissue characterized by swelling and the accumulation of pus. It can be external and visible, on the skin, or internal. When it is suppurating it is called an apostema. Abscesses appear when an area of tissue becomes infected and the body is able to "wall off" the infection and prevent it from spreading. White blood cells, which are the body's defense against some types of infection, migrate through the walls of the blood vessels to the area of infection and accumulate within the damaged tissue. During this process, pus forms, which is an accumulation of fluids, living and dead white blood cells (mainly polymorphonuclear neutrophils, PMNs), dead tissue and bacteria or any other foreign material or invader. Abscesses can form in almost any part of the body and can be caused by infectious organisms, parasites and foreign materials. Abscesses in the skin are easily visible, red, raised and painful, whereas abscesses that form in other areas of the body may not be as obvious but can cause a great deal of damage if they involve vital organs.

entities/acidez-estomacal/description.text: Heartburn is a painful burning sensation in the chest or throat that occurs when stomach acid flows back into the esophagus, the tube that carries food from the mouth to the stomach. The pain originates in the chest and can radiate to the neck, throat or angle of the jaw. Pregnancy, some foods, alcoholic beverages and some medicines can cause heartburn.

entities/acido-urico/description.text: Uric acid is an organic compound of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and hydrogen. Its chemical formula is C5 H4 N4 O3. It is a weak acid produced in the liver, muscles, intestines, kidneys and vascular endothelium as the end product of the catabolism (the part of the metabolic process that consists of transforming complex biomolecules into simple molecules and properly storing chemical energy) of purines (adenine and guanine) through the action of the enzyme xanthine oxidase. It is found in the urine in small amounts. In some animals, such as birds, reptiles and many arthropods, it is the main waste product and is expelled with the feces. In human blood, the uric acid concentration in men is 3.6 to 6.5 mg/dl, and for women it is 2.5 to 6.5mg/dl, although lower levels can be found in vegetarians. Gout in humans is associated with abnormal levels of uric acid in the system. Saturation of uric acid in human blood can give rise to a type of kidney stone (nephrolithiasis) when the acid crystallizes in the kidney. A considerable percentage of gout patients come to have uric acid kidney stones. The greater the increase in uric acid in the blood, the greater the chances of suffering kidney, arthritic and other conditions.

entities/acne/description.text: Acne, also known as common acne or acne vulgaris, is a chronic inflammatory skin disease involving the pilosebaceous units (hair follicle and sebaceous glands), characterized by the formation of comedones, papules, pustules, nodules and scars, which appear mainly on the face and upper trunk.

entities/acromegalia/description.text: Acromegaly is a condition in which there is too much growth hormone in the body. It occurs when the pituitary gland produces too much growth hormone. The pituitary gland is a pea-sized endocrine gland located at the base of the brain that controls, produces and secretes several hormones, for example growth hormone. The cause of the secretion of too much growth hormone is generally a noncancerous (benign) tumor of the pituitary gland. Excessive production of growth hormone in children produces gigantism instead of acromegaly. Elephantiasis is a syndrome characterized by significant enlargement of some parts of the body, especially the lower limbs and the external genital organs. It can be produced by various persistent inflammatory diseases caused by various spirochetes, treponemes and parasites. Elephantiasis is due to obstruction of the lymphatic vessels (producing severe inflammation) and to blood parasites such as filariae (parasites that inhabit the lymphatic vessels, body cavities, the heart and other places in the body depending on the species). It also causes bone malformation, which progressively deforms the body as far as the deformation allows.

entities/actinomicosis/description.text: Actinomycosis is a disease caused by an anaerobic bacterium called Actinomyces israelii, which is a common organism that normally does not cause disease (non-pathogenic) and is found in the nose and throat. Given the normal location of the bacterium in the nose and throat, actinomycosis appears most commonly on the face and neck. The infection is not contagious. Symptoms occur when the bacterium enters the facial tissues due to trauma, surgery or infection. A common cause is a dental abscess or oral surgery. Once it has become localized in the tissue, it forms an abscess, producing a deep red to reddish-purple swelling, often on the jaw, from which its common name of "lumpy jaw" derives. Finally, the abscess breaks through the surface of the skin to produce a draining sinus tract. Actinomycosis can occasionally occur in the chest (pulmonary actinomycosis) and the abdomen or other areas of the body.

entities/actinomyces/description.text: Actinomyces is a genus of Gram-positive bacteria. Some species are anaerobic, while others are facultative anaerobes. Actinomyces species do not form spores and, while the individual bacteria are spherical, the colonies form structures similar in shape to fungal hyphae. Many Actinomyces are opportunistic pathogens of humans and other mammals, particularly in the oral cavity. In rare cases, these bacteria can cause actinomycosis, a disease characterized by the formation of abscesses in the mouth, lungs or gastrointestinal tract. Some species are responsible for the vegetal smell of the earth, which is often particularly noticeable after rain.

entities/acufenos/contagion.text: They can be caused by a large number of causes, generally traumatic, or be the result of a symptom of blocked ears or of Ménière's disease. They can also be caused by stressful situations from studies, work, the family, economic or social environment, or exposure to noise.

entities/acufenos/description.text: Tinnitus or acouphenes, which consists of a perceptual phenomenon in which knocking or sounds are perceived in the ear that do not come from any external source. They generally consist of whistling, roaring, buzzing, whispering, blowing, hissing or ringing, and sometimes become so loud that the patient is unable to hear a normal conversation.

entities/adenoides/description.text: The adenoids are lymphatic tissue found in the upper airway between the nose and the back of the throat. They are similar to the tonsils. Adenoid hypertrophy means that the tissue is swollen. The adenoid vegetations help the body prevent or fight infections by removing bacteria and germs. Infections can cause the adenoid vegetations to become inflamed. Children with adenoid hypertrophy often breathe through the mouth because the nose is blocked. Mouth breathing occurs mainly at night, but may be present during the day. Mouth breathing can lead to the following symptoms: bad breath, cracked lips, dry mouth, persistent rhinorrhea or nasal congestion, sleep problems, heavy snoring, episodes of absence of breathing during sleep (sleep apnea). Children with adenoid hypertrophy may also have more frequent ear infections.

entities/adenoma-de-hipofisis/descriptio.text: Pituitary adenomas are slow-growing benign tumors that originate in the cells that make up the pituitary gland. The pituitary gland is considered the “master gland,” which regulates the function of other glands of the body. Pituitary adenomas are relatively common, occurring in approximately 1 in every 1,000 adults, and are in the vast majority benign (noncancerous), slow-growing tumors.

entities/adenoma-de-prostata/description.text: A prostate adenoma or benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) consists of a non-malignant (non-cancerous) growth in the size of the prostate. As the prostate grows, it can progressively compress the urethra and therefore cause difficulty urinating. This happens because this compression impedes the flow of urine from the bladder into the urethra and out of the body. Possible consequences are urine retention in the bladder or reflux of urine toward the kidneys, and a need to urinate frequently. If the inflammation is very severe, the urinary system can become completely blocked. BPH is a very common disease in men: although it generally begins from the age of 30, it very rarely becomes manifest before 40. At approximately 60 years of age, more than 50% of men have BPH, and between 70 and 80 years of age up to 90% present some of its symptoms.

entities/adenovirus-serotype-33/descript.text: Respiratory problems. Adenoviruses (Adenoviridae) are a family of viruses that infect both humans and animals. They are non-enveloped double-stranded DNA viruses that can cause respiratory tract infections, conjunctivitis, hemorrhagic cystitis and gastroenteritis. They can also cause fever and abdominal distension; it affects the adenoids and lymph nodes.

entities/adenovirus-serotype-36/descript.text: Adenoviruses (Adenoviridae) are a family of viruses that infect both humans and animals. They are non-enveloped double-stranded DNA viruses that can cause respiratory tract infections, conjunctivitis, hemorrhagic cystitis and gastroenteritis. They can also cause fever and abdominal distension; it affects the adenoids and lymph nodes.

entities/adenovirus/description.text: Adenoviruses (Adenoviridae) are a family of viruses that infect both humans and animals. They are non-enveloped double-stranded DNA viruses that can cause respiratory tract infections, conjunctivitis, hemorrhagic cystitis and gastroenteritis. They can also cause fever and abdominal distension; it affects the adenoids and lymph nodes.

entities/adicciones/description.text: Drug addiction. Addictions. Epilepsy. Dyslexia. Drug addiction --> Organic problem. Alcoholism --> Emotional problem. The terms drug addiction and drug dependence refer to the addiction generated by repeated exposure to a drug, whether a medication or a psychoactive substance. It is a need to consume repeated doses of the substance in order to feel well or to avoid feeling unwell. The desire to consume and obtain it is very strong; there is a tendency to increase the doses and a psychological, and sometimes physical, dependence as a consequence of the drug's effects.

entities/aftosavirus/contagion.text: Dairy products. It especially attacks toddlers, although it can appear at any age. This happens particularly when it is hot, usually in summer or early fall.

entities/agnosia-de-caras/description.text: Agnosia is the disruption of the ability to recognize previously learned stimuli, or to learn new stimuli, without any deficiency in perception, language or intellect. In agnosia, the difficulty in recognizing stimuli cannot be attributed to sensory defects, such as loss of vision due to an eye disorder, or to unfamiliarity with the stimulus presented. In visual agnosia, for example, the subject can see normally, since their visual system functions correctly, but is unable to interpret, describe or recognize what they are seeing. The person with agnosia has no deficit whatsoever in their general mental abilities.

entities/agresividad/description.text: Corrects problems related to extreme aggressiveness and criminality. The term aggressiveness refers to a set of activity patterns that can manifest with varying intensity, ranging from physical fighting to the gestures or verbal outbursts that appear in the course of any negotiation. There are several types of aggressiveness: physical (blows, kicks, etc.), verbal (insults), facial (gestures), indirect (toward objects belonging to the affected person), sexual (rape). Aggressiveness can manifest at each of the levels that make up the individual: physical (physical fights), emotional (rage, anger), cognitive (destructive fantasies) and social (acting out of aggressiveness). In its strictest sense, aggressiveness can be understood as behavior aimed at causing harm to another person.

entities/ah1n1/description.text: Influenzavirus A subtype H1N1, better known as human influenza A H1N1, is a subtype of influenzavirus type A of the influenza virus. H1N1 has mutated into various subtypes that include Spanish flu (extinct in the wild), swine flu, avian flu and bovine flu. Avian influenza, also known as bird flu, designates a viral infectious disease that affects birds, although it has sufficient potential to infect various species of mammals, including humans, pigs and domestic cats.

entities/ah1n7/description.text: Influenzavirus A subtype H1N7, better known as human influenza A H1N7, is a subtype of influenzavirus type A of the influenza virus. Avian influenza, also known as bird flu, designates a viral infectious disease that affects birds, although it has sufficient potential to infect various species of mammals, including humans, pigs and domestic cats.

entities/alergias/description.text: Allergies caused by foods, mainly seafood. Skin allergies. Allergies in general. Allergy is an immune reaction of the body to a substance that is generally innocuous (harmless) to the host, which manifests with characteristic signs and symptoms when the host is exposed to it by inhalation, ingestion or skin contact. For a long time allergy was considered equivalent to hypersensitivity (an older term), and for that reason it was mistakenly regarded as an exaggerated immune reaction to a substance. But allergy is the clinical expression of the body's normal immune response mechanisms against possible invaders; the error lies not in the type of response or its intensity but in the target, which poses no threat. The final consequence of this error of the immune system is disease of the host, caused by the collateral effects suffered by the tissues where the immune system tries to defend itself against that harmless substance. The clinical manifestations of this disease are diverse, since they depend on the causative substance and the organ affected. At present, more than a third of the world's population has some disease of allergic origin.

entities/alexia/description.text: Alexia is the partial or total loss of the ability to read due to a brain injury, when that ability had previously been acquired. It is generally accompanied by loss of writing skill (agraphia), although the person can speak and understand spoken language. It is therefore an acquired defect.

entities/alopecia/description.text: Alopecia is a disease in which there is abnormal loss or thinning of the hair; the term is considered a synonym of baldness. It can affect the scalp or other areas of the skin where there is hair, such as the eyelashes, eyebrows, armpits, genital region and beard. Alopecia can be classified into a multitude of groups according to its origin and manifestations, but the most frequent form is androgenic alopecia, also called androgenetic alopecia or common baldness, which is responsible for 95% of cases and mainly affects men, less frequently women, and owes its name to the fact that it is caused by the action of male hormones or androgens on the hair follicle, causing its progressive miniaturization. Other common forms of alopecia are alopecia areata, in which the hair loss is not permanent and is commonly confined to a specific area; alopecia universalis, which is the extensive form of alopecia areata; and cicatricial alopecia, which is caused by destruction of the hair follicle and is therefore irreversible. There are many less frequently occurring varieties of alopecia that can originate from genetic causes, medications, skin infections, trauma, nutritional deficiencies and certain skin or systemic diseases.

entities/alteraciones-nerviosas/descript.text: The symptoms that characterize a nervous breakdown vary considerably according to the type of mental disorder that causes it. For example, if it is caused by a neurosis, the symptoms may be depression, an irrational fear of traveling, especially by plane, or of interacting with strangers, extreme anxiety, crying, constant startling and heart palpitations. A person suffering a nervous breakdown may well lose control of their emotions, although they retain their mental activity. Cyclothymia, or excessive and rapid mood swings, frequently occurs, and outbursts of anger may alternate with periods of calm and indifference. The emotional pairs should be checked.

entities/altivez/description.text: Haughtiness or arrogance refers to a person's excessive pride in relation to themselves, which leads them to believe in and demand more privileges than they are entitled to. It is frequently used with a negative connotation.

entities/alvaro/description.text: Pair related to hormonal dysfunction. Alvaro Echeverría is the son of Luis Echeverría (former president of Mexico). He asked Dr. Goiz to name a pair after him, and Dr. Goiz did so. He is a very good therapist.

entities/alzheimer/description.text: Alzheimer's disease is a neurodegenerative disease that manifests as cognitive decline and behavioral disorders. In its typical form it is characterized by a loss of immediate memory and of other mental capacities (such as higher cognitive abilities) as nerve cells (neurons) die and different areas of the brain atrophy. After diagnosis the disease usually has an average duration of approximately 10 years, although this may vary in direct proportion to the severity of the disease at the time of diagnosis. Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia; it is incurable and terminal, and it appears most frequently in people over 65 years of age. In rare cases, however, it can develop from the age of 40. In Alzheimer's disease there is a significant decrease in the enzyme choline acetyltransferase due to the weakening of its receptors, which leads to an increase in senile plaques. It produces dementia states through neuropathological and neurotransmitter changes. It is a syndrome of progressive cognitive decline. Some medicinal plants that have shown benefits in treating Alzheimer's disease are the following: Ginkgo (Ginkgo biloba), Turmeric root (Curcuma longa) and Green tea (Thea sinensis). Blood circulation should be stimulated in the upper parietal - temporal - frontal region.

entities/ameba/contagion.text: Infection occurs through contamination of water, vegetables, fruit or other raw foods that are poorly washed or undercooked with infectious cysts from contaminated feces.

entities/ameba/description.text: The amoeba is an intestinal parasite of the Entamoeba histolytica type. They are small organisms that live as intestinal parasites in humans and dogs. At the beginning of their life cycle, before reaching the parasitic phase, they remain in a latent state in a cyst covered with chitin, a substance that protects them from the outside. Once the cyst is consumed, they are released in the stomach, producing amoebiasis. These parasites feed basically on bacteria and nutrient remnants in their host's stomach. Some symptoms of amoebiasis are intense fatigue, diarrhea, nausea, weight loss, occasional fever, abdominal pain, intestinal gas and flatulence. Occasionally amoebas can settle in other areas of the body, producing more serious infections and symptoms, such as a liver abscess (a pus-filled mass inside the liver).

entities/amebiasis-intestinal/descriptio.text: Amoebas. When it invades the intestine it can produce dysentery (an inflammatory disorder of the intestine, especially the colon, that produces severe diarrhea containing mucus and/or blood in the stool). Of every 10 people in whom the parasite is detected, one will develop symptoms, which may range from mild diarrhea to more serious cases. The disease develops in two phases: 1) Acute phase: this is the most serious and may last from weeks to months. The patient has severe abdominal pain and bloody stools. 2) Chronic phase: may last for years and, if untreated, can lead to death. In this case, mild diarrhea alternates with constipation.

entities/amebiasis/contagion.text: Amoeba parasite. Infection occurs through contamination of water, vegetables, fruit or other raw foods that are poorly washed or undercooked with infectious cysts from contaminated feces.

entities/amebiasis/description.text: Amebiasis or amoebiasis is a parasitic disease produced by the amoebae Entamoeba histolytica, Entamoeba dispar and Entamoeba moshkovskii, rhizopod protozoa widespread in warm and tropical climates. Their usual habitat is the large intestine. They can invade the intestinal mucosa, producing ulcerations, and spread to other organs. The parasite is generally acquired in its cyst form through oral ingestion of contaminated food or fluids. When it invades the intestine, it can produce dysentery, which is an inflammatory disorder of the intestine, especially the colon, that produces severe diarrhea containing mucus and/or blood in the stool. If untreated, dysentery can be fatal.

entities/amenorrea/description.text: Amenorrhea is the absence of menstruation because it never began or because it later stopped. It can be normal (physiological) or indicative of disease (pathological). In the latter case, amenorrhea is not the diagnosis but rather a symptom of an anatomical, genetic or neuroendocrine disease.

entities/amigdalitis/description.text: Tonsillitis is inflammation of one or both palatine tonsils (large, fleshy, oval masses of tissue located on the lateral wall of the oropharynx on each side of the throat). These clusters of tissue contain the cells that produce antibodies useful in fighting infection.

entities/amnesia/description.text: Before defining amnesia, it is necessary to define the concept of memory. Memory is the capacity of our Central Nervous System to learn, organize and fix events from our past, and it is closely linked to the function of attention. It is able to store data through ultra-complex mechanisms that unfold in three stages: encoding, storage and retrieval. The presence of amnesia prevents this capacity from developing properly. Amnesia is determined when it is verified that someone has lost or has a weakened memory. The person suffering from this disorder is unable to store or retrieve information previously received, whether for organic or functional reasons. Amnesia is the partial or complete loss of memory. In medical terms, it is a disorder of memory function during which the individual is unable to retain or retrieve previously stored information.

entities/ana-alicia/description.text: Pair related to tachycardia. Ana Alicia Gándara is a physician who practices biomagnetism; she was the second president of the Mexican College of Biomagnetism and the discoverer of this pair.

entities/anemia-hemolitica/description.text: Hemolytic anemia is a group of hemolytic disorders (whether intravascular or extravascular) that cause a decrease in red blood cell mass. Unlike non-hemolytic anemias (due to iron deficiency, for example), in hemolytic anemias the survival of red blood cells in peripheral blood (normally between 90 and 120 days) is shortened.

entities/anemia/description.text: Anemia is defined as a low concentration of hemoglobin in the blood. Hemoglobin is a molecule found inside the red blood cells that serves to carry oxygen to the tissues. Therefore, when there is severe anemia, the body's tissues and organs do not receive enough oxygen; the person feels tired, their pulse is rapid, they tolerate exertion poorly and they feel short of breath. It is detected by a laboratory test that reveals a lower-than-normal hemoglobin level in the blood. It may be accompanied by other altered parameters, such as a decrease in the number of red blood cells or a decrease in hematocrit, but it is not correct to define it as a decrease in the quantity of red blood cells, since these blood cells can vary considerably in size; sometimes the number of red blood cells is normal and yet there is anemia. Anemia is not a disease but a sign that can originate from multiple causes. Iron deficiency precedes the onset of iron-deficiency anemia, which is the main cause of all possible forms of anemia.

entities/aneurisma/description.text: An aneurysm is a small, balloon-shaped, blood-filled bulge that forms in the walls of blood vessels. Any vessel can have one, but it is most common in the aorta, the cerebral vessels, the popliteal artery, the mesenteric artery and the splenic artery. A cerebral aneurysm can occur in veins or arteries at the base of the brain (in the circle of Willis), and an aortic aneurysm occurs in the main artery that carries blood from the left ventricle of the heart to the brain. When the size of an aneurysm increases, there is a significant risk of rupture, which can result in severe hemorrhage, other complications or death. Aneurysms can be hereditary or caused by diseases that weaken the walls of blood vessels.

entities/angeles/description.text: Pair related to improvement of the immune system. Ángeles is a physician who motivated Dr. Goiz to go on with his research when the health authorities tried to stop him. She told him that the discovery he had made was not Dr. Goiz's but God's through the doctor, and that it was a legacy for humanity.

entities/angustia/description.text: Anguish is a distressing affective state characterized by appearing as a reaction to an unknown danger or a shock. It is usually accompanied by intense psychological distress and by small alterations in the organism, such as an elevated heart rate, tremors, excessive sweating, and a sensation of tightness in the chest or shortness of breath (in fact, “angustia” refers to “narrowing”).

entities/anisakis/description.text: Anisakiasis. It affects the brain. Lesions in the digestive tract. Abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting. Sometimes the larvae are expelled by coughing. If the larvae pass into the intestine, a severe eosinophilic granulomatous response can occur even one or two weeks after the infestation. This reaction causes symptoms similar to those of Crohn's disease. Bioenergetically, the parasite responds as a virus.

entities/anorexia/description.text: Anorexia consists of an eating disorder involving weight loss induced by the patients themselves that leads to a state of starvation. Anorexia is characterized by fear of gaining weight and by a distorted and delusional perception of one's own body that makes the patient see themselves as fat even when their weight is below what is recommended. For this reason they begin a progressive reduction in weight through fasting and reduced food intake.

entities/ansiedad/description.text: Anxiety is an involuntary anticipatory response of the organism to stimuli that may be external or internal, such as thoughts, ideas, images, etc., which are perceived by the individual as threatening and dangerous, and it is accompanied by an unpleasant feeling or somatic symptoms of tension. It is a warning signal that alerts to imminent danger and allows the person to take the necessary measures to face a threat.

entities/antibioticoterapia-prolongada/d.text: Therapeutic treatment consisting of the use of antibiotics, that is, medications that fight infections caused by bacteria, either by killing them or by preventing them from reproducing. Also known as antibiotic therapy.

entities/antrax/contagion.text: Wool and cotton sorters' disease. Contact with infected animals or their contaminated products (hide, wool and blood), either directly through handling them or indirectly carried by various blood-feeding insects. This is the most common mode of transmission. Infection is also possible after inhaling spores; this mode of infection is associated with processes such as hide tanning or wool processing. Infection can also occur by inhalation, or by the digestive route after eating meat from infected animals; consumption of milk does not appear to transmit the disease, and person-to-person transmission is very rare.

entities/antrax/description.text: Anthrax (carbunco; anthrax in English, also known in Spanish as ántrax maligno or ántrax) is a contagious, acute and serious disease that can affect all homeotherms (organisms that keep their body temperature within certain limits, regardless of the ambient temperature), including humans, caused by Bacillus anthracis, a gram-positive, strictly aerobic, spore-forming bacillus found in the soil. The severity of anthrax in humans varies according to the mode of infection and the speed of treatment; cutaneous anthrax, the most common manifestation of the disease, has low mortality. In contrast, pulmonary anthrax is lethal in most cases. It causes nasopharyngeal problems, nasal polyps, pain, poor vision, mucus, cysts, otitis (inflammation of the ear and/or its tissues and parts), laryngitis (inflammation of the larynx), conjunctivitis, photophobia (abnormal intolerance to light). In combination with other pathogens, it can cause a tumor called pituitary adenoma.

entities/apendicitis/description.text: Appendicitis is inflammation of the appendix, which is located in the cecum (the portion where the large intestine begins). Cases of appendicitis normally require a surgical procedure called appendectomy, which consists of removing the inflamed appendix. In untreated cases the mortality rate is high, mainly due to complications such as peritonitis and septic shock (particularly when the inflamed appendix ruptures).

entities/arritmia-cardiaca/description.text: Cardiac arrhythmia is a disturbance in the succession of heartbeats. It may be due to changes in heart rate, either because it speeds up (tachycardia) or because it slows down (bradycardia); these are not necessarily irregular, just faster or slower. But very often arrhythmia involves an irregular rhythm, which occurs when there are abnormalities in the heart's physiological pacemaker (sinus node) or in the heart's conduction system, or due to the appearance of abnormal (ectopic) pacemaker zones. "Bradyarrhythmias", or slow heart rhythm disorders, result from inadequate production of impulses from the sinus node or from a block in the propagation of the impulse and can cause loss of consciousness. "Tachyarrhythmias", or fast heart rhythm disorders, may be of atrial origin; in this case they may allow adequate cardiac output and are less dangerous than sustained ventricular arrhythmias, which more often produce collapse or death. It may be related to pericarditis and inflammation of the heart.

entities/arterioesclerosis/description.text: Arteriosclerosis is a condition in which plaque is deposited along the walls of the arteries. Plaque is a sticky substance made up of fat, cholesterol, calcium and other substances found in the blood. Over time, this plaque hardens and narrows the arteries. That limits the flow of oxygen-rich blood and can lead to serious problems such as: Coronary artery disease. These arteries carry blood to your heart. When they become blocked, you can suffer angina or a heart attack. Carotid artery disease. These arteries carry blood to your brain. When they become blocked, you can suffer a stroke. Peripheral artery disease. These arteries are in your arms, legs and pelvis. When they become blocked, you can suffer numbness, pain and sometimes infections. Arteriosclerosis generally causes no symptoms until an artery narrows too much or closes completely. Many people do not know they have this condition until they have a medical emergency. Treatments include medications, medical procedures and surgery. A change in lifestyle can also help. This includes a healthy diet, exercise, maintaining a healthy weight, quitting smoking and managing stress.

entities/artritis-reumatoide-deformante/.text: Deforming rheumatoid arthritis is a systemic autoimmune inflammatory disease characterized by persistent inflammation of the joints, which typically affects the small joints of the hands and feet, producing their progressive destruction and generating varying degrees of deformity and functional disability. Although the disorder is of unknown cause, autoimmunity plays a primary role in its origin, its chronicity and the progression of the disease. The disease is associated with the presence of autoantibodies. Extra-articular manifestations sometimes appear, which can affect various organs and systems, such as the eyes, lungs, heart, skin or blood vessels. Untreated rheumatoid arthritis usually follows a progressive, deforming and disabling course.

entities/artritis/description.text: Arthritis is the inflammation of one or more joints. A joint is the area where two bones meet. There are more than 100 different types of arthritis. Arthritis involves the breakdown of cartilage, which normally protects a joint, allowing it to move smoothly. Cartilage also absorbs shock when pressure is applied to the joint, as happens when one walks. Without the usual amount of cartilage, the bones rub together, causing pain, swelling (inflammation) and stiffness.

entities/artrosis-de-cadera/description.text: Arthrosis is a degenerative process that develops in the hyaline cartilage, which decreases in thickness due to loss of its capacity to retain water. As a person ages, the frequency of hip arthrosis increases. But age is not the only factor that brings on arthrosis; so do use and some local and general pathologies. The young hip has smooth, transparent, thick, steel-colored cartilage. With use, this cartilage decreases in thickness and becomes opaque, less elastic, less shiny and yellowish. On the weight-bearing surfaces it becomes less smooth.

entities/artrosis/description.text: Chronic arthrosis, also called osteoarthritis, which is a disease produced by wear of the cartilage, the tissue that acts as a cushion by protecting the ends of the bones and that facilitates joint movement. It is the most frequent rheumatic disease, especially among elderly people. In general, a temporary pair is one that appears as a consequence of a well-defined traumatic process and that disappears spontaneously when the acute painful and/or inflammatory problem resolves. This type of pair should be scanned and treated with the same principles that apply to common pairs.

entities/ascaris/description.text: Ascaris is a genus of ascaridid nematodes of the family Ascarididae. It includes several species of parasitic worms that cause ascariasis. The effects it produces in the body depend on where it is located and on its developmental form. Larval forms, as they pass through the lungs, can cause hemorrhage and inflammation, which in massive form is known as Löffler syndrome. Occasionally the larvae may fail to reach the lung and lodge in other organs, provoking a granulomatous reaction. In the intestinal mucosa they produce irritation because of their size and movement. Serious complications can also occur, such as intestinal obstruction and even migration of adult individuals to other organs of the body, such as the common bile duct and the biliary tract. These parasites can reach 20 to 30 cm. in length; a large number of parasites may be present in one individual and can cause intestinal obstruction. The adult Ascaris lives in the host; the female can produce close to 200,000 particularly resistant eggs per day, which are passed to the outside together with the feces. In adverse environments, the eggs can go through dormant states lasting up to 10 years; under favorable conditions, however, the egg completes its development in three or four weeks. If an egg is ingested (together with food, soil, water or feces), the larvae pass through various organs such as the heart and lungs until they lodge in the intestine, where the parasite completes its development to maturity. Ascaris does not need an intermediate host to complete its life cycle.

entities/ascitis/description.text: Ascites is the presence of serous fluid in the space between the visceral peritoneum and the parietal peritoneum. In general, if the accumulation of fluid in the abdomen is slight, no symptoms are produced, but it may cause abdominal distension, heartburn, indigestion and lower back pain between L2 and L5, in addition to breathing difficulties (dyspnea). In some patients with ascites, the ankles swell (edema) because of the weight of the excess fluid on the great inguinal vessels. Pain is not a characteristic symptom of ascites. Portal hypertension causes collateral circulation to develop, with new and prominent superficial abdominal veins appearing.

entities/asfixia/contagion.text: Other causes of asphyxia include drowning, gas poisoning, fouling of the air breathed, narcotic overdose, electrocution, obstruction of the airways by foreign bodies and strangulation.

entities/asfixia/description.text: Asphyxia occurs when oxygen stops flowing to the lungs or bronchi due to an obstruction in the throat or trachea. To avoid irreparable brain damage when tissue oxygenation stops, some form of artificial respiration must be established immediately. Most people, plants and animals die four to six minutes after respiratory arrest if they are not artificially ventilated.

entities/asma-paroxistica/description.text: Paroxysmal asthma is a disorder characterized by episodes of breathing difficulty, usually occurring after several hours of sleep in a reclining position. It is commonly produced by pulmonary edema resulting from congestive heart failure. The episodes may be accompanied by coughing, a feeling of suffocation, cold sweats and tachycardia.

entities/asma/description.text: Bronchial asthma. Allergic asthma. The adrenal glands are not producing corticosteroids. Breathing difficulty caused by constriction of the airways (bronchi). Asthma is a disease of the respiratory system characterized by chronic inflammation of the airways, whose clinical manifestations are heterogeneous and variable over time and consist of wheezing (noise when breathing), breathing difficulty, chest tightness, shortness of breath and cough. For the "Adrenal gland" – "Entire front of the body" pair, the entire front of the thorax and abdomen must be checked. 8 points can be identified, 4 on each side, starting at the upper part of the chest and ending at the level of the navel. The negative pole is placed on one of the adrenal glands and 8 positive poles are placed on the front of the thorax and abdomen.

entities/aspergillus/description.text: Aspergillus is a genus of about 600 fungi (molds) and is ubiquitous (present everywhere). Fungi can be classified into two basic morphological forms: yeasts and hyphae. Aspergillus is a filamentous fungus (composed of chains of cells, called hyphae). Aspergillus is an opportunistic fungus and one of those that take advantage of immunocompromised people. Among the most frequent pathologies are: 1) Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis: especially important in the immunosuppressed. 2) Onychomycosis: disease of the nails. 3) Otomycosis: disease mainly of the external ear. 4) Allergic sinusitis. 5) It can generate glaucoma; combined with other pathogens it can cause dangerous ophthalmic diseases. 6) Mycoses (infections caused by fungi) of the scalp.

entities/ataxia-cerebelosa/description.text: Cerebellar ataxia. Dizziness, clumsy and staggering gait, balance problems and aggressive behavior. Muscular coordination of the thorax. Ataxia is characterized by lack of coordination in the movement of the body parts of any animal, including humans. This lack of coordination can affect the fingers and hands, the arms and legs, the body, speech, eye movements, the swallowing mechanism, etc.

entities/autismo/description.text: Autism is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by impaired social interaction and communication (both verbal and nonverbal) and restricted and repetitive behavior. Parents generally notice signs in the first two years of their child's life. These generally develop gradually, but some children with autism reach their developmental milestones at a normal pace and then suffer regressive autism.

entities/autoestima/description.text: Self-esteem is a set of perceptions, thoughts, evaluations, feelings and behavioral tendencies directed toward ourselves, toward our way of being and behaving, and toward the features of our body and our character. In short, it is the evaluative perception of ourselves. The importance of self-esteem lies in the fact that it concerns our being, our way of being and the sense of our personal worth. Therefore, it can affect how we are, how we act in the world and how we relate to others. Nothing in our way of thinking, feeling, deciding and acting escapes the influence of self-esteem.

entities/avaricia/description.text: Avarice is the eagerness or inordinate desire to possess riches, goods or objects of abstract value with the intention of hoarding them for oneself, far beyond the amounts required for basic survival and personal comfort. The term is applied to an excessive desire in the pursuit of riches, status and power.

entities/babesia/description.text: Babesia is a genus of parasitic protists that cause the disease babesiosis in animals and humans. The parasite is transmitted by ticks and attacks red blood cells, where it reproduces. It is a very dangerous parasite. It causes hemolytic anemia. It can produce lesions in the heart, lung, liver, spleen, kidney and digestive system, such as infarctions at the level of the valves, hemorrhages and alveolar edema, hepatomegaly, fatty degeneration, a friable and brownish spleen, glomerulonephritis, tubulonephritis, ulcerative gastritis, and desquamative to hemorrhagic enteritis and hemorrhages.

entities/bacterias-reservorio/descriptio.text: Reservoir of bacteria. Very rare; impact and scan everything again. The Pleura-Peritoneum and Peritoneum-Pleura pairs are bilateral, which means that 2 pairs of magnets are needed, one on each half of the body: 1) Right pleura - Right peritoneum & 2) Left pleura - Left peritoneum.

entities/balanitis/description.text: Balanitis is inflammation of the glans of the penis. When it also affects the foreskin it is called balanoposthitis. The inflammation may be due to an infection (bacterial, fungal or viral), but it could also be due to the use of unsuitable (irritating) soaps. In addition, balanitis may be a symptom of other inflammatory or dermatological diseases. Lack of aeration and hygiene can cause smegma (a secretion that tends to accumulate on the genitals) to produce inflammation and edema. Some studies indicate that balanitis is more frequent in uncircumcised males.

entities/balantidium-coli/contagion.text: The hosts of Balantidium coli include pigs, wild boars, rats, primates (including humans), horses, cows and guinea pigs. Infection is produced among these species by fecal-oral transmission. Pigs are the most common reservoirs, although very few show symptoms.

entities/balantidium-coli/description.text: Balantidium coli is a species of parasitic ciliate protist. It has two phases: cyst and trophozoite. The host generally acquires the cyst through contaminated water or food. After ingestion, excystation occurs in the small intestine and the trophozoites colonize the large intestine. The trophozoites reside in the lumen of the large intestine. Some trophozoites invade the colon wall. In the lumen, trophozoites may disintegrate or encyst. Encystation is initiated by dehydration of the intestinal contents, which usually occurs in the large intestine but can also occur in the feces outside the host. Symptoms may be local, due to irritation of the intestinal mucosa, or systemic in nature, and include diarrhea and dysentery.

entities/balastidiosis/description.text: It is produced by Balantidium coli, a large ciliated protozoan that infects humans and other primates and inhabits the cecum and colon. Its infective form is the cyst; the person acquires the parasite by ingesting food and water contaminated with the cysts. Ulcerations occur throughout the colon, the rectosigmoid being the most affected. It produces dysentery, characterized by an acute picture of diarrhea with mucus, blood, straining and tenesmus (need to evacuate, accompanied by pain).

entities/ballantidium-tifo/contagion.text: The hosts of Balantidium coli include pigs, wild boars, rats, primates (including humans), horses, cows and guinea pigs. Infection is produced among these species by fecal-oral transmission. Pigs are the most common reservoirs, although very few show symptoms.

entities/ballantidium-tifo/description.text: The excrement of Ballantidium Tifo goes to the brain, causing seizures or epilepsy. It creates a membrane that covers the bronchial walls, causing respiratory failure, fluid retention, inflammation (edema). It produces dysentery (severe diarrhea containing mucus and/or blood).

entities/bartolinitis/description.text: Bartholinitis is inflammation of the Bartholin's glands, located on both sides of the vagina, between the labia majora and the vaginal wall, whose function is vaginal lubrication. When the small opening through which the fluid secreted by the gland exits becomes obstructed, the fluid continues to be produced but, having no outlet, it accumulates and a round lump begins to form at the edge of the vagina, which may grow to the size of an orange, although most often it reaches the size of a walnut. This process is accompanied by pain in the affected area. When there is infection, the lump fills with a purulent fluid with a very unpleasant odor.

entities/benavides/description.text: Universal reservoir of viruses and bacteria. Related to autism and Down syndrome. Benavides is the surname of a very active engineer who lives in Nuevo Laredo, Tamaulipas.

entities/bienestar/description.text: Well-being (bien ser, in the sense of being a good person in multiple respects such as honesty, kindness, solidarity, inclination to selfless service, neatness, order, responsibility, etc.), which is often presented as equivalent to or integrated with wellness (bienestar, in the sense of fulfillment, feeling good about oneself, feeling satisfied with oneself, feeling at peace with oneself, or feeling content with the life one has been given), is a state of personal satisfaction, ease and comfort that, separately or jointly, regards as positive and/or appropriate such aspects as health or psychobiological well-being, social and economic success, professional success, personal pleasure, the joy of living, harmony with oneself and with one's surroundings, the sensation of feeling fulfilled for having been able to reach certain goals, the presumption of having achieved adequate personal and cultural development, the belief that one is a good person in accordance with the opinions of third parties, etc.

entities/bilis/description.text: Bile, colloquially known as gall, is a yellowish, brownish or olive-green, bitter-tasting liquid substance produced by the liver of many vertebrates. It takes part in the digestive processes by acting as an emulsifier of fatty acids (that is, it turns them into very small droplets that can be attacked more easily by the digestive juices). It contains bile salts, proteins, cholesterol, hormones and water (the largest component, about 97 % of the total content). Its secretion by the liver is continuous; in the interdigestive periods it is stored in the gallbladder and it is released into the duodenum after food intake. When we eat, bile leaves the gallbladder through the bile ducts into the small intestine and mixes with the fats in the food. Bile salts emulsify the fats in the aqueous contents of the intestine, in the same way that detergents emulsify the grease in frying pans. Once the fats are emulsified, the enzymes of the pancreas and of the intestinal mucosa digest them. In addition to its digestive and penetrating function, bile serves as an excretion route for the product resulting from the breakdown of hemoglobin (bilirubin) created by the spleen, which gives bile its characteristic color. It also neutralizes any excess stomach acid before it enters the ileum, the final section of the small intestine. Bile salts are bactericidal, eliminating microbes that enter with food, and they are also detoxifying, especially for excess alcohol and for some drugs. Sometimes, when a person is under high levels of stress or has fits of anger, the bile stored in the gallbladder spills unnecessarily, causing abdominal pain.

entities/bipolaridad/description.text: Bipolar disorder is a condition in which a person has periods of depression or periods in which they are extremely happy, bad-tempered or irritable. Bipolar disorder, also known as bipolar affective disorder (BAD) and formerly as manic-depressive psychosis (MDP), is the psychiatric diagnosis that describes a mood disorder characterized by the presence of one or more episodes with abnormally elevated levels of energy, cognition and mood. This situation commonly becomes more pronounced at times and/or in situations of direct confrontation that refer to their personal and health problems; these people tend to become flustered in the face of constructive criticism.

entities/blastocystis-hominis/contagion.text: Ingestion of water or food contaminated with fecal matter from a carrier. Farm animals, birds, rodents, reptiles, fish, pigs, monkeys and even cockroaches.

entities/blastocystis-hominis/descriptio.text: Blastocystis hominis is a protozoan that can be found in the human intestine and cause diarrheal episodes, nausea, anorexia and abdominal spasms. Main cause of seizures or epilepsy.

entities/blastomyces-coccidioides/descri.text: Blastomyces coccidioides is a fungus pathogenic to humans that lodges in the lungs. The clinical manifestations differ according to the patient's immune status. In the immunocompetent host, the infection may be asymptomatic, whereas immunocompromised patients are at risk of severe disseminated disease.

entities/blastomyces-dermatitidis/contag.text: The ideal habitat for this mycelial form is moist soil with abundant organic matter. Infection usually occurs by inhaling the fungus and less frequently through the skin. Once the infection has occurred, the process is not contagious.

entities/blastomyces-dermatitidis/descri.text: Blastomycosis is an uncommon pyogranulomatous disease affecting humans, dogs and cats, produced by the dimorphic fungus called Blastomyces dermatitidis, frequently found in soil and on wood. A febrile pneumonia occurs, with cough, asthenia and dyspnea (difficulty breathing), first on exertion and then continuous and progressive; often congestion and induration of the cervical and submandibular lymph nodes. The mediastinal lymph nodes appear radiographically as a dense mass at the bifurcation of the trachea and usually produce dysphagia (difficulty swallowing). Boils, abscesses and skin ulcers may also occur, sometimes with regional lymphadenopathy; hypopyon, panophthalmitis or blindness. Once established, the process is usually rapidly debilitating and fatal. The pneumonia may be focal, with few large pyogranulomatous lesions, or diffuse, with a multitude of lardaceous-looking miliary granulomas.

entities/bloqueo-aorta/description.text: It corresponds to a narrowing of the aortic opening. An obstruction can cause chest pain or a feeling of losing consciousness when active. The aorta is the main artery of the human body, which in adults has an average diameter of 2.5 cm. The aorta gives rise to all the arteries of the circulatory system except the pulmonary arteries, which arise from the right ventricle of the heart. The function of the aorta is to transport and distribute oxygen-rich blood to all the arteries. It arises directly from the base of the left ventricle of the heart and, forming an arch called the aortic arch, descends toward the abdomen where, at the level of the IV lumbar vertebra, it bifurcates into two arteries, the common or primitive iliac arteries, and the median sacral artery.

entities/bloqueo-del-has-de-hiz/descript.text: A right bundle branch block (RBBB) is a medical term used for a defect in the electrical conduction system of the heart, characterized by a delay in electrical conduction through the right branch of the bundle of His and, consequently, through the anterolateral wall of the heart. The mammalian heart has specialized cardiac muscle cells, electrical impulses and intercellular junctions, with a mechanism called the gap junction. These cells form the cardiac conduction system. The sinus node is located in the posterosuperior part of the right atrium; it is oval in shape and is the largest of the cardiac pacemakers. From the sinus node, the electrical impulse travels, spreading through the atria via the internodal pathways, producing atrial depolarization and its consequent contraction. The electrical wave then reaches the atrioventricular (AV) node, or node of Aschoff-Tawara, an oval structure located on the left side of the right atrium, in the interatrial septum. Here the electrical wave undergoes a pause of approximately 0.1 second. The cardiac impulse then spreads through a bundle of fibers that forms a bridge between the atrioventricular node and the ventricular branches, called the bundle of His. Myocardial cells are striated muscle cells composed of actin and myosin filaments. They are surrounded by a membrane called the sarcolemma, which thickens at its ends, serving as the junction point of two myocardial cells. These junction points are known as intercalated discs, which have low electrical impedance and therefore a great capacity for conducting the electrical stimulus from one myocardial cell to another.

entities/bloqueo-vena-pulmonar/descripti.text: This corresponds to a narrowing of the opening of the pulmonary veins. The pulmonary veins are the set of veins responsible for carrying blood from the lungs to the heart. The pulmonary veins originate from the capillary networks of the pulmonary lobules and the last bronchial divisions. They are large, short veins and lack valves. Through them, oxygenated blood from the lung is carried to the heart, emptying into the upper portion of the left atrium. This blood reaches the heart after being oxygenated through the process of hematosis, which takes place across the blood-air (alveolar-capillary) barrier in the lung. Next, from the left atrium, the blood passes into the left ventricle through the mitral valve and, leaving it through the aortic valve, enters the aorta to be distributed to the rest of the body.

entities/bocio/description.text: Goiter is the enlargement of the thyroid gland. Externally it appears as a swelling in the anteroinferior part of the neck just below the larynx. When the thyroid gland enlarges, it can produce too much, too little or enough thyroid hormone.

entities/bonilla/description.text: Pair related to aggressiveness and criminality. Dr. Bonilla told Dr. Goiz that all the great psychopaths have the right temporal lobe affected. Bonilla is a psychiatrist from Ecuador, the best of his kind. This pair was named in his honor. Estrellita is an extraordinary therapist from Ecuador.

entities/bordetela-pertussis/description.text: Bordetella pertussis is a gram-negative, strictly aerobic, non-spore-forming, fimbriated, encapsulated coccobacillus of the genus Bordetella. Bordetella pertussis is the agent responsible for whooping cough. Unlike Bordetella bronchiseptica, Bordetella pertussis is non-motile. Humans are the only hosts of Bordetella pertussis. The bacteria lodge in the respiratory system, attaching first to the ciliated epithelium of the respiratory tract and then to the pulmonary alveoli, causing necrosis. Whooping cough (pertussis) is a highly contagious acute infectious disease of the upper respiratory tract caused by the gram-negative bacterium Bordetella pertussis. It is characterized by tracheobronchial inflammation and typical bouts of violent, spasmodic coughing with a sensation of suffocation that end with a shrill noise during inspiration. It is a serious disease that can cause permanent disability in infants and even death. Chronic cough. It causes problems in the digestive tract, diarrhea, flatulence. In women it causes vaginal discharge.

entities/borrelia/description.text: Borrelia is a genus of bacteria of the phylum Spirochaetes, characterized by its helical shape. 52 species of Borrelia have been identified, all of them transmitted by blood-feeding arthropods. Infections by many Borrelia species are characterized by relapsing fevers, with two main forms distinguished: the epidemic forms, transmitted by lice, and the endemic forms, transmitted by ticks. Borrelia causes Lyme disease: Stage 1) Erythema migrans: reddening of the skin shaped like an eye at the center surrounded by a reddish oval approx. 5 cm in diameter. Stage 2) Multiple migrans-type erythematous lesions (reddening of multiple points of the skin), neurological symptoms such as palsy of the seventh (facial) cranial nerve, meningoencephalitis, cardiac symptoms such as atrioventricular block, myopericarditis, and asymmetric oligoarticular arthritis. Stage3) Dermatitis, neurological disease, asymmetric oligoarticular arthritis, chronic fatigue. For the Costohepatic - Costohepatic pair, the magnets are placed as follows: the negative pole on the axillary line, at the level of the liver, on the last rib, and the positive pole 2 fingerbreadths above the gallbladder.

entities/botulismo/contagion.text: Clostridium botulinum is found in soils and in non-potable waters throughout the world. It produces spores that survive in poorly preserved or poorly canned foods, where they generate the toxin. Infection occurs through wounds, pickled, canned and bottled foods, and dairy products. Pickling (encurtido) is the name given to foods that have been immersed (marinated) in a salt solution and that ferment on their own or with the help of a harmless microorganism (such as Lactobacillus plantarum), whereby the pH drops and acidity increases in order to extend their shelf life. Among the foods most exposed to botulism are raw meats or fish preserved through deficient salting or smoking processes, or some low-acid vegetables or those that may lose their natural acidity through the action of other microorganisms.

entities/botulismo/description.text: Clostridium botulinum is the name of a species of anaerobic Gram-positive bacillus that is generally found in soil and produces botulinum toxin, the causative agent of botulism. Botulism is an intoxication caused by botulinum toxin, a bacterial neurotoxin produced by the bacterium Clostridium botulinum. The toxin acts by blocking the release of acetylcholine at the myoneural junction, preventing the transmission of the nerve impulse. Botulinum toxin is one of the most toxic substances known, so that merely tasting the contaminated food can produce serious poisoning that can even lead to death. It can cause flaccid paralysis of the skeletal muscles and parasympathetic failure. Symptoms generally appear between 8 and 36 hours after eating the contaminated food. There is no fever with this infection. Symptoms can include the following: palpebral ptosis (drooping eyelid(s)), mydriasis (both pupils dilated, nonreactive), abdominal cramps (not always present), breathing difficulty that can lead to respiratory failure, difficulty swallowing and speaking, double vision, dry mouth, nausea, temporary absence of breathing, vomiting, weakness with paralysis (equal on both sides of the body), constipation, decreased mental alertness, intestinal problems, muscle pain, gas.

entities/bradicardia/contagion.text: - Damage to heart tissue from heart disease or a heart attack. - High blood pressure (hypertension). - Abnormalities in the heart that originated before birth (congenital heart disease). - Infection of the heart tissues

entities/bradicardia/description.text: Bradycardia, also known as bradyarrhythmia, is a slow heart rate, below 60 beats per minute at rest. Symptoms do not normally appear until it drops below 50 beats per minute. Symptoms can be fatigue, weakness, dizziness, fainting. High-performance athletes may have athlete's heart syndrome, which results in a low heart rate that helps prevent tachycardia when performing their physical activity.

entities/bronquitis/description.text: Bronchitis is an inflammation of the lower airways. It occurs when the bronchi, located between the lungs, become inflamed due to an infection or for other reasons. Symptoms include: cough with mucus (sometimes blood-streaked), inflammation of the bronchi (branches of the airways between the trachea and the lungs), inflammation (edema) of the bronchial walls, obstruction of the alveoli, whistling or wheezing, fatigue, bubbling (referring to the sound effect heard when the patient is auscultated with a stethoscope), difficulty breathing, hoarseness, general malaise. In chronic bronchitis, the following symptoms may also occur: swelling of the ankles, feet and legs, bluish discoloration of the lips caused by low blood oxygen levels, susceptibility to respiratory infections (such as colds and flu).

entities/brucella-abortus/contagion.text: Main hosts: calf, buffalo, ram, yak. It is transmitted by ingestion of contaminated food, especially through consumption of unpasteurized dairy products such as milk and cheese from infected animals, by direct contact with an infected animal, or by inhalation of aerosols in contaminated environments.

entities/brucella-abortus/description.text: Brucella abortus is a gram-negative bacterium in the family Brucellaceae; in women it produces problems in pregnancy, inflames the pelvic cavity and can produce miscarriages. Brucella abortus generally causes miscarriages in the second third of gestation; miscarriage rates are around 80%.

entities/brucella/description.text: Brucella is a genus of gram-negative bacteria, known mainly for causing the disease brucellosis, a zoonosis (transmitted to humans by an animal). Brucella species are facultative intracellular, flagellated coccobacilli that lack a capsule or native plasmids and do not form spores. Ten species of Brucella are known, some of them with different biotypes, each of which differs in host specificity: B. melitensis (sheep, goat, camel); B. abortus (calf, buffalo, camel, yak); B. suis (pig, hare, reindeer, rodent, caribou); B. canis (dog); B. neotomae (rodents) and B. ovis (sheep).Four additional species have recently been described: B. ceti and B. pinnipedialis for species hosted in cetaceans and seals respectively; B. microti for species hosted in red foxes and field rodents; and B. inopinata, isolated in 2009 from a human infection.

entities/brucelosis/contagion.text: Bacteria of the genus Brucella. Dairy products (milk and cheese). Contact with the following animals: sheep, goat, camel, calf, buffalo, yak, pig, hare, reindeer, rodent, caribou, dog, rodents. It is transmitted by ingestion of contaminated food, especially through consumption of unpasteurized dairy products such as milk and cheese from infected animals; by direct contact with an infected animal; or by inhalation of aerosols in contaminated environments.

entities/brucelosis/description.text: Common brucella, brucellosis or Malta fever is an infectious disease produced by bacteria of the genus Brucella that attacks several species of mammals, among which is the human being, in whom it produces a nonspecific febrile picture, acute undulant fever, headache, night sweats, fatigue and anorexia. False leukemia. Respiratory and pulmonary problems such as bronchitis.

entities/bruxismo/description.text: Bruxism is the involuntary habit of clenching or grinding the teeth without functional purpose. Bruxism affects between 10 % and 20 % of the population and can lead to headache and pain in the muscles of the jaw, neck and ear. The grinding can wear down the teeth and be very annoying to other people with misophonia (a psychiatric disorder consisting of intolerance to everyday sounds produced by other people's bodies, such as eating, sipping, coughing, chewing, or also to sounds produced when using certain objects, which can trigger anxiety and aggressive behavior in the patient).

entities/bulimia/description.text: Bulimia is a disease in which the person overeats or has regular episodes of excessive food intake and feels a loss of control. The person then uses various methods, such as vomiting or taking laxatives in excess, to avoid weight gain. Many people with bulimia, though not all, also suffer from anorexia nervosa.

entities/burkholderia-cepacia/contagion.text: The bacterium is commonly found in water and soil and can survive for prolonged periods in moist environments. Person-to-person spread is documented. Hospitals, clinics and camps for cystic fibrosis patients must be strictly isolated to avoid infection with Burkholderia cepacia.

entities/burkholderia-cepacia/descriptio.text: Burkholderia cepacia is an important human pathogen frequently causing pneumonia in patients with debilitating lung diseases such as cystic fibrosis or who are immunocompromised, as in chronic granulomatous disease. Infected individuals must be treated in areas separate from uninfected patients to limit spread, because of the extreme severity the infections can cause, with rapid lung decline ending in death.

entities/bursitis/contagion.text: Related to the Actinomyces bacterium. Bursitis is often the result of overuse. It can be caused by a change in activity level, such as training for a marathon, or by being overweight. Bursitis can also be caused by trauma, rheumatoid arthritis, gout or infections. Sometimes the cause cannot be determined.

entities/bursitis/description.text: Bursitis is the swelling and irritation of a bursa, a fluid-filled sac that acts as a cushion between muscles, tendons and joints. Bursitis commonly occurs in the shoulder, knee, elbow and hip. Other areas that may be affected include the Achilles tendon and the foot. Some of the most common symptoms are the following: joint tenderness and pain when pressing around the joint, stiffness and pain when the affected joint is moved, and swelling, warmth or redness over the joint. It is a prolonged (chronic) bacterial infection that commonly affects the face and neck. These bacteria cause shoulder stiffness or shoulder bursitis. It signifies fear.

entities/calambre/description.text: A muscle spasm or cramp is a sustained, involuntary contraction of a muscle or group of muscles, accompanied by mild or intense pain, that can cause those muscles to harden or bulge. It can be caused by insufficient oxygenation of the muscles, or by loss of fluids and mineral salts as a consequence of prolonged exertion, sudden movements or cold. In most cases it is harmless and disappears after a few minutes (it is also known as a muscle "pull"). Poisoning or certain diseases can also cause cramps, particularly in the stomach. They can normally be relieved or eliminated by stretching the affected area and resting. A spasm should be distinguished from a muscle contracture. The latter, while also a painful, involuntary shortening of a muscle, lasts longer (it can last from days to months) and is less painful than a muscle cramp; moreover, stretching or massage does not relieve the symptoms. Possible causes of a contracture are nervous tension, poor posture, excessive exercise, fibromyalgia, psycho-emotional problems and other pathologies that cause muscle blockage.

entities/calcificacion-lumbar/descriptio.text: Calcification is a process in which calcium accumulates in body tissue, causing that tissue to harden. This can be a normal or an abnormal process. Ninety-nine percent of the calcium that enters the body is deposited in the bones and teeth. The remaining calcium is dissolved in the blood. When a disorder affects the balance between calcium and certain chemicals in the body, calcium can be deposited in other parts of the body, such as the arteries, kidneys, lungs and brain. Calcium deposits can cause problems with the way these organs and blood vessels function. Calcifications can generally be seen on X-rays.

entities/calculos-biliares/description.text: Cholelithiasis, commonly known as gallstones or biliary lithiasis, refers to the formation of stones (solid deposits) in the bile ducts, above all in the gallbladder. They are accretions of solid matter that may be as small as grains of fine sand or, in exceptional cases, so large that they fill the entire gallbladder. Most, however, are of intermediate size, that is, 20 mm or less. Most of these crystals (about 80%) consist of cholesterol crystals; the rest are black pigmented crystals.

entities/calculos-renales/description.text: Corrects renal or kidney stones or colic. These colics are sudden pains of great intensity generally produced by the presence of a stone in the duct running from the kidneys to the urinary tract near the urethra. In medical history this pain is known as the most intense that exists, and it is commonly seen in emergency medicine, described as worse than childbirth, broken bones, gunshot wounds, burns or surgery.

entities/campylobacter-jejuni/contagion.text: Transmission through milk, water and undercooked food, particularly poultry. More frequent in summer and in children under 5 years. Bacteria of the genus Campylobacter can be found in all species of poultry.

entities/campylobacter-jejuni/descriptio.text: Campylobacter jejuni is a species of the genus Campylobacter. It is a bacillus that stains negative with Gram staining and is motile by means of one or two flagella. Campylobacter jejuni causes intestinal infections. The clinical picture manifests as acute diarrhea, which may or may not be accompanied by vomiting, abdominal pain, headache and general malaise. The incubation period is 1 to 10 days; the clinical picture is highly self-limiting and lasts 2 to 5 days. Some studies suggest that Campylobacter is the leading cause of diarrhea in developed countries. Campylobacter invades cells of the small intestine, damages them and impairs fluid absorption.

entities/cancer-de-colon/description.text: Colorectal cancer, also called colon cancer, includes any type of neoplasm (an abnormal mass of tissue produced because the cells that make it up multiply at a higher-than-normal rate; it is benign when it extends only locally and malignant when it behaves aggressively, compresses nearby tissues and spreads to distant sites) of the colon, rectum and appendix. Many cases of colorectal cancer are thought to arise from an adenomatous polyp in the colon. These mushroom-shaped cell growths are usually benign, but occasionally become cancerous over time.

entities/cancer-de-estomago/description.text: Stomach cancer or gastric cancer is a type of malignant cell growth with the capacity to invade and destroy other tissues and organs, in particular the esophagus and the small intestine. In the metastatic forms, tumor cells can infiltrate the lymphatic vessels of the tissues, spread to the lymph nodes and, crossing this barrier, enter the bloodstream, after which the way to virtually any organ of the body is open.

entities/cancer-de-higado/description.text: Hepatocellular carcinoma, or hepatocarcinoma, is a cancer of the liver that constitutes 80-90% of primary malignant liver tumors. Its incidence is more frequent in men than in women, generally in people between 50 and 60 years of age. This tumor is due to hepatic cirrhosis in about 90% of cases. The causes of hepatocarcinoma are those that can produce hepatic cirrhosis (hepatitis C virus infection, alcoholism, hemochromatosis, etc.); other risk factors for the development of hepatocarcinoma are tobacco use and prolonged use of oral contraceptives.

entities/cancer-de-ovario/description.text: Ovarian cancer is a malignant tumor that arises in any part of the ovary. The ovary is a very complex organ that can be the site of numerous tumors of very different morphological type, some of which are endowed with hormonal function, which explains the great variety of classifications. The most frequent location is the epithelium covering the ovary. It also develops from the germ cells or from the connective tissue around the ovary. In general, ovarian cancer produces no symptoms. This is why most cases are detected when the disease is already advanced. Sterility and drugs used for ovarian stimulation in treatments lasting more than one year increase the incidence of ovarian cancer.

entities/cancer-de-pancreas/contagion.text: The main known risk factors for pancreatic cancer are: 1. Tobacco - It is the main known risk factor for developing pancreatic cancer. 2. Diet - Pancreatic cancer occurs more frequently in populations that consume the so-called Western diet, characterized by a high content of refined sugars, fats and proteins of animal origin. 3. Diseases - pancreatitis, diabetes mellitus, cholecystitis and liver cirrhosis. 4. Alcohol - this habit acts as a causal factor in a variety of digestive diseases such as tumors of the oropharynx and esophagus. Alcohol is a promoter of carcinogenesis in the laboratory. In addition, alcohol, together with high-fat diets, is an important determinant of chronic calcifying pancreatitis. 5. Urban and rural incidence - pancreatic cancer is more frequent among inhabitants of urban areas and therefore less frequent among inhabitants of rural areas.

entities/cancer-de-pancreas/description.text: Pancreatic cancer is a high-mortality tumor that originates in the pancreatic gland. Pancreatic cancer does not cause symptoms right away. When symptoms appear, they are usually vague or imperceptible. They include yellowish discoloration of the skin and eyes, pain in the abdomen and back, weight loss and fatigue. It is one of the most aggressive neoplasms (abnormal mass of tissue) because of its early spread, its lack of specific early symptoms and its late diagnosis (at the time of diagnosis, patients usually have locally advanced or even metastatic disease, which precludes curative surgery).

entities/cancer-de-piel/description.text: Skin cancer is a condition in which malignant (cancerous) cells form in the tissues of the skin. There are different types of cancer that begin in the skin. Skin color and exposure to ultraviolet rays can increase the risk of developing skin cancer. There are three main types of skin cancer: cutaneous melanoma, basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma. Cutaneous melanoma is the most aggressive of the skin cancers and is highly invasive owing to its capacity to metastasize. Basal cell carcinoma is a type of skin cancer that originates in the basal cells (small, round cells located in the lowest part (or base) of the epidermis, which is the outermost layer of the skin). Squamous cell carcinoma (spinocellular carcinoma) is a type of skin cancer that begins in the squamous cells, which are thin, flat cells that resemble fish scales; they are found in the tissue that forms the surface of the skin and in the lining of the hollow organs of the body, such as the passages of the respiratory and digestive tracts. It is also known as epidermoid carcinoma. Other, less frequent types of skin cancer are the following: cutaneous lymphoma (mycosis fungoides), Kaposi's sarcoma, dermatofibrosarcoma or malignant histiosarcoma, and Merkel cell carcinoma.

entities/cancer-de-prostata/description.text: Prostate cancer is cancer that develops in one of the glandular organs of the male reproductive system called the prostate. Cancer occurs when some prostate cells mutate and begin to multiply uncontrollably.
