These could also spread from the prostate to other parts of the body, especially to the bones and lymph nodes, giving rise to metastasis. This condition can cause pain, difficult urination and erectile dysfunction, among other symptoms.

entities/cancer-de-pulmon/description.text: Lung cancer is a group of diseases resulting from the malignant growth of cells of the respiratory tract, particularly of lung tissue, and one of the most frequent types of cancer worldwide. Lung cancer usually originates from epithelial cells and can lead to metastasis and infiltration of other tissues of the body. The most frequent symptoms are usually breathing difficulty, cough (including bloody cough) and weight loss, as well as chest pain, hoarseness and swelling of the neck and face. Lung cancer is classified into two main types according to the size and appearance of the malignant cells: small cell lung cancer (microcytic) and non-small cell lung cancer (non-microcytic). The most common cause of lung cancer is smoking, with 95 % of lung cancer patients being smokers or ex-smokers. In nonsmokers, the onset of lung cancer is the result of a combination of genetic factors and exposure to radon gas, asbestos and air pollution, including secondhand smoke (passive smokers). Lung cancer is one of the most serious diseases and one of the cancers with the highest incidence in humans, responsible for the highest cancer mortality rates worldwide. It is the leading cause of cancer death in men and the third, after colon and breast cancer, in women, causing more than one million deaths each year worldwide.

entities/cancer-de-rinon/description.text: Renal cell carcinoma is the most frequent form of kidney cancer, especially in adults; it originates in the renal tubules. The most common risk factors include smoking, genetic factors and hemodialysis. The classic triad of kidney cancer is blood in the urine, flank pain and the appearance of an abdominal mass. This triad is known as the too-late triad, because by the time the patient presents all three symptoms the disease has progressed beyond a curable point. Today, most kidney tumors are asymptomatic and are detected incidentally during an imaging examination, usually performed to look for unrelated causes.

entities/cancer-de-seno/description.text: Breast cancer is a malignant proliferation of the epithelial cells lining the mammary ducts or lobules. It is a clonal disease, in which an individual cell, as a result of a series of somatic or germline mutations, acquires the ability to divide without control or order, causing it to reproduce until it forms a tumor. The resulting tumor, which begins as a mild abnormality, becomes serious, invades neighboring tissues and, finally, spreads to other parts of the body. The main risk factors for developing breast cancer include advanced age, first menstruation at an early age, advanced age at the time of first childbirth or never having given birth, a family history of breast cancer, the use of hormones such as estrogen and progesterone, alcohol consumption and being of the white race.

entities/cancer-de-testiculo/description.text: Testicular cancer is a type of cancer that generally originates in the testicle, a part of the male reproductive system, although it can also first manifest in the abdomen or in the thorax (mediastinum). Its cause is so far unknown. It is a disease that has gone from being extremely rare at the beginning of the twentieth century to being, at present, the most common type of malignant tumor among young men. Over a lifetime, the probability of developing testicular cancer is 1 in 250 (0.4%), although the incidence varies by race. The great majority of testicular cancer cases are detected by the patient himself. It does not produce general symptoms that might raise suspicion of a medical problem, such as fever or pain. A monthly testicular self-examination is recommended after a hot shower, when the scrotum is most relaxed. The man should gently examine each testicle, feeling for hard lumps, and then compare the two. Symptoms include: a small, fixed lump in the testicle itself, usually painless; slight pain or heaviness in a testicle (without having received any recent blow); a sudden accumulation of fluid in the scrotum; slight enlargement or discomfort of the nipples or breasts; dull pain in the lower abdomen or groin; significant increase or decrease in the size of a testicle.

entities/cancer-de-tiroides/description.text: Thyroid cancer groups together a small number of malignant tumors of the thyroid gland, which is the most common malignancy of the endocrine system. Malignant tumors of the thyroid generally originate in the follicular epithelium of the gland and are classified according to their histological characteristics. The most common symptom is the presence of a nodule in the thyroid, although it should be clarified that only 5% of such nodules are malignant. Sometimes the first sign is an enlarged lymph node. Other symptoms present are pain, voice changes and symptoms of hypotension or hypertension. Thyroid neoplasms can arise in any type of cell found in the gland, including follicular cells, calcitonin-producing cells (C cells), lymphocytes and vascular elements. From the point of view of their pathological characteristics, primary thyroid neoplasms are classified into 4: differentiated carcinomas (papillary carcinoma, follicular carcinoma, Hürthle cell carcinoma), medullary carcinoma, undifferentiated carcinoma and lymphoma. The most common (papillary and follicular) grow slowly, and these forms are rarely fatal in patients under 45 years of age.

entities/cancer-de-tobillo/description.text: Ankle cancer is cancer that develops in the lower part of the leg. Cancer occurs when some cells mutate and begin to multiply uncontrollably. These could also spread from the ankle to other parts of the body.

entities/cancer-de-vejiga/description.text: Bladder cancer, or vesical cancer, is a type of malignant tumor that appears in the urinary bladder. The main factors in the development of bladder cancer include specific chemicals, found mainly in cigarette smoke, and certain parasitic infections. Superficial bladder cancer is distinguished from invasive cancer. When the disease is associated with widespread metastasis, curing the patient is complicated. The inside of the bladder is lined with transitional cells, which are responsible for most bladder cancers. Progression depends largely on the aggressiveness of the tumor. Advanced age and coexisting diseases are associated with higher all-cause mortality rates. Hematuria (presence of blood in the urine) is the most frequent symptom of bladder cancer. The degree of hematuria does not correlate with the extent of the disease. It may be macroscopic hematuria, frank or visible to the patients themselves, or detected in a urinalysis. Any degree of hematuria, however, requires ruling out bladder cancer, even if there are other possible causes of hematuria, such as urinary stones, bacterial cystitis, etc.

entities/cancer-oseo/description.text: Primary bone cancer is an uncommon type of cancer that affects the human skeleton. Unlike secondary bone cancer, it originates in the bone and is not the result of cancer from another part of the body that has spread to the bone. Its most frequent symptom is pain, although it can also cause swelling, fractures, loss of mobility, fever, anemia, etc. There are three types of bone cancer: 1) Osteosarcoma: the most common variant, it develops in the new tissue of growing bones (osteoid). 2) Chondrosarcoma: it originates in cartilage between the ages of 50 and 60. 3) Ewing's sarcoma: it arises in immature nerve tissue, usually in the bone marrow. It is more frequent during the growth years. The risk factors are: being young (except in chondrosarcoma), having received radiotherapy or chemotherapy, having Paget's disease and, in some cases, there may be a hereditary component.

entities/cancer-vesical/contagion.text: The exact cause of bladder (vesical) cancer is unknown. However, several things can increase the risk of developing it. Smoking enormously increases the risk of developing bladder cancer; up to half of all bladder cancers in men and some in women may be caused by smoking. Approximately one in four cases of bladder cancer is caused by occupational exposure to cancer-causing chemicals, called carcinogens; the people at greatest risk are painters, truck drivers and those who work in the leather, aluminum and rubber industries, as well as those who spray insecticides. The chemotherapy drug cyclophosphamide can increase the risk of bladder cancer. Women who have received radiotherapy for the treatment of cervical cancer have a greater risk of bladder cancer. Prolonged (chronic) bladder irritation or infection can lead to a certain type of bladder cancer.

entities/cancer-vesical/description.text: Bladder cancer is a cancer that begins in the bladder, the part of the body that holds and releases urine and that is located in the center of the lower abdomen. Symptoms of bladder cancer may include the following: abdominal pain, blood in the urine, bone pain or tenderness if the cancer spreads to the bone, fatigue, painful urination, pollakiuria (increased number of urinations, usually of small volume), vesical tenesmus (an urgent desire to urinate that forces one to go to the bathroom without being able to urinate), urine leakage (incontinence), weight loss.

entities/candida-albicans/description.text: Candida albicans is an asexual, diploid, saprophytic fungus (it depends for its nutrition on residues from other organisms). It is usually found in the oral cavity, in the gastrointestinal tract and in the vagina. It plays a relevant role in the digestion of sugars through a fermentation process. It causes candidiasis or thrush. Candidiasis includes infections ranging from superficial ones, such as oral candidiasis and vaginitis, to systemic and potentially fatal ones, known as candidemias, which are generally limited to immunocompromised people. In the scan it is also necessary to find a virus; the fungus needs it to survive.

entities/candidiasis-rectal/description.text: Although women are more prone to rectal candidiasis, it cannot be ruled out that it may develop in men. Among the most common symptoms of rectal candidiasis is constant itching, or what is called “pruritus,” which often becomes unbearable.

entities/candidiasis-vaginal/description.text: Vaginal mycosis is an infection of the vagina. Most women have vaginal candidiasis at some point. Candida albicans is a common type of fungus that is often found in small amounts in the vagina, the mouth, the digestive tract and on the skin. Most of the time it causes neither infection nor symptoms. Candida and many other microorganisms that normally live in the vagina keep one another in balance. Sometimes, however, the amount of Candida albicans increases, leading to candidiasis. This can happen in pregnancy, in overweight, in diabetes, or when taking antibiotics used to treat other types of infections. Antibiotics change the normal balance among the microorganisms of the vagina. Candidiasis is not spread through sexual contact. However, some men will develop symptoms such as itching and a rash on the penis after sexual contact with an infected partner. Having many vaginal Candida infections can be a sign of other health problems. Other vaginal infections and discharges can be mistaken for vaginal candidiasis. Some symptoms are the following: abnormal vaginal discharge (the discharge can range from a slightly watery white secretion to a thick, abundant white discharge (like cottage cheese)), burning and itching of the labia and vagina., painful intercourse, painful urination, redness and swelling of the skin just outside the vagina (vulva).

entities/cansancio/description.text: Tiredness is the lack of energy after physical, intellectual or emotional exertion, or from lack of rest. But it can be a symptom of a disease if there is no prior activity to justify it.

entities/caracter/description.text: Controls people's explosive temper. It also applies to people who have no character, who obey everything. A person's character is understood as their personality or way of being.

entities/caries-dental/contagion.text: Veillonella bacterium. Errors in hygiene techniques. Lack of tooth brushing. Not knowing how to properly perform mouth-rinsing movements. No use of dental floss. Genetic etiology. Saliva pH.

entities/caries-dental/description.text: Dental caries is a multifactorial disease characterized by the destruction of the tissues of the tooth as a consequence of demineralization caused by the acids generated by bacterial plaque. The bacteria make this acid from the food residues of the diet left exposed to them. Chemical destruction of the teeth is associated with the intake of sugars and acids contained in drinks and foods. The influence of salivary pH in relation to caries has likewise been demonstrated. After destroying the enamel, it attacks the dentin and reaches the dental pulp, producing its inflammation, pulpitis, and subsequent necrosis (pulp death). If the tooth is not treated, it can subsequently lead to inflammation of the area surrounding the apex (tip of the root), producing apical periodontitis, and can even cause a dental abscess, cellulitis or even Ludwig's angina.

entities/carmen/description.text: Pair related to ovarian dysfunction. Carmen is a woman who was treated by Dr. Goiz. Her husband died and she was left with her children. The psychological impact and the absence of pregnancies and sexual relations caused her ovarian dysfunction.

entities/cataratas/description.text: A cataract is the partial or total opacity of the lens. The opacity causes light to scatter within the eye so that it cannot be focused on the retina, creating blurred images. It is the most common cause of blindness that is treatable with surgery. It has various causes, but it is mostly attributed to age, although there are also many other causes. Over time, yellowish-brown particles are deposited that gradually make the lens opaque. Cataracts cause problems with perceiving colors, changes in contrast and problems with everyday activities such as driving, reading, etc.

entities/ceguera/description.text: Blindness is a physical disability consisting of total or partial loss of the sense of sight. There are several types of partial blindness depending on the degree and type of vision loss, such as low vision, scotoma, and partial blindness (in one eye).

entities/celiaquia/description.text: Celiac disease (CD) is a chronic, multiorgan autoimmune process that primarily damages the intestine and can damage any organ or tissue of the body. It is produced by a permanent intolerance to gluten (a set of proteins present in wheat, oats, barley and rye – TACC – and products derived from these cereals). Traditionally considered a purely digestive disorder, it is now known to be in fact a systemic disease, since the abnormal immune response caused by gluten can give rise to the production of different autoantibodies that can attack virtually any part of the body. Although a "permanent intolerance" to gluten occurs, it is not a simple food intolerance, much less an allergy. It is an autoimmune disease that, without strict treatment, can lead to very serious health complications, among which are various types of cancer, cardiovascular diseases (especially cardiomyopathies), neurological and psychiatric disorders (known as "neurogluten"), other autoimmune diseases and osteoporosis. There are no different degrees of severity of celiac disease, but rather different presentations: regardless of whether or not there are symptoms, of their type or intensity, or of the organs they affect, the damage and the risk of serious complications are always present if gluten is consumed, even minimal traces from cross-contamination.

entities/celos/description.text: Jealousy is an emotional response that arises when a person perceives a threat to something they consider their own. The term commonly refers to the suspicion or unease at the possibility that the loved one may pay attention to someone else. It also refers to the feeling of envy toward another person's success or possessions.

entities/celulas-madre/description.text: The negative pole of the magnet is placed on the navel and the positive pole on any tissue, organ or system that presents some dysfunction. This achieves the regeneration of any tissue; presumably the damaged cells are replaced by stem cells. Research carried out by Dr. Humberto Lucio Castañeda. The name comes from the Mayan word “Gen,” which means egg. The point is located on the omphalomesenteric artery, that is, the navel. Dr. Humberto Lucio uses the word “Gen” instead of navel.

entities/celulitis/description.text: Cellulitis is a common skin infection caused by bacteria, the most common being staphylococcus and streptococcus. Normal skin has many types of bacteria living on it; when there is a break in it, these bacteria can cause a skin infection. The skin in the infected area will become red, hot, irritated and painful.

entities/cervicitis/description.text: Inflammation of the tissues of the cervix is known as cervicitis. Cervicitis in women has much in common with urethritis in men, and many of the causes are sexually transmitted. It can be caused by several infections, the most common of which are Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Trichomonas vaginalis and herpes simplex are less common causes of cervicitis.

entities/chagas/description.text: Chagas disease is caused by Trypanosoma cruzi, a parasite related to the African trypanosome that causes African trypanosomiasis or sleeping sickness. In the heart it causes heart disease or heart failure, inflating the pericardial cavity. In the lungs it causes ventilatory insufficiency. In the pancreas it causes false diabetes. Chagas disease has two phases: acute and chronic. The first may occur without symptoms or with very mild symptoms. The symptoms may be: fever, a feeling of general indisposition (general malaise), swelling of one eye if the bite is near it, and an inflamed, reddened area at the site of the insect bite. After the acute phase, the disease goes into remission and no other symptoms appear for many years. When symptoms finally appear, they may include: constipation, digestive problems, heart failure, abdominal pain, palpitations, difficulty swallowing.

entities/chapingo/description.text: Pair related to epilepsy. Dr. Goiz gave it the name Chapingo because it was the first Mexican university to accept his research. With this, the Mexican health and government system stopped convulsing.

entities/chikunguna-o-chikungunya/descri.text: Chikungunya, also known as chikungunya epidemic arthritis or chikungunya fever, is an alphavirus-type virus transmitted to people through the bite of carrier Aedes mosquitoes, both Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus. The virus is transmitted in a similar way to dengue fever and causes a disease with an acute febrile phase lasting 2 to 5 days, followed by a period of pain in the joints of the extremities; this pain may persist for weeks, months or even years in a percentage that may be around 12 % of cases. Chikungunya can occur only once. Afterward, antibodies develop that will protect the people who were ill and, according to the evidence available to date, the immunity would be lifelong.

entities/chlamydia-intestinalis/descript.text: Chlamydia intestinalis is a pathogenic bacterium. The most common clinical manifestations are abdominal pain, bloating, gas, diarrhea and gastrointestinal problems in general.

entities/chlamydia-pneumoniae/descriptio.text: Chlamydia pneumoniae is a pathogenic bacterium. The most common clinical manifestations are pneumonia and bronchitis, followed less frequently by pharyngitis and sinusitis. A combination of these pictures may also occur. However, asymptomatic infection is the most frequent. It affects the coagulation systems and produces bleeding. In women it causes vaginal discharge and epistaxis bleeding (hemorrhage in the nasal cavities). In combination with Chlamydia trachomatis it produces rectal and vaginal bleeding.

entities/chlamydia-psittaci/contagion.text: Chlamydia psittaci is transmitted from birds to mammals by inhalation, contact or ingestion. Birds are excellent vectors for spreading chlamydial infection because they eat the detritus of infected animals.

entities/chlamydia-psittaci/description.text: Chlamydia psittaci is a species of intracellular bacterium that causes chlamydiosis, an epidemic avian disease in mammals, and respiratory psittacosis in humans (a form of zoonosis). Psittacosis in birds and in humans frequently begins with flu-like symptoms and progresses to pneumonia.

entities/chlamydia-trachomatis/descripti.text: Chlamydia trachomatis (chlamydia) is a bacterium belonging to the genus Chlamydia. It is an obligate intracellular bacterium that infects only humans; it causes trachoma and blindness, oculogenital infections and pneumonias. Some individuals will develop reactive arthritis. Pterygia: fleshy growth in front of the eye. It is related to enteroviruses.

entities/cianosis/description.text: Cyanosis is the bluish coloration of the skin, mucous membranes and nail beds (nails), usually due to the presence of concentrations equal to or greater than 5 g/dL of deoxygenated hemoglobin in the blood vessels near the surface of the skin, or of abnormal hemoglobin pigments (methemoglobin or sulfhemoglobin) in the erythrocytes or red blood cells. Because cyanosis depends on the amount, and not on a percentage, of deoxygenated hemoglobin, it is much easier to find in states with an increased red cell volume (polycythemia) than in cases with decreased red cell mass (anemia). It can be difficult to detect in patients with very pigmented skin. Although human blood always has a reddish color (except in rare cases of hemoglobin-related diseases), the optical properties of the skin distort the dark red color of unoxygenated blood so that it appears bluish. The basic principle behind cyanosis is that deoxygenated hemoglobin is more prone to optical bluish coloration, and it also produces vasoconstriction, which makes it more evident. The color scattering that produces the blue color of veins and cyanosis is similar to the process that makes the sky look blue: some colors are refracted and absorbed more than others. During cyanosis, the tissues have unusually low concentrations of oxygen, and therefore tissues that are normally full of bright oxygenated blood fill with dark, deoxygenated blood. Dark blood is much more prone to the optical effects, and therefore oxygen deficiency (hypoxia) leads to bluish coloration of the lips and other mucous membranes. The name derives from the color cyan, which means "blue."

entities/circulacion-sanguinea/descripti.text: Blood circulation is improved. The main function of the circulation is the transport of water and of substances carried by the blood so that an organism can carry out its vital activities. In humans, the circulatory system is made up of arteries, capillaries, the heart and veins. Arteries are made of three layers of tissue, a muscular one in the middle and an inner layer of epithelial tissue. Capillaries are embedded in the tissues, also allowing the exchange of gases within the tissue. Capillaries are very thin and fragile, being only one epithelial layer thick. The heart is a muscular organ located in the thoracic cavity, between the two lungs. Veins carry blood at lower pressure than arteries and are not as strong as they are. Blood is delivered to the veins by the capillaries after the exchange between oxygen and carbon dioxide has taken place. Veins carry waste-rich blood back to the heart and lungs. Veins have valves inside them that ensure that low-pressure blood always moves in the right direction, toward the heart, without allowing it to flow backward. The waste-rich blood returns to the heart and then the whole process repeats.

entities/cirrosis-hepatica/description.text: Liver cirrhosis. Liver destruction. The main abnormality of liver cirrhosis is the presence of fibrosis, which consists of the deposition of collagen fibers in the liver. Liver cirrhosis is the end result of chronic liver damage caused by chronic liver disease.

entities/cisticerco-reservorio/descripti.text: Universal reservoir. Cysticercus reservoir. The cysticercus is a heteroxenous parasite, that is, one with two different evolutionary forms: the adult parasite and the juvenile, intermediate or larval stage, also called the metacestode. Each develops in hosts of two different species (although in some cases the same host can harbor both forms). Two examples of juvenile cysticerci that affect humans are those belonging to the genus Taenia: Taenia saginata and Taenia solium. They lodge in the subcutaneous connective tissue, the interfascicular connective tissue of the skeletal muscles and of the serous membranes and, eventually, of other organs such as the heart, lungs, liver, eye and brain, giving rise to the picture known as cysticercosis. Cysticercoses are diseases caused by the presence in the tissues of cysticerci, metacestodes or larval, juvenile or intermediate forms of various species of cestodes of the genus Taenia. The symptoms depend on the organs involved, their presence in the CNS (central nervous system) being particularly important, in which case symptoms range from constant, severe headaches and disorientation to, in severe cases, seizures, partial memory loss and even death.

entities/cisticercosis/description.text: Universal reservoir. Cysticercoses are diseases caused by the presence in the tissues of cysticerci, metacestodes or larval, juvenile or intermediate forms of several species of cestodes of the genus Taenia. The symptoms depend on the organs involved, their presence in the CNS (central nervous system) being particularly important, in which case the symptoms range from constant and severe headaches and disorientation to, in serious cases, seizures, partial memory loss and even death.

entities/citomegalovirus/description.text: It attacks the spinal cord and produces multiple sclerosis; it is curable as long as there is no spinal cord damage. Muscle weakness. Paralysis. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a form of herpesvirus; in humans, it is known as Human herpesvirus 5 (HHV-5). It belongs to the subfamily Betaherpesvirinae of the family Herpesviridae. Its name alludes to the increase in size seen in infected cells as a result of the weakening of the cytoskeleton. This virus is one of the main causes of infectious mononucleosis. CMV affects both immunocompetent and immunosuppressed people. It is in immunosuppressed patients that it produces severe complications. However, in others, conditions such as mononucleosis-like syndrome, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy or arthralgia have also been described. CMV mainly attacks the salivary glands and can be a serious or fatal disease for fetuses during pregnancy.

entities/claustrofobia/description.text: Claustrophobia is the fear of enclosed spaces; those who suffer from it tend to avoid elevators, tunnels, the subway, small rooms, and the use of medical diagnostic techniques such as CT or MRI. The claustrophobic person is not afraid of the enclosed space itself, but of the possible negative consequences of being in that place, such as being shut in forever or suffocating from believing that there is not enough air in that place. Most small, enclosed spaces involve a risk of being shut in and a restriction of movement, so people with claustrophobia can feel very vulnerable when their movements are restricted in this way. When a person who suffers from claustrophobia anticipates entering, or enters, an enclosed space, they experience an intense anxiety reaction such as shortness of breath, palpitations or dizziness.

entities/climaterio/description.text: The climacteric is a transition period lasting for years, before and after menopause, as a consequence of ovarian depletion, associated with decreased estrogen production, during which the ovary loses over the years the capacity to produce hormones, follicles and oocytes. In women, it is often confused with menopause, which is the last menstrual period. During the climacteric, the chain of processes that, from the month following puberty, have prepared the woman for pregnancy comes to an end. By the beginning of the climacteric all the ovarian follicles have already been used up, and the hormones that regulate the monthly cycle are no longer produced. In many cases, the menstrual cycle becomes progressively longer.

entities/clostridium-botulinum/contagion.text: Clostridium botulinum is found in soils and in non-potable waters throughout the world. It produces spores that survive in poorly preserved or poorly canned foods, where they generate the toxin. Infection occurs through wounds, pickled, canned and bottled foods, and dairy products. Pickling (encurtido) is the name given to foods that have been immersed (marinated) in a salt solution and that ferment on their own or with the help of a harmless microorganism (such as Lactobacillus plantarum), whereby the pH drops and acidity increases in order to extend their shelf life. Among the foods most exposed to botulism are raw meats or fish preserved through deficient salting or smoking processes, or some low-acid vegetables or those that may lose their natural acidity through the action of other microorganisms.

entities/clostridium-botulinum/descripti.text: Clostridium botulinum is the name of a species of anaerobic Gram-positive bacillus that is generally found in soil and produces botulinum toxin, the causative agent of botulism. Botulism is an intoxication caused by botulinum toxin, a bacterial neurotoxin produced by the bacterium Clostridium botulinum. The toxin acts by blocking the release of acetylcholine at the myoneural junction, preventing the transmission of the nerve impulse. Botulinum toxin is one of the most toxic substances known, so that merely tasting the contaminated food can produce serious poisoning that can even lead to death. It can cause flaccid paralysis of the skeletal muscles and parasympathetic failure. Symptoms generally appear between 8 and 36 hours after eating the contaminated food. There is no fever with this infection. Symptoms can include the following: palpebral ptosis (drooping eyelid(s)), mydriasis (both pupils dilated, nonreactive), abdominal cramps (not always present), breathing difficulty that can lead to respiratory failure, difficulty swallowing and speaking, double vision, dry mouth, nausea, temporary absence of breathing, vomiting, weakness with paralysis (equal on both sides of the body), constipation, decreased mental alertness, intestinal problems, muscle pain, gas.

entities/clostridium-difficile/contagion.text: Fecal-oral route. The bacterium's spores are resistant to heat and antibiotics and can survive on almost any surface, so infections commonly occur in hospitals. The use of chlorine disinfectants is recommended to destroy these organisms in the environment.

entities/clostridium-difficile/descripti.text: Clostridium difficile is a bacterial species of the genus Clostridium, which are spore-forming, strictly anaerobic Gram-positive bacilli. The toxin produced by the bacterium Clostridium difficile is responsible for antibiotic-associated gastrointestinal diseases, ranging from relatively benign, self-limited diarrhea to severe, life-threatening pseudomembranous colitis. The bacterium colonizes the intestine of a small proportion of healthy individuals (less than 5%), and it is exposure to antibiotics that is associated with overgrowth and subsequent disease (endogenous infection). Some conditions related to Clostridium difficile are: pancreatitis or inflammation of the pancreas, pancreatic dysfunction, digestive problems, diabetes mellitus.

entities/clostridium-malignum/descriptio.text: Clostridium is a genus of anaerobic, gram-positive, parasitic and saprophytic bacilli; some of them sporulate and are motile, generally by means of peritrichous flagella. Clostridium malignum affects various organs such as the liver and lung. It can produce respiratory failure.

entities/clostridium-perfringens/contagi.text: It is found in the intestines of humans and of various homeothermic animals (which regulate their body temperature), in soil, in water, and in food (especially in meat that is not well cooked).

entities/clostridium-perfringens/descrip.text: Clostridium perfringens is an anaerobic, Gram-positive, encapsulated, spore-forming, nonmotile bacterium that is widely distributed in the environment and has great ecological plasticity. It does not usually appear in spore form, either in pathological specimens or in cultures. It is found in the intestines of humans and of various homeothermic animals (organisms that keep their body temperature within certain limits), in soil, in water and in food (especially undercooked meat), among other places. The diseases it causes can be fatal. It is the most important etiological agent of gas gangrene. It is also responsible for other clinical pictures such as food-borne toxic infections, necrotizing enteritis, cellulitis and nonspecific infections. Symptoms appear after an incubation period of 8 to 24 hours, and the clinical picture is characterized mainly by the onset of abdominal pain and severe diarrhea. It runs its course without fever, and the illness is of short duration, with favorable recovery, except in children and debilitated persons. Necrotizing enteritis is a very uncommon but serious clinical picture that appears after an incubation period of less than 24 hours and is characterized by abdominal pain, diarrhea, vomiting and acute inflammation of the small intestine, with necrosis and gangrene in various portions of it.

entities/clostridium-tetani/description.text: Clostridium tetani is a spore-forming, anaerobic Gram-positive bacterium. Found in nature as spores in the soil or as a parasite in the gastrointestinal tract of animals, it causes very serious infections in humans and produces the disease tetanus: cephalic tetanus, wound tetanus and neonatal tetanus. It causes urinary tract problems, affects the nervous system and produces violent muscle contractions. It produces toxins that can lead to death. Low back pain, hypertension, edema, mental confusion, fever, catarrh.

entities/codo-de-tenista/contagion.text: This injury is common in people who play a lot of tennis or other racquet sports, hence its name "tennis elbow." The backhand is the most common stroke that causes symptoms. However, any activity that involves repetitive twisting of the wrist (such as using a screwdriver) can lead to this condition. Therefore, painters, plumbers, construction workers, cooks and butchers are all more prone to developing tennis elbow, or humeral epicondylitis. This condition can also be due to constant use of the computer mouse and keyboard.

entities/codo-de-tenista/description.text: Tennis elbow --> Elbow pain. The pair corrects the problem and, consequently, the pain disappears. The most common symptoms are elbow pain that gradually worsens, pain radiating from the outside of the elbow to the forearm and back of the hand when gripping or twisting something, and a weak grip. Tennis elbow is an inflammation or pain on the outer (lateral) side of the upper arm near the elbow. The part of the muscle that attaches to a bone is called a tendon. Some of the muscles in the forearm attach to the bone on the outside of the elbow. When these muscles are used over and over again, small tears appear in the tendon. Over time, this leads to irritation and pain where the tendon attaches to the bone.

entities/colera/description.text: Cholera is an acute, infectious and contagious intestinal disease caused by serotypes 01 and 0139 of the bacterium Vibrio cholerae; it produces a secretory diarrhea characterized by rice-water stools with a marked fishy odor, a high amount of sodium, bicarbonate and potassium, and a scant amount of protein. In its severe form, it is characterized by high-volume watery diarrhea that rapidly leads to dehydration.

entities/colesterol-alto/description.text: Cholesterol is a sterol (lipid) found in the body tissues and blood plasma of vertebrates. Although high blood cholesterol levels have harmful consequences for health, it is an essential substance for creating the plasma membrane that regulates the entry and exit of substances in the cell. It is abundant in fats of animal origin. Too high a concentration of cholesterol in the blood, in combination with other factors such as inflammation of the arteries, can cause it to adhere to the arteries and form what is commonly known as plaque. Plaque can narrow the arteries or even block them. There are two main types of cholesterol: 1) HDL stands for high-density lipoproteins. It is called "good" cholesterol because it transports cholesterol from other parts of the body to the liver. The liver then eliminates the cholesterol from the body. 2) LDL stands for low-density lipoproteins. It is called "bad" cholesterol because a high LDL level can lead to an accumulation of cholesterol in the arteries if they are inflamed. The most common cause of arterial inflammation is related to excessive consumption of refined carbohydrates such as sugar and flours. Cholesterol levels can be reduced with exercise and a diet based on fruits and vegetables. It has been clinically established that the levels of total plasma cholesterol (the sum of the cholesterol present in all classes of lipoproteins) recommended for the general population should be below 200 mg/dL (milligrams per deciliter). Values above these may imply a high cardiovascular risk, and it is recommended to begin a change in lifestyle, especially regarding diet and physical exercise.

entities/colico-nefritico/description.text: Nephritic or renal colic is a sudden, very intense pain generally produced by the presence of stone(s) in the duct that runs from the kidneys to the urinary tract near the urethra. In medical history, this pain is known as the most intense that exists, and it commonly presents in emergency medicine described as worse than childbirth, broken bones, gunshot wounds, burns or surgery. The pain originates in the lower back and from there spreads throughout it. It is described as a kind of intense pressure that presents as pronounced throbbing that may induce fainting.

entities/colicos-estomacales/description.text: The Stomach-Stomach pair is universal for all types of stomach colic. Colic is a type of stomachache that occurs when the muscles that make up the digestive organs begin to contract in continuous spasms. Normally, this stomach discomfort is accompanied by a certain degree of tension in the abdominal wall.

entities/colicos-menstruales/description.text: Dysmenorrhea or painful menstruation is an irregularity of menstrual function characterized by painful periods that appear with menstruation. Some symptoms may be the following: leg cramps, intense pelvic or abdominal pain, lower back pain (at kidney level), headache, nausea, dizziness, vomiting, excessive sweating, fainting, fatigue, as well as anxiety, irritability or depression.

entities/colitis-ulcerosa/description.text: Ulcerative colitis is an inflammatory disease of the colon (the large intestine) and the rectum. It is characterized by inflammation and ulceration (an open lesion of the skin or mucous membrane with loss of substance) of the inner wall of the colon. Typical symptoms include diarrhea (sometimes bloody) and frequently abdominal pain.

entities/complejo-de-edipo/description.text: Oedipus complex, which is characterized by childhood emotions and feelings marked by the simultaneous and ambivalent presence of loving and hostile desires toward the parents. In general terms, Freud defines the Oedipus complex as the unconscious desire to have a sexual (incestuous) relationship with the parent of the opposite sex and to eliminate the parent of the same sex (parricide). The Oedipus complex is generally associated with males, that is, the boy's attraction to the maternal figure; likewise, the Electra complex is the female counterpart of the Oedipus complex, that is, the girl's affective attraction to the father figure.

entities/complejo-de-electra/description.text: The Electra complex is the term designating the female counterpart of the Oedipus complex. It consists of an affective attraction of the girl toward the father figure. The Electra complex is a psychological concept that seeks to explain female maturation. The Electra complex is something very common to all girls at some point in childhood although, on some occasions, it goes further. The affective fixation or infatuation with the father can generate a situation of rivalry with the mother. It is supposed to be a normal dynamic in the development of little girls, which can be observed from the age of 3 and which usually resolves naturally within two years. Unlike in boys, this circumstance is less clear and goes more unnoticed, since girls have a very close bond with their mothers, which makes it difficult for them to sustain competitiveness with her.

entities/concentracion/description.text: Mental concentration is a psychic process carried out by means of reasoning; it consists of voluntarily focusing all of the mind's attention on a goal, object or activity being performed or being considered at that moment, setting aside the whole series of events or other objects that may be capable of interfering with its achievement or with one's attention.

entities/condiloma/description.text: Condylomas are sexually transmitted diseases produced by the human papillomavirus that cause warts in the anal or genital area.

entities/confusion-mental/description.text: Mental confusion is the inability to think as clearly and quickly as one normally does. One may feel disoriented and have difficulty paying attention, remembering and making decisions. Confusion can appear quickly or slowly over time, depending on the cause. Often it is temporary, while at other times it is permanent and incurable.

entities/congreso/description.text: Pair related to parasites. Dr. Goiz called it "congreso" (Congress) because the Congress of the Union, made up of deputies and senators, are parasites who live off the people.

entities/conjuntivitis/description.text: Conjunctivitis is swelling (inflammation) or infection of the membrane lining the eyelids (conjunctiva). Some of the most common symptoms of conjunctivitis are the following: blurred vision, crusts that form on the eyelid during the night, eye pain, a gritty feeling in the eyes, increased tearing, itchy eyes, red eyes and sensitivity to light.

entities/convulsiones/description.text: Seizures are symptoms of a brain problem. They occur due to the sudden onset of abnormal electrical activity in the brain. There are many types of seizures and some have mild symptoms. Seizures are divided into two main groups: focal seizures, which occur in one part of the brain, and generalized seizures, which are the result of abnormal activity on both sides of the brain. Most seizures last from 30 seconds to 2 minutes and do not cause lasting damage. It may be indicative of epilepsy if the person has recurrent seizures.

entities/coronavirus/description.text: Coronaviruses are a genus of vertebrate RNA viruses of the family Coronaviridae. Their symptoms are confused with renal failure. It affects the respiratory system and the intestinal tract. Urethral bleeding may appear.

entities/corynebacterium-diphtheriae/con.text: It is transmitted through dairy products. It is transmitted to others through direct contact by sneezing, the throat, skin, eyes or any other type of secretion from infected people.

entities/corynebacterium-diphtheriae/des.text: Corynebacterium diphtheriae is a Gram-positive, aerobic, catalase-positive, chemoorganotrophic bacterium that causes diphtheria. Diphtheria is characterized by causing tracheobronchial problems, chronic cough, generalized edema, diarrhea, and inflammation of the arteries. It is an acute epidemic infectious disease. It usually affects the tonsils, throat, nose, myocardium, nerve fibers or skin. It can also cause a burning sensation in the throat when swallowing food, difficulty breathing and/or states of imminent shock (cold skin, restlessness, fever, grayish mucous exudate). Another symptom that may occur is torticollis, in which the neck muscles (particularly the sternocleidomastoid muscle, levator scapulae and, to a lesser extent, the scalene muscles) contract involuntarily and cause the head to tilt.

entities/coxiella-burnetii/description.text: Coxiella burnetii is a species of intracellular pathogenic bacterium. The genus Coxiella is morphologically similar to the rickettsiae, but with certain genetic and physiological differences. C. burnetii is a small Gram-negative bacillus, with two growth phases as well as an inactive spore form in the soil. It can survive common disinfectants and is resistant to many other changes in the environment. The ID50 (the dose needed to infect 50% of experimental subjects) is one. It occurs by inhalation, that is, inhalation of a single organism produces the disease in 50% of the population. The disease occurs in two stages: an acute stage with headache, chills and respiratory symptoms, and an insidious chronic phase.

entities/coxsackie-virus/contagion.text: The virus can be transmitted by hands and contaminated surfaces or objects and may be involved in outbreaks, especially among children in schools and daycare centers.

entities/coxsackie-virus/description.text: It prevents food from passing. Some diseases caused by coxsackievirus are: myocarditis, pericarditis, acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis, pleurodynia (Bornholm disease), "hand, foot and mouth" disease or "human foot-and-mouth disease", meningitis, onychomadesis (detachment of the nail beginning at the lunula), acute cystitis, herpangina.

entities/criminalidad/description.text: Criminal behavior is related to people who commit crimes. A crime is defined as atypical, unlawful, imputable, culpable conduct subject to a criminal penalty and sometimes to objective conditions of punishability. It implies an infringement of criminal law. That is, an action or omission defined and punished by law.

entities/criptoceles-primordialis/descri.text: Royal Rife identified some viruses in the first half of the 20th century and built a microscope capable of observing them alive in their natural environment, something that today's electron microscope cannot do. He showed that it is possible to eliminate pathogens by exposing them to specific vibrational frequencies, documenting those frequencies for a large number of viruses and bacteria. He built a machine that emitted those frequencies and eliminated pathogens without using drugs and without side effects. He is considered a genius for what he achieved; however, the economic interests of power groups linked to the pharmaceutical industry destroyed his work and consigned him to oblivion. He named a group of viruses "Cryptocides primordialis", viruses linked to the formation of cancerous tumors. http://www.rifemachines.com/ http://www.qigonginstitute.org/html/papers/NenahSylver-Healing%20with%20Electromedicine.pdf

entities/crohn/description.text: Crohn's disease is a chronic inflammatory disease with intermittent manifestations that mainly affect the gastrointestinal tract throughout its length (from the mouth to the anus), whose origin, not yet determined, lies in genetic and environmental components. Together with ulcerative colitis it is one of the so-called inflammatory bowel diseases. Crohn's disease produces significant symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, fecal incontinence, rectal bleeding, weight loss and fatigue. Extraintestinal symptoms may involve the skin, joints, biliary tract and eyes.

entities/crueldad/description.text: Cruelty is defined as the emotional response of obtaining pleasure from the suffering and pain of others, or the action that unnecessarily causes such suffering or pain. It is considered a sign of psychological maladjustment.

entities/cryptococcus/description.text: It affects the brain. In humans it can cause pulmonary cryptococcosis and atypical acute pneumonia. The main clinical problem they generate is meningitis. . On breathing, the fungus enters through the respiratory tract and reaches the lungs, where it can generate infection or disseminate, provided the immune system is not in adequate condition. It can also pass via the lymphatic route to major organs, such as the central nervous system, and cause death. Cryptococcosis is an opportunistic disease generated by fungi of the genus Cryptococcus. The condition generally does not develop in the immunocompetent population, only in the immunosuppressed.

entities/culpabilidad/description.text: Guilt is, like negligence, the failure to calculate the possible and foreseeable consequences of an act. Guilt is an affective state in which the person experiences conflict for having done something they believe they should not have done or, conversely, for not having done something the person believes they should have done.

entities/debilidad-muscular/description.text: Muscle weakness is the reduction of strength in one or more muscles; it may be generalized or only in one area, one side of the body, one limb or one muscle. Weakness is more noticeable when it is in one area, in which case it may occur after a stroke, after a nerve injury or during an exacerbation of multiple sclerosis.

entities/demencia-senil/description.text: Senile dementia is the name given to a syndrome characterized by the affected person progressively losing many of their mental capacities, especially cognitive ones. The term senile is an adjective referring to senescence or old age, although current medical studies show a minority of cases of senile dementia at relatively early chronological ages. Senile dementia includes the deterioration of cognitive functions. One of the most sensitive functions, and therefore one of the most affected, is memory. The capacity to store new information is reduced in patients suffering from senile dementia (anterograde amnesia), and at the same time there may be loss of previously formed memories (retrograde amnesia). Patients may also have difficulty recognizing faces or recognizing prominent places. Another cognitive function affected in the patient with senile dementia is the ability to produce and understand language. Behavioral changes can occur at any point in the disease. Their intensity and frequency are not necessarily progressive, and they do not appear in all cases of senile dementia. The most frequent are erratic wandering, agitation-aggressiveness, catastrophic reactions, disinhibition, complaining, negativism, intrusiveness, and eating and sexual behavior disorders.

entities/dengue-hemorragico/contagion.text: Dengue is transmitted by the bite of the female of a hematophagous (blood-feeding) mosquito, popularly known as the white-legged mosquito, whose scientific name is Aedes aegypti. This mosquito lives mainly in urban habitats and completes part of its life cycle in artificial water reservoirs such as flower vases, ponds, abandoned tires, etc. It bites humans during the day.

entities/dengue-hemorragico/description.text: Dengue is an infectious disease caused by the dengue virus. They secrete large amounts of mucoproteins. The initial symptoms of dengue hemorrhagic fever are similar to those of dengue fever, but after several days the patient becomes irritable, restless and sweaty. These symptoms are followed by a shock-like state. Bleeding appears as small spots of blood on the skin (petechiae) and larger patches of blood under the skin (ecchymoses). Minor injuries can cause bleeding. Shock can lead to death. If the patient survives, recovery begins after a one-day crisis period. When impacting, they are likely to vomit.

entities/dengue-virus/contagion.text: Dengue is transmitted by the bite of the female of a hematophagous (blood-feeding) mosquito, popularly known as the white-legged mosquito, whose scientific name is Aedes aegypti. This mosquito lives mainly in urban habitats and completes part of its life cycle in artificial water reservoirs such as flower vases, ponds, abandoned tires, etc. It bites humans during the day.

entities/dengue-virus/description.text: Dengue is an infectious disease caused by the dengue virus. The infection causes flu-like symptoms and fever, and sometimes progresses to a potentially fatal condition called severe dengue or dengue hemorrhagic fever. Bright red skin rashes sometimes appear. Joint pain.

entities/depresion/description.text: Depression is the psychiatric diagnosis that describes a mood disorder, transient or permanent, characterized by feelings of dejection, unhappiness and guilt, in addition to causing a total or partial inability to enjoy things and the events of daily life (anhedonia). Depressive disorders may be accompanied, to a greater or lesser degree, by anxiety. The medical term refers to a syndrome or set of symptoms that mainly affect the affective sphere: such as constant sadness, low spirits, irritability, a feeling of malaise, helplessness and frustration with life, and it can reduce performance at work or limit usual life activity. Depression is a complex disease in which biological, genetic and biochemical factors are involved. Imbalance of the neurotransmitters serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine is related to depression. Some medicinal plants that have shown benefits in treating depression are the following: St. John's wort (Hypericum perforatum), licorice (Glycyrrhiza glabra) and kola nut (Cola acuminata).

entities/dermatitis-atopica/description.text: Atopic dermatitis is a long-lasting (chronic) skin disorder consisting of itchy, scaly rashes. Atopic dermatitis is due to a reaction (similar to an allergy) in the skin, which leads to ongoing swelling and redness. People with atopic dermatitis may be more sensitive because their skin lacks certain proteins. Atopic dermatitis is most common in infants; many people outgrow it by early adulthood. People with atopic dermatitis often have asthma or seasonal allergies. People with atopic dermatitis often test positive on allergy skin tests; however, this dermatitis is not caused by allergies. The following factors can make the symptoms of atopic dermatitis worse: allergies to pollen, mold, dust mites or animals, colds and dry air in winter, flu, contact with irritating materials and chemicals, contact with rough materials such as wool, dry skin, emotional stress, drying of the skin from taking many baths or showers or swimming very often, getting too cold or too hot, sudden changes in temperature, and perfumes or dyes added to skin lotions or soaps.

entities/dermatitis/description.text: Dermatitis is a condition in which the skin becomes red and sore after direct contact with a substance. There are two types of contact dermatitis: irritant and allergic. Irritant dermatitis, the most common type of contact dermatitis, is caused by contact with acids, alkaline materials such as soaps and detergents, fabric softeners, solvents or other chemicals. The reaction usually resembles a burn. Allergic contact dermatitis is caused by exposure to a substance or material to which the person has become very sensitive or allergic.

entities/derrame-pleural/description.text: Pleural effusion is an accumulation of fluid between the layers of tissue lining the lungs and the chest cavity. The body produces pleural fluid in small amounts to lubricate the surfaces of the pleura; a pleural effusion is an abnormal and excessive accumulation of this fluid. There are two different types: transudative pleural effusions are caused by fluid leaking into the pleural space, which is brought about by elevated pressure in the blood vessels or low protein content in the blood; exudative effusions are caused by blocked blood vessels or lymphatic vessels, inflammation, lung injury and tumors. Some of the symptoms of pleural effusion are the following: chest pain, usually a sharp pain that worsens with coughing or deep breathing, cough, fever, hiccups, rapid breathing, difficulty breathing. Sometimes there are no symptoms.

entities/desbloqueo-energetico/descripti.text: Energetically unblocks people. Sometimes there is a blockage in detecting the pairs; this pair helps unblock it. On one occasion, in a course Dr. Goiz was teaching, there was a somewhat drowsy student who was being fondled by a pretty classmate he had just met who was sitting next to him. Dr. Goiz sees him and says: How about we switch places? You come up here and present, and I'll sit there. He placed this pair on him and he woke up completely.

entities/desequilibrio-del-sistema-linfa.text: Improves lymphatic flow / the lymphatic system; helps with inflammation in the arms and legs. The Optic chiasm – Optic chiasm pair adjusts the morbid processes in which lymphatic flow is altered, whether on its own or as a consequence of infectious or traumatic pathologies with local or generalized edema. The lymphatic system is a network of tissues and organs. It is made up mainly of lymphatic vessels, lymph nodes and lymph. The lymphatic vessels, which are different from blood vessels, carry a fluid called lymph throughout the body. Lymph contains white blood cells that protect the body against germs. Along the vessels there are lymph nodes. Together with the spleen, these nodes are where white blood cells fight infections. The bone marrow and the thymus produce the cells found in lymph. They are also part of the system. The lymphatic system eliminates infection and maintains the balance of the body's fluids. If it does not work properly, fluid accumulates in the tissues and causes swelling called lymphedema. Other problems of the lymphatic system can include infections, blockages and cancer.

entities/deshidratacion/description.text: Dehydration is the alteration or lack of water and mineral salts in the plasma of a body; it can also be defined as the loss of body water above 3%. It can be produced by being in very hot conditions (especially if humidity is high), intense exercise, lack of drink or a combination of these factors. It also occurs in those diseases in which fluid and electrolyte balance is altered. To prevent it, one should drink water or isotonic drinks such as lemonade. Drinking very sugary drinks, such as colas, is not very advisable. Water should be drunk whenever one is thirsty; it is not advisable, as is often said, to drink two liters of water a day, or to drink without the body asking for it, since we could cause water poisoning, a phenomenon known as overhydration. The symptoms of dehydration, apart from the dryness of the mucous membranes that causes thirst, may be: nausea, lack of strength or reduced performance, mental and physical fatigue, and the fact that, when the skin is pinched without digging in the nail, the mark remains. To reduce the amount of water eliminated, the kidneys concentrate the urine more, and even the urine already in the bladder can be reconcentrated further. Urine can be concentrated to the point of producing only 500 ml a day, but its production does not decrease further; sweating can account for a greater loss of water than urine. Dehydration disappears quickly; most of its symptoms disappear within half an hour to an hour after drinking water without any restriction, even with dehydration of up to 10 percent of body weight.

entities/desnutricion/description.text: Undernutrition is a disease caused by an inappropriate, hypocaloric and hypoproteic diet. It can also be caused by poor absorption of nutrients, as in celiac disease. The difference between undernutrition and malnutrition is that in undernutrition there is a deficiency in the intake of calories and proteins, whereas in malnutrition there is a deficiency, excess or imbalance in the intake of one or more nutrients the body needs.

entities/desprendimiento-de-retina/descr.text: Retinal detachment is the separation of the light-sensitive membrane (retina) at the back of the eye from its supporting layers. Some of the symptoms of retinal detachment may be flashes of bright light (especially in peripheral vision), blurred vision, floaters in the eye, and a shadow or blindness in part of the visual field of one eye.

entities/diabetes-insipida/description.text: Diabetes insipidus. Intense thirst. Polyuria (excess urine). Severe hyperglycemia (excessive amount of glucose in the blood). Metabolic disease. Diabetes insipidus is a disease produced by an absolute or relative deficiency of vasopressin, or by resistance to its effect. Vasopressin is a hormone produced in the hypothalamus that is stored and released through the neurohypophysis; it controls the reabsorption of water molecules by concentrating the urine and reducing its volume in the renal tubules, thereby affecting tubular permeability. It receives its name because it plays a key role as a homeostatic regulator of fluids, glucose and salts in the blood. Diabetes insipidus can begin gradually or abruptly at any age. Usually the only symptoms are exaggerated thirst and excessive urine production. A patient may drink enormous amounts of fluid (4 to 10 liters a day) to compensate for the losses that occur in the urine. When this compensation is not possible, dehydration can develop rapidly and, consequently, a drop in blood pressure and shock. The affected person continues to urinate in large quantities and frequently during the night, having to wake up every few hours. There are two kinds: central diabetes insipidus (the most frequent in humans) and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. The alteration in central diabetes insipidus results from a deficiency of antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin). In the case of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, the alteration occurs at the level of the type II aquaporin channels in the collecting tubule, which prevents vasopressin from functioning properly even though its plasma levels are within the normal range.

entities/diabetes-mellitus/description.text: True diabetes. The only diabetes caused by deficient production of insulin by the pancreas; since there is no insulin production, it must be injected. Less than 1% of detected diabetes cases. They may be genetic. The false ones are curable. Diabetes mellitus is a group of metabolic disorders that share the common feature of persistently or chronically elevated blood glucose concentrations (hyperglycemia). It is classified into 3 types: type 1 diabetes mellitus, in which there is total destruction of the cells, leading to an absolute insulin deficiency; type 2 or non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, which arises as a consequence of a progressive defect in insulin secretion, together with a background of peripheral resistance to it; gestational diabetes, which is diagnosed during pregnancy; and other types of diabetes brought about by different causes. It is caused by several disorders, the main one being low production of the hormone insulin, secreted by the cells of the islets of Langerhans of the endocrine pancreas, or its inadequate use by the body, which will affect the metabolism of carbohydrates, lipids and proteins. The main symptoms of diabetes mellitus are excessive urination (polyuria), an abnormal increase in the need to eat (polyphagia), increased thirst (polydipsia), and weight loss for no apparent reason. These three symptoms (polyuria, polyphagia and polydipsia, or the 3 P rule) are sometimes taken as a reference for suspecting type 2 diabetes, since they are mostly the most common ones in the population. Diabetes is a chronic condition that is triggered when the body loses its ability to produce enough insulin or to use it effectively. Insulin is a hormone made in the pancreas that allows glucose from food to pass into the body's cells, where it is converted into energy so that the muscles and tissues can function. As a result, a person with diabetes does not absorb glucose properly, so it remains circulating in the blood (hyperglycemia) and damages tissues over time. This deterioration causes potentially lethal health complications.

entities/diarrea/description.text: Diarrhea is an alteration of the feces characterized by an increase in the volume, fluidity and frequency of bowel movements compared with normal physiological conditions, which entails poor absorption of fluids and nutrients, and may be accompanied by abdominal pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, weakness or loss of appetite. In addition to the large loss of water involved in diarrheal evacuations, patients, usually children, lose dangerous amounts of important salts, electrolytes and other nutrients. The medical definition of diarrhea involves more than three bowel movements a day or an increase in the amount of stool to more than 200 g /24 h in adult subjects. The patient perceives it as a decrease in stool consistency that causes urgency and/or abdominal discomfort. This urge to evacuate, often uncontrollable, is usually the only or main problem, very often accompanied by cramps and, depending on the etiology, it may be accompanied by mucus, pus or blood in the stool.

entities/difteria/contagion.text: Corynebacterium diphtheriae bacterium. It is transmitted through dairy products. It is transmitted to others through direct contact by sneezing, the throat, skin, eyes or any other type of secretion from infected people.

entities/difteria/description.text: Corynebacterium diphtheriae is a Gram-positive, aerobic, catalase-positive, chemoorganotrophic bacterium that causes diphtheria. Diphtheria is characterized by causing tracheobronchial problems, chronic cough, generalized edema, diarrhea, and inflammation of the arteries. It is an acute epidemic infectious disease. It usually affects the tonsils, throat, nose, myocardium, nerve fibers or skin. It can also cause a burning sensation in the throat when swallowing food, difficulty breathing and/or states of imminent shock (cold skin, restlessness, fever, grayish mucous exudate). Another symptom that may occur is torticollis, in which the neck muscles (particularly the sternocleidomastoid muscle, levator scapulae and, to a lesser extent, the scalene muscles) contract involuntarily and cause the head to tilt.

entities/discapacidad-intelectual/descri.text: Intellectual or developmental disabilities are anomalies in the learning process, understood as the slow and incomplete acquisition of cognitive abilities during human development, which lead to substantial limitations in ordinary development. They are characterized by highly variable intellectual functioning, occurring together with associated circumstances in two or more of the following areas of adaptive skills: communication, self-care, home living, social skills, community use, self-direction, health and safety, functional academic skills, leisure and work.

entities/discinesia/description.text: Dyskinesia is a term used to designate abnormal and involuntary movements in nervous diseases. The abnormal movements include repetitive chewing, oscillatory movement of the jaw or facial grimacing. They occur in both striated and smooth musculature, tremor being a typical symptom.

entities/disenteria/description.text: Dysentery (formerly known as the flux or bloody flux) is an inflammatory disorder of the intestine (gastroenteritis), especially of the colon, that produces severe diarrhea containing mucus and/or blood in the stool. If left untreated, dysentery can be fatal. Dysentery is generally caused by a bacterial or protozoan infection or a parasitic infestation, but it can also be caused by a chemical irritant or a viral infection. The two most frequent causes are infection with an enterobacterium of the genus Shigella and infection by an amoeba, Entamoeba histolytica. When it is caused by Shigella it is called bacillary dysentery (because of its bacillus shape), and when it is caused by an amoeba it is called amoebic dysentery. In addition, shigella dysentery or bacillary dysentery can produce meningeal signs that are mistaken for meningoencephalitis: this was the cause of epidemics on ships in ancient times; likewise, in the great wars it was at times the cause of more deaths than the war itself.

entities/disfuncion-auditiva/description.text: Auditory dysfunction, hearing loss or hearing impairment is a problem in which one or more parts of the ear interrupt the way sound travels through the auditory system to the brain. Someone who has hearing loss might be able to hear most sounds, hear only some, or possibly hear none.

entities/disfuncion-bazo/description.text: Spleen dysfunction. It alters blood factors. A malfunctioning spleen produces three conditions: 1) Thrombocytopenia: a decrease in platelets. 2) Anemia: low concentration of hemoglobin (responsible for carrying oxygen to the tissues). 3) Leukemia: uncontrolled increase in leukocytes or white blood cells. What does the spleen do? 1) It sequesters 30% of the platelets 2) It destroys red blood cells that have already done their job 3) It stimulates the generation of red and white blood cells. The spleen is a parenchymal organ present in almost all vertebrates. Its main function is the destruction of old red blood cells, the production of some new ones and the maintenance of a blood reserve. It forms part of the lymphatic system and is the center of activity of the immune system. The human spleen is flattened, oblong and very friable. It lies in the upper left quadrant of the abdominal cavity, related to the pancreas, the hemidiaphragm and the left kidney. Although its size varies from person to person, it is usually 12 cm long, 8 cm wide and 4 cm thick, and weighs approximately 200 g.

entities/disfuncion-duodeno/description.text: Duodenal dysfunction. It produces nervous colitis and irritable bowel, since the duodenum ferments food. In the digestive system, the duodenum is the part of the small intestine that connects the stomach with the jejunum. The duodenum is located in the posterior and upper part of the abdomen, in the retroperitoneum, being the only portion of the small intestine that is fixed, and it is made up entirely of smooth muscle. It begins at the pylorus, the opening in the lower part of the stomach through which it empties its contents into the intestine. It ends at the duodenojejunal flexure, which separates it from the jejunum. Its inflammation gives rise to duodenitis, and it is usually associated with gastritis and/or ulcers. After food is combined with gastric acid, it descends into the duodenum, where it mixes with bile from the gallbladder and digestive juices from the pancreas. The absorption of vitamins, minerals and other nutrients begins in the duodenum.

entities/disfuncion-erectil/description.text: Corrects the problem of erectile dysfunction. It can happen to young men who lose this ability after a strong emotional event. Erectile dysfunction, or impotence, is the repeated inability to achieve or maintain an erection firm enough to have satisfactory sexual intercourse.

entities/disfuncion-hipofisis/descriptio.text: Dysfunction of the pituitary gland. The pituitary gland governs the function of the other glands. Its dysfunction produces a failure in the endocrine system. The hypophysis, or pituitary gland, is an endocrine gland that secretes hormones responsible for regulating homeostasis, which is the property of living organisms consisting of their ability to maintain a stable internal condition by compensating for changes in their environment through the regulated exchange of matter and energy with the exterior, including the trophic hormones that regulate the function of other glands of the endocrine system; it depends in part on the hypothalamus, which in turn regulates the secretion of some hormones. It is a complex gland housed in a bony space called the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone, located at the base of the skull, in the middle cranial fossa, which connects with the hypothalamus through the pituitary stalk or hypophyseal stalk. The endocrine system, also called the system of internal-secretion glands, is the set of organs and tissues of the body that secrete a type of substance called hormones, which are released into the bloodstream and regulate some of the body's functions. It is a signaling system similar to that of the nervous system, but in this case, instead of using electrical impulses at a distance, it works exclusively by means of substances (chemical signals). Hormones regulate many functions in organisms, including, among others, mood, growth, tissue function and metabolism, through specialized cells and endocrine glands. Endocrine organs are also called ductless glands or endocrine glands, because their secretions are released directly into the bloodstream, whereas exocrine glands release their secretions onto the internal or external surface of cutaneous tissues, the gastric mucosa or the lining of the pancreatic ducts.

entities/disfuncion-intestinal/descripti.text: Colon malfunction, intestinal dysfunction, intestinal residues, gas, flatulence. Improves intestinal flow; helps people who do not go to the bathroom very often or who struggle to evacuate. Gastrointestinal dysfunctions and possible obesity not related to glandular dysfunctions. Linked to phenomena of sluggish bowel and excessive intestinal absorption.

entities/disfuncion-nervio-vago/descript.text: Vagus nerve dysfunction. The vagus nerve or pneumogastric nerve is the tenth of the twelve cranial nerve pairs. It arises from the medulla oblongata and innervates the pharynx, esophagus, larynx, trachea, bronchi, heart, stomach, pancreas, liver and the viscera supplied by the superior mesenteric artery, through periarterial plexuses that reach the myenteric plexuses where the parasympathetic postsynaptic fibers are located. This nerve provides sensation to the following structures: tonsillar region, back of the nose and throat, larynx, ear, stomach. It stops hiccups when pressure is applied. It provides the parasympathetic component to various viscera, including: heart, bronchi, stomach, esophagus, intestine, pancreas and liver, on which it has various effects. It is not only responsible for collecting sensation from the larynx but also provides its motor component, through two branches: the recurrent laryngeal nerve and the superior laryngeal nerve. Lesions of this nerve can occur in its branches; if they occur in the pharyngeal branches, dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) results. In the laryngeal branches: paralysis of the cricothyroid muscle and a weak voice. A lesion can also occur in the recurrent laryngeal nerve: vocal cord paralysis, dysphonia and hoarse voice. Both of its laryngeal nerves may be affected, which produces aphonia.

entities/disfuncion-ocular/description.text: Corrects problems of ocular dysfunction such as myopia and hyperopia. Visual disturbances. When one or more elements of the functional unit that makes up the ocular surface (tear film, lacrimal glands, eyelids and reflex neural arcs) are altered or fail, an alteration of the ocular surface results that can produce anything from non-specific symptoms of eye irritation with few ophthalmological signs, to severe ophthalmological diseases accompanied by loss of vision due to corneal opacification. There are many types of eye problems and visual disturbances, among which the following can be mentioned: halos, blurred vision (loss of visual acuity and inability to see small details), blind spots or scotomas (dark "holes" in the visual field in which nothing can be seen). Loss of vision and blindness are the most serious visual problems.

entities/disfuncion-ovarica/description.text: Ovarian dysfunction. Corrects menstrual problems, cramps, amenorrhea (absence of menstruation), dysmenorrhea (painful menstruation) and problems related to menopause. Impacting the pair restores normal menstrual function. Amenorrhea can arise from different causes, including: psychological shocks, malnutrition, postpartum, contraceptive intoxication, pituitary alterations, miscarriages, pelvic infections and others. The ovary is the female gonad or reproductive organ that produces and secretes sex hormones and ova. They are paired, almond-shaped structures weighing about 6 to 7 grams, grayish-white in color, attached on both sides of the uterus by the utero-ovarian ligaments and to the pelvic wall by the infundibulopelvic ligaments. The female ovaries are the equivalent of the male testicles. The hormones secreted by the ovary are the estrogens, which are responsible for the growth of the endometrium during the proliferative phase of the menstrual cycle; progesterone, the hormone that prevents the shedding of the glycogen-rich endometrium during the secretory phase of the menstrual cycle; and inhibin, which inhibits the secretion of follicle-stimulating hormone from the pituitary gland. With the help of these hormones, the ovum will eventually implant in the endometrium. Insignificant amounts of testosterone are also produced in the ovary.

entities/disfuncion-pancreas/description.text: The pancreas is an organ located in the abdomen that has an exocrine secretion made up of digestive enzymes that pass into the small intestine, and an endocrine secretion made up of hormones that pass into the blood, such as insulin, glucagon, pancreatic polypeptide and somatostatin. Since the pancreas has an exocrine part, whose function is digestive, and an endocrine part, with metabolic functions, it is considered an amphicrine gland. It is conical in shape and is divided into several regions called the head, neck, body and tail. In humans it measures between 15 and 23 cm in length, 4 in width and 5 in thickness, with a weight ranging between 70 and 150 g. The head is located in the concavity of the duodenum, or duodenal loop, formed by the first three portions of the duodenum, and ascends obliquely to the left; it lies against the posterior wall at the level of the first and second lumbar vertebrae next to the adrenal glands, behind the stomach, forming part of the contents of the retroperitoneal space. The head of the pancreas lies within the middle and upper duodenal curvature. The neck of the pancreas lies anterior to the superior mesenteric vessels. Posterior to it is the portal vein. To the right of the head. The body of the pancreas continues posterior to the stomach toward the left, ascending slightly. The tail of the pancreas ends after passing between the layers of the splenorenal ligament, the only intraperitoneal part of the pancreas. The main pancreatic duct, or duct of Wirsung, begins in the tail and runs to the right through the body. In the head it changes direction downward. In the lower portion of the head it joins the common bile duct, ending in the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater), which enters the descending duodenum (second part of the duodenum). The accessory pancreatic duct, or duct of Santorini, is formed by two branches, the first coming from the descending portion of the main duct and the second from the uncinate process. A dysfunction of the pancreas can lead to one or more of the following diseases: acute pancreatitis, chronic pancreatitis, pancreatic cancer, cystic fibrosis and diabetes mellitus.
