entities/esquizofrenia/description.text: Schizophrenia is a complex mental disorder that makes it difficult to tell the difference between what is real and unreal, to think clearly, to have normal emotional responses and to act normally in social situations. Schizophrenia is a complex disease. Mental health experts are not sure what causes it. The symptoms of schizophrenia generally appear slowly over months or years. Sometimes the person may have many symptoms and at other times only a few. People with schizophrenia may have difficulty keeping friends and working. They may also have problems with anxiety, depression and suicidal thoughts or behaviors. Early symptoms may include: feeling irritable or tense, difficulty concentrating, difficulty sleeping. As the illness continues, the person may have problems with thinking and emotions, such as: strange behaviors, hearing or seeing things that do not exist (hallucinations), isolation, decreased emotion, problems paying attention, strongly held beliefs that are not real (delusions), thoughts that "jump" between different topics (loose associations).

entities/esterilidad-masculina/descripti.text: Male fertility requires erection, normal ejaculation and correct semen quality. The fertile man, on ejaculating during intercourse, deposits at least 12 million motile, normal spermatozoa at the back of the vagina. Some disorders that can cause sterility are the following. Erectile dysfunction: an erection insufficient to penetrate the woman causes sterility. Anejaculation: absence of ejaculation means sterility, since a man who does not ejaculate cannot deposit semen in the vagina. The most frequent causes are diabetes and spinal cord injuries from accidents that cause paraplegia; other causes are hormonal or psychological. These men produce spermatozoa but cannot expel them. Obstructive azoospermia: spermatozoa are produced in the testicles, but the ducts that connect the testicles to the penis are obstructed. Oligoasthenozoospermia: a decrease in the number and motility of spermatozoa. The causes are multiple: chromosomal, genetic, hormonal, infectious, partial obstructions of the seminal ducts, varicocele (varicose veins of the testicle), etc.

entities/estrabismo/description.text: Strabismus is the deviation of the alignment of one eye relative to the other, preventing bifoveal fixation. The absence of bifoveal fixation reduces or abolishes depth perception, or stereopsis. When strabismus is congenital or develops during childhood, it can cause amblyopia, a pathology in which the neurological structures responsible for vision do not develop correctly, which is why, on reaching adulthood, even though the pathology that gave rise to the amblyopia (strabismus, refractive error, etc.) is corrected, vision with the amblyopic eye is insufficient and cannot be corrected with any treatment. Amblyopia is reversible during childhood and occasionally adolescence with appropriate therapeutic measures.

entities/estrenimiento/description.text: Constipation is a condition consisting of a lack of regular bowel movements, producing infrequent or strained defecation, generally of scant and hard stools. Normal defecation frequency varies between people, from a couple of times a day to three times a week. It can be considered a disorder depending on whether or not it affects quality of life.

entities/estres/description.text: Stress is a physiological reaction of the body in which various defense mechanisms come into play to face a situation perceived as threatening or as an increased demand. Physiological or biological stress is an organism's response to a stressor such as an environmental condition or a stimulus. Stress is a body's way of reacting to a challenge. Depending on the stressful event, the body's way of responding to stress is through activation of the sympathetic nervous system, which gives rise to the fight-or-flight response. Because the body cannot maintain this state for long periods of time, the parasympathetic system tends to return the body to more normal physiological conditions (homeostasis). In humans, stress normally describes a negative condition (distress) as opposed to a positive condition (eustress), which can have a mental and physical effect, and even an effect on well-being or malaise, in a human being. Symptoms may be nervousness (trembling) or restlessness, a racing heart, dilated pupils, sweating, flushed skin and goose bumps. Stress = Tension.

entities/estrogenos/description.text: Estrogens are steroid sex hormones (derived from cholesterol), mainly of the female type, produced by the ovaries, by the placenta during pregnancy and, in smaller amounts, by the adrenal glands. Estrogens induce cell proliferation in organs, mainly the endometrium, the breast and the ovary itself. They have a certain preventive effect against cerebrovascular disease and, on the endometrium, they act in coordination with the gestagens, another class of female sex hormone that induces maturation. Estrogens reach their highest concentration in the first 7 days of the menstrual cycle. Estrogens act on various cell groups of the body, especially some related to sexual activity, to the brain, to endocrine function and also to neurotransmitter function. By regulating the menstrual cycle, estrogens affect the reproductive tract, the urinary tract, the blood vessels and heart, the bones, the breasts, the skin, the hair, the mucous membranes, the pelvic muscles and the brain. Secondary sexual characteristics, such as pubic and underarm hair, also begin to grow when estrogen levels increase. Many of the organ systems, including the musculoskeletal and cardiovascular systems and the brain, are affected by estrogens.

entities/etmoiditis/description.text: Ethmoiditis is an infection of the ethmoid air cells in the paranasal sinuses. These are the air-filled spaces located behind the nose and between the eyes. Most ethmoid sinus infections are caused by bacteria. Some types of fungi and viruses may also be involved.

entities/exantema-subito/description.text: Roseola, or exanthem subitum, is a childhood disease, especially of children under two years of age, whose external manifestations are usually limited to a transient eruption or "exanthem" that appears after three days of fever.

entities/exantema/description.text: An exanthem is a skin rash that appears acutely. It frequently appears with general infectious diseases such as measles, rubella, chickenpox, scarlet fever, dengue or typhus. An exanthem can also be the consequence of a drug incompatibility (drug eruption). The causes of an exanthem in a child can be very varied and numerous, but we can divide them into four groups: infectious agents: viruses and bacterial toxins (more than 50 have been described), medications, inflammatory diseases and the effects of some viral vaccines (measles, rubella and mumps).

entities/eyaculacion-precoz/description.text: Premature ejaculation is the most frequent sexual problem in men. Premature ejaculation is a lack of control over the ejaculatory reflex; it is therefore a disorder of the orgasm phase during sexual intercourse. The vast majority of men have experienced premature ejaculation at some point in their sexual life. In the most severe cases, the man ejaculates before penetrating his partner or seconds after doing so. Urologists and sex therapists find that premature ejaculation causes frequent emotional problems, both for the patient and for his partner, in addition to the abrupt end of the sexual act.

entities/fagos-reservorio/description.text: Atopic dermatitis. Urogenital diseases. Painful abdominal disorders. Bacteriophages, also called phages, are viruses that exclusively infect bacteria. When a bacterium is attacked by a phage, it can be destroyed by lysis or rupture of its cell membrane; phages replicate within the cellular parenchyma, sharing and/or using genomic fractions of the bacteria without apparently affecting the bacterium up to that point. Phages carry pathogenicity information in their genome that gives bacteria the capacity to be more dangerous, since they increase their toxic capacity and turn nonpathogenic elements into pathogenic ones. Hence the need to detect their presence in higher organisms and end their cycle. In lysis, the interdependence established between the bacteriophage and the microbial cell (some authors report that the infection also extends to some fungi) ends with the destruction of the individual cell, but it initiates a process of release of the virus and subsequently the invasion of new cells.

entities/falso-embarazo/description.text: False pregnancy. An ultrasound and an antigen test certifying that she is not pregnant are required, since the Uterus - Uterus pair causes miscarriages. True pregnancy is identified by the Uterus - Ovary pair; ectopic pregnancy (outside the uterus --> in the tubes) is identified by the Fallopian tube - Ovary pair. Once both have been ruled out with biomagnetism and with medical studies, this pair is depolarized. It corrects problems related to amenorrhea (absence of menstruation) and abnormal enlargement of the abdomen caused by an ascaris (parasite) lodged in the uterus; once the pair is depolarized, the parasites are expelled vaginally.

entities/falta-de-aire/description.text: Corrects problems of breathlessness or shortness of breath. Pulmonary surfactants are substances present in the lungs, specifically in the alveoli; they are composed of phospholipids (80%), neutral lipids (8%) and proteins (12%), and their main function is to reduce the surface tension of the alveoli during expiration, preventing the alveolar collapse that would produce breathing difficulties; they also have an immunological function. The effects of pulmonary surfactant are as follows: it improves lung function, that is, it improves oxygenation, improves ventilation/perfusion, increases functional residual capacity, decreases the elastic recoil of the lung, improves alveolar expansion and increases lung compliance. This pair helps regenerate the surfactant (membrane) of the bronchial alveolus. It works very well for mine workers and smokers. Also for newborns. A deficiency in the quantity and/or quality of surfactant leads to significant alterations in lung function. One example is respiratory distress syndrome, which occurs in premature neonates who, at birth, do not yet have a sufficient amount of pulmonary surfactant in their alveoli, which enormously increases the work they must do with each inspiration to draw air in; this can cause death from exhaustion if not treated in time.

entities/faringitis/description.text: Pharyngitis, or sore throat, is discomfort, pain or scratchiness in the throat that often makes swallowing painful. Pharyngitis is caused by swelling (inflammation) of the pharynx, which is at the back of the throat, between the tonsils and the larynx. Most sore throats are caused by a viral infection. Some viruses can cause specific types of sore throat, such as coxsackie infection or mononucleosis. Bacteria that can cause pharyngitis include group A streptococci, which lead to strep throat in some cases. Other less common bacteria that cause sore throats include Corynebacterium, gonorrhea and chlamydia. Most cases of pharyngitis occur during the colder months and the illness frequently spreads among family members. The main symptom is sore throat, and it may be accompanied by fever, headache, muscle and joint aches, skin rash, and swollen lymph nodes in the neck.

entities/fasciola-hepatica/contagion.text: Fasciolopsis buski parasite. Domestic herbivores: sheep, goats, cows, donkeys, pigs, rats. Ingestion of aquatic plants. Contaminated liver. Contaminated water. Contaminated vegetables (aquatic and terrestrial).

entities/fasciola-hepatica/description.text: Fasciola hepatica, which affects herbivorous vertebrate animals (cows, sheep and goats, among others) and humans, is an infection that is divided into 2 stages. In the first stage, also called the acute or invasive phase, the clinical picture includes: pain localized in the epigastrium and/or right upper quadrant radiating to the scapula on the same side, hepatomegaly, irregular febrile episodes, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, hyporexia, myalgia, arthralgia, and fleeting urticaria with occasional dermographism. The second stage, also called the chronic (or established) phase, appears about 3 - 5 months post-infection, and its clinical manifestations are associated with the presence of flukes in the bile ducts. The parasites cause hyperplasia of the duct walls with marked fibrosis, and extensive damage to the hepatic architecture, due largely to parasitic enzymes. It is characterized by signs and symptoms related to biliary obstruction (partial, or complete in more severe cases) and to the degree of inflammation: abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, soft hepatomegaly, fever.

entities/fasciolopsis-buski/contagion.text: Domestic herbivores: sheep, goats, cows, donkeys, pigs, rats. Ingestion of aquatic plants. Contaminated liver. Contaminated water. Contaminated vegetables (aquatic and terrestrial).

entities/fasciolopsis-buski/description.text: The liver fluke (Fasciola hepatica) is a species of trematode flatworm (fluke) of the subclass Digenea, characterized by its lanceolate shape, with two suckers, one oral and one ventral, and a biological cycle with two generations (digenean) in two hosts, an amphibious gastropod mollusk and a mammal. It is a parasite of the bile ducts and gallbladder of herbivores and omnivores, including humans; it is the causative agent of one of the most widespread parasitic diseases of livestock, fascioliasis (or fasciolosis), which is considered one of the most important parasitic diseases of domestic ruminants in the world. The liver fluke is a flat, unsegmented, fleshy worm measuring 2 to 3.5 cm in length by 1 to 1.5 cm in width. It is whitish in color, with shades ranging from ash gray to brownish. The anterior or cephalic portion has an oral sucker measuring approximately 1 mm and a larger one in the ventral area, of approximately 1.6 mm. Two periods are distinguished in fasciolosis. The first period, called the initial or invasion period, extends from the moment the metacercariae are ingested until the juvenile parasites become established in the bile ducts. They produce inflammation of the peritoneum with serosanguineous exudate; Glisson's capsule shows thickening and leukocyte infiltrate due mainly to eosinophils; the liver enlarges, with the presence of microabscesses and necrosis. High, irregular fever occurs. Pain in the right hypochondrium of variable intensity. Painful hepatomegaly due to inflammation of the parenchyma; urticaria. In the blood there is up to 80% leukocytosis with eosinophilia; there is hypergammaglobulinemia. The second period, the established stage, extends from the time the juvenile distomes reach sexual maturity and remain in the lumen of the bile ducts until their death. The bile ducts dilate and become sclerotic, with a chronic inflammatory reaction around the periphery of the ducts. When the number of parasites is large, there is atrophy of the hepatic parenchyma due to compression and periportal cirrhosis. The main location of adult Fasciola hepatica is the bile ducts, although they can move to other sites such as the cystic duct, common bile duct, gallbladder and ampulla of Vater. On rare occasions, the juvenile parasites do not follow the usual route and head toward other sites in the body, producing erratic fasciolosis. The sites they frequently invade erratically are the lungs, peritoneum, skin, liver and sites near the liver. The adult parasites in their definitive habitat produce digestive-type symptoms. Liver problems. Tracheal problems. Biliary-type dyspepsia with anorexia, flatulence, nausea, vomiting, a feeling of abdominal fullness, constipation with periods of diarrhea, biliary colic. Transient jaundice, hepatomegaly and fever usually occur. Heart problems. It obstructs normal flow in the liver. It causes hyporexia (partial loss of appetite).

entities/fatiga-cronica/description.text: Chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS) is considered a serious neurological disease. It can progressively affect the immune, neurological, cardiovascular and endocrine systems. Some of the symptoms of chronic fatigue are: severe fatigue, low-grade fever or fever, unrefreshing sleep, intolerance to light (photophobia), intolerance to sound (hyperacusis), intolerance to temperature changes, muscle pain, joint pain, multiple chemical sensitivities, electromagnetic sensitivity and sensitivity to other environmental factors, a feeling of permanent flu-like state, chronic pharyngitis, substantial loss of concentration and memory, spatial disorientation, intolerance to emotional stress and to physical activity, among others.

entities/fatiga/description.text: Fatigue is a feeling of lack of energy, exhaustion or tiredness. Fatigue is different from drowsiness. In general, drowsiness is the feeling of a need to sleep, whereas fatigue is a lack of energy and motivation. Drowsiness and apathy (a feeling of not caring what happens) may be symptoms that accompany fatigue. Fatigue can be a normal and important response to physical exertion, emotional stress, boredom or lack of sleep. When fatigue is not relieved by sleeping well, eating well or having a low-stress environment, it should be evaluated.

entities/fibromialgia/contagion.text: The etiology and pathogenesis of fibromyalgia are not completely understood. Its relation with disorders of the central and peripheral nervous system, altered neurotransmitters and hormones, sleep disturbances, genetic factors, immune system alterations, psychiatric alterations, physical or mental stress, and alteration of the peripheral tissues has been observed. In some cases it has been related to other rheumatological diseases, infections, physical trauma, chemical substances and vaccines.

entities/fibromialgia/description.text: Fibromyalgia produces joint pain; arthritis deforms the joints, fibromyalgia does not. In the United States you are given Tylenol for life when fibromyalgia is detected. Fibromyalgia is a chronic disease characterized by generalized musculoskeletal pain, with exaggerated hypersensitivity (allodynia and hyperalgesia) at multiple predefined points (tender points), without demonstrable organic alterations. It is usually related to a wide variety of symptoms, notably persistent fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, generalized stiffness and anxiety-depressive symptoms. Both kidneys should be scanned.

entities/fibrosis-pulmonar/description.text: Pulmonary fibrosis is an interstitial lung disease characterized by the replacement of lung tissue by collagenous tissue. Radiological studies show the presence of scars in the lungs. This replacement generates changes in the physical characteristics of the lungs, producing major hemodynamic and clinical changes that can lead to death. Gradually, the alveoli are replaced by fibrotic tissue. As a scar forms, the tissue becomes thicker, causing an irreversible loss of gas-exchange capacity that progressively decreases overall tissue oxygenation; it may become complicated to the point of pulmonary infarction, abscess or bronchiectasis.

entities/fibrosis-quistica/description.text: Cystic fibrosis is a disease that mainly affects the lungs, and to a lesser extent the pancreas, liver and intestine, causing the accumulation of thick, sticky mucus in these areas. It is one of the most common types of chronic lung disease in children and young adults and is a potentially fatal disorder; patients usually die from lung infections due to Pseudomonas or Staphylococcus.

entities/fiebre-aftosa/contagion.text: Produced by coxsackievirus and enterovirus. Dairy products. It especially attacks toddlers, although it can appear at any age. This happens particularly when it is hot, usually in summer or early fall.

entities/fiebre-aftosa/description.text: Human foot-and-mouth disease (hand, foot and mouth disease) is a mild viral illness whose main symptoms are pain in the mouth and the presence of small blisters, ulcers or sores on the hands, feet and mouth. The two types of virus that cause it are Coxsackievirus and Enterovirus. It should not be confused with the other foot-and-mouth disease (glosopeda), which is a disease of livestock and is probably much better known. The symptoms of the disease begin three to six days after exposure and are initially: low-grade fever (37.5 to 39 °C), loss of appetite, mouth pain, and a nonlocalized feeling of illness. After a couple of days, small but normal-looking blisters begin to appear. These can vary in size from 2 to 4 mm. The blisters are surrounded by a small reddish area. They generally appear in the mouth, forming some shallow, painful ulcerations. They also appear on the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet and, less frequently, on the buttocks, the upper arms and legs, or the genitals.

entities/fiebre-escarlatina/description.text: Scarlet fever is a disease caused by infection with group A streptococcal bacteria (the same bacteria that cause strep throat), which produce a toxin that leads to the distinctive reddish rash of the disease. The main risk factor is infection with the bacteria that cause strep throat. The time between becoming infected and the onset of symptoms is short, usually 1 to 2 days. The disease classically begins with fever and a sore throat. The rash usually appears first on the neck and chest and then spreads to the rest of the body. This condition is described as feeling like "sandpaper." The texture of the rash is more important than its appearance in confirming the diagnosis. The rash can last about a week and, as it fades, peeling of the skin (desquamation) may occur around the fingertips, the toes and the groin area. The following symptoms are also likely to occur: abdominal pain, intense red coloration in the folds of the armpit and groin, chills, fever, general malaise (indisposition), headache, muscle aches, sore throat, redness and swelling of the tongue (strawberry tongue), vomiting.

entities/fiebre-malta/contagion.text: Bacteria of the genus Brucella. Dairy products (milk and cheese). Contact with the following animals: sheep, goat, camel, calf, buffalo, yak, pig, hare, reindeer, rodent, caribou, dog, rodents. It is transmitted by ingestion of contaminated food, especially through consumption of unpasteurized dairy products such as milk and cheese from infected animals; by direct contact with an infected animal; or by inhalation of aerosols in contaminated environments.

entities/fiebre-malta/description.text: Common brucella, brucellosis or Malta fever is an infectious disease produced by bacteria of the genus Brucella that attacks several species of mammals, among which is the human being, in whom it produces a nonspecific febrile picture, acute undulant fever, headache, night sweats, fatigue and anorexia. False leukemia. Respiratory and pulmonary problems such as bronchitis.

entities/fiebre-q/description.text: Q fever is a zoonosis (a disease transmitted to humans by an animal) caused by the bacterium Coxiella burnetii (small, Gram-negative). This organism is not common but can be found in livestock, cattle, sheep, goats and other domestic mammals. It produces no symptoms in animals. When there are symptoms, they occur after an incubation period of 10 to 40 days. The most classic presentation corresponds to a flu-like syndrome with high fever (lasting between one and two weeks), severe headache, myalgia, arthralgia, confusion, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, as well as respiratory symptoms such as pleuritic pain and dry cough. During the course of the infection, the disease can progress to atypical pneumonia. Less frequently, Q fever causes granulomatous hepatitis.

entities/fiebre-reumatica/description.text: Rheumatic fever is an inflammatory disease that can occur after an infection with group A streptococcal bacteria (such as strep throat or scarlet fever). The disease can affect the heart, joints, skin and brain. Some of the symptoms of rheumatic fever are the following: abdominal pain, fever, heart (cardiac) problems that may be asymptomatic or may cause difficulty breathing and chest pain, joint pain, arthritis (mainly in the knees, elbows, ankles and wrists), joint swelling, redness or warmth, nosebleeds (epistaxis), skin nodules, skin rash (erythema marginatum), skin rash on the trunk and upper part of the arms or legs, rashes that may look ring-shaped or snake-like, Sydenham's chorea (emotional instability, muscle weakness and rapid, uncoordinated, jerky spasmodic movements mainly affecting the face, feet and hands).

entities/fiebre-tifoidea/description.text: Typhoid fever, or enteric fever, is an infectious disease produced by Salmonella enterica subgroup enterica serotype Typhi, bacteria of the genus Salmonella. Its reservoir is the human, and the mechanism of transmission is fecal-oral, through water and food contaminated with excreta. Not to be confused with typhus, which is produced by several species of the genus Rickettsia transmitted by external parasites (lice). The bacterium enters by the digestive route, reaches the intestine and passes into the blood, which causes a phase of bacteremia toward the first week of the disease; it subsequently settles in various organs and produces inflammatory and necrotic phenomena, which are due to the release of endotoxins. Finally, the salmonellae are eliminated to the exterior in the feces. In the incubation period, which lasts 10 to 15 days, there is a disturbance of the general condition and a bacteremic phase with fever that rises progressively until it reaches 39-40 degrees Celsius, at which point it plateaus, along with headache, stupor, rose spots on the abdomen, swelling of the nasal mucosa, coated ("toasted") tongue, ulcers on the palate and sometimes hepatosplenomegaly and diarrhea. The disease may progress to recovery in 2 weeks or be prolonged with focal localizations from the fifth week onward. If it is not adequately treated, serious complications may arise, such as intestinal hemorrhage and perforation, and septic shock.

entities/fiebre/description.text: Fever is a syndrome (set of symptoms and signs) whose main sign is hyperthermia (increased temperature), although this is not essential, since there can be fever without hyperthermia. We say that hyperthermia is the main sign: the most frequent, the easiest to measure, and the first to appear. Fever is the body's response to agents of an infectious nature (which is most frequent) or to non-infectious causes (resorption toxins, lesions in certain nervous territories, etc). We thus speak of septic fever in the first case and aseptic fever in the second. The biomagnetic pairs that help bring down fever are the following: Orbital floor - Orbital floor, Kidney - Kidney, Temporal - Temporal. However, a complete review of the client will be necessary to eliminate the cause of the fever in question.

entities/filaria/contagion.text: They are transmitted in the form of larvae or microfilariae to vertebrates by an arthropod, generally mosquitoes, among them the Culex mosquito. Also by ingestion of contaminated water.

entities/filaria/description.text: Filariae are nematode parasites of the order Spirurida that produce the disease called lymphatic filariasis or elephantiasis, which consists of thickening of the skin and underlying tissue (it turned out to be the first infectious disease discovered to be transmitted by insects). Elephantiasis is caused when the parasite obstructs the lymphatic system. Elephantiasis mainly affects the lower limbs, whereas the ears and mucous membranes are rarely affected; however, the extent of symptoms depends on the filarial species involved. It can affect the legs, arms, vulva and breasts.

entities/flatulencias/description.text: Flatulence, also known as gas or farts, is the mixture of intestinal gases expelled through the anus, with a characteristic sound and odor. These intestinal gases come from three sources: 1) gases produced from food by colonies of intestinal bacteria and symbiotic yeasts that live in the gastrointestinal tract of mammals; 2) carbon dioxide (CO2), produced by the neutralization of gastric acid; 3) swallowed air. Gases originating from bacterial fermentation (mainly hydrogen and methane) account for approximately three quarters of total flatulence. When there is excessive production and passage of odorous gases, it can become socially disabling for some people. In general, the cause is fermentation of undigested substances by the colonic microflora. It is a multifactorial problem and may be the manifestation of an organic ailment, such as malabsorption disorders. All animals pass flatus, including many invertebrates, birds, worms, ants, fish and reptiles. Because of their different diet, the flatus of carnivores is generally more odorous than that of herbivores. Human flatulence is composed of nitrogen (ingested, 70-85%), hydrogen (microbes, 0-50%), carbon dioxide (microbes, ingested, 10-30%), methane (microbes, 0-10%), oxygen ( ingested, 0-10%). Flatus also contains aerosolized particles of excrement, although in minuscule amounts. Although the humor of flatulence is likely to be considered amusing, many cultures consider it impolite to pass gas in public.

entities/flaviviridae/description.text: Flaviviridae is a family of viruses spread mainly by arthropod vectors (especially ticks and mosquitoes). It includes the following genera: Genus Flavivirus: the type species is yellow fever virus; it also includes West Nile virus, dengue virus and Zika virus. A total of 67 viruses have been identified in humans and animals. Genus Hepacivirus: the type species is hepatitis C virus; it also includes GBV-B virus. Genus Pestivirus: the type species is bovine viral diarrhea virus; also classical swine fever and, in small ruminants, border disease virus. Genus Pegivirus: the type species is human pegivirus, previously called hepatitis G virus. Several species of this genus have been discovered in animals. The main diseases caused by the Flaviviridae family include: dengue, Japanese encephalitis, Kyasanur Forest disease, Murray Valley encephalitis, St. Louis encephalitis, tick-borne meningoencephalitis, West Nile encephalitis, yellow fever, and hepatitis C.

entities/florencia/description.text: Pair related to metalloid poisoning. Florencia is a Chilean woman whose father had problems of consciousness; he was completely shut down. He ate only oats, milk and sugar. The oats were toasted in old machines that contaminated them with metalloids. With this pair his problem was corrected.

entities/flujo-vaginal/description.text: Vaginal discharge is a fluid that lubricates the vagina and is produced both in preparing the organ for the sexual act and in the initial and final phases of menstruation, during ovulation, and in many other cases. It has a characteristic odor that intensifies if there are infections in the organ.

entities/forunculo/description.text: A furuncle or boil is an inflammation of the skin caused by infection of a hair follicle and the surrounding subcutaneous tissue, usually by the bacterium Staphylococcus aureus. Sometimes several boils join together to form a larger lesion, in which case the condition is known as furunculosis or carbuncle. Boils usually appear in moist hairy areas of the body such as the face, neck, armpits, groin, legs and breasts, especially where there is friction with clothing. Poor hygiene, obesity and diseases such as diabetes or immunodeficiency increase the risk of infection. It can also be spread by contagion to other parts of the body or to other people.

entities/fotofobia/description.text: Photophobia is eye discomfort in the presence of bright light. Severe photophobia can occur with eye problems and can cause intense eye pain even in relatively dim light. Some of the causes of photophobia are the following: iritis or acute uveitis (inflammation inside the eye), eye burns, corneal abrasion, corneal ulcer, excessive use of contact lenses or poorly fitted contact lenses, meningitis, eye disease, injury or infection (such as chalazion, episcleritis and glaucoma), drugs such as amphetamines, atropine, cocaine, cyclopentolate, idoxuridine, phenylephrine, scopolamine, trifluridine, tropicamide and vidarabine.

entities/frigidez/description.text: Frigidity is the absence of any kind of pleasure in sexual relations. In some cases, though less frequently, the frigid person also does not enjoy masturbation. Frigidity may exist from the beginning of sexual life (primary or total frigidity) or appear later (secondary or partial frigidity) and mainly affects women. Male frigidity also exists but is less frequent.

entities/frustracion/description.text: Frustration is a common emotional response to opposition, related to anger and disappointment, that arises from the perception of resistance to the fulfillment of individual will. The greater the obstruction and the will, the greater the frustration is also likely to be. The cause of frustration may be internal or external.

entities/galactorrea/description.text: Galactorrhea occurs when any fluid comes out of the nipple area of the breast. Nipple discharge is not usually a symptom of breast cancer, but it is important to find out the cause and receive treatment. Nipple discharge that is not normal has the following characteristics: it contains blood, comes from only one nipple, comes out on its own without squeezing or touching the nipple. Nipple discharge is more likely to be normal if it comes from both nipples and occurs when the nipples are squeezed. The color of the discharge does not indicate whether it is normal or not. It is considered galactorrhea when the discharge occurs outside the breastfeeding period; in some cases it can occur in males.

entities/gardnerella-vaginalis/contagion.text: It is not transmitted through sexual intercourse. Gardnerella vaginalis is a bacterium that is always present in the woman's body; it is a normal inhabitant of the body that is harmless throughout life and helps maintain the proper bacterial level; however, accumulations of this bacterium can form visible colonies of up to 5 cm and cause discomfort.

entities/gardnerella-vaginalis/descripti.text: Gardnerella vaginalis is a bacillus involved in the disease called bacterial vaginosis, characterized by an imbalance in the normal saprophytic flora of the vagina with a decrease in Lactobacillus spp. and population overgrowth of Gardnerella vaginalis and other aerobic and anaerobic bacteria. It is a non-motile, facultatively anaerobic, non-encapsulated bacterium that does not form endospores. It was formerly known as Haemophilus vaginalis. Its natural habitat is the human vagina. In women it causes vaginitis, vaginal discharge, bleeding, miscarriages and vaginal problems. In men it causes problems in the urethra. Bacterial vaginosis is the main cause of vaginal discharge and odor, although 50% of women may be asymptomatic. It was previously believed to be a sexually transmitted disease, but today it is known that it is not. Gardnerella is not a venereal disease.

entities/gastritis-cronica/description.text: Chronic gastritis is an inflammation of the stomach lining that develops gradually and persists for a considerably prolonged time. It may last from one month up to one year. Type A chronic gastritis: affects the body and fundus of the stomach without involving the antrum, usually associated with pernicious anemia. It is presumed to have an autoimmune etiology. Type B chronic gastritis: this is the most frequent form. It affects the antrum in young patients and the entire gastric mucosa in older people, and is caused by the bacterium Helicobacter pylori.

entities/gastritis/contagion.text: There are several causes of gastritis, among them poor eating habits, stress, analgesic abuse, autoimmune disorders or Helicobacter pylori infection.

entities/gastritis/description.text: Gastritis is inflammation of the gastric mucosa, which on gastroscopy appears reddened, presenting as reddish patches that represent irritation or subepithelial hemorrhages. However, the precise diagnosis is obtained by endoscopic examination. This will show whether only one part of the stomach is affected or the entire gastric sphere. Sometimes there are no symptoms, but most commonly there is burning or pain in the epigastrium, accompanied by nausea, dizziness, vomiting, etc. Symptoms related to gastroesophageal reflux, such as acidity in the stomach, are frequently found. The burning in the epigastrium usually subsides in the short term with food intake. But about two hours after eating, the food passes into the duodenum and the hydrochloric acid secreted for digestion remains in the stomach, which makes the symptoms worse. Upper abdominal pain (which may worsen with eating), indigestion or loss of appetite may also appear. If there is a bleeding ulcerative component, there may be vomiting of blood or of material resembling coffee grounds, and dark stools.

entities/giardia-lamblia/contagion.text: Contaminated food. Feces of an infected person or animal. Present in drinking water containing the parasite. Fruits and vegetables not properly washed or that were grown using contaminated fertilizer. Contact with people who do not wash their hands well or with the cutlery of infected people, since chlorine does not inactivate the parasite. This parasite is protected by an outer covering that allows it to survive outside the body and in the environment for long periods.

entities/giardia-lamblia/description.text: Giardia lamblia, intestinalis or duodenalis is a pathogenic flagellate protozoan that parasitizes the digestive tract of humans and other mammals, producing a condition called giardiosis, giardiasis or lambliasis. The pathology caused by G. lamblia is mainly due to the effects caused by the mechanical action of adhering and attaching to the intestinal epithelium. These effects produce an alteration of the microvilli, which lose exposed surface area as they thicken, and this leads to the appearance of various physiological alterations of greater or lesser severity, depending on the degree of impairment of the absorption process. The symptoms produced by giardiasis can range from none at all to symptoms such as mucous diarrhea without traces of blood, meteorism (abdominal distension caused by the production and accumulation of an excessive amount of gas in the gastrointestinal tract), abdominal pain, anorexia. In the most severe cases, malabsorption syndrome may occur, due to the destruction of the epithelial cells of the small intestine. This forces a constant renewal of the epithelium with immature cells that are not yet capable of absorbing or digesting certain molecules, which results in malabsorption of lipids, carbohydrates and proteins. It is characterized by the appearance of steatorrhea (fatty, copious stools) and, later, protein and vitamin deficiencies (especially fat-soluble vitamins). Flatulence, belching, nausea, vomiting, cephalalgia (headache), short stature syndrome, jaundice (yellowish skin color; it occurs rarely), urticaria (edematous skin lesions), fever, dyspnea (shortness of breath). People who have giardia generally have an aggressive personality and sometimes mistreat people in their work environment. They also show uncontrolled growth of the buttocks. Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, putrid diarrhea. Giardiasis is a diarrheal disease caused by Giardia intestinalis (also known as Giardia lamblia), a microscopic single-celled parasite that lives in the human intestine (the anterior portion of the small intestine (duodenum)).

entities/gingivitis/description.text: Gingivitis is inflammation of the gums; it is a form of periodontal disease in which inflammation and infection destroy the supporting tissues of the teeth. This can include the gums, the periodontal ligaments and the tooth sockets (alveolar bone). Gingivitis is due to the long-term effects of plaque deposits on the teeth. Plaque is a sticky material made up of bacteria, mucus and food debris that builds up on the exposed parts of the teeth. It is also a major cause of tooth decay. If plaque is not removed, it turns into a hard deposit called tartar (or calculus) that becomes trapped at the base of the tooth. Plaque and tartar irritate and inflame the gums. The bacteria and the toxins they produce cause the gums to become infected, inflamed and tender. Some of the symptoms of gingivitis are: bleeding gums (blood on the toothbrush even with gentle brushing), bright red or reddish-purple appearance of the gums, gums that are tender to the touch (but painless), mouth ulcers, swollen gums, shiny-looking gums.

entities/glaucoma/description.text: Glaucoma refers to a group of eye disorders that can cause damage to the optic nerve, the nerve that sends the images you see to the brain. In most cases, damage to the optic nerve is caused by increased pressure in the eye, called intraocular pressure. Glaucoma is the second most common cause of blindness. The front part of the eye is filled with a clear fluid called aqueous humor; this fluid is produced in an area behind the colored part of the eye (the iris); this fluid leaves the eye through channels where the iris and cornea meet; this area is called the anterior chamber angle or simply the angle. The cornea is the transparent covering at the front of the eye that covers the iris, pupil and angle. Any factor that slows or blocks the flow of this fluid will cause a buildup of pressure in that organ.

entities/goiz/description.text: Cerebral, pulmonary or renal dysfunction. If, before starting the patient's scan, one foot is longer than the other, it is necessary to place the positive pole on the kidney on the same side as the shortened foot and the negative pole on the contralateral parietal (on the opposite side). If the foot problem is not corrected, then it is an anatomical problem and the patient must be referred to an orthopedist. Dr. Goiz has corrected problems of up to 10 cm. of difference between one foot and the other. Most cases of asthmatic bronchitis and asthma are due to this biomagnetic pair. Check polarities; people already come with one hemibody shorter, which must be corrected. The symptoms produced by this pair are very varied and may be of the central nervous system, the bronchopulmonary system or the renal system. Central nervous system symptoms may include hemicrania (unilateral headache that preferentially affects the ocular, temporal or frontal region, always on the same side, in short-lasting episodes of between 2 and 45 minutes, but recurring very frequently, up to 40 times a day; the pain is very intense and is accompanied by a series of symptoms, such as ocular redness, tearing, nasal blockage, rhinorrhea (nasal discharge and congestion) and palpebral ptosis (drooping eyelids)), motor disorders of the contralateral hemibody and even mild behavioral disorders. The bronchopulmonary symptoms are associated with bronchospasm-dyspnea and recurrent bronchitis. The renal symptoms may produce dysuria or a tendency to urinary tract infection. Renal congestion, heavy head with deafness and tiredness. If there is no resonance with the contralateral parietal, resonance should be sought at other points of the skull, such as the temporal and the ear, and also at the contralateral parotid and parathyroid gland. When there is resonance with the parotid or the parathyroid gland, it mimics a picture of hypocalcemia and muscle weakness. Only the kidney can cause shortening of the lower limb; there is no other organ that causes it.

entities/gonorrea/description.text: Gonorrhea, also called blennorrhagia, blennorrhea and gonococcal infection. It mainly affects the mucous membranes of the genital and urinary tract, but it can also affect the ocular conjunctiva, the pharynx and the rectum. Its most common features are purulent discharge from the urethra in men and the consequence of infertility in women. Gonorrhea is caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae and can be spread by any type of sexual activity. It can be contracted through contact with the mouth, vagina, penis or anus. The bacteria proliferate in warm, moist areas of the body, including the tube that carries urine out of the body (urethra). In women, the bacteria can be found in the reproductive tract (which includes the fallopian tubes, uterus and cervix). This bacterium can even proliferate in the eyes. Symptoms of gonorrhea generally appear 2 to 5 days after infection; however, in men, symptoms can take up to a month to appear. Some people have no symptoms; they may be completely unaware that they have acquired the disease and therefore do not seek treatment. This increases the risk of complications and the chances of transmitting the infection to another person. Symptoms in men include: pain and burning on urination, increased urinary frequency or urgency, discharge from the penis (white, yellow or green), red or inflamed opening of the penis (urethra), tender or swollen testicles, sore throat (gonococcal pharyngitis). Symptoms in women can be very mild and can be mistaken for another type of infection. These symptoms include: vaginal discharge, pain and burning on urination, increased urination, sore throat, painful sexual intercourse, severe pain in the lower abdomen (if the infection spreads to the fallopian tubes and the stomach area), fever (if the infection spreads to the fallopian tubes and the stomach area). If the infection spreads to the bloodstream, the symptoms include: fever, rash, arthritis-like symptoms. It can also produce dental disorders, gingivitis, bad breath, and yellowish or blackish teeth. Meningococcus (Neisseria meningitidis) + Gonococcus (Neisseria gonorrhoeae) produces deforming rheumatoid arthritis. Rheumatism is related to arthritis.

entities/gota/contagion.text: Unhealthy lifestyles, obesity, excessive intake of alcohol or foods rich in purines, such as red meat, organ meats, oily fish or shellfish. Hepatitis.

entities/gota/description.text: Gout is a disease produced by an accumulation of monosodium urate crystals (a salt derived from uric acid) in different parts of the body, above all in the joints, soft tissues and kidneys. The typical acute gout attack usually begins at night and consists of arthritis that causes intense pain and redness in the metatarsophalangeal joint of the big toe. Gout is one of the types of microcrystalline arthritis. The fundamental factor causing gout is hyperuricemia (elevated blood uric acid levels). The two main reasons why blood uric acid levels are too high are increased production by the body and decreased elimination by the kidney.

entities/granuloma/description.text: A granuloma is a more or less spherical mass of immune cells that forms when the immune system tries to isolate foreign substances it has been unable to eliminate. Such substances include infectious organisms such as bacteria and fungi, as well as other materials such as keratin and sutures. A granuloma is therefore a special type of inflammation that can occur in a wide variety of diseases. They are also due to chronic inflammatory processes.

entities/gripe/contagion.text: Through virus-laden aerosol droplets (from nasal or bronchial secretions or saliva containing any of them), which are emitted when coughing or sneezing or simply when talking. The droplets are inhaled directly or, more frequently, are transmitted from hand to hand through handshakes or objects such as door handles, and are then introduced into the nasal passages when the hand touches the nose, mouth or eyes. It is also transmissible through blood and through surfaces or objects contaminated with the virus, which are called fomites. Influenza viruses survive longer in dry, cold environments. They can retain their infectivity for one week at human body temperature, for 30 days at 0 °C and for much longer at lower temperatures. It can be easily inactivated by detergents or disinfectants.

entities/gripe/description.text: Flu, grippe or influenza is an infectious disease caused by more than 200 serologically different viral types. The virus most frequently involved is a rhinovirus (30-50%), a type of picornavirus with 99 known serotypes. Other viruses involved include: coronaviruses (10-15%), influenza viruses (5-15%), human parainfluenza viruses, and respiratory syncytial viruses, adenoviruses, enteroviruses and metapneumoviruses. It affects the respiratory tract. Initially it may resemble a cold and is often accompanied by general symptoms such as sore throat, weakness, sneezing, nasal discharge and congestion, watery eyes, muscle aches (myalgia), stomach ache, joint pain (arthralgia) and headache (cephalalgia), with cough (generally dry and without mucus), general malaise, tiredness and some signs such as fever. In some more serious cases it can be complicated by pneumonia, which can be fatal, especially in young children and above all in the elderly. Although it can be confused with the common cold (catarrh), flu is a more serious disease and is caused by a different type of virus. It is one of the most common diseases and generally lasts between 3 and 10 days. Although the common cold has no cure, the symptoms generally resolve spontaneously in 7 to 10 days. To treat flu or influenza, all of the following pairs must be placed: 1) Gallbladder - Right / Left Kidney 2) Kidney - Kidney 3) Pancreas: Pancreatic ligament - Spleen 4) Bladder - Pituitary gland 5) Cranial vault - Cranial vault 6) Trachea - Trachea 7) Eyelid – Eyelid

entities/haemophilus-influenzae/descript.text: It causes nosebleeds, rhinitis, laryngitis, influenza. Haemophilus influenzae, formerly called Pfeiffer's bacillus or Bacillus influenzae, are nonmotile Gram-negative coccobacilli. It is generally aerobic but can grow as a facultative anaerobe. H. influenzae was erroneously considered the cause of common influenza until 1933, when the viral etiology of influenza became apparent. However, H. influenzae is responsible for a wide range of diseases such as meningitis, epiglottitis, pneumonia, sepsis and others of lesser severity. Most strains of H. influenzae are opportunistic pathogens, that is, they live in their host without causing disease, but they can cause problems when other factors (such as a viral illness that reduces the immune response) create an infectious opportunity.

entities/halitosis/description.text: Halitosis is a clinical sign characterized by bad breath or unpleasant mouth odor. It is generally caused by bacteria and affects 25% of the population. The causes of halitosis can be multiple, ranging from poor oral hygiene to diseases as serious as lung cancer, including chronic gastritis, although the vast majority originate in the mouth itself. Bad mouth odor is produced by bacterial decomposition of food remains between the teeth, of saliva, of cells of the oral mucosa or of blood.

entities/hanta-virus/description.text: Causes cancer in moles that grow. The magnet is placed on any mole on the body. High fever in a previously healthy person, chills, headache, musculoskeletal pain and gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain). Hantaviruses generally produce two types of conditions in humans: a type of viral hemorrhagic fever, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS); or hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a very serious lung condition.

entities/hechiceria/description.text: Witchcraft is the group of beliefs, practical knowledge and activities attributed to certain people who are supposedly endowed with certain magical abilities that they use for various purposes to cause harm.

entities/helicobacter-pylori/contagion.text: Helicobacter pylori lives exclusively in the stomach; it is the only known organism that survives in such an acidic environment. The bacterium has been isolated from the feces, saliva and dental plaque of infected patients. Gastro-oral or fecal-oral route. Contaminated water and food, or even oral transfer of fluids with a contaminated person.

entities/helicobacter-pylori/description.text: Helicobacter pylori is a bacterium that infects the human gastric epithelium and causes ulcers and some types of gastritis. It alters sperm production in the testicle, poor digestion, diaphragmatic hernia. At first it causes severe gastritis, then gastric ulcer.

entities/hematoquiluria/description.text: Hematochyluria is the presence of the main elements of blood in the urine, giving it an appearance that is both milky and pink. Hematochyluria is one of the main symptoms of filariasis.

entities/hematuria/description.text: Hematuria is the presence of blood in the urine, a frequent condition in human and veterinary medicine. The color of the urine can vary from blood red (or bright red) to brown, depending on whether the blood is fresh or has been transformed into acid hemoglobin by the effect of urinary pH.

entities/hemofilia/description.text: Hemophilia is an uncommon disorder in which the blood does not clot normally. Hemophilia usually occurs in men. People with hemophilia lack a clotting factor or have it in low amounts. Clotting factors are proteins needed for normal blood clotting. Without it, people can bleed for a long time after an injury or accident. They can also bleed internally in the knees, ankles and elbows. Bleeding into the joints causes pain and, when untreated, can lead to arthritis. Brain hemorrhages are a very serious complication of hemophilia and require emergency treatment. The main signs and symptoms of hemophilia are excessive bleeding and easy bruising. Blood tests can detect it. The main treatment is injection of the missing clotting factor into the bloodstream. It can be done regularly or only when the person needs it.

entities/hemorragia-gastrica/description.text: A gastric hemorrhage is any recent-onset blood loss originating from a lesion of the digestive tract. It manifests with the appearance of bloody stools. The amount of hemorrhage can range from minimal, with no hemodynamic repercussion, to one of greater magnitude and severity. A gastric hemorrhage is not a disease but a clinical sign through which different diseases manifest.

entities/hemorragia-intracraneal/descrip.text: An intracranial hemorrhage is a type of bleeding that occurs inside the skull. Bleeding around or inside the brain itself is called a cerebral hemorrhage (or intracerebral hemorrhage). Bleeding caused by the rupture or leakage of a blood vessel in the brain is called a hemorrhagic stroke. All bleeding inside the skull is called intracranial hemorrhage. Bleeding inside the skull or brain usually occurs suddenly, from either external or internal causes. A hemorrhage can damage the brain and nerves very quickly and can be fatal. Because the brain cannot store oxygen, it depends on a series of blood vessels to supply oxygen and nutrients. The accumulation of blood from an intracranial or cerebral hemorrhage puts pressure on the brain and deprives it of oxygen. When a hemorrhage or stroke interrupts the flow of blood around or inside the brain, depriving it of oxygen for more than three or four minutes, the brain cells die. In addition, the affected nerve cells and the related functions they control are damaged. The "Temporo-occipital region - Temporo-occipital region" pair helps eliminate the blood accumulated in the skull.

entities/hemorragia-nasal/description.text: A nosebleed is the loss of blood from the tissue lining the nose. Bleeding most often occurs in only one nostril. Nosebleeds are very common, and most occur because of colds or minor irritations. These bleeds can be alarming for some patients, but they are rarely potentially serious. The nose contains a large number of tiny blood vessels that bleed easily. The movement of air through the nose can dry out and irritate the membranes lining its interior, forming crusts that bleed when they are irritated by rubbing, picking or blowing the nose. The lining of the nose is more likely to become dry and irritated because of low humidity, allergies, colds or sinusitis. Thus, nosebleeds are more frequent during winter, when viruses are common and the hot air of heated indoor areas dries out the nasal passages. Most of these bleeds occur in the front part of the nasal septum, the tissue that separates the two sides of the nose. Occasionally, nosebleeds may be a sign of other disorders such as bleeding disorders or arterial hypertension.

entities/hemorragia-rectal/description.text: Rectal bleeding is often discovered by seeing bright red blood on toilet paper, or because the toilet water turns red, usually after a bowel movement. Rectal bleeding can also cause an extremely dark stool, ranging from deep red/maroon to black, sometimes with a tarry appearance (melena). The color of the blood can indicate where the bleeding is occurring. Bright red blood usually indicates that the bleeding is in the lower part of the colon or the rectum. Dark red or maroon blood usually indicates that the bleeding is higher up, in the colon or the small intestine. Melena (black, sticky, foul-smelling stools due to the presence of degraded blood from the upper digestive tract) usually indicates that the bleeding is in the stomach, for example bleeding from ulcers. Not all rectal bleeding is visible to the eye. In some cases, evidence of rectal bleeding can only be seen through microscopic examination of a stool sample.

entities/hemorragias/description.text: A hemorrhage is the escape of blood from the circulatory system, caused by the rupture of blood vessels such as veins, arteries or capillaries. It is an injury that triggers a loss of blood, either internal or external, and depending on its volume it can give rise to various complications such as anemia (low concentration of red blood cells or hemoglobin in the blood) or hypovolemic shock (major bleeding involving a loss of blood volume approaching 70%). Coagulation factors are all those proteins native to the blood that take part in and form part of the blood clot. There are thirteen coagulation factors, designated by Roman numerals; all of them require activation cofactors such as calcium and phospholipids. Coagulation factors are essential for coagulation to occur, and their absence can lead to serious bleeding disorders such as hemophilia. The different types of hemorrhage, classified according to their anatomical origin, are the following: 1) Internal hemorrhage - rupture of a blood vessel inside the body. 2) External hemorrhage - rupture of blood vessels through the skin; this type of hemorrhage is frequently produced by open wounds. 3) Exteriorized hemorrhage - through natural orifices of the body, such as the mouth when vomiting (hematemesis) or coughing (hemoptysis), the nose (epistaxis), any part of the digestive tract (gastrointestinal hemorrhage), the rectum (rectal bleeding), the vagina (metrorrhagia), the urethra (hematuria), the ear (otorrhagia) and the eye (hyposphagma). According to the type of blood vessel ruptured, hemorrhages can be classified as: 1) Capillary hemorrhage - this is the most frequent and the least serious, since blood capillaries are the most abundant vessels and those with the lowest blood pressure. 2) Venous hemorrhage - the bleeding comes from an injured vein, and the blood flows out continuously but without force; it is dark red in color. 3) Arterial hemorrhage - this is the most serious and, if not treated in time, can lead to death; the bleeding comes from an injured artery and the blood comes out in an intermittent, bright red spurt.

entities/hemorroides/description.text: Hemorrhoids are swollen cushions of tissue in the anus or the lower part of the rectum that contain many arteries and veins. Hemorrhoids result from increased pressure in the anus. This can occur during pregnancy or childbirth or because of constipation. This pressure causes the anal cushions to swell. This tissue can bleed, often during bowel movements. Hemorrhoids can be caused by straining during bowel movements, constipation, sitting for long periods of time (especially on the toilet), and diseases such as liver cirrhosis. Hemorrhoids can be inside or outside the body. Internal hemorrhoids occur just inside the anus, where the rectum begins. When they are large they can protrude (prolapse). The most common problem with internal hemorrhoids is bleeding during bowel movements. External hemorrhoids occur outside the anus and can cause difficulty cleaning the area after a bowel movement. If a blood clot forms in an external hemorrhoid, it can be very painful (thrombosed external hemorrhoid). Hemorrhoids are generally not painful, but if a blood clot forms they can cause a great deal of pain.

entities/hepadnaviridae/description.text: Hepadnaviridae is a family of viruses that cause liver infections in humans and animals. Hepadnaviruses have a very short circular DNA genome, partly double-stranded and partly single-stranded. It comprises two genera: genus Orthohepadnavirus: hepatitis B virus, and genus Avihepadnavirus: duck hepatitis B virus.

entities/hepatitis-a/description.text: Hepatitis A is characterized by acute inflammation of the liver in most cases. Hepatitis A cannot become chronic and does not cause permanent damage to the liver. Following an infection, the immune system produces antibodies and confers immunity on the individual against future infections. Transmission can occur through contact with the feces and blood of an infected person. The pathogen is present approximately 15 to 45 days before symptoms occur and during the first week of the illness. Symptoms usually appear 2 to 6 weeks after exposure to the hepatitis A pathogen; they are generally mild but can last up to several months, especially in adults. Symptoms include: dark urine, fatigue, itching, loss of appetite, low-grade fever, nausea and vomiting, clay-colored or pale stools, yellow skin (jaundice).

entities/hepatitis-b/description.text: The only viral hepatitis. Hepatitis B is characterized by irritation and swelling (inflammation) of the liver due to infection with the hepatitis B virus. Hepatitis B infection is caused by the hepatitis B virus. This disease can be contracted through contact with the blood or body fluids (such as semen, vaginal secretions and saliva) of a person who has the virus. The symptoms of hepatitis B may not appear until 6 months after the time of infection. Initial symptoms may include: loss of appetite, fatigue, low-grade fever (moderate, prolonged fever), muscle and joint aches, nausea, vomiting, yellow skin and cloudy urine. The symptoms will disappear within a few weeks or months if the body is able to fight off the infection. Some people never get rid of the hepatitis B virus, which is called chronic hepatitis B. People with chronic hepatitis may have no symptoms and may not know they are infected. Over time, some people may develop symptoms of chronic liver damage and cirrhosis of the liver. When hepatitis B is combined with another virus, it can give rise to a disease called Kaposi's sarcoma, a malignant tumor of the lymphatic endothelium characterized by the appearance of bluish-red, flat or raised, irregularly shaped lesions, bleeding from gastrointestinal lesions, difficulty breathing due to lung lesions, and bloody sputum, also due to lung lesions.

entities/hepatitis-c/contagion.text: Toxins. Yellow fats. Raw oils. Foods. Mayonnaise, ketchup, vegetable oils, raw fats, oils in salads, margarine, vegetable shortening. Allopathic medicines. Chocolate should be 100% cacao so that vegetable oils are not added. Here it is difficult to find 100% cacao chocolate.

entities/hepatitis-c/description.text: Hepatitis C is characterized by swelling (inflammation) of the liver. Infection can occur if the blood of someone with hepatitis C enters the body, whether through a wound, the eyes or the mouth. Most people who were recently infected with hepatitis C have no symptoms. Some people have yellowish skin (jaundice) that goes away. Chronic infection usually causes no symptoms, but tiredness, skin disorders and other problems may occur. People who have a long-term (chronic) infection often have no symptoms until their liver becomes scarred (cirrhosis). Most people with this condition are ill and have many health problems. The following symptoms may occur with hepatitis C infection: pain in the upper right quadrant of the abdomen, abdominal swelling due to fluid (ascites), clay-colored or pale stools, cloudy urine, fatigue, fever, itching, jaundice (yellowish discoloration of the eyes and/or skin), loss of appetite, nausea and vomiting.

entities/hepatitis-e/description.text: Hepatitis E is a disease that affects the liver. It is caused by the bacterium Klebsiella pneumoniae. The characteristic signs and symptoms of hepatitis E are: jaundice (yellowish coloration of the skin and the sclera of the eyes, dark urine and pale stools), anorexia (loss of appetite), an enlarged liver that is tender on palpation (hepatomegaly), abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, fever.

entities/hepatitis-reservorio/descriptio.text: The viruses lodged in the gallbladder are generally hepatitis B and HIV 1. Once the pair has been depolarized, treatment must follow immediately, looking for the pair that forms when the virus leaves the gallbladder. This organ is a virus reservoir where viruses come to lodge in their effort to survive when they are besieged, whether by drugs or by some other procedure. Viruses have the intelligence or intuition to hide in one place and later return to their usual pair; therefore, when depolarizing this pair, it is necessary to carry out a complete scan to find the pair where the virus is lodged and impact it. Hepatitis is an inflammatory disease that affects the liver. Its cause can be infectious (viral, bacterial, etc.), immune (due to autoantibodies, autoimmune hepatitis) or toxic (for example, due to alcohol, toxic substances or drugs). Depending on its etiology, it is also considered a sexually transmitted disease. There are viruses specific to hepatitis (hepatotropic viruses), that is, those that cause only hepatitis. There are many viruses: A, B, C, D, E, F and G. The most important are viruses A, B and C; to a lesser extent D and E, with the last ones, F and G, being the least studied.

entities/hernia-diafragmatica/descriptio.text: A diaphragmatic hernia is a congenital anomaly in which there is an abnormal opening in the diaphragm, the muscle that helps one breathe. This opening allows part of the abdominal organs (stomach, spleen, liver and intestines) to move up into the chest cavity near the lungs. A diaphragmatic hernia is caused by improper joining of structures during fetal development. As a result, abdominal organs such as the stomach, small intestine, spleen, part of the liver and the kidney appear in the chest cavity. In this way, the lung tissue on the affected side is not allowed to develop completely; in most cases they affect the left side. Some of the symptoms of people with a diaphragmatic hernia are the following: severe difficulty breathing, bluish coloration of the skin due to lack of oxygen, rapid breathing (tachypnea), rapid heart rate (tachycardia).

entities/hernia-discal/description.text: A herniated disc is a disease in which part of the intervertebral disc (nucleus pulposus), located between the vertebrae, is displaced toward the nerve root, compresses it and produces neurological lesions resulting from this injury. Herniations may be contained (deformation only, also called disc protrusion) or with rupture. The hernia causes pain in the lumbar area. Pain arises from inflammation of the periosteum of the vertebrae, the joints, the dura mater, the annulus fibrosus, the posterior longitudinal ligament and the lumbar muscles of the spine. A herniated disc can produce a series of clinical manifestations, the most frequent being lumbago and sciatica.

entities/hernia-hiatal/description.text: Hiatal hernia is a condition in which the upper part of the stomach bulges through an opening in the diaphragm. The diaphragm is the muscular wall that separates the stomach from the thorax. The diaphragm helps prevent acid from passing into the esophagus. When there is a hiatal hernia, it is easier for acid to rise. The passage of acid from the stomach into the esophagus is called gastroesophageal reflux. Gastroesophageal reflux can cause symptoms such as: heartburn, problems swallowing, dry cough, bad breath. Hiatal hernias are common, especially in people over 50 years of age. It is recommended to eat small portions, avoid certain foods, not smoke or drink alcohol, and lose weight. The physician may recommend antacids or other medicines. Surgery may be required.

entities/hernia-inguinal/description.text: An inguinal hernia is a protrusion of the contents of the abdominal cavity through a weak point of the inguinal canal. There are two types of inguinal hernia, one direct and the other indirect. In direct inguinal hernias, the abdominal contents, specifically the small intestine, pass through a weakness in the abdominal musculature and protrude in the area of Hesselbach's triangle. Direct hernias present as an oval swelling, are reducible and rarely enter the scrotum. As a rule, they do not travel along the inguinal canal. Indirect inguinal hernias occur when the abdominal contents protrude through the internal or deep inguinal ring. They descend along the inguinal canal, parallel to the spermatic cord, and over time usually reach the scrotum. They are the most frequent inguinal hernias and are very common in children. They can occur in women and, when complete, produce labial inguinal hernias.

entities/hernia-umbilical/description.text: For the "Navel - Rectum" pair it is also suggested to place the magnets on the soles of the feet, the negative on the right side of the body and the positive on the left side. An umbilical hernia is a protrusion of the contents of the abdominal cavity through a weak point of the umbilical ring due to a defect in closure of the abdominal wall. It is a very common hernia in children and adults, especially the obese and women. The protrusion involves the small intestine, peritoneum and omentum, and other viscera, and carries a high incidence of strangulation of the herniated contents. It becomes visible above and outside the umbilical scar as an oval bulge over the navel, occasionally painful. It is occasionally associated with diastasis, that is, separation of the rectus abdominis muscles.

entities/herpes-1-zoster/description.text: Ulcerations in the intercostal spaces. Herpes zoster is a disease produced by a reactivation of the latent varicella-zoster virus, which affects the peripheral nerves (ganglioradicular neuropathy) and the skin, where it can produce small, painful, ring-shaped blisters grouped along a dermatome. Colloquially it is known as shingles (in Spanish: faja de la reina, culebrilla, culebrina or culebrón).

entities/herpes-2/description.text: Thrush in the mouth. Urogenital diseases. Herpes simplex is an inflammatory infectious disease of viral type characterized by the appearance of skin lesions formed by small vesicles grouped in clusters and surrounded by a red ring. It is caused by the herpes simplex virus, or herpesvirus hominis, type I (HSV-1), which affects the face, lips, mouth and upper body, and type II (HSV-2), which occurs more frequently on the genitals and lower body. Vesicles that ulcerate may appear in the pharynx.

entities/herpes-4/description.text: Cold sores in the mouth. Herpes simplex is an inflammatory infectious disease of viral type characterized by the appearance of skin lesions formed by small vesicles grouped in clusters and surrounded by a red ring. It is caused by the herpes simplex virus, or herpesvirus hominis, type I (HSV-1), which affects the face, lips, mouth and upper body, and type II (HSV-2), which occurs more frequently on the genitals and lower body.

entities/herpes-7/description.text: Herpes 7. It can cause exanthem subitum (roseola, rash), acute respiratory illnesses, fever, rash, vomiting, diarrhea, and a drop in the lymphocyte count. Most of the time no symptoms at all appear.

entities/herpes-facial/description.text: Facial herpes is very common and is also known as cold sores, fever blisters, orofacial herpes, herpes labialis and herpes febrilis. Facial herpes is characterized by a group of fluid-filled blisters that appear on red, inflamed areas of the skin or mucous membranes. A burning sensation is often present just before the skin lesions develop. The blisters heal without scars but tend to recur.

entities/hhv-5/description.text: It attacks the spinal cord and produces multiple sclerosis; it is curable as long as there is no spinal cord damage. Muscle weakness. Paralysis. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a form of herpesvirus; in humans, it is known as Human herpesvirus 5 (HHV-5). It belongs to the subfamily Betaherpesvirinae of the family Herpesviridae. Its name alludes to the increase in size seen in infected cells as a result of the weakening of the cytoskeleton. This virus is one of the main causes of infectious mononucleosis. CMV affects both immunocompetent and immunosuppressed people. It is in immunosuppressed patients that it produces severe complications. However, in others, conditions such as mononucleosis-like syndrome, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy or arthralgia have also been described. CMV mainly attacks the salivary glands and can be a serious or fatal disease for fetuses during pregnancy.

entities/hhv-6/description.text: Herpes 6. Allergies in the groin, itching. Human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6), or herpesvirus type 6, formerly also known as human B-lymphotropic virus (HBLV), is a virus of the Herpesviridae family, one of the 8 (HHV-1 to HHV-8) that infect humans. It usually causes fever. In 10% of cases it causes exanthema subitum (roseola, rash). It is associated with several more serious complications, such as encephalitis, lymphadenopathy, myocarditis and myelosuppression. After primary infection, the virus establishes itself in myeloid tissue and the bone marrow and remains latent for the lifetime of the host. The virus periodically reactivates from the latent state, with HHV-6 DNA. In most cases these reactivations are often asymptomatic, but in immunosuppressed individuals there can be serious complications. HHV-6 has also been found in multiple sclerosis patients and implicated as a cofactor in several other diseases, including chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, AIDS, and temporal lobe epilepsy.

entities/hhv-7/description.text: Human herpesvirus 7 or HHV-7 is a virus of the beta subfamily of Herpesviridae. It is characterized by a genome organization similar to that of HHV-6. Present in coinfections with HHV-6, whether it is a pathogen is debated: some authors indicate that there is no clear evidence that it is involved in any human disease, while others state that it causes roseola infantum, pityriasis rosea, neurological disorders and transplant complications.

entities/hhv-8/description.text: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) or Kaposi's sarcoma virus is a rhadinovirus that was identified in 1994 as responsible for Kaposi's sarcoma cancer. This cancer attacks immunosuppressed people. The virus quickly became the herald or messenger of a new epidemic, that of AIDS. In AIDS patients, the cancer can develop rapidly and can also involve the skin, lungs, digestive tract and other organs.

entities/hidrocele/description.text: A hydrocele is the pathological accumulation of serous fluid inside a cavity in the human body. It is popularly known as a water cyst, although this term is inappropriate because what accumulates is not exactly water. The most common type of hydrocele is hydrocele testis, the excessive accumulation of fluid in the spermatic cord.

entities/higado-graso/description.text: The liver is the largest organ inside the body. It helps digest food, store energy and eliminate toxins. Fatty liver disease, or hepatic steatosis, is a condition in which fat accumulates in the liver. There are two main types: nonalcoholic fatty liver disease and alcoholic fatty liver disease, also called alcoholic hepatic steatosis. There are two types of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease: simple fatty liver and nonalcoholic hepatic steatosis. In simple fatty liver disease there is fat in the liver but little or no inflammation or damage to the liver cells; in general, simple fatty liver is not serious enough to cause damage or complications to the liver. In nonalcoholic hepatic steatosis there is inflammation and damage to the liver cells as well as fat; the inflammation and damage to the liver cells can cause fibrosis or scarring of the liver; steatosis can cause cirrhosis or liver cancer. Alcoholic fatty liver disease is due to high alcohol consumption; the liver breaks down most of the alcohol so that it can be eliminated from the body, but the breakdown process can generate harmful substances. These substances can damage liver cells, cause inflammation and weaken the body's natural defenses. The more alcohol is consumed, the more the liver is damaged. Alcoholic fatty liver disease is the earliest stage of alcoholic liver disease; the following stages are alcoholic hepatitis and cirrhosis.

entities/hiperactividad/description.text: Hyperactive behavior usually refers to constant activity, a tendency to be easily distracted, impulsivity, inability to concentrate, aggressiveness and similar behaviors. Characteristic behaviors may include: fidgeting or constant movement, wandering, talking excessively, difficulty participating in quiet activities (such as reading).

entities/hiperglucemia/description.text: Hyperglycemia (hyperglycaemia) means an excessive amount of glucose in the blood. It is the basic finding in all types of diabetes mellitus, when it is uncontrolled or in its early stages. The opposite term is hypoglycemia. Hyperglycemia and insulin resistance have effects on patient outcomes: they reduce resistance to infection, favoring superinfection by gram-negative bacteria and fungi, they favor the onset of polyneuropathies and multiorgan dysfunction and, ultimately, they increase patients' crude mortality rate. In the fasting state, a person's blood glucose should not exceed 126 mg/dl, and 200 mg/dl the rest of the time. Maintaining high blood glucose levels for years contributes to seriously worsening the long-term complications of diabetes.

entities/hiperhidrosis/description.text: Hyperhidrosis is a disorder consisting of excessive sweating produced by a failure of our autonomic (sympathetic) nervous system, causing our body to produce more sweat than it needs to regulate body temperature. Many people who have this disease see their quality of life affected and feel a loss of control over it, since perspiration occurs regardless of temperature and emotional state. According to the regions affected by excessive perspiration, the following are distinguished: palmar sweating, axillary sweating and facial sweating (a phenomenon associated with facial sweating is facial blushing, which consists of reddening of the face). In addition, primary hyperhidrosis and secondary hyperhidrosis can be distinguished: the former can begin at any point in life; the latter may be due to disorders of the thyroid or pituitary gland, diabetes mellitus, tumors, menopause or certain drugs.
