It is estimated that 1 % of the population has primary hyperhidrosis; it affects men and women equally. In its most severe forms it can cause fungal infections, scaling, bad odor, irritation and pigmentation of the skin.

entities/hiperplasia-benigna-prostatica/.text: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) consists of a non-malignant (non-cancerous) growth in the size of the prostate. This enlargement of the prostate gland is the product of androgenic stimulation. As the prostate grows, it can progressively compress the urethra and therefore cause difficulty urinating. This happens because this compression impedes the flow of urine from the bladder into the urethra and out of the body. Possible consequences are urine retention in the bladder or reflux of urine toward the kidneys, and a need to urinate frequently. If the inflammation is very severe, the urinary system can become completely blocked. BPH is a very common disease in men: although it generally begins from the age of 30, it very rarely becomes manifest before 40. At approximately 60 years of age, more than 50% of men have BPH, and between 70 and 80 years of age up to 90% present some of its symptoms.

entities/hipersexualidad/description.text: Hypersexuality is a sudden increase in, or extreme frequency of, libido or sexual activity. Although hypersexuality can occur due to some medical problems, the use of some medications and the ingestion of drugs, in most cases the cause is unknown.

entities/hipertension-arterial/descripti.text: Blood pressure is a measurement of the force exerted against the walls of the arteries as the heart pumps blood through the body. Hypertension is a term used to describe high blood pressure. Blood pressure readings are usually given as two numbers. For example, 120 over 80 (written as 120/80 mmHg). One or both of these numbers may be too high. The top number is called the systolic blood pressure and the bottom number the diastolic blood pressure. Normal blood pressure is a blood pressure below 120/80 mmHg most of the time. High blood pressure (hypertension) is a blood pressure of 140/90 mmHg or higher most of the time. Some factors that alter blood pressure are the following: the amount of water and salt in the body, the state of the kidneys, the nervous system and the blood vessels, and the levels of different hormones in the body. Arterial hypertension increases the likelihood of suffering a stroke, a heart attack, heart failure, kidney disease and early death. Some factors that increase the risk of developing arterial hypertension are: obesity, stress, anxiety, excess alcohol, excess salt, diabetes, smoking.

entities/hipertension-ocular/description.text: Intraocular pressure is the pressure exerted by the intraocular fluids against the wall of the eye, which is necessary for this organ to remain distended. Its mean value is 16 mmHg, and it can easily be measured with the help of a device called a tonometer. The balance between production and reabsorption of the aqueous humor is the main factor determining the level of intraocular pressure. On the other hand, elevated intraocular pressure, or ocular hypertension, is the main risk factor for developing an eye disease known as glaucoma. Ocular hypertension is considered to be present when intraocular pressure is above 21 mmHg in two consecutive measurements; values between 11 and 21 mmHg are considered normal. The eye is in fact a hollow sphere full of fluid, which exerts pressure on its walls, thanks to which it remains distended. The fluid inside the eye is divided into two parts of different compositions and textures. The first is the vitreous humor, which is found in the back of the organ, between the posterior surface of the lens and the retina. It is a gelatinous substance in which its components diffuse slowly. It occupies 80 % of the interior of the eye; its renewal is scant and very slow. The second is the aqueous humor, which is found in the front of the eye, between the lens and the cornea. The aqueous humor occupies 3 % of the interior of the eye and is constantly renewed; production and reabsorption are continuous and remain balanced under normal circumstances. If an imbalance occurs due to excess production or blocked reabsorption, intraocular pressure rises above the values appropriate for the proper functioning of the eye.

entities/hipertiroidismo/description.text: Hyperthyroidism is a type of thyrotoxicosis characterized by a metabolic disorder in which excess function of the thyroid gland leads to hypersecretion of thyroid hormones (free thyroxine (T4) or free triiodothyronine (T3), or both) and abnormally elevated plasma levels of these hormones. As a consequence, symptoms such as tachycardia, weight loss, nervousness and tremors appear. In humans, the main causes of this condition are Graves' disease or diffuse toxic goiter, toxic thyroid adenoma, toxic multinodular goiter, subacute thyroiditis and the effects of some medications. Excess thyroid hormones (TH) induce an overall increase in metabolism, with a rise in energy expenditure, heat production and oxygen consumption. Protein synthesis increases, but overall catabolism predominates over anabolism, so a negative nitrogen balance results. In addition, the sensitivity of tissues to the action of catecholamines increases, probably due to a potentiation of adrenergic receptors. Because of the catabolic effect, weight loss occurs (barely noticeable when there is polyphagia). The skin becomes thin, hair loss increases, and the nails become brittle and tend to separate from the nail bed (Plummer's nails). Excess thyroid hormones produce an increase in intestinal motility, so the number of bowel movements increases. The cardiovascular system is overloaded because of the increased tissue requirements for nutrients and oxygen, the need to dissipate the excess heat produced, and cardiac hypersensitivity to catecholamines. Heart rate increases and arrhythmias may appear. In the neuromuscular system, excess thyroid hormones manifest as nervousness, irritability, insomnia, mental disorders that may range from anxiety to delirium, fine distal tremor, hyperreflexia and weakness of the girdle muscles. Sometimes dyspnea occurs, caused by oxygen consumption and anxiety. It must be distinguished from the dyspnea that a large goiter can cause by narrowing the airway.

entities/hipo/description.text: Hiccups are a spasmodic, involuntary and repetitive contraction of the diaphragm and intercostal muscles that causes a sudden inspiration of air. The diaphragm is a fundamental muscle for breathing in mammals. When it contracts, the chest expands and air enters the lungs through the trachea (inspiration). In contrast, when the diaphragm relaxes, the chest contracts and air leaves the lungs through the mouth and nose (expiration). The phrenic nerve controls the contraction and relaxation of the diaphragm. If the phrenic nerve sends abnormal impulses, the diaphragm contracts suddenly, causing an abnormal sudden inspiration and abrupt closure of the glottis, producing hiccups. Some of the situations that can provoke hiccups are: eating too fast, gastric distension due to aerophagia or consumption of carbonated drinks, alcohol abuse and anxiety. Most of the time, hiccups last only a few minutes. However, they sometimes persist for days or weeks.

entities/hipocalcemia/description.text: Hypocalcemia is a condition in which blood calcium levels are low. Calcium is an important salt in many body systems, especially in heart and muscle function. A prolonged deficit in calcium levels can lead to bone malformation, which can result in brittle bones prone to fracture.

entities/hipoglucemia/description.text: Hypoglycemia (not to be confused with its antonym, hyperglycemia) is a state defined by an abnormally low blood glucose concentration, below 50-60 mg / 100 ml. It is often called insulin shock, because of how frequently it occurs in patients with diabetes mellitus treated with insulin. It is generally associated with alterations or loss of consciousness. Hypoglycemia can be due to various causes. In healthy people it is usually the consequence of very prolonged fasting, because the body continues to use glucose once there is no glycogen left in the liver to produce it. Intense exercise accompanied by little prior intake can cause hypoglycemia, since physical activity promotes the use of glucose by the tissues. In people with diabetes mellitus it is very common. In this case it is usually due to a failure in the administration of exogenous insulin. It must be watched for especially in children under 6 years of age, since it can impair brain development. Glucose is a monosaccharide with the molecular formula C6 H12 O6. Glucose, free or combined, is the most abundant organic compound in nature. It is the primary source of energy synthesis for cells, through its catabolic oxidation, and it is the main component of structurally important polymers such as cellulose and of energy-storage polymers such as starch and glycogen. Photoautotrophic organisms, such as plants, synthesize glucose in photosynthesis from inorganic compounds such as water and carbon dioxide, according to the reaction: 6(CO2) + 6 (H2O) ---> C6 H12 O6 + 6 (O2) in the presence of sunlight as a catalyst.

entities/hipomania/description.text: Hypomania is an affective state characterized by a persistently expansive, hyperactive and/or irritable mood, as well as by thoughts and behaviors consequent to that mood, which is distinguishable from a normal mood. Individuals in a hypomanic state have less need for sleep and rest, may be hyperempathic and have an enormous amount of energy. This pathological mood constitutes one of the phases of bipolar disorder and of cyclothymia (alternating hypomania and depression).

entities/hipopotasemia/description.text: Hypopotassemia, also known as hypokalemia, is a disorder of the body's fluid and electrolyte balance characterized by a decrease in the levels of potassium ion (K) in the plasma, with levels below 3.5 mmol/L. Hypokalemia can be caused by various abnormalities. Among the most frequent are: diarrhea, burns, decreased intake and intestinal diseases. Decreased intake as a cause of low potassium is uncommon, because the kidneys have the capacity to reabsorb potassium (K), which is found in most foods. Potassium is the main intracellular cation in humans, and therefore it has a large number of physiological functions, which, when there is an alteration in the homeostasis of the ion, produce a series of abnormalities. Notable functions of potassium include the following: it regulates the water content of cells, preventing its leakage; it maintains acid-base balance and, together with sodium, regulates the amount and normal distribution of water in the body; in balance with calcium and magnesium, it contributes to the regulation of all cellular functions, especially the excitability of the heart, the nervous system and the muscles; it is indispensable for the movement of the myocardium and activates enzyme systems; it is involved in building proteins; it increases neuromuscular excitability, and it is responsible for facilitating the transmission of the nerve impulse across the cell membrane. Some fruits rich in potassium are bananas and oranges.

entities/hiporexia/description.text: Hyporexia is the partial loss of appetite, which differs from anorexia because the latter is a total loss. Although it can occur at any age, this problem is frequent in older adults or the elderly due to several factors. Among these are sensory losses, whether of taste, smell or sight, since this affects proper appetite and food consumption.

entities/hipotiroidismo/description.text: Hypothyroidism. For our body to function properly, it is very important to have adequate concentrations of the hormones T3 and T4. When these are not adequate, we speak of thyroid dysfunction. If the thyroid gland is underactive, it does not produce sufficient amounts of thyroid hormones and metabolic processes are slower, so the body slows down, and hypothyroidism is said to be present. The thyroid gland is an important organ of the endocrine system. It is located in the front of the neck, just above where the clavicles meet. The thyroid produces hormones that control the way every cell in the body uses energy. This process is called metabolism. The most common cause of hypothyroidism is thyroiditis; swelling and inflammation damage the cells of the thyroid gland. Some causes of hypothyroidism are the following: an immune system that attacks the thyroid gland, viral infections (common cold) or other respiratory infections, pregnancy, radiation therapy to the neck, radioactive iodine, pituitary tumor or pituitary surgery. Some early symptoms of hypothyroidism are: hard stools or constipation, increased sensitivity to cold, fatigue or feeling slowed down, heavy or irregular menstrual periods, muscle or joint pain, pallor or dry skin, sadness or depression, brittle and weak hair or nails, weakness, weight gain. Some late symptoms of hypothyroidism are: diminished sense of taste and smell, hoarseness, swelling of the face, hands and feet, slow speech, thickening of the skin, thinning of the eyebrows.

entities/histoplasma-capsulatum/descript.text: Histoplasma capsulatum is a yeast that in the saprophytic state (organisms that depend for their nutrition on residues from other organisms) grows in mycelial form. It causes acute pulmonary histoplasmosis, a lung infection that impairs oxygenation. It can cause weight loss. It atrophies the spleen. Continuous urge to urinate.

entities/histoplasmosis/description.text: Histoplasmosis is a fungal infection. The fungus Histoplasma grows as a mold in the soil. The disease appears when the spores produced by this fungus are inhaled. Soil containing bird or bat droppings may have larger amounts of this fungus. The threat is greater after an old building is demolished, or in caves. Having a weakened immune system increases the risk of contracting or reactivating this disease. People who are very young or very old, or those with AIDS, cancer, an organ transplant or a chronic lung disease (emphysema, bronchiectasis), have more severe symptoms. In immunocompetent people it is usually asymptomatic. In the immunodeficient, it can present with pneumonia-like pictures with fever and respiratory distress, and in approximately 20% of patients it progresses to septic shock, kidney failure and coagulopathy, leading to death. If symptoms occur, they are generally the following: fever, chills, cough, chest pain, joint pain, mouth sores, and red bumps on the skin called erythema nodosum. The infection may be active for a short period of time and then the symptoms disappear. Sometimes the lung infection can become chronic.

entities/hongos-bucales/description.text: Oral fungus, frequently called oral candidiasis, is a relatively common medical condition. When fungus develops in the mouth, the tongue and the inner cheeks will appear to be covered with white lesions. Sometimes these lesions may form on the throat, gums, tonsils and even the palate. Since most fungi generally develop rapidly, it may become a chronic condition if not treated properly and/or if the cause of the infection is not identified; the fungus may spread to other parts of the body such as the skin, lungs and liver.

entities/hongos-en-los-pies/description.text: This is a fungal infection produced by dermatophyte fungi (which feed on keratin) or by yeasts (in very rare cases with immune system impairment). It affects the interdigital folds, the sole and the edges of the foot. The risk of contracting this condition increases if you wear closed footwear, especially if it is plastic-lined, if you keep your feet damp for prolonged periods, if you sweat a lot, or if you have a minor injury to the nails or skin. The most common symptom is cracked, scaly, peeling skin between the toes or on the sides of the foot. Other symptoms may include red, itchy skin, burning or stinging, and blisters that ooze (discharge fluid) or crust over. If the fungus spreads to the nails, they may become discolored, thickened and may even fall off.

entities/hostilidad/description.text: Hostility encompasses a wide range of offensive behaviors. It is normally understood as conduct intended to disturb or upset. To harass is to bother someone or mock them insistently. In the legal sense, it is behavior that is found threatening or disturbing.

entities/htlv-1/description.text: Human T-lymphotropic virus. These are human T-cell lymphotropic viruses. HTLV-I was the first known human oncogenic retrovirus. It causes a malignant hematologic disease called adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATL), and also gives rise to a subacute myelopathy called tropical spastic paraparesis (TSP) or HTLV-I-associated myelopathy (HAM).

entities/htlv-2/description.text: Human T-lymphotropic virus. These are human T-cell lymphotropic viruses. HTLV-2 has not been clearly related to any disease, but it has been associated with several cases of myelopathy.

entities/huntington/description.text: Huntington's disease (HD) is a serious, rare, hereditary and degenerative neurological disease. The course of the disease can follow very different paths, even among siblings and close relatives. The disease produces psychiatric and motor impairment that progresses very slowly over a period of 15 to 20 years. The external feature most associated with the disease is exaggerated movement of the limbs (choreic movements) and the appearance of sudden grimaces. In addition, speaking and remembering become progressively difficult. In the final stages of the disease, the duration of the movements lengthens, holding the limbs in awkward and painful positions for a time that can extend to hours. However, severe psychiatric disorders, which normally precede the muscular ones, are the characteristic features of the disease. It can trigger repeated depressive episodes with negative repercussions on those close to the patient. Cognitive faculties decline, as does memory, and the ability to concentrate worsens. The disease ends up causing dementia in patients. It should also be said that the suffering brought on by the disease itself and its sequelae can lead to suicidal wishes.

entities/ictericia/description.text: Jaundice makes the skin and the whites of the eyes turn yellow. Excess bilirubin causes jaundice. Bilirubin is a yellow chemical substance contained in hemoglobin, the substance that carries oxygen in red blood cells. As red blood cells break down, the body develops new cells to replace them. The broken-down cells are processed in the liver. If the liver cannot handle the blood cells as they break down, bilirubin accumulates in the body and the skin may look yellow.

entities/inapetencia/description.text: Appetite is the desire to ingest food, felt as hunger. Appetite exists in all higher life forms and serves to regulate adequate energy intake to maintain metabolic needs. It is regulated by a close interaction between the digestive system, adipose tissue and the brain. Lack of appetite is a phenomenon that occurs in both children and adults. The Parathyroid-Parathyroid pair makes it possible to regulate appetite.

entities/inconciencia/description.text: The term unconscious is used as an adjective to describe a mental state or disposition of a subject who carries out their behavior inadvertently, that is, without realizing it, and which, in general, does not depend on their will to perform it.

entities/incontinencia-urinaria/descript.text: Urinary incontinence is the loss of bladder control or the inability to hold back the outflow of urine; it involves a significant psychological and social impact. It can condition the patient's lifestyle, although it is common for the patient affected by incontinence not to give it the importance it deserves. The causes are multiple, notably detrusor instability (spastic bladder), overflow incontinence, stress incontinence, fecal impaction in elderly patients, or simply false (functional) incontinence.

entities/infarto-agudo-de-miocardio/desc.text: The term acute myocardial infarction (acute means sudden, myo muscle and cardio heart), frequently abbreviated as AMI or MI and known colloquially as a heart attack, cardiac attack or infarction, reflects the death of cardiac cells caused by the ischemia that results from an imbalance between the demand for and the supply of blood flow through the coronary circulation. The main cause is coronary artery disease with insufficient blood flow, which produces tissue damage in a part of the heart caused by obstruction of one of the coronary arteries, frequently due to rupture of a vulnerable atheromatous plaque. The ischemia, or deficient oxygen supply, resulting from such an obstruction produces angina pectoris, which, if recanalized early, does not cause death of cardiac tissue, whereas if the anoxia (lack of oxygen in a tissue) or hypoxia (decreased oxygen supply) persists, myocardial injury and finally necrosis, that is, infarction, occur. Myocardial infarction is the leading cause of death in men and women worldwide. The propensity to produce arrhythmias, mainly ventricular fibrillation, is the most frequent cause of death in acute myocardial infarction during the first minutes, which is why there is a tendency to place automated external defibrillators in busy public places. The main risk factors predisposing to an infarction are atherosclerosis or other coronary disease, a history of angina pectoris, a previous infarction or heart rhythm disorders, as well as age, mainly in men over 40 years and women over 50 years. Certain modifiable habits, such as smoking, excessive consumption of alcoholic beverages, obesity and high stress levels, also contribute significantly to a higher risk of having an infarction.

entities/infeccion-garganta/description.text: A throat infection is an invasion of the throat by a pathogenic microorganism, its multiplication in the tissues, and the reaction of the throat to its presence and to that of its possible toxins. Infections can be due to bacteria, fungi, viruses, protozoa or prions.

entities/infeccion-por-deficiencia-inmun.text: Immunodeficiency or immune deficiency is a pathological state in which the immune system does not fulfill its protective role, leaving the organism vulnerable to infection. Immunodeficiencies make affected people highly susceptible to infections and cause a higher prevalence of cancer. People with immunodeficiency are normally treated with passive immunity to overcome infections.

entities/infeccion-renal/description.text: Pyelonephritis, kidney infection or upper urinary tract infection is an infection of the kidney involving the renal parenchyma, the renal pelvis and the renal calyces. Normally, the microorganisms that produce it ascend from the bladder to the parenchyma. It is characterized by pain on urination, fever, chills, flank and lumbar pain, nausea and vomiting. A kidney infection requires prompt medical attention. If not treated properly, the kidney infection may cause permanent damage to the kidneys, or the bacteria may spread into the bloodstream and cause a potentially life-threatening infection.

entities/infeccion-uterina/description.text: Uterine infections are generally caused by sexually transmitted diseases, such as chlamydia, gonorrhea or herpes, or by the use of devices inserted in the pelvic area, allergy to spermicides (used for birth control), allergy to the latex of condoms or exposure to certain chemicals. Uterine infections can last months or years, and in certain cases can cause some fertility problems. There are 3 types of uterine infection: cervicitis (inflammation of the cervix), endometriosis (infection of the lining of the uterus) and myometriosis (infection of the musculature of the uterus). Some of the symptoms that can help identify a uterine infection are: abnormal vaginal bleeding, unusual vaginal discharge that does not go away (it may be white, gray or yellow, and may even have a very strong and unpleasant odor), pain during sexual intercourse, irregular menstruation, permanent vaginal pain, pressure or heaviness in the pelvic area or the lower abdomen.

entities/infertilidad/description.text: Infertility is a disease affecting the couple, in which they are unable to conceive a child naturally or to carry a pregnancy to term. Infertility affects approximately 15% of couples. Approximately 33% of cases are due to a female factor, 21% are due to a male factor, 40% are of mixed type and the rest (6%) are due to unexplained causes.

entities/inflamacion-ganglionar/descript.text: Inflammation of the lymph nodes can be due to many causes, from minor infections to serious diseases. The lymph nodes act as filters of tissue fluid (lymph). The lymphatic system runs through the body, like the blood vessels, and serves to defend the immune system against pathogens. Lymphatic cells (lymphocytes) are part of the white blood cells. Lymph nodes are distributed throughout the body: in the neck, in the groin, in the armpits and in the internal organs. Lymph nodes have different shapes and sizes.

entities/inflamacion-persistente/descrip.text: The Adrenal gland - Adrenal gland pair helps reduce any inflammation in the body, whatever its cause. Inflammation is the way many diseases manifest themselves. It is a nonspecific response to aggressions from the environment and is generated by inflammatory agents. The inflammatory response occurs only in vascularized connective tissues (those containing blood vessels) and arises for the defensive purpose of isolating and destroying the harmful agent, as well as repairing the damaged tissue or organ. It is therefore considered a mechanism of innate immunity. In medicine, inflammation is identified by the suffix -itis. The greatest problem arising from inflammation is that the defense may be directed at both harmful and non-harmful agents, thus causing injury to healthy tissues or organs.

entities/influenza/contagion.text: Through virus-laden aerosol droplets (from nasal or bronchial secretions or saliva containing any of them), which are emitted when coughing or sneezing or simply when talking. The droplets are inhaled directly or, more frequently, are transmitted from hand to hand through handshakes or objects such as door handles, and are then introduced into the nasal passages when the hand touches the nose, mouth or eyes. It is also transmissible through blood and through surfaces or objects contaminated with the virus, which are called fomites. Influenza viruses survive longer in dry, cold environments. They can retain their infectivity for one week at human body temperature, for 30 days at 0 °C and for much longer at lower temperatures. It can be easily inactivated by detergents or disinfectants.

entities/influenza/description.text: Flu, grippe or influenza is an infectious disease caused by more than 200 serologically different viral types. The virus most frequently involved is a rhinovirus (30-50%), a type of picornavirus with 99 known serotypes. Other viruses involved include: coronaviruses (10-15%), influenza viruses (5-15%), human parainfluenza viruses, and respiratory syncytial viruses, adenoviruses, enteroviruses and metapneumoviruses. It affects the respiratory tract. Initially it may resemble a cold and is often accompanied by general symptoms such as sore throat, weakness, sneezing, nasal discharge and congestion, watery eyes, muscle aches (myalgia), stomach ache, joint pain (arthralgia) and headache (cephalalgia), with cough (generally dry and without mucus), general malaise, tiredness and some signs such as fever. In some more serious cases it can be complicated by pneumonia, which can be fatal, especially in young children and above all in the elderly. Although it can be confused with the common cold (catarrh), flu is a more serious disease and is caused by a different type of virus. It is one of the most common diseases and generally lasts between 3 and 10 days. Although the common cold has no cure, the symptoms generally resolve spontaneously in 7 to 10 days. To treat flu or influenza, all of the following pairs must be placed: 1) Gallbladder - Right / Left Kidney 2) Kidney - Kidney 3) Pancreas: Pancreatic ligament - Spleen 4) Bladder - Pituitary gland 5) Cranial vault - Cranial vault 6) Trachea - Trachea 7) Eyelid - Eyelid

entities/inmunodeficiencia/description.text: Immunodeficiency is a pathological state in which the immune system does not fulfill its protective role, leaving the body vulnerable to infection. Immunodeficiencies make affected people highly susceptible to infections. The immune or immunological system, also known simply as the immune system, is the set of biological structures and processes within an organism that protects it against disease by identifying and attacking pathogenic agents. It detects a wide variety of agents, from viruses to intestinal parasites, and needs to distinguish them from the organism's own healthy cells and tissues in order to function correctly. The immune system is composed mainly of leukocytes (lymphocytes, other leukocytes, antibodies, T cells, cytokines, macrophages and neutrophils, among other components that help it function). Detection is complicated, since pathogens can evolve rapidly, producing adaptations that evade the immune system and allow the pathogens to successfully infect their hosts.

entities/inseguridad/description.text: Emotional insecurity is a feeling of unease, nervousness or fearfulness associated with a multitude of contexts, which can be triggered by the perception that one is vulnerable, or a feeling of vulnerability and instability that threatens one's self-image or ego. A person who is insecure has no confidence in their own worth and abilities, lacks confidence in themselves or others, may think that others will let them down and fear letting others down themselves, or distrusts that current positive circumstances are anything more than temporary. This is a common trait that differs between people only in the degree of the symptom.

entities/insomnio/description.text: Insomnia is a disease defined as difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep, and it may manifest as difficulty falling asleep (initial insomnia), frequent waking during the night, or waking very early in the morning, earlier than planned (terminal insomnia). According to the duration of the problem, it can also be divided into acute insomnia if it lasts less than 4 weeks, subacute when it lasts between 4 weeks and 6 months, or chronic if it lasts more than 6 months. The most frequent complaint associated with insomnia is daytime sleepiness, poor concentration and inability to feel active during the day. Insomnia can be due to many causes, including primary insomnia, stress, psychiatric disorders such as anxiety or depression, use of contraceptives and others.

entities/insuficiencia-cardiaca/descript.text: Heart failure is spoken of when the function of the heart is altered or it does not pump enough blood to supply the organs, muscles and tissues of the body. When the heart begins to fail, the body detects it immediately and sets compensatory mechanisms in motion, so many patients do not notice the abnormal symptoms manifested by the heart. These mechanisms are effective only for a certain time, so a point is reached at which the body cannot remedy the failure of the heart's pumping. The most common cause of heart failure is coronary disease, such as angina pectoris and, especially, myocardial infarction. Another common cause is arterial hypertension, which must be detected and controlled in time to prevent and avoid the development of HF. Blood pressure should be below 140/90. Excessive alcohol consumption can also lead to HF, since it damages the heart muscle and gives rise to so-called dilated cardiomyopathy, a progressive dilation of the heart due to thinning and weakening of its walls. The first symptom of heart failure appears when the patient is subjected to any situation in which greater pumping by the heart and a greater amount of blood to the body are needed. The patient will feel breathlessness and shortness of breath while exercising or carrying out activities that were previously well tolerated. Some other symptoms are the following: Dyspnea: a feeling of shortness of breath. At first it appears with physical exertion, walking quickly or climbing stairs, but little by little the episodes become more intense and appear when performing any task, such as dressing or washing, and even at rest. Orthopnea: difficulty breathing when lying down, so that the patient is forced to sleep with two or three pillows or in a somewhat upright position. Fatigue: muscular tiredness is due to insufficient pumping of blood. Edema: swelling of the legs caused by water and salt retention. In severe cases the edema can be very pronounced. Oliguria: means eliminating a smaller amount of urine than usual (less than 400 milligrams a day). Dyspnea and edema are usually preceded by oliguria. In HF the kidneys abnormally retain water and salt, which will later accumulate in the lungs and tissues, producing dyspnea and edema. It is often accompanied by nocturia, which is increased diuresis at night, when the recumbent position is adopted and venous return increases. Other symptoms of HF are gastric fullness, intestinal discomfort, abdominal swelling, pain in the right side of the abdomen, congestion of the neck veins, palpitations, dizziness, syncope, lack of appetite or anorexia. When the heart does not pump well, the blood that reaches the heart to be pumped stagnates in the veins leading to the heart, and these become congested.

entities/insuficiencia-hepatica/descript.text: Liver insufficiency or liver failure is the inability of the liver to carry out its synthetic and metabolic function as part of normal physiology. Two forms are recognized: acute liver failure and chronic liver failure. During acute liver failure, hepatic encephalopathy develops (confusion, stupor and coma), and there is a decrease in the production of proteins (such as albumin and clotting proteins) within the four weeks following the appearance of the first symptoms (such as jaundice) of a liver problem. Liver failure is said to be "hyperacute" if this interval is 7 days or less, while it is "subacute" liver failure if the interval is 5 to 12 weeks. Chronic liver failure generally occurs in the context of liver cirrhosis, which in turn can be the consequence of many possible causes, such as excessive intake of alcoholic beverages, hepatitis B or C, autoimmune, hereditary and metabolic causes such as hemochromatosis (excessive accumulation of iron) or Wilson's disease (excessive accumulation of copper), or nonalcoholic steatohepatitis.

entities/insuficiencia-pancreatica/descr.text: Pancreatic insufficiency (PI) is a serious disorder that occurs when the pancreas does not produce digestive enzymes or produces them in insufficient quantity, which means the body cannot digest food as well, causing inadequate absorption of nutrients from food (malabsorption). PI is an important consequence of a wide range of serious diseases that alter normal pancreatic function, some of which are: Acute pancreatitis (AP): AP can cause a release of pancreatic digestive enzymes at the wrong time, leading to PI. Chronic pancreatitis (CP): CP can damage the cells that produce pancreatic digestive enzymes and obstruct the pancreatic duct through calcifications, preventing the release of the enzymes, causing a spillage of these enzymes and leading to PI. Pancreatic cancer: patients with pancreatic cancer may have reduced availability of pancreatic enzymes due to destruction of enzyme production, causing malabsorption associated with PI. Pancreatic surgery: surgical alteration of pancreatic tissue can cause PI. Gastric surgery: gastric (stomach) surgery can alter the production, activation and deactivation of pancreatic enzymes, which can cause PI. Cystic fibrosis: cystic fibrosis can alter the enzyme-producing cells and cause blockage of the channels that transport the digestive enzymes to the pancreas, in both cases causing PI. Diabetes: diabetes can decrease insulin levels; low insulin concentrations are one of the ways in which diabetes can lead to PI.

entities/insuficiencia-pulmonar/descript.text: Pulmonary or respiratory deficiency occurs when not enough oxygen flows from the lungs to the heart. Respiratory failure also occurs when the lungs cannot remove carbon dioxide (a waste gas) from the blood. Having too much carbon dioxide in the blood can end up harming the organs. Diseases and conditions that affect breathing can cause respiratory failure. Some examples of lung diseases are: COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease), pneumonia, pulmonary embolism and cystic fibrosis. Some examples of conditions include those that affect control of the nerves and muscles, such as spinal cord trauma, muscular dystrophy and stroke. Damage to the tissues and ribs around the lungs has a similar effect.

entities/insuficiencia-renal/description.text: Kidney failure is the loss of the kidneys' ability to eliminate waste and help with the balance of fluids and electrolytes in the body. Some causes are the following: acute tubular necrosis, autoimmune kidney disease, a blood clot from cholesterol (cholesterol embolus), decreased blood flow due to very low blood pressure (caused by burns, dehydration, hemorrhage, injury, septic shock, surgery), disorders that cause clotting within the blood vessels of the kidney, urinary tract obstruction and some complications during pregnancy. Some symptoms of kidney failure are the following: bloody stools, bad breath and a metallic taste in the mouth, a tendency to bruise, changes in mental status or mood, loss of appetite, decreased sensation, especially in the hands or feet, fatigue, flank pain (between the ribs and the hips), hand tremor, arterial hypertension, nausea or vomiting that may last for days, nosebleeds, persistent hiccups, prolonged bleeding, epileptic seizures, lethargic and slow movements, swelling due to fluid retention in the body, swelling, usually in the ankles, feet and legs, and changes in urination.

entities/integridad-anatomica/descriptio.text: This pair occurs when there is an alteration of anatomical integrity, when there is dissatisfaction over losses, over the lack of a limb, over miscarriages or unwanted pregnancies. It corrects sophrological (body-mind balance) and psychological problems. The pair occurs when there is self-criticism (common in women), and also in people with emotional traumas from lacking organs or limbs. The growth gland is affected by all of the above.

entities/integridad-moral/description.text: Moral integrity. Shame; they steal or lie. Unethical people. Ethics is the branch of philosophy that studies behaviors insofar as they can be considered good or bad. Its focus is human actions and those aspects of them that relate to the good, virtue, duty, happiness and a fulfilled life.

entities/intolerancia-a-la-lactosa/descr.text: Lactose intolerance occurs when the small intestine is unable to digest lactose, a type of sugar found in milk and other dairy products. The reason for this problem is that the intestine does not produce enough of the enzyme lactase. Enzymes help the body absorb food. Not having enough lactase is called lactase deficiency. A baby's body produces lactase in order to digest milk, including breast milk. Premature babies sometimes have lactose intolerance. Children born at term generally show no signs of this intolerance until they are at least three years old. Lactose intolerance is hardly dangerous and is very common in adults. Symptoms frequently appear 30 minutes to two hours after eating or drinking dairy products, and are often relieved by not eating or drinking these products. Symptoms include: abdominal distension, abdominal cramps, diarrhea, gas (flatulence), nausea.

entities/intolerancia-alimentaria/descri.text: Food intolerance is caused by the inability to metabolize certain substances present in foods, due to various enzyme deficiencies. What is the difference between food allergy and food intolerance? Adverse reactions to foods are frequently confused with food allergies. In many cases, such reactions are due to some other factor - perhaps food poisoning, a psychological aversion to a food, or an intolerance to an ingredient in a food. Food allergy is a specific form of intolerance to a food or one of its components that activates the immune system. An allergen (the causative food protein, which in most people produces no adverse reactions) triggers a series of chain reactions in the immune system, including the production of antibodies. These antibodies cause the release of chemicals, such as histamine, which produce various symptoms such as itching, runny nose, cough or respiratory disorders. Allergies to foods or their components are frequently inherited and are usually identified in the first years of life. Food intolerance affects metabolism, but not the body's immune system.

entities/intoxicacion-alimentaria/descri.text: Food poisoning is the clinical manifestation of toxicity (intoxication) resulting from exposure to toxic substances carried by foods, both solid and liquid. Poisoning occurs after ingesting foods that are contaminated with organic or inorganic substances harmful to the body, such as: poisons, toxins, pathogenic biological agents, heavy metals, etc. Food poisoning can affect one person or a group of people who have eaten the same contaminated food. It occurs most commonly after eating food at outdoor meals, large social gatherings or restaurants. Most cases of food poisoning are actually foodborne toxic infections, caused by pathogenic bacteria, viruses, prions or parasites, and/or their metabolic products. This contamination usually arises from improper handling, preparation or storage of food. The monitoring and control of food to ensure that it will not cause food poisoning is called bromatology (food science).

entities/intoxicacion-cronica/descriptio.text: Chronic poisoning is a form of poisoning in which cumulative damage to various organs and systems is produced by various poisons. It may take months or years to present as a clinically recognizable entity. Toxicants that act in this way are called "cumulative toxicants"; the organic accumulation of the toxicant generally goes unnoticed until, once a damage threshold is exceeded, it manifests as a clinically recognizable entity.

entities/intoxicacion-etilica/descriptio.text: The effects of alcohol on the body are numerous and diverse. Alcohol, specifically ethanol, is a potent psychoactive drug with a large number of tertiary effects that can seriously affect our body. The amount and circumstances of consumption play an important role in determining the duration of intoxication. For example, when alcohol is consumed after a large meal, visible signs of intoxication are less likely to occur than on an empty stomach. Hydration also plays an important role, especially in determining the duration of hangovers. Alcohol has a biphasic effect on the body, that is, its effects change over time. Initially, it produces feelings of relaxation and cheerfulness, but further consumption can lead to blurred vision and coordination problems. Cell membranes are highly permeable to alcohol, so once alcohol is in the bloodstream, it can spread into almost all the tissues of the body. After excessive consumption, unconsciousness may occur, and extreme levels of consumption can lead to alcohol poisoning and death (a blood concentration of 0.55% – approx. 5 grams of alcohol per liter of blood – could kill half of those affected through cardiorespiratory arrest). Death can also be caused by asphyxia, if vomit – a frequent result of excessive intake – obstructs the trachea and the individual is too drunk to respond. An appropriate first-aid response to an unconscious, drunk person is to place them in the recovery position. When alcohol reaches the blood (between 30 and 90 minutes after being ingested), there is a decrease in the sugars present in the bloodstream, which causes a feeling of weakness and physical exhaustion. This is because alcohol accelerates the transformation of glycogen (a substance responsible for storing sugar in the liver) into glucose, and the glucose is eliminated more rapidly. Another action of alcohol is that it inhibits vasopressin, a hormone synthesized by the hypothalamus and then released by the neurohypophysis. This hormone is responsible for maintaining the body's fluid balance by instructing the kidney to reabsorb water from the urine. If vasopressin function fails, the kidney begins to eliminate more water than is ingested, which causes the body to seek water from other organs. This causes the meninges (membranes covering the brain) to lose water, and therefore headache appears. Alcohol decreases the body's levels of vitamin B1.

entities/intoxicacion-por-arsenico/descr.text: Ingestion of high concentrations of arsenic can cause death. Arsenic has been linked to an increased risk of cancer of the lung, skin, bladder, liver, kidney and prostate. Symptoms of arsenic exposure include: thickening of the skin, skin discoloration, small "bumps" or "warts" on the palms of the hands, the soles of the feet and the torso, stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, decreased production of red and white blood cells, abnormal heart rhythm, damage to blood vessels, numbness of the hands and feet, partial paralysis, blindness, garlic-smelling breath, seizures.

entities/intoxicacion-por-bismuto/descri.text: Bismuth poisoning usually occurs from the continuous consumption of drugs containing this substance; the most common symptoms are: depression, diarrhea, headache, rheumatic pains, stomatitis, fever, gingivitis, eye and respiratory irritation, nausea, bad breath, loss of appetite and weight, sleep disorders and a metallic taste.

entities/intoxicacion-por-medicamentos-o.text: Iatrogenesis is harm to health caused or provoked by a medical act. It can be produced by a drug or by a medical or surgical procedure performed by any professional associated with the health sciences, whether physician, therapist, psychologist, pharmacist, nurse, dentist, etc. It can also be caused by a physician who practices alternative therapies. It can occur due to an error or incorrect choice of treatment, or through negligence, inexperience, recklessness or abandonment of the patient. However, it can also result from medical procedures performed within a correct indication, with skill, prudence and diligence. Drug poisoning is one of the leading causes of death in the population. According to an article published in the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) in the year 2000, physicians are the third leading cause of death in the United States, surpassed only by heart disease and cancer. In the United States alone, 225,000 people died from iatrogenic causes. Of these, 5% were due to unnecessary surgery, 3% to medication errors in hospitals, 9% to other errors in hospitals, 36% to hospital-acquired infections and 47% to the negative side effects of prescribed medications. A pancreatic belt should be applied, which consists of placing 4 magnets around the pancreas (-,+,-,+) at the following points: head, body, tail and tip. The pancreatic belt releases the toxic elements of ingested medications that have accumulated in the pancreas.

entities/intoxicacion-por-metales-pesado.text: Pancreatic poisoning from excess heavy metals. Manganese, chromium, arsenic, lead, mercury, copper and others. Generally present in shellfish and seafood. Poisoning can also occur from an excess of medications or proteins.

Place a pancreatic belt, which consists of placing 4 magnets around the pancreas (-,+,-,+) at the following points: head, body, tail and tip. With the pancreatic belt, the heavy metals accumulated in the pancreas are released. There are different types of metals, and the symptoms and effects on the body vary depending on each of them. This biomagnetic pair serves to detoxify the body of any of the following metals. Manganese (Mn): manganese is a transition metal indispensable in steel production; it is also a component of welding materials and their fumes. It is present in paints and insecticides, as a gasoline antiknock agent, and it is also used as an animal nutrient. Its main route of entry is respiratory, and its half-life is 39 days. High exposures to manganese alter the speed of visual response and fine movement of the hand and forearm and give rise to fine tremor. Above certain levels it has toxic effects on the respiratory system, through deposition and interference with local immunity, and on the central nervous system, through alteration of catecholamine and melatonin metabolism. The neurological clinical picture of manganese poisoning has been classified into three stages according to the intensity of the manifestations, which range from anorexia, fatigue and headache; to intention tremor, muscle pain, vertigo and ataxia; up to severe motor alterations that hinder gait or make it rigid (like a rooster's steps) and impair speech articulation and facial expression (mask-like face). It shows some similarities with Parkinson's disease, but both the organic lesions and their pathophysiology are different. Chromium (Cr): chromium is a metal that has several valences: 0, +2, +4, +5, +6 . But the chromium that matters in industrial hygiene corresponds to valence +3, which is carcinogenic, with no dermal absorption but with absorption through the gastrointestinal route. Meanwhile, chromium +6, which is absorbed through the skin and readily enters cells, where it is reduced to +3, is also dangerous. Chromium +3 causes lung cancer, perforation of the nasal septum, bronchitis, asthma and contact dermatitis. The most exposed workers are those who work in the productive sectors of steel, chrome plating, chromium and ferrochromium smelting, and paints that use it as a pigment. Arsenic (As): Arsenic acts by inhibiting the immune system and causes chromosomal aberrations in lymphocytes. Chronic exposure is the most typical. A topical reaction of the skin and mucous membranes. Very characteristic is the appearance of white spots on the skin (punctate leukomelanoderma) and the formation of punctate calluses resembling corns on the palms and soles. In addition, goose bumps, bronzed patches, striae, and hyperkeratosis localized especially on the scrotum, armpits, groin and face. There is damage to the central nervous system, with a sensation of numbness, burning, tingling, pruritus, spasms, tremor and paralysis of the extremities resembling tetraplegia. In the liver it can cause hepatic cirrhosis, and it can also affect the kidney. There is a clear association of arsenic levels with lung, pleural and kidney cancer. In situations of acute exposure, an intestinal picture occurs with gastroenteritis, esophagitis, vomiting, diarrhea, nausea and abdominal pain, which may progress to shock. Workers are usually monitored by measuring arsenic in the urine. The maximum permitted concentration is 200 milligrams / liter. Unlike other metals, the toxic fraction here is the inorganic one, since the organic fractions are excreted very rapidly. Lead (Pb): Hematological and cardiovascular effects and evidence of impaired renal function have been detected in subjects with elevated plasma lead levels. Likewise, damage to the respiratory system is reflected in the increase in pneumonias associated with elevated levels of lead in the air. Inhibition of phagocytes and various effects on pulmonary immunity have been detected. At low-dose levels, there is evidence of neurological and neurobehavioral damage, which could be expressed as learning disorders and attention deficit. There are also associations in workers exposed to lead with higher mortality from tumors in general. Other effects have to do with the reproductive system; for example, the sustained decline in sperm counts in Europe in recent decades is associated with lead toxicity. Mercury (Hg): Mercury is toxic to the central nervous system and the kidney. The symptoms of chronic poisoning are basically three: erethism, tremor and stomatitis. Irritability, hyperactivity, emotional lability, shyness and memory loss make up mercurial erethism, or “Mad Hatter” disease. This latter name comes from the hatters who were poisoned during the hat-drying process, when the felt gave off mercury vapors from the mercury residues left after treating the pelts of rodents (rabbits, hares, muskrats, coypus, beavers) with mercury nitrate. Nowadays, hydrogen peroxide and barium are used for these tasks. Other symptoms are gastrointestinal disturbances such as gastritis, gastroduodenitis, nausea, abdominal pain, vomiting and diarrhea. There is also headache, dermatitis, visual disturbances and grayish-brown spots on the lens, gingivitis (which increases with poor hygiene), bleeding and bluish lines on the gums.

entities/intoxicacion-por-metaloides/con.text: Metalloid poisoning. Contaminated boxed cereals. The Teflon of kitchen frying pans is composed of tungsten and molybdenum; when released, they poison the person. Cyanide poisoning. Lead poisoning.

entities/intoxicacion-por-metaloides/des.text: Poisoning occurs through exposure to, ingestion, injection or inhalation of a toxic substance, provided that it is of chemical composition, since if the compound is natural it would be called excessive intake, and this applies to any substance, whether natural, chemical, processed or created. Accidental or voluntary poisonings due to the consumption of medications are the most frequent. Other toxic agents are: industrial, household and gardening products, drugs, carbon monoxide and alcohol in excessive use. The severity of the poisoning depends on the toxicity of the product, the route of introduction, the dose ingested and the age of the victim. Together with metals and nonmetals, semimetals (also known as metalloids) make up one of the three categories of chemical elements in a classification according to bonding and ionization properties. They are characterized by behavior intermediate between that of metals and nonmetals.

entities/intoxicacion-por-pesticidas/des.text: A plaguicide, or pesticide, is any substance intended to prevent, destroy, attract, repel or combat any pest, including unwanted species of plants or animals, during the production, storage, transport, distribution and processing of food, agricultural products or animal feed. The term includes substances intended for use as plant growth regulators, defoliants, desiccants, fruit-thinning agents or germination inhibitors, and substances applied to crops before or after harvest to protect the product against deterioration during storage and transport. The definition of pest includes insects, weeds, birds, mammals, mollusks, fish, nematodes or microbes that compete with humans for food, destroy property, spread diseases or are vectors of them, or cause nuisance. Pesticides are not necessarily poisons, but they can be toxic to humans or other animals. However, according to the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants, 9 of the 12 most dangerous and persistent organic compounds are pesticides. The term pesticide is more widespread than the exact generic name: biocide (literally: killer of life). During the 1980s, the massive application of pesticides was generally considered a revolution in agriculture. They were relatively inexpensive and highly effective. Their application became a common practice as a preventive measure even without any visible attack. Since then, experience has shown that this method not only harms the environment but is also ineffective in the long run. Where pesticides have been used, pest species have become resistant and difficult or impossible to control. In some cases resistance has developed in the main disease vectors (e.g. malaria mosquitoes), or new agricultural pests have emerged.

entities/intoxicacion-por-quimioterapia/.text: Detoxification from chemotherapy one year after it was administered. Chemotherapy is a therapeutic technique that consists of administering chemical substances to treat diseases. It is currently one of the most widely used therapeutic methods in the treatment of cancer, using a wide variety of antineoplastic drugs for this purpose. The development of anticancer drugs, such as those used in chemotherapy, has now become a multibillion-dollar industry. Chemotherapy treatment can cause deterioration in cancer patients, since the drugs also destroy normal cells, especially those that divide most rapidly. These effects, although usually transient, can become chronic, which can weaken the patient extremely, especially if it is administered for long and continuous periods of time. In some cases, when the side effects are very intense, toxicity occurs, which can lead to temporary discontinuation of antineoplastic treatment. The side effects depend on the chemotherapeutic agent, and the most important are: alopecia (hair loss), nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, anemia (due to destruction of the bone marrow, which decreases the number of red blood cells), immunosuppression (decreased effectiveness of the immune system), hemorrhages (due to the lack of platelets from destruction of the bone marrow), cardiotoxicity (there is an increased risk of cardiovascular disease), hepatotoxicity (affects the liver and its functions), nephrotoxicity (affects the kidneys and their functions), tumor lysis syndrome (a metabolic imbalance characterized by the rapid release of intracellular potassium, phosphorus and nucleic acid into the blood after the death of malignant cells), decreased blood coagulation factors, sterility (destruction of the cells that produce sex hormones and gametes), asthenia (a generalized feeling of tiredness, fatigue, and physical and mental weakness), cognitive disorders (mental disorders that affect cognitive functions, mainly memory, perception and problem-solving).

entities/intoxicacion/contagion.text: Bismuth poisoning (e.g., Pepto-Bismol). Poisoning from ingesting food (usually vegetables) with toxins derived from insecticides and pesticides, generally bismuth-based.

entities/intoxicacion/description.text: Poisoning is produced by exposure to, or ingestion, injection or inhalation of, a toxic substance, provided it is of chemical composition, since if the compound is natural it would be called excessive intake, and this applies to any substance, whether natural, chemical, processed or created. Accidental or voluntary poisonings due to the consumption of medications are the most frequent. Other toxic agents are: industrial, household and gardening products, drugs, carbon monoxide and alcohol in excessive use. The severity of poisoning depends on the toxicity of the product, the route of introduction, the dose ingested and the age of the victim. On the other hand, food poisoning occurs when one ingests food or water containing bacteria, parasites, viruses or toxins produced by these microorganisms. Most cases of food poisoning arise from common bacteria such as Staphylococcus or Escherichia coli. It is essential to detect signs of vital risk: check the level of consciousness, breathing and also the pulse. The quadriceps femoris is the most powerful and voluminous muscle in the entire human body. It is the one that supports our weight and allows us to walk, stroll, sit and run. It is called the quadriceps because it has four muscle heads.

entities/ira/description.text: Anger, rage or annoyance is an emotion expressed through resentment, fury or irritability. The physical effects of anger include increased heart rate, blood pressure and levels of adrenaline and noradrenaline. Some see anger as part of the brain's fight-or-flight response to a perceived threat or harm. Anger becomes the predominant feeling behaviorally, cognitively and physiologically when a person makes the conscious decision to take action to immediately stop the threatening behavior of another external force. Anger can have many physical and mental consequences.

entities/isaac/description.text: Pair related to migraine. The pair bears the name of Dr. Goiz. In the lung, 4 drainages take place that must be kept in kinetic equilibrium to allow proper pulmonary ventilation: air, blood, lymph and humors. In the lung, as in no other organ, phenomena of intrathoracic rheologism take place that obey the laws of elementary physics, such as the one that states: "in a closed space through which fluids circulate, the increase of one conditions the decrease of the others".

entities/juan-ramon/description.text: Pair related to diarrhea. In honor of Juan Ramón de la Fuente, who, as Secretary of Health of the Mexican government, rejected Dr. Goiz's healing method and threatened him if he continued his research.

entities/kawasaki/description.text: Kawasaki disease is a multisystem, idiopathic disease characterized by vasculitis affecting small and medium-caliber vessels, especially the coronary arteries, classically causing aneurysms in them; in addition, it is usually associated with a mucocutaneous syndrome. The acute disease presents fever, erythema, conjunctival and oral erosion, edema of the limbs, erythema of the soles and hands, skin rashes and hyperplasia of the cervical lymph nodes, and occasionally inflammation of the heart and the major joints.

entities/klebsiella-pneumoniae/descripti.text: Klebsiella pneumoniae is the most clinically relevant species within the bacterial genus Klebsiella, composed of Gram-negative bacteria of the family Enterobacteriaceae, which play an important role as a cause of opportunistic infectious diseases. It is the causative agent of urinary tract infections, pneumonias, bronchitis, sepsis (potentially fatal physiological, pathological and biochemical abnormalities associated with an infection), soft tissue infections and surgical wound infections. Patients admitted to intensive care units, neonates, and patients with COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease), diabetes mellitus or alcoholism are especially susceptible.

entities/lactancia/description.text: Improves lactation in women. Breastfeeding is feeding with milk from the mother's breast; it is an unequaled way of providing the ideal food for the proper growth and development of children. Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended during the newborn's first six months. After six months, it is recommended to continue breastfeeding and to offer the baby other foods appropriate for its age, up to a minimum of two years. It is not known what the "normal" duration of breastfeeding is in the human species. The references regarding the terms and characteristics of breastfeeding are understood from the cultural context of the nursing mothers, such that breastfeeding periods can vary as widely as the variety of cultures existing in the world. Worldwide we can cite cases where it is considered an act only for babies a few weeks or months old, and there are also cases in which breastfeeding has been maintained for several years.

entities/laringitis/description.text: Laryngitis is characterized by swelling and irritation (inflammation) of the larynx, generally associated with hoarseness or loss of voice. The larynx is located in the upper part of the airway leading to the lungs (trachea). The larynx contains the vocal cords and, when these become inflamed or infected, they swell. This can cause hoarseness. Sometimes the airways can become blocked. The most common form of laryngitis is an infection caused by a virus, such as those of the common cold or flu. It can also be brought on by: allergies, bacterial infection, bronchitis, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), injury, irritants and chemicals, pneumonia. Laryngitis is considered acute if it lasts a couple of days. It is considered chronic if it lasts more than two weeks.

entities/legionella/contagion.text: Air-conditioning systems are a relevant source of Legionella; their filters must be changed and cleaned regularly. They live in stagnant water over a wide temperature range, preferably above 35 degrees Celsius. Their growth is favored by the presence of organic matter. Water systems of large buildings, hotels and hospitals, humidifiers, misting machines, spas and thermal water fountains.

entities/legionella/description.text: Legionella is the common name of the genus Legionella, which groups rod-shaped Gram-negative bacteria. Their growth is favored by the presence of organic matter. They have aerobic respiration and a flagellum for movement. Within this genus there are 48 species and a total of about 78 serotypes. In humans it produces obstruction of the upper airways and affects the bronchi and lungs. Some of the symptoms of Legionella are the following: high fever, gastrointestinal disturbances (abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea), nonproductive cough, sometimes with sputum, headache, muscle pain, chest pain, breathing difficulty (especially as the disease progresses), lethargy, lack of coordination, fatigue and general malaise.

entities/leishmania/description.text: Leishmania is a genus of protists responsible for the disease known as leishmaniasis, which occurs in 3 forms: 1) Cutaneous: skin ulcers, 2) Mucocutaneous: ulcers on the skin, mouth and nose, 3) Visceral leishmaniasis: skin ulcers, fever, low red blood cells, inflammation of the spleen and liver.

entities/leishmaniasis/description.text: Cutaneous leishmaniasis affects the skin and mucous membranes. Skin sores usually begin at the site of the sand fly bite. In a few people, sores can develop on the mucous membranes. The symptoms of cutaneous leishmaniasis depend on where the lesions are located and may include: difficulty breathing, skin sores that can turn into a skin ulcer that heals very slowly, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea and nosebleed, difficulty swallowing, ulcers and wearing away (erosion) in the mouth, tongue, gums, lips, nose and nasal septum. Systemic or visceral leishmaniasis affects the entire body and is a form that occurs 2 to 8 months after the person is bitten by the sand fly. Most people do not remember having had a skin sore. This form can lead to fatal complications. The parasites damage the immune system by decreasing the number of disease-fighting cells. In children, visceral and systemic infection generally begins suddenly with: cough, diarrhea, fever, vomiting. Adults usually present a fever lasting from 2 weeks to 2 months, accompanied by symptoms such as fatigue, weakness and loss of appetite. The weakness increases as the disease worsens. other symptoms of visceral and systemic leishmaniasis may be: abdominal discomfort, fever that lasts weeks and may come and go in cycles, cold sweats, scaly, grayish, dark and pale skin, thinning hair, weight loss.

entities/lepra/contagion.text: Caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium leprae. Transmitted by rats. Transmission through contact or living with an infected person - coughing, sneezing. The main source of leprosy contamination is the breast milk of a contaminated mother.

entities/lepra/description.text: Leprosy is a disease that causes skin ulcers, neurological damage and muscle weakness that worsens over time. Leprosy is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium leprae. It is not very contagious and has a long incubation period (time before symptoms appear), which makes it difficult to know where and when someone contracted the disease. Children are more likely than adults to contract it. Leprosy has two common forms: tuberculoid and lepromatous. Both forms cause ulcers on the skin, but the lepromatous form is the more severe and produces large lumps and swellings (nodules). Some of its symptoms are the following: skin lesions that are lighter than the normal skin color, lesions with decreased sensitivity to touch, heat or pain, lesions that do not heal after a few weeks or months, muscle weakness, numbness or absence of sensation in the hands, arms, feet and legs.

entities/leptospira/description.text: Leptospira is a genus of bacteria of the order Spirochaetales, which includes a small number of pathogenic and saprophytic species. It produces flatulence. It produces Weil's disease, whose main symptoms in most cases are fever, cephalalgia, muscle, joint and bone pain, jaundice, renal failure, hemorrhages and involvement of the meninges. It is similar to scabies; it produces problems in the digestive tract, airways and mucous membranes.

entities/lesion-en-medula-espinal/descri.text: Spinal cord injury, or myelopathy, is an alteration of the spinal cord that can cause a loss of sensation and/or mobility. The two main causes of spinal cord injury are trauma and disease. Trauma: car accidents, falls, gunshots, ruptured intervertebral disc. Diseases: poliomyelitis, spina bifida, primary or metastatic tumors, Friedreich's ataxia, hypertrophic osteitis of the spine. It is important to point out that the spinal cord does not have to be completely severed for a loss of function to occur. In fact, most spinal cords remain intact after a spinal cord injury. A spinal cord injury is not always related to a back or neck injury such as ruptured discs, spinal stenosis, etc. It is possible to injure the neck or back without the spinal cord suffering any damage.

entities/leucemia/description.text: True leukemia. Spinal cord disorders. Destroys the marrow that produces white blood cells. Confused with brucellosis. Lung problems. Anemias. Leukemia (meaning “white blood”) is a group of malignant diseases of the bone marrow (hematologic cancer) that causes an uncontrolled increase of leukocytes (white blood cells) in it. The body uses leukocytes to fight infections and other foreign substances. Damage occurs in the bone marrow in the form of displacement of the normal bone marrow cells by a greater number of immature white blood cells. All of this results in a lack of platelets in the blood, which are essential in the blood-clotting process, so people with leukemia can easily develop bruises and excessive bleeding or pinpoint hemorrhages (petechiae). White blood cells, involved in the body's defense, may be deficient or dysfunctional. This can leave the patient's immune system unable to fight a simple infection. Because leukemia prevents the immune system from functioning normally, some patients experience frequent infections, ranging from infected tonsils, mouth sores, diarrhea and pneumonia to opportunistic infections. Finally, the deficiency of red blood cells produces anemia, which can cause dyspnea (difficulty breathing) and pallor.

entities/libido/description.text: Libido means sexual desire, sexual behavior, and is also identified as psychic, physiological and emotional energy, energy associated with sexual behavior. Sigmund Freud saw the libido as linked not only with sexual desire but with all constructive human activities.

entities/linfedema/description.text: Lymphedema refers to the type of edema produced by an obstruction in the body's lymphatic channels. This situation arises from the accumulation of lymph (composed of a clear fluid rich in proteins and fibroblasts) in the interstitial spaces (the area between the different cells of a tissue), within the subcutaneous cellular tissue. It is generally due to a failure or insufficiency of the lymphatic system, and results in an increase in the volume of the limbs, completely or partially, and the disappearance of the contours normally visible beneath the skin.

entities/linfogranuloma-venereo/descript.text: Lymphogranuloma venereum (or venereal granuloma) is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the invasive serovars L1, L2 or L3 of the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis; the first symptoms appear 3 to 12 days after infection, and a painless blister appears that turns into an ulcer; it heals so quickly that it may go unnoticed. Then the lymph nodes of the groin enlarge and become tender to the touch. The disease is characterized by painless genital ulcerations that can be confused with syphilis. In addition, they progress to destroy internal and external tissues, with pus and blood. Fistulas, abscesses and strictures are common. The destructive nature of lymphogranuloma also increases the risk of superinfection by other pathogenic microorganisms.

entities/linfoma-de-burkitt/description.text: Burkitt's lymphoma or Burkitt cell leukemia is a rare form of cancer of the lymphatic system – associated mainly with B lymphocytes – that predominantly affects young people, described most frequently in central Africa, although it has also been described in other areas of the world. Burkitt's lymphoma results from a characteristic chromosomal translocation affecting the Myc gene. A chromosomal translocation means that the chromosome has broken, allowing it to join other chromosomal parts. In Burkitt's lymphoma it affects chromosome 8 (Myc gene locus), which changes the expression pattern of the Myc gene, altering its natural function of controlling cell growth and proliferation. The most frequent variant produces a translocation from chromosome 8 to 14, while other variants include translocations to other chromosomes.

entities/listeria/description.text: Listeria is a bacterium that causes a disease called listeriosis. This disease mainly affects pregnant women, newborns, adults with a depressed immune system and elderly people. Its two main manifestations are sepsis and meningitis. Meningitis is often complicated by encephalitis. The disease has low morbidity (people infected) but very high mortality (30%). At onset, mild intestinal problems and flu-like symptoms appear, but later the following manifest: 1) In pregnant women: miscarriage, even at term, or birth of infants with septicemia. 2) In children, the elderly and the immunosuppressed: a serious tendency to septicemia (blood infection), meningitis (infection of the brain or cerebrospinal fluid), endocarditis (infection of the heart) and pneumonia (lung infection). 3) In healthy adults: meningitis, meningoencephalitis and respiratory disorders. It can also present in milder forms such as: abscesses, conjunctivitis, gastroenteritis or skin lesions.

entities/logorrea/description.text: Logorrhea is a communication disorder, sometimes classified as a mental illness, characterized by incoherent talkativeness. "Verbosity" or "verbal incontinence" are used as synonyms. It presents as a symptom of some psychiatric disorders, as alterations of the language faculties, as with a brain injury, or due to a progressive disease. Logorrhea is characterized by an abundance of words in speech. It refers not only to talking a lot; it becomes impertinent and annoying, or describes someone who commits an indiscretion. An abundance of vain and idle words (useless, unnecessary, unfounded). Talking a lot and without substance. Talking indiscreetly.

entities/loja/description.text: Pair related to energy unblocking. This pair was named in honor of the city of Loja, Ecuador, where his thesis on the tumor phenomenon was accepted for the first time. The University of Loja published his thesis and keeps it as part of its heritage. With this step began the process of energetically unblocking diseases in the world.

entities/lumbalgia/description.text: Low back pain. The lower back is an intricate structure of interconnected and overlapping elements: 1) Tendons, muscles and other soft tissues. 2) Highly sensitive nerve roots and nerves running from the lower back to the legs and feet. 3) Small, complex joints. 4) Intervertebral discs with their gelatinous nuclei. Irritation of or a problem in any of these structures can cause low back pain or pain that radiates to or is felt in other parts of the body. Pain caused by the resulting lumbar muscle spasms can be severe, and there are several syndromes that produce pain that may become chronic. Although low back pain is extremely common, its symptoms and severity can vary greatly. For example, a simple lumbar muscle strain can be so intense that it requires a visit to the emergency room, while disc degeneration might cause nothing more than mild, intermittent discomfort.

entities/lupus/description.text: Lupus is a systemic and chronic rheumatic disease; that is, in addition to affecting the joints and muscles, it can damage the skin and almost all organs. Its basis is autoimmune, since it is produced by the formation of antibodies. The disease evolves in phases of flare-ups and others in which the effects of the disease remit. Likewise, there are very severe forms of lupus and others that are less serious, such as those that manifest with skin conditions. This pathology mainly affects women, and at a fertile period of life (between 20 and 40 years). Cases have also been described in children and the elderly. The cause is unknown. However, since it is an autoimmune disease, there are different factors that can influence the immune system and trigger lupus. Several hypotheses have been considered, including genetics and the environment. Exposure to sunlight could also be a triggering factor for the pathology. In fact, many individuals with lupus have photosensitivity to ultraviolet rays. Likewise, hormones, specifically female estrogens, may be responsible for the disease. In fact, it has been observed that birth control pills can accelerate its onset in genetically predisposed women. Since it is a multisystem disease, it affects several organs. On the one hand, it presents general symptoms: Easy tiring, unexplained weight loss, prolonged fever that is not due to any infectious process, and temperature changes. In addition, joint and muscle symptoms are among the most frequent clinical manifestations. 90 percent of patients with lupus suffer from pain and inflammation in the joints (arthritis), most frequently in the hands, wrists, elbows, knees and feet. Morning joint stiffness may also appear. Skin involvement is also frequent. The best-known lesion, though not the most frequent, is the so-called “butterfly-wing erythema”, which consists of redness and eruption of the skin on the cheeks and nose. Hair loss is also frequent when the disease is active. On the other hand, lupus patients suffer from hypersensitivity to ultraviolet rays. If they are exposed to the sun without protection, the disease can reactivate. When it affects the heart and lungs, the lining layers of the heart (pericardium) and of the lungs (pleura) become inflamed due to the disease. This gives rise to pericarditis and pleuritis. Both have similar symptoms: chest pain and fever. On other occasions, lupus affects the lungs or the heart valves, causing cardiorespiratory insufficiency. When it affects the kidney, lupus always affects both kidneys at the same time. The most frequent lesion is inflammation (nephritis), which sometimes prevents the kidney from properly eliminating the body's waste, so that the waste accumulates in the blood. Because of this inflammation, the kidney is often unable to assimilate and retain proteins. As a result, they are eliminated in the urine and swelling of the face and legs occurs. When it affects the brain, lupus can affect the nervous system. Although it is generally of little importance, it is a problem that must be monitored. It manifests with headaches, depression or episodes of hyperactivity.
