These are very frequent manifestations in the general population and may be due to a mild cerebral inflammation from lupus or to many other circumstances. Likewise, the depression may not be triggered by the disease, but rather because the patient becomes depressed on learning that he or she faces this pathology, of unknown origin and capable of affecting so many organs of the body. There are several types of lupus. Systemic lupus erythematosus: this is the most common; it can be mild or severe and can affect many parts of the body, including the joints, skin, kidneys, heart, lungs, blood vessels and brain. Discoid lupus: causes a skin rash that does not go away. Subacute cutaneous lupus: causes blisters after being in the sun. Drug-induced lupus: caused by certain medicines; it usually disappears when the medication is stopped. Neonatal lupus: this is not common and affects newborns; it is probably caused by certain antibodies from the mother.

entities/luxacion/description.text: A luxation or dislocation is any capsuloligamentous injury with loss of contact between the articular surfaces due to severe trauma, which may be total (luxation) or partial (subluxation). In medicine, a dislocation is a separation of two bones at the place where they meet in the joint. A dislocated bone is a bone that is no longer in its normal position. A dislocation can also cause damage to ligaments and nerves. A luxation is the permanent separation of the two parts of a joint; that is, it occurs when extreme force is applied to a ligament, producing separation of the ends of two connected bones.

entities/lyme/description.text: Borrelia causes Lyme disease: Stage 1) Erythema migrans: reddening of the skin shaped like an eye at the center surrounded by a reddish oval approx. 5 cm in diameter. Stage 2) Multiple migrans-type erythematous lesions (reddening of multiple spots on the skin), neurological symptoms such as palsy of the seventh (facial) cranial nerve, meningoencephalitis, cardiac symptoms such as atrioventricular block, myopericarditis, and asymmetric oligoarticular arthritis. Stage3) Dermatitis, neurological disease, asymmetric oligoarticular arthritis, chronic fatigue. For the Costohepatic - Costohepatic pair, the magnets are placed as follows: the negative pole on the axillary line, at the level of the liver, on the last rib, and the positive pole 2 fingers above the gallbladder.

entities/maculopatias/description.text: Macular edema. Maculopathy is inflammation of the macula. The term maculopathy identifies any disease that affects the macula, the area of the retina specialized in fine detail vision, which serves us, among other things, to be able to read and to distinguish people's faces. In the center of the macula - which is itself in the center of the retina - lies the fovea, which is a depression of the retina at whose center is the foveola, where there are only cones: these are the photoreceptors - cells that can transform light signals into electrochemical impulses - responsible for central vision and color perception (unlike rods, which are used for night vision and are abundant in the peripheral retina). The main symptom of maculopathy is a characteristic loss of visual function: those who suffer from macular disease progressively lose vision in the center of the visual field, which should not be confused with seeing a black spot in the central field. Another common symptom of maculopathy is distortion of images (metamorphopsia). For example, the grout lines between tiles no longer look straight. Other less frequent symptoms involve misperceptions of the size of the objects observed. The Macula-Cerebellum pair is used to improve vision.

entities/mal-de-addison/description.text: Addison's disease is a hormonal deficiency caused by damage to the adrenal gland, resulting in primary adrenocortical hypofunction or insufficiency. Addison's original description of this disease is: languor and general weakness, hypokinetic activity of the heart, gastric irritability and a peculiar change in skin coloration.

entities/mal-olor-axilas/description.text: Bromhidrosis is bad body odor, usually associated with excessive sweating. When it is intense, it can become a health problem with an impact on the private, working and social life of those who suffer from it. The body odor is unpleasant and pungent despite the use of deodorants, antiperspirants or perfume, which in many cases actually make the situation worse. The axilla or armpit is the area of the human body located below the junction between the shoulder and the arm, as distinct from the groin, between the leg and the hip. In this area hair grows in both men and women from adolescence onward. Women in various cultures remove it because it is frowned upon in those cultures. In men, not having axillary hair, or hair in other parts of the anatomy, culturally seems to indicate a lack of virility or sexual maturity. The armpits are prone to accumulating bad odor due to sweat and some conditions. To correct the bad odor, it is necessary to place the magnets repeatedly until the odor disappears.

entities/mal-olor-pies/description.text: The foot is the terminal portion of a limb that bears the body's weight and allows locomotion. It is an anatomical structure found in many vertebrates. Foot odor is generally the product of a fungal infection produced by dermatophyte fungi (which feed on keratin) or by yeasts (in very rare cases with an altered immune system). It affects the interdigital folds, the sole and the edges of the foot. To correct the bad odor, the magnets must be placed repeatedly until the odor disappears.

entities/mala-digestion/description.text: Poor digestion or dyspepsia is the more or less habitual inability to digest food properly. Digestion takes place slowly and heavily and is accompanied by other symptoms indicating that the digestive system is not working well. A distinction must be made between dyspepsia, or poor digestion, and indigestion. In dyspepsia, poor digestion occurs as a recurrent phenomenon that habitually repeats with a certain frequency over a period of three months. Indigestion occurs occasionally, usually lasts a short time and then disappears.

entities/malaria/contagion.text: Parasites of the genus Plasmodium. Blood transfusion. Pregnant mother to fetus. Bite of various species of infected mosquitoes of the genus Anopheles. As is known, only the females of this mosquito feed on blood in order to mature their eggs; the males do not bite and cannot transmit diseases, since they feed only on nectar and plant juices. The infected female Anopheles carries Plasmodium in her salivary glands.

entities/malaria/description.text: Malaria or paludism is a disease produced by parasites of the genus Plasmodium, and some scientific studies suggest that it may have been transmitted to humans through western gorillas. The disease can be caused by one or several of the different Plasmodium species: Plasmodium falciparum, Plasmodium vivax, Plasmodium malariae, Plasmodium ovale or Plasmodium knowlesi. The symptoms are very varied, beginning with fever, chills, sweating and headache. In addition, there may be nausea, vomiting, cough, bloody stools, muscle aches, jaundice (yellowish discoloration of the skin and mucous membranes), blood clotting defects, shock, kidney or liver failure, central nervous system disorders and coma. Fever and chills are cyclical symptoms, recurring every two or three days. Both kidneys must be scanned.

entities/malassezia-furfur/description.text: Malassezia furfur is a species of fungus that is part of the normal flora of human skin and is the cause of dandruff and of an infectious, non-contagious skin disease called pityriasis versicolor, which is a superficial skin infection characterized by spots on the skin (reddish hypo- or hyperpigmented macules) and is usually otherwise asymptomatic. It mimics scarlet fever or psoriasis (a chronic inflammatory skin disease that produces thickened, inflamed, scaly lesions, frequently appearing on the elbows, knees, scalp, abdomen and back). Skin spots.

entities/malignidad/description.text: Evil, wickedness or malignity is a relative negative condition attributed to human beings that indicates the absence of morality, goodness, charity or natural affection for their environment and those around them. Acting with wickedness also implies deliberately contravening, by means of cunning, the officially correct codes of conduct, morality or behavior in a social group.

entities/mareos/description.text: Dizziness is an unpleasant sensation that usually occurs when turning the head repeatedly, bending over or getting up. The term is imprecise and can be confused with vertigo and with kinetosis. Vertigo is a subjective sensation of movement of the objects around us or of our own body, usually a spinning sensation. Kinetosis or motion sickness is the disorder due to movement, whether by sea, air, car, train or that produced by some amusement rides, whose main symptoms are vomiting, nausea and loss of balance, produced by repetitive linear and angular acceleration and deceleration. In biomagnetism there are three balance centers: 1) Horizontal --> Ear - Ear 2) Vertical --> Frontal hairline pole - Frontal hairline pole 3) Position --> Medulla oblongata - Cerebellum.

entities/materialismo/description.text: Materialism is a philosophical doctrine that consists of admitting matter as the only substance, denying spirituality and the immortality of the human soul. It is an attitude of a person who places excessive value on material things, such as money or property.

entities/mediastinitis/description.text: Mediastinitis is an uncommon disease characterized by acute or chronic inflammation of the mediastinum, generally caused by germs that colonize this anatomical region. The most frequent causes are esophageal perforation, a complication of cardiac surgery (postsurgical mediastinitis) and extension into the mediastinum of nearby infectious processes of pulmonary, pleural or dental origin. Acute mediastinitis is a serious infectious process with high mortality, above all from septic shock. The inflammation normally appears in the area of the thorax (chest) between the lungs (mediastinum); this area contains the heart, the great blood vessels, the trachea, the esophagus, the thymus gland, the lymph nodes and the connective tissues.

entities/megacolon/description.text: Megacolon is a potentially fatal complication of other intestinal conditions that causes widening (dilation) of the large intestine over a period of one to several days. Toxic megacolon arises as a complication of an inflammatory bowel disease, such as ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease and infections of the colon. The term "toxic" means that this complication occurs with infection or inflammation and is very dangerous. This is different from other forms of megacolon such as pseudo-obstruction, acute colonic ileus or congenital dilation of the colon, which occur without infection or inflammation. The rapid widening of the colon can cause the following symptoms: abdominal pain, abdominal distension, abdominal tenderness, fever, rapid heart rate, shock.

entities/melatonina/description.text: Dysfunction of the pineal gland. Vitiligo appears as a result of pineal gland dysfunction + liver dysfunction + an emotional problem. It is a degenerative skin disease in which the melanocytes (the cells responsible for skin pigmentation) die, so that melanin (the substance that produces skin pigmentation) stops being produced in the area where cell death has occurred. The pineal gland acts on pigmentation, sexuality and the adrenal glands. Its dysfunction affects the production of corticosteroids, which are a variety of hormones of the steroid group (produced by the cortex of the adrenal glands) and their derivatives. Corticosteroids are involved in a variety of physiological mechanisms, including those that regulate inflammation, the immune system, carbohydrate metabolism, protein catabolism and plasma electrolyte levels and, finally, those that characterize the response to stress. The pineal gland, also known as the pineal body, conarium or epiphysis cerebri, is a small endocrine gland (it secretes hormones) in the brain of vertebrates. It produces melatonin, a hormone derived from serotonin that affects the modulation of sleep patterns, both circadian and seasonal rhythms. Its shape resembles a small pine cone (hence its name), and it is located in the epithalamus near the center of the brain, between the two hemispheres, tucked into a groove where the two halves of the thalamus join. The pineal gland is responsible for producing melatonin. This pair normalizes the generation of melatonin. In Homo sapiens there is a constant synthesis of melatonin that decreases abruptly around 30 years of age; from adolescence onward, calcifications called corpora arenacea usually form in the gland. It has been observed that the functions of melatonin include, among others, regulating the biological clock and reducing oxidation. Melatonin deficits may be accompanied by insomnia and depression and could cause a gradual acceleration of aging. Melatonin is the most potent endogenous antioxidant known. Its functions are the following: 1) Its primary function is to coordinate and regulate biological rhythms (hunger, sleep, etc.) 2) It harmonizes the autonomic system with the environment. 3) It controls the functioning of the body's neuroendocrine centers. 4) It combats jet lag. 5) It regulates body temperature. 6) It regulates sleep, helps you sleep better and allows you to wake up more rested. 7) It participates in a wide variety of cellular and neurophysiological processes. 8) It prevents premature calcification in childhood, favoring bone growth. 9) It controls the onset of puberty. 10) It protects the central nervous system 11) It enhances and stimulates the immune system. 12) It helps prevent and treat diseases, including cancer. 13) It promotes the function of other glands. 14) It calms tension and stress and relaxes the muscles, promoting drowsiness. 15) It improves mood and the sense of well-being. 16) It causes apoptosis (programmed cell destruction or death brought about by the organism itself) of cancer cells in the thymus. Some diseases that can be prevented or treated with adequate generation of melatonin are the following: diseases of aging (Parkinson's, Alzheimer's), neurodegenerative diseases, cardiovascular diseases, headaches, erectile dysfunction, depression, macular degeneration, edema, ulcerative colitis, cephalalgia, asthma, sleep disturbances, anxiety, arteriosclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, cancer, tiredness, cataracts, cystitis, respiratory insufficiency, arrhythmias, gastroesophageal reflux, burns, tuberculosis, circadian rhythm disorders (cyclical physical and mental changes (24 hours)), memory problems, high blood pressure, infections, maculopathies, skin lesions, migraine, tachycardia, aluminum or lead toxicity, wounds, intestinal disorders, osteoarthritis, pancreatitis, hyperpigmentation, hypertension, glaucoma.

entities/meningitis-aseptica/description.text: Aseptic meningitis is a common, rarely fatal condition, generally caused by certain viruses. Fortunately, most people exposed to these viruses experience no symptoms or experience mild symptoms without meningitis. Meningitis means inflammation of the membranes that cover the brain and spinal cord. Because several different viruses can cause aseptic meningitis, the way the virus spreads depends on the type of virus involved. The most common viruses enter through the mouth, multiply in the body and are excreted in the feces. Unwashed hands can carry the virus and transmit it to another person (this is called fecal-oral transmission). The viruses that commonly cause aseptic meningitis can be transmitted for weeks after infection. Aseptic meningitis generally begins with fever, headache, stiff neck and general malaise. Depending on the virus, a rash or eruption may appear. Certain viruses can also cause gastrointestinal symptoms (diarrhea, vomiting) and respiratory symptoms (common cold, sore throat). Symptoms generally appear 3 to 6 days after exposure to the disease.

entities/meningitis-bacteriana/descripti.text: Bacterial meningitis is caused by a bacterium; it is a rapid-onset inflammation of the layers of tissue that cover the brain and spinal cord (meninges) and of the fluid-containing space located between the meninges (subarachnoid space). Older children and adults develop neck stiffness that makes it difficult or impossible to lower the chin to the chest, usually accompanied by fever and headache. The brain and spinal cord are covered by three layers of tissue called meninges. The subarachnoid space is located between the middle layer and the inner layer of the meninges, which cover the brain and spinal cord. This space contains the cerebrospinal fluid, which flows through the meninges, fills the internal spaces of the brain and acts as a cushion for the brain and spinal cord. When bacteria invade the meninges and the subarachnoid space, the immune system reacts against the invaders and immune cells gather to defend the body against them. The result is inflammation (meningitis), which can cause complications such as: blood clots, brain swelling (cerebral edema), increased pressure inside the skull (intracranial or endocranial pressure), excess fluid in the brain, inflammation of the cranial nerves, subdural empyema (accumulation of pus beneath the meninges), septic shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation, among others.

entities/meningitis/contagion.text: Meningitis is an infection that in 80% of cases is caused by viruses, 15 to 20% by bacteria, and in the remaining cases is due to poisoning, fungi, medications and other diseases.

entities/meningitis/description.text: Meningitis is an infection of the membranes that cover the brain and spinal cord (meninges). It can lead to sclerosis. The most common causes of meningitis are viral infections, which generally improve without treatment. However, bacterial meningeal infections are extremely serious and can result in death or brain damage, even with treatment. Meningitis can also be caused by: chemical irritation, drug allergies, fungi, parasites, tumors. Most viral meningitis is due to enteroviruses, which are viruses that can also cause intestinal disease. Likewise, viral meningitis can be caused by the herpes virus, the same virus that can cause cold sores and genital herpes. However, people with cold sores or genital herpes are not at greater risk of developing herpetic meningitis. The viruses that can cause mumps and HIV can cause aseptic meningitis. Recently, West Nile virus, which is spread through mosquito bites, has become a cause of viral meningitis. Viral meningitis occurs more frequently than bacterial meningitis. Symptoms usually appear rapidly and may include: fever, chills, changes in mental status, nausea, vomiting, sensitivity to light (photophobia), intolerance to sounds, severe headache, stiff neck (meningismus), agitation, bulging fontanelles in infants, decreased level of consciousness, poor feeding or irritability in children, rapid breathing, unusual posture with the head and neck arched backward (opisthotonus). Meningitis is an important cause of fever in children and newborns. Meningitis can cause serious long-term consequences such as deafness, epilepsy, hydrocephalus or cognitive deficit. The medulla oblongata stops sending messages to the ventilatory muscles, causing death from ventilatory failure.

entities/menopausia/description.text: Menopause is defined as the permanent cessation of menstruation and has physiological correlates, with the decline in estrogen secretion due to loss of follicular function. It is a step within a slow and long process of reproductive aging. This term is often confused with the climacteric.

entities/menstruacion-irregular/descript.text: Irregular or dysfunctional bleeding in women. Metrorrhagia is any vaginal hemorrhage, coming from the uterus, not associated with the menstrual cycle by its rhythm or by the amount of flow. The causes of this abnormality are generally local, that is, of the uterus or the pelvis. Its remote causes may be related to the endocrine glands or to the general state of health.

entities/meteorismo/description.text: Meteorism is the abdominal distension caused by the production and accumulation of an excessive amount of gas in the gastrointestinal tract, either in the intestine (meteorismus intestinalis) or in the stomach.

entities/metrorragia/description.text: Metrorrhagia is any vaginal hemorrhage, coming from the uterus, not associated with the menstrual cycle by its rhythm or by the amount of flow. The causes of this abnormality are generally local, that is, of the uterus or the pelvis. Its remote causes may be related to the endocrine glands or to the general state of health. Alterations in menstrual cycles are frequent in the two years following the first menstruation (menarche) and in the three years before menopause (cessation of menstruation).

entities/miastenia-gravis/description.text: Myasthenia gravis (MG) is a chronic autoimmune neuromuscular disease characterized by varying degrees of weakness of the body's skeletal (voluntary) muscles. The name comes from Latin and Greek and means «grave muscle weakness». It begins with an insidious picture of loss of strength, which quickly recovers with rest but reappears when exercise is resumed. It usually begins in the periocular muscles. On rare occasions the onset is acute. The main characteristic of myasthenia gravis is muscle weakness that increases during periods of activity and decreases after periods of rest. Certain muscles -such as those that control eye and eyelid movement, facial expression, chewing, speech and deglutition (swallowing)- are often affected by this disorder. The muscles that control breathing and movements of the neck and limbs may also be affected, but later.

entities/micoplasmosis-aviar/description.text: Mycobacterium tuberculosis avis was thought to be a virus. It is the smallest known bacterium. It causes brain disorders, psychological problems, pain and inflammation. It can cause torticollis, in which the neck muscles (particularly the sternocleidomastoid muscle, the levator scapulae and, to a lesser extent, the scalene muscles) contract involuntarily and cause the head to tilt. When there is no drainage of cerebrospinal fluid, the pressure in the head increases and it has to be drained. This is called hydrocephalus. It is cured with biomagnetism. Avian mycoplasmosis is a disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis avis; it first involves the respiratory system, followed by the joint system and, less frequently, other regions. The bacteria that produce it, the mycoplasmas, lack a cell wall, which makes them resistant to some antibiotics. Mycoplasmas are transmitted horizontally by the airborne route, by direct contact with other birds or by indirect contact through people, animals, food, water, fomites, etc. Vertically they are transmitted through the egg. The incubation period varies from 6 to 21 days. Some of its characteristic signs are tracheal rales, nasal discharge and cough. Secondary invasion by bacteria, especially Escherichia coli, is frequent.

entities/micosis-de-cuero-cabelludo/desc.text: Scalp mycosis, or tinea capitis, is an infection of the scalp caused by a type of fungus called a dermatophyte, which parasitizes keratinized tissue. These fungi are keratinophilic (they show an affinity for keratin) and keratinolytic (they metabolize keratin), which means that they can parasitize the skin, hair and nails in humans and animals. Scalp mycosis occurs most commonly in children. It is very rare in adults. The fungus thrives in warm, moist environments. Factors that can contribute to tinea capitis include heat, humid weather and excessive sweating. Factors that can increase your likelihood of having tinea capitis include: age under 10 years, African ancestry, day care centers, exposure to pets with the infection, poor hygiene, sharing combs, brushes or hats, diabetes, and immune system disorders such as human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). Symptoms of tinea capitis include itching of the scalp (not always present), bald patches, inflamed areas, ulcers or irritated skin. If not treated correctly, it can cause permanent hair loss and scarring.

entities/micosis-de-pulmon/description.text: Pulmonary mycosis is a fungal infection of the lungs. The disease used to be called Pneumocystis carinii or PC pneumonia. This type of pneumonia is caused by the fungus Pneumocystis jiroveci. This fungus is common in the environment and rarely causes disease in healthy people. However, it can cause a lung infection in people with an immune system weakened by cancer, chronic use of corticosteroids or other medications that weaken the immune system, HIV/AIDS, or organ or bone marrow transplantation. Pneumocystis jiroveci was a relatively rare infection before the AIDS epidemic. Pneumocystis pneumonia in people with AIDS usually develops slowly over days to weeks or even months and is less severe. People with this type of pneumonia who do not have AIDS generally become ill more quickly and the disease is more acute. Symptoms include cough, often mild and dry, fever, rapid breathing, and difficulty breathing, especially with activity (exertion).

entities/micosis-de-unas/description.text: Tinea unguium, onychomycosis or ringworm of the nails is a superficial infection of the nails, of both the hands and the feet, that leaves them abnormal in thickness and color. It is caused by a type of fungus called a dermatophyte, which parasitizes keratinized tissue. These fungi are keratinophilic (they show affinity for keratin) and keratinolytic (they metabolize keratin), which means they can parasitize the skin, hair and nails of humans and animals. Transmission from one area to another or from one person to another is very frequent. Nail mycosis occurs when a fungus proliferates in or around a toenail or fingernail. Fungi can live in the dead tissues of the hair, nails and outer skin layers. Common fungal infections include: athlete's foot, jock itch (tinea cruris), and ringworm of the skin of the body or the head. Fungal nail infections are seen more frequently in adults and are generally preceded by a fungal infection of the feet. Toenails are affected more frequently than fingernails. People who frequent public swimming pools, gyms or showers and those who sweat a lot often have these infections. The fungi that cause them thrive in warm, moist areas. The chances of contracting a fungal nail infection increase if the person has manicures and pedicures using utensils that have been used on other people, has minor injuries to the skin or nails, has a nail deformity or disease, has skin that stays moist for a long time, has immune system problems or wears closed shoes. Symptoms include nail changes (abnormal coloration or malformation) in one or more nails (usually the toenails) such as: brittleness, change in the shape of the nail, crumbling of the outer edges of the nail, debris (breakdown of a solid mass into particles) trapped under the nails, loosening or lifting of the nail, thickening of the nail, yellow or white streaks on the side of the nail.

entities/micosis-genital/description.text: Genital mycosis is one of the most common causes of vaginal discharge, with Candida albicans being the fungus most frequently found responsible. Candida albicans infections do not depend on external contagion, since this microorganism is part of the normal flora of the genital region; it has been observed that 20 to 60% of healthy women are intestinal carriers and around 10% are vaginal carriers. The infection develops through the appearance of certain factors that favor the growth of the fungus. Among the factors predisposing to the development of these infections we can highlight: taking oral contraceptives, pregnancy (due to the variation in hormone levels), diabetes, prolonged treatment with corticosteroids or medications that lower the defenses, exposure to radiation therapy, a diet excessive in carbohydrates, and having a sexual partner who carries the fungus. It usually begins as a burning sensation and intense itching in the vulvar region. Subsequently a scant, yellowish or whitish, lumpy discharge appears. It also causes difficulty urinating and discomfort during sexual intercourse. All these complaints generally increase in the days before menstruation. On viewing the vagina with a speculum, its walls are seen to be reddened and covered by whitish plaques firmly adhered to them. This type of mycosis can also be spread sexually, producing in men an infection of the glans and foreskin, where the complaints are very similar to those experienced by women.

entities/microsporum/description.text: Microsporum is a genus of fungi that cause tinea capitis and tinea corporis (dermatophytosis), among other mycoses. It is a keratinophilic filamentous fungus included in the dermatophyte group. Fungus that causes dandruff. Mycosis (infection caused by a fungus) in the mouth, ear, eye, nose. After clearing the mycosis, impact Elbow-Elbow. It may be related to liver dysfunction; it manifests with dandruff in the pubic hair of men or women.

entities/miedo/description.text: Fear or dread is an emotion characterized by an intense unpleasant sensation caused by the perception of a danger, real or supposed, present, future or even past. It is a primary emotion derived from the natural aversion to risk or threat. The maximum expression of fear is terror. Fear is related to anxiety.

entities/mielomeningocele/description.text: Myelomeningocele is a birth defect in which the spinal column and the spinal canal do not close before birth. This condition is a type of spina bifida. Normally, during the first month of pregnancy, the two sides of the spinal column (backbone) join to cover the spinal cord, the spinal nerves and the meninges (the tissues covering the spinal cord). Spina bifida refers to any congenital defect involving incomplete closure of the spinal column. Myelomeningocele is the most common type of spina bifida. It is a neural tube defect in which the bones of the spine do not form completely, resulting in an incomplete spinal canal. This causes the spinal cord and the meninges (the tissues covering the spinal cord) to protrude (stick out beyond their normal boundaries) from the child's back. Spina bifida occulta is a condition in which the bones of the spine do not close, but the spinal cord and meninges remain in place and the skin usually covers the defect. Another type of spina bifida is called meningocele, a condition in which the tissue covering the spinal cord protrudes through the defect in the spine, but the spinal cord remains in place.

entities/migrana/description.text: The Temple – Temple pair improves blood supply to the brain, helping headaches and migraines to disappear. It corrects lung problems such as pulmonary emphysema (when Mycobacterium leprae is present), pulmonary bronchiectasis, pulmonary tuberculosis and mycoses. It helps correct hypertension. It regulates intracranial microcirculation. Migraine is a type of headache that can occur with symptoms such as nausea, vomiting or sensitivity to light. In many people, a throbbing pain is felt on only one side of the head. Some people who suffer from migraines have warning symptoms, called an aura, before the actual headache begins. An aura is a group of symptoms that include changes in vision. It is a warning sign that a severe headache is about to occur. Migraine produces a very severe headache, with nausea and vomiting. It is a neurological disorder. During a migraine attack there are changes in serotonin that affect the blood vessels in the brain, causing abnormal activity. The decrease in serotonin causes the blood vessels to dilate, producing a painful inflammation, which results in the headache. The nausea and vomiting are a consequence of the pathway or influence of the neurotransmitter in the gastrointestinal tract. Serotonin is a neurotransmitter monoamine that is synthesized in the serotonergic neurons of the central nervous system and in the enterochromaffin cells of the gastrointestinal tract. A migraine is caused by abnormal brain activity, which can be triggered by many factors; however, the exact chain of events remains unclear. Most medical experts believe that the attack begins in the brain and involves nerve pathways and chemicals. The changes affect blood flow in the brain and surrounding tissues. Migraine attacks can also be triggered by caffeine withdrawal, changes in hormone levels during women's menstrual cycle or with the use of birth control pills, changes in sleep patterns, drinking alcohol, loud noises or bright lights, exercise or other physical stress, skipping meals, odors and perfumes, smoking or exposure to smoke, stress and anxiety. Some medicinal plants that have shown benefits in the treatment of migraine are the following: Matlali (Chrysanthemum parthenium), ginger (Zingiber officinalis) and eucalyptus leaf (Eucalyptus globulus). Efforts should be made to stimulate blood circulation in the occipital, temporal and parietal regions.

entities/miocarditis/description.text: Myocarditis is a medical term describing inflammation of the myocardium, which is the muscular portion of the heart. It is generally due to a viral or bacterial infection and presents as chest pain, sudden signs of heart failure and sudden death. A long list of causes leading to myocarditis has been identified: viruses, bacteria, spirochetes, protozoa, fungi, parasites.

entities/mioma-uterino/description.text: A uterine myoma is a benign, noncancerous tumor that grows in the muscular tissue of the uterus, or myometrium, in women. Its real name is uterine leiomyoma, since they originate from the smooth muscle tissue of the myometrium. Only 0.5% of myomas become malignant tumors (sarcomas) in women.

entities/mixovirus-parotiditis/descripti.text: It causes the disease known as parotitis or mumps. Located mainly in one or both parotid (salivary) glands. It can affect different glands of the body, the central nervous system and the testicles. The most frequent complications are meningitis and testicular inflammation, which can lead to infertility. Extreme dryness of the mucous membranes. It affects the bladder. True Sjögren's syndrome.

entities/mononucleosis/contagion.text: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). Its transmission requires close personal contact, and it is transmitted through saliva, in which it remains active for several hours. For this reason, mononucleosis is also known as the "kissing disease" or "lovers' fever".

entities/mononucleosis/description.text: Mononucleosis is a viral infection that causes fever, sore throat and swelling of the lymph nodes, especially in the neck. Mononucleosis is often spread through saliva and close contact. It is known as the "kissing disease" and occurs most frequently between 15 and 17 years of age; however, the infection can develop at any age. Mononucleosis is generally linked to Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), but it can also be caused by other microorganisms such as cytomegalovirus (CMV). Mononucleosis may begin slowly with fatigue, general indisposition, headache and sore throat. The sore throat slowly gets worse. The tonsils become swollen and develop a yellowish-white coating. The lymph nodes in the neck also frequently become swollen and painful. Symptoms of mononucleosis include: drowsiness, fever, general discomfort, restlessness or a general feeling of illness, loss of appetite, muscle stiffness or aches, skin rash, sore throat, swollen lymph nodes, especially in the neck and armpit, and swollen spleen.

entities/moquillo/contagion.text: It is transmitted through the air and through contact with infected body fluids, including food and water contaminated by these fluids. Household animals with distemper, inhalation of respiratory droplets from an infected person, contaminated food or drink, bites from mosquitoes, ticks and other insects, skin contact, allergic reaction to vaccines, autoimmune disease, bacteria such as those of Lyme disease, syphilis and tuberculosis, parasites such as nematodes, cysticercosis and toxoplasmosis in patients with AIDS and other people with a weakened immune system, effects of cancer.

entities/moquillo/description.text: Viral encephalitis. Distemper, also known as Carré's disease, is an infectious and contagious disease of viral origin that affects animals of all ages, which are particularly vulnerable early in life and in old age. The symptoms depend on the direct action of the virus on the affected organs or tissues and on the bacteria that proliferate in them. According to the system involved, we can classify them as: General: Fever, of the biphasic type, with a rise at the onset of the disease, which then subsides and reappears with the onset of secondary bacterial infections. It is during this period that diagnostic tests for distemper are recommended. Loss of appetite. General malaise. Weight loss. Dehydration. Respiratory: Nasal discharge, ranging from serous to mucopurulent. Cough. Dyspnea (difficulty breathing). Ocular: Corneal edema (red eye). Change in corneal color (blue eye). Conjunctivitis with ocular discharge (eye crust). Dry keratitis, resulting from the action of the virus on the lacrimal glands. Corneal ulcer. Digestive: Vomiting. Diarrhea. Dehydration. Cutaneous: Hyperkeratosis (hardening) of the footpads. Eruptions (exanthem). Dental: Hypoplasia (incomplete development) of the dental enamel. Neurological: Ataxia (incoordination of movements), which may progress to paresis (partial absence of movement) and then to paralysis. Tics, chorea or flexor spasm, that is, the involuntary movement of a muscle or group of muscles, especially of the head and limbs. Seizures, of the epileptiform type. Apoplexy (cerebrovascular accidents or attacks). A particular animal may present a few or most of the symptoms described, depending on the severity of the infection. The course of the disease may be only 10 days, and it can extend to several weeks and even months, with intermittent periods of improvement followed by relapse.

entities/moraxella-catarrhalis/descripti.text: Moraxella catarrhalis is a gram-negative, aerobic, oxidase-positive diplococcus-shaped bacterium that can colonize and cause respiratory tract infection in humans. Clinically, these bacteria are known to cause otitis media, bronchitis, sinusitis and laryngitis.

entities/morganella-morganii/description.text: Morganella morganii is a bacterial species of the family Enterobacteriaceae, gram-negative bacilli. They commonly inhabit the environment and the intestinal tract of humans, mammals and reptiles as saprophytic flora and occasionally cause urinary tract infections and other nosocomial infections.

entities/morganella-tifo/description.text: Morganella Tifo. It causes severe liver and digestive disorders, diarrhea, anorexia. Its proper eradication prevents liver transplantation. It tests positive on febrile agglutination tests (diseases that cause fever). It can cause preeclampsia, which is a medical complication of pregnancy associated with pregnancy-induced hypertension and with high levels of protein in the urine (proteinuria). Associated with cellulite, which is the accumulation of adipose tissue in certain areas of the body, forming fatty adipose nodules.

entities/mycobacterium-bovis/description.text: Mycobacterium bovis is a slow-growing, microaerophilic (survives with very low levels of oxygen) mycobacterium that causes bovine tuberculosis. It can also infect and cause tuberculosis in humans. Tuberculosis produces kidney stones and gallstones. Abscesses in the body. It is possibly the most prevalent infectious disease in the world. Although tuberculosis is predominantly a disease of the lungs, it can also affect the central nervous system, the lymphatic system, the circulatory system, the genitourinary system, the digestive system, the bones, the joints and even the skin. The classic symptoms of tuberculosis are a chronic cough with blood-tinged sputum, fever, night sweats and weight loss.

entities/mycobacterium-leprae/contagion.text: Transmitted by rats. Transmission through contact or living with an infected person - coughing, sneezing. The main source of leprosy contamination is the breast milk of a contaminated mother.

entities/mycobacterium-leprae/descriptio.text: Leprosy. It is the deadliest bacterium. Cause of bubonic plague; black lumps appear all over the skin; it usually kills the patient. If a black ulcer appears on the skin, it is probably leprosy. A disease brought from Europe to America. Only if this bacterium is present can it be confirmed that the patient has cancer; if it is not present, there is no cancer. Most cancers detected by traditional medicine are only abscesses. It produces toxins such as limosina, goes to the skin and destroys it, and produces clubbed fingers.

entities/mycobacterium-lepromatosis/desc.text: Leprosy. Mycobacterium lepromatosis is a bacterium (with many similarities to Mycobacterium leprae) that was identified in 2008 at the University of Texas and also causes leprosy.

entities/mycobacterium-tuberculosis-avis.text: Mycobacterium tuberculosis avis was thought to be a virus. It is the smallest known bacterium. It causes brain disorders, psychological problems, pain and inflammation. It can cause torticollis, in which the neck muscles (particularly the sternocleidomastoid muscle, the levator scapulae and, to a lesser extent, the scalene muscles) contract involuntarily and cause the head to tilt. When there is no drainage of cerebrospinal fluid, the pressure in the head increases and it has to be drained. This is called hydrocephalus. It is cured with biomagnetism. Avian mycoplasmosis is a disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis avis; it first involves the respiratory system, followed by the joint system and, less frequently, other regions. The bacteria that produce it, the mycoplasmas, lack a cell wall, which makes them resistant to some antibiotics. Mycoplasmas are transmitted horizontally by the airborne route, by direct contact with other birds or by indirect contact through people, animals, food, water, fomites, etc. Vertically they are transmitted through the egg. The incubation period varies from 6 to 21 days. Some of its characteristic signs are tracheal rales, nasal discharge and cough. Secondary invasion by bacteria, especially Escherichia coli, is frequent.

entities/mycobacterium-tuberculosis-o-ba.text: Tuberculosis is spread through the air when infected people cough, sneeze or spit. A growing number of people worldwide contract tuberculosis because their immune system is compromised by immunosuppressive drugs, drug abuse or AIDS. Oral sex with an infected person.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis is a bacterium responsible for the largest number of tuberculosis cases in the world. Robert Koch described it for the first time, hence the heteronym (nickname) of this bacterium: "Koch's bacillus". Tuberculosis is a contagious bacterial infection that mainly involves the lungs but can spread to other organs. Tuberculosis is possibly the most prevalent infectious disease in the world. Although tuberculosis is predominantly a disease of the lungs, it can also affect the central nervous system, the lymphatic system, the circulatory system, the genitourinary system, the digestive tract, the bones, the joints and even the skin. The classic symptoms of tuberculosis are a chronic cough with blood-streaked sputum, fever, night sweats and weight loss. Infection of other organs causes a wide variety of symptoms: kidney stones and gallstones, abscesses in the body, sterility in men and women, kidney pain, edema and a sensation of cold. It can cause torticollis, in which the neck muscles (particularly the sternocleidomastoid muscle, the levator scapulae and, to a lesser extent, the scalene muscles) contract involuntarily and cause the head to tilt. Mental disorders.

entities/mycoplasma-pneumoniae/descripti.text: Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a bacterium that causes diseases of the respiratory system, such as tracheobronchitis and atypical pneumonia. They are the smallest free-living bacteria. They are peculiar due to the absence of a cell wall and the presence of sterols in their cell membrane. At 2-3 weeks after exposure, low-grade fever, malaise, headache and dry cough without expectoration appear. Acute pharyngitis may also appear. The symptoms gradually worsen over the following days and may persist for 2 weeks or more. The bronchial passages become infiltrated by lymphocytes and plasma cells.

entities/mycoplasma/contagion.text: Mycoplasmas are frequently found in research laboratories as contaminants of cell cultures. Contamination occurs through carriers or due to contaminated culture media.

entities/mycoplasma/description.text: Mycoplasmas (Mycoplasma) are bacteria that lack a cell wall. There are more than 100 recognized species of the genus Mycoplasma. Because of the absence of a cell wall, mycoplasmas are not sensitive to antibiotics that block cell-wall synthesis, such as penicillin and others. Several species are human pathogens, such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae, the causative agent of an important atypical pneumonia and other respiratory disorders. Some may cause or contribute to some cancers. A mycoplasma cell generally measures less than 1 μm, and they are therefore difficult to detect with a conventional microscope. Mycoplasmas can induce cellular changes, such as changes in metabolism and cell growth, and severe infections can destroy a cell line. They can cause lung and skin problems.

entities/nausea/description.text: Nausea is a sensation indicating that vomiting is near, and the efforts that accompany the need to vomit. It presents as discomfort in the upper part of the stomach, giving the patient the sensation that there will be a violent, spasmodic expulsion of the stomach contents through the mouth, which frequently does not occur. When this situation is prolonged, it can become a debilitating symptom.

entities/negatividad/description.text: Negativity or pessimism is a state of mind and a philosophical doctrine holding that we live in the worst of all possible worlds, a world where pain is perpetual and our destiny is to try to obtain what we will never have. Pessimism denies the progress of civilization and of human nature. From the psychological point of view, it constitutes one of the most notable traits or symptoms of the disease known as depression.

entities/neisseria-gonorrhoeae/descripti.text: Gonorrhea, also called blennorrhagia, blennorrhea and gonococcal infection. It mainly affects the mucous membranes of the genital and urinary tract, but it can also affect the ocular conjunctiva, the pharynx and the rectum. Its most common features are purulent discharge from the urethra in men and the consequence of infertility in women. Gonorrhea is caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae and can be spread by any type of sexual activity. It can be contracted through contact with the mouth, vagina, penis or anus. The bacteria proliferate in warm, moist areas of the body, including the tube that carries urine out of the body (urethra). In women, the bacteria can be found in the reproductive tract (which includes the fallopian tubes, uterus and cervix). This bacterium can even proliferate in the eyes. Symptoms of gonorrhea generally appear 2 to 5 days after infection; however, in men, symptoms can take up to a month to appear. Some people have no symptoms; they may be completely unaware that they have acquired the disease and therefore do not seek treatment. This increases the risk of complications and the chances of transmitting the infection to another person. Symptoms in men include: pain and burning on urination, increased urinary frequency or urgency, discharge from the penis (white, yellow or green), red or inflamed opening of the penis (urethra), tender or swollen testicles, sore throat (gonococcal pharyngitis). Symptoms in women can be very mild and can be mistaken for another type of infection. These symptoms include: vaginal discharge, pain and burning on urination, increased urination, sore throat, painful sexual intercourse, severe pain in the lower abdomen (if the infection spreads to the fallopian tubes and the stomach area), fever (if the infection spreads to the fallopian tubes and the stomach area). If the infection spreads to the bloodstream, the symptoms include: fever, rash, arthritis-like symptoms. It can also produce dental disorders, gingivitis, bad breath, and yellowish or blackish teeth. Meningococcus (Neisseria meningitidis) + Gonococcus (Neisseria gonorrhoeae) produces deforming rheumatoid arthritis. Rheumatism is related to arthritis.

entities/neisseria-meningitidis/contagio.text: The bacterium is transmitted from person to person through droplets of respiratory or throat secretions. Spread of the disease is facilitated by close and prolonged contact (kissing, sneezing, coughing, dormitories, shared dishes and cutlery) with an infected person. It can be transmitted to the fetus when the mother's uterus is infected; it is not a hereditary or genetic problem.

entities/neisseria-meningitidis/descript.text: On its own, the meningococcus produces arthritis. Meningococcus (Neisseria meningitidis) + gonococcus (Neisseria gonorrhoeae) produces deforming rheumatoid arthritis. Rheumatism is related to arthritis. Neisseria meningitidis, often called meningococcus, is a gram-negative bacterium that can cause meningitis and other forms of meningococcal disease, for example meningococcemia, a potentially fatal type of sepsis. This bacterium is known as a coccus because it is round, and more specifically as a diplococcus because it tends to form pairs. About ten percent of adults are carriers of meningococci in the nasopharynx. As an exclusively human pathogen, N. meningitidis is the main cause of bacterial meningitis in children and young adults and causes developmental impairment and death in ten percent of cases. Meningococci produce the only known form of epidemic bacterial meningitis. When the meningococcus is found with the Thoracic spine - Lumbar spine pair, it is because it has settled in the spinal canal (spinal column), and it may cause spina bifida. It is the route of entry of the cysticercus into the brain.

entities/nerualgia-del-trigemino/descrip.text: Trigeminal neuralgia is a nerve disorder that causes stabbing or electric-shock-like pain in parts of the face. The pain of trigeminal neuralgia comes from the trigeminal nerve. This nerve carries sensations of touch and pain from the face, eyes, sinuses and mouth to the brain. The disease generally affects adults, but it can affect anyone at any age. Trigeminal neuralgia may be part of the normal aging process. Trigeminal neuralgia can be caused by: multiple sclerosis, or pressure on the trigeminal nerve from a tumor or a swollen blood vessel; frequently no cause is found. Very painful spasms normally appear, like piercing electrical pulses that generally last a few seconds or minutes, but they can become constant. The pain is usually on only one side of the face, often around the eye, the cheek and the lower part of the face. The pain can be triggered by touch or sounds. Painful episodes of trigeminal neuralgia can be triggered by common everyday activities such as: brushing the teeth, chewing, drinking, eating, lightly touching the face, shaving.

entities/nervio-optico/description.text: Reduces inflammation of the optic nerve. Edema problems in the optic nerve. The optic nerve or second cranial nerve is a sensory nerve responsible for transmitting visual information from the retina to the brain.

entities/neumonia-fulminante/description.text: Pneumonia is a disease of the respiratory system consisting of inflammation of the alveolar spaces of the lungs. Most of the time pneumonia is infectious, but this is not always the case. Pneumonia can affect an entire lung lobe (lobar pneumonia), a segment of a lobe, the alveoli near the bronchi (bronchopneumonia) or the interstitial tissue (interstitial pneumonia). Pneumonia makes the tissue that forms the lungs look reddened and swollen, and it becomes painful. Many patients with pneumonia are treated by family doctors and are not admitted to hospital. Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) or extrahospital pneumonia is that acquired outside hospitals, whereas nosocomial pneumonia (NP) is that acquired during a hospital stay. Pneumonia can be a serious disease if not detected in time, and it can be fatal, especially among elderly people and the immunosuppressed.

entities/neumonia/contagion.text: The microorganisms that cause pneumonia spread rapidly through the air and can be propagated by sneezing, coughing and mucus; a patient who has had pneumonia may be left with sequelae of it in their organism for a long time, which makes them potentially contagious, and the people most prone to contracting it are those in the course of a flu or an asthmatic episode, among other diseases of the respiratory system.

entities/neumonia/description.text: Pneumonia is a disease of the respiratory system consisting of inflammation of the alveolar spaces of the lungs. Most of the time pneumonia is infectious, but this is not always the case. Pneumonia can affect an entire lung lobe (lobar pneumonia), a segment of a lobe, the alveoli near the bronchi (bronchopneumonia) or the interstitial tissue (interstitial pneumonia). Pneumonia makes the tissue that forms the lungs look reddened and swollen, and it becomes painful. Many patients with pneumonia are treated by family doctors and are not admitted to hospital. Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) or extrahospital pneumonia is that acquired outside hospitals, whereas nosocomial pneumonia (NP) is that acquired during a hospital stay. Pneumonia can be a serious disease if not detected in time, and it can be fatal, especially among elderly people and the immunosuppressed.

entities/neumonitis/description.text: Pneumonitis is the term for pulmonary inflammation limited to the interstitium, as occurs in viral pneumonia, pneumonia of unknown etiology and radiation pneumonia, including the fibrotic type. This inflammation is sometimes produced by allergic reactions. It is commonly confused with pneumonia because of the similarity of the words. The difference between the two is that, whereas in pneumonia the inflammatory exudate accumulates inside the alveoli, in pneumonitis the inflammatory exudate accumulates around them, that is, in the interstitial tissue.

entities/neuralgia-ciatalgica/descriptio.text: Sciatic neuralgia, also called sciatalgia, is a condition characterized by pain from the hip along the back of the thigh and leg that can become very intense. In some cases it has no demonstrable etiology and is attributed to rheumatism (essential or rheumatic sciatica), and in other cases it is caused by a multitude of factors that can act at any point along the course of the great sciatic nerve, but above all on its radicular fibers, fifth lumbar and first sacral (symptomatic sciatica). Sciatic neuralgia is the most frequent neuralgia and especially affects adults between thirty and sixty years of age, predominating in males in a proportion of 5 to 3, and especially in those who perform heavy occupations, such as gardeners, farmers, bricklayers, porters, etc. It should be remembered that the sciatic nerve is the largest and longest nerve and that it is formed by fibers from the fourth and fifth lumbar roots and the first, second and third sacral roots, all components of the cauda equina.

entities/neurocisticercosis/contagion.text: Neurocysticercosis is caused by ingestion of Taenia solium eggs, by the fecal-oral route, from a person with taeniasis (T. solium) to a healthy person. Poor hygiene, deficient sanitation and the use of untreated or poorly treated sewage water facilitate the spread of the disease.

entities/neurocisticercosis/description.text: Neurocysticercosis is a disease of the central nervous system of parasitic origin that generates high morbidity. It mainly causes chronic epilepsy, is caused by the pork cysticercus, may be asymptomatic and has a good prognosis if treated in time.

entities/neurodermatitis/description.text: Neurodermatitis is an extremely variable eczematous skin disease that is presumed to be a response to vigorous scratching, rubbing or picking to relieve intense itching. It varies in intensity, severity, course and morphological expression in different individuals. In most cases this pathology has a high emotional component.

entities/neurosis/description.text: Neurosis is a condition of the nervous system that has consequences for how a person handles their emotions, leading them to develop a pathology that prevents them from building empathy with their surroundings. It should be clarified that this concept has a double meaning: on the one hand, it is used to denote a symptom of various anxiety-related alterations of the psyche; on the other, in colloquial speech it appears as a synonym for a certain nervous state or even as a synonym for obsession. In the field of psychology, neurosis is described as an imbalance of the mind caused by anxiety that occurs without any organic damage. It manifests through maladaptive or repetitive behaviors whose purpose is to reduce stress. As specialists explain, human beings protect themselves from distress through various defense mechanisms, among them denial, displacement and repression. That is, through them an individual's psychic structure compensates for excessive distress; therefore, in order to reduce the stress that a given situation or feeling causes them, the neurotic person tends to repeat certain behaviors constantly. A person suffering from neurosis behaves in an unhealthy way and is unable to analyze their surroundings coolly and look for solutions, so they keep going around in circles and resort to denial so as not to accept what disturbs them.

entities/newcastle/description.text: Newcastle disease is a zoonotic disease of birds caused by the Newcastle disease virus (NDV); it is highly contagious and affects many species of domestic and wild birds. It most notably affects poultry because of their high susceptibility. Humans acquire the disease by eating one of these infected birds when undercooked, usually by sucking on the bones. Some of the symptoms that occur with the disease are: impaired balance, vertigo, dizziness, muscular incoordination of the thorax, cerebellar ataxia.

entities/nocardia-americana/description.text: Nocardia is a genus of Gram-positive bacteria found in organic-rich soils throughout the world. It produces facial paralysis of the seventh cranial nerve, earache or deafness. Tinnitus (knocking or sounds are perceived in the ear that do not come from any external source) due to water or pressure differences.

entities/norwalk/description.text: Norovirus (or Norwalk-like virus) is a genus of RNA viruses of the family Caliciviridae and is responsible for approximately 50% of gastroenteritis outbreaks due to food poisoning. Norovirus can affect people of any age. Norovirus infection is characterized by nausea, vomiting, watery diarrhea and abdominal pain. In general, affected patients feel weak, lose their appetite, and present muscle aches, headache, cough and mild fever. The disease has a benign course; severe infections are rare. Although suffering a Norovirus infection is extremely unpleasant, it is generally not dangerous and most people who contract the disease recover in two or three days. Norovirus is inactivated by high temperatures or by chlorine-based disinfectants. The virus is resistant to alcohols and detergents.

entities/obesidad-morbida/description.text: Obesity is a preventable chronic disease of multifactorial origin characterized by excessive accumulation of fat or general hypertrophy of the adipose tissue in the body; that is, when the natural energy reserve of humans and other mammals, stored in the form of body fat, increases to a point where it endangers health or life. Overweight and obesity are the fifth leading risk factor for human death in the world. Obesity forms part of the metabolic syndrome and is a known risk factor, that is, an indication of predisposition to various diseases, particularly cardiovascular diseases, type 2 diabetes mellitus, sleep apnea, stroke and osteoarthritis, as well as to some forms of cancer and dermatological and gastrointestinal conditions. Morbid obesity, severe obesity or class III obesity is the term for obesity characterized by a BMI (body mass index) of 40 or greater, or a BMI of 35 or greater in the presence of at least one other significant disease or severe disability and handicap due to excess weight. In addition to reducing life expectancy, morbid obesity causes disability, handicap and problems of social exclusion. Because of its collective effects, it is a public health problem in many countries and one that has been increasing as a result of changes in social and eating habits. Morbid obesity: if the pancreas appears in the scan, a pancreatic belt should be applied, which consists of placing 4 magnets around the pancreas (-,+,-,+) at the following points: head, body, tail and tip.}

entities/obstruccion-coronaria/descripti.text: Coronary obstruction, also called atherosclerosis, is a common disorder of the arteries in which fat, cholesterol and other substances accumulate in the arterial walls. The most extensive accumulations are called atheromas or plaques and can damage the arterial walls and obstruct blood flow. When blood flow to the heart muscle is severely restricted, symptoms such as chest pain occur.

entities/obstruccion-del-piloro/descript.text: The pylorus is a small portion of the stomach that serves as the entrance gate to the duodenum (the beginning of the small intestine), closing or opening to prevent or allow the passage of food. This function allows food to be digested by the stomach by preventing food from passing prematurely into the intestine under the effect of gravity. When the process of gastric digestion has finished, the pylorus opens, letting the chyme pass (a dense liquid formed by the food bolus and gastric juices) into the intestine, where a different type of digestion takes place. When the pylorus becomes obstructed, the passage of stomach contents into the duodenum is prevented, encouraging them to return to the esophagus (the duct connecting the mouth with the stomach). This action irritates the esophagus, causing heartburn and other symptoms. When food is in the stomach, a ring of muscle fibers prevents the food from going back up into the esophagus; these muscle fibers are called the lower esophageal sphincter, or LES. If the sphincter muscle does not close properly, stomach contents can flow back into the esophagus, which is called reflux or gastroesophageal reflux. Some of the most common symptoms of pyloric obstruction are the following: feeling that food is stuck behind the breastbone, nausea after eating, heartburn or burning pain in the chest (below the breastbone) that increases when bending over, leaning the body, lying down or eating.

entities/obstruccion-intestinal/descript.text: Intestinal obstruction is a mechanical or functional interruption of the intestines that prevents the normal transit of the products of digestion. It can occur at any level of the small intestine distal to the duodenum or of the colon. With biomagnetism, intestinal obstruction caused by stress, neurological dysfunction or inadequate diet can be corrected. In a proper diet, the basic components must be balanced: proteins, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins and minerals.

entities/obstruccion-pulmonar/descriptio.text: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a lung disorder characterized by the presence of airway obstruction that is generally progressive and irreversible. A higher incidence is found in people exposed to tobacco smoke, and its main symptom is a decrease in breathing capacity, which progresses slowly over the years and causes considerable deterioration in the quality of life of those affected, and may lead to premature death. The main types of COPD are chronic bronchitis and emphysema. The main cause of this disease is prolonged exposure to substances that irritate and damage the lungs, such as cigarette smoke, environmental pollution, chemical fumes and dust. At first, COPD may cause no symptoms or only very mild ones. As the disease progresses, the symptoms worsen and become more severe. They include: cough with a lot of phlegm, difficulty breathing (especially when exercising), wheezing, chest tightness.

entities/odio/description.text: Hatred is a feeling of deep antipathy, dislike, aversion, enmity or repulsion toward a person, thing or phenomenon, as well as the desire to avoid, limit or destroy it. Hatred can be based on fear, whether justified or not, or beyond the negative consequences of relating to it. Hatred can generate aversion, feelings of destruction, destruction of harmonious balance and occasionally self-destruction. Hatred is not justifiable from a rational point of view because it undermines the possibility of dialogue and shared construction. Hatred is an intense feeling of displeasure. It can occur in a wide variety of contexts, from hatred of inanimate objects or animals, to hatred of oneself or other people, entire groups of people, people in general, existence, society, or everything.

entities/ojeras/description.text: Dark circles under the eyes, better described in medical vocabulary as idiopathic hyperchromia of the orbital ring, correspond to an alteration in the coloration of the skin located below the eyes due to excessive melanin production and dilation of the capillaries close to the skin surface. These changes are usually produced by increased melanin and changes in the small spider veins that supply the area, but factors such as tiredness, insomnia and sun are also known to cause them.

entities/onchocerca-volvulus/description.text: Onchocerciasis is a chronic parasitic disease caused by a nematode worm called Onchocerca volvulus. The parasitic infestation causes potentially severe lesions in the skin and eyes and has become the second most important cause of blindness in the world. In the skin it causes itching, swelling, inflamed eruptions and rashes.

entities/oncocercosis/description.text: Onchocerciasis is a chronic parasitic disease caused by a nematode worm called Onchocerca volvulus. The parasitic infestation causes potentially severe lesions in the skin and eyes and has become the second most important cause of blindness in the world. In the skin it causes itching, swelling, inflamed eruptions and rashes.

entities/orf-virus/contagion.text: Orf virus is a virus that in sheep and goats produces the disease called contagious ecthyma, also called scabby mouth (contagious pustular dermatitis and sores and scabs in the mouth). It can also infect humans. The term orf comes from Old English and means rough. Contagious ecthyma is a zoonotic disease, that is, humans can contract the disease through direct contact with sheep and goats or through infected materials.

entities/orf-virus/description.text: It affects the retina. It causes keratoconus, an uncommon condition in which the cornea (the transparent part at the front of the eye) is abnormally thinned and protrudes forward in a cone shape, causing narrowed vision. In the disease contagious ecthyma (orf), the virus causes a purulent papule that appears locally and generally does not cause systemic symptoms. Infected sites include the fingers, hands, arms, face and even the penis (due to contact with the hand during urination). In the eyes it can cause serious damage, even among healthy people. The papule may persist for 7 to 10 weeks and heals spontaneously.

entities/osteomielitis/description.text: Osteomyelitis is a sudden or long-standing infection of the bone or bone marrow, usually caused by a pyogenic bacterium or mycobacteria and fungi. Risk factors are recent trauma, diabetes, hemodialysis and intravenous drug use. Staphylococcus aureus is the organism most commonly isolated in all forms of osteomyelitis. Hematogenously initiated osteomyelitis is frequently seen in children, and almost 90% of cases are caused by Staphylococcus aureus. It is an inflammation or swelling of bone tissue that usually occurs as the result of an infection.

entities/osteoporosis/description.text: Osteoporosis is a disease that affects the bones and is caused by a decrease in the bone mass that forms them, both of the proteins that make up their matrix or structure and of the calcium mineral salts they contain. As a consequence, the bone is less resistant and more fragile than normal, has less resistance to falls and breaks relatively easily after trauma, producing fractures or microfractures. Bone is a living tissue that is constantly being replaced by new bone. Osteoporosis occurs when the body is unable to produce enough new bone, or when a large amount of existing bone is reabsorbed by the body, or both. There are no symptoms in the initial stages of osteoporosis. Many times, people will have a fracture before they know they have the disease. Pain almost anywhere in the spine can be caused by fractures of the vertebrae, which often occur without an injury. The pain may come on suddenly or slowly. There may be a loss of height (up to 15 cm) over time.

entities/otitis/description.text: Otitis is inflammation of the ear or its tissues and parts. According to their anatomical location they are classified as otitis externa and otitis media. Otitis is usually more common during children's growth stages and may be associated with the arrival of spring. Its onset is also often linked to other more severe infectious processes, such as meningitis and encephalitis. The Eustachian tube runs from the middle ear to the back of the throat. This tube drains fluid that is normally produced in the middle ear. If the Eustachian tube becomes blocked, fluid may accumulate, which can cause an infection.

entities/oxiuros/contagion.text: It mainly infects children under 12 years of age, who can acquire it by eating contaminated food or by scratching the anus due to the itching produced by egg-laying in the perianal area and then putting their hands to their mouth.

entities/oxiuros/description.text: Enterobius vermicularis is a small nematode parasite of humans popularly known as pinworm. It causes the intestinal disease known as oxyuriasis or piduyes, whose correct name is enterobiasis. Symptoms may include intense pain and itching around the anus, especially during nighttime rest, sleep disturbance and weight loss.

entities/palidez/description.text: Pallor is an abnormal loss of color of the skin or mucous membranes. Pallor of the skin is probably not a serious condition and will not require treatment, unless it also appears on the lips, tongue, palms of the hands, inside of the mouth or in the lining of the eyes. Generalized pallor affects the whole body and is most easily observed in the face, the lining of the eyes, the inside of the mouth and the nails. Localized pallor usually affects a single limb. The ease of diagnosing pallor varies with skin color and with the thickness and number of blood vessels in the subcutaneous tissue. In blond or red-haired people, pallor may be normal. It can be very difficult to detect in a person with dark skin and sometimes becomes noticeable only in the lining of the eyes and mouth. Pallor can be the result of a decrease in blood supply to the skin (cold, fainting, shock, hypoglycemia) or a reduction in the number of red blood cells (anemia); it is different from loss of skin pigment, since pallor is related to blood flow in the skin rather than to the deposit of melanin in this part of the body.

entities/paludismo/contagion.text: Parasites of the genus Plasmodium. Blood transfusion. Pregnant mother to fetus. Bite of various species of infected mosquitoes of the genus Anopheles. Only the females of this mosquito feed on blood in order to mature their eggs; the males do not bite and cannot transmit diseases, since they feed only on nectar and plant juices. The infected female Anopheles carries Plasmodium in her salivary glands.

entities/paludismo/description.text: Malaria or paludism is a disease produced by parasites of the genus Plasmodium, and some scientific studies suggest that it may have been transmitted to humans through western gorillas. The disease can be caused by one or several of the different Plasmodium species: Plasmodium falciparum, Plasmodium vivax, Plasmodium malariae, Plasmodium ovale or Plasmodium knowlesi. The symptoms are very varied, beginning with fever, chills, sweating and headache. In addition, there may be nausea, vomiting, cough, bloody stools, muscle aches, jaundice (yellowish discoloration of the skin and mucous membranes), blood clotting defects, shock, kidney or liver failure, central nervous system disorders and coma. Fever and chills are cyclical symptoms, recurring every two or three days. Both kidneys must be scanned.

entities/pancreatitis/description.text: Pancreatitis is the sudden swelling and inflammation of the pancreas. The pancreas is an organ located behind the stomach that produces chemicals called enzymes, as well as the hormones insulin and glucagon. Most of the time, the enzymes are only active after they reach the small intestine, where they are needed to digest food. When these enzymes somehow become active inside the pancreas, they eat (and digest) the pancreatic tissue. This causes swelling, bleeding (hemorrhage) and damage to the pancreas and its blood vessels. The inflammation can be sudden (acute) or progressive (chronic). Acute pancreatitis generally involves a single "attack", after which the pancreas returns to its normal state. Severe acute pancreatitis can be life-threatening. In chronic pancreatitis, permanent damage to the pancreas and its function occurs, which usually leads to fibrosis (scarring). Apply a pancreatic belt, which consists of placing 4 magnets around the pancreas (-,+,-,+) at the following points: head, body, tail and tip. With the pancreatic belt, the heavy metals accumulated in the pancreas are released.

entities/paperas/description.text: Parotitis, popularly called mumps, is a contagious disease that can be acute or chronic, located mainly in one or both parotid glands, which are major salivary glands located behind the ascending rami of the mandible. It is caused by the mumps virus (Myxovirus parotitidis), which belongs to the Paramyxoviridae family. This virus normally causes the disease in children and adolescents, although it can also cause infections in susceptible adults. As a rule, the disease confers lifelong immunity, so it can be prevented by administration of a vaccine. Mumps can affect different glands of the body, the central nervous system and the testicles. The most frequent complications are meningitis and testicular inflammation, which can lead to infertility.

entities/papiloma/description.text: Human papillomavirus (HPV) comprises diverse groups of DNA viruses belonging to the family Papillomaviridae. It produces condyloma and warts on the vagina and penis. No virus can generate cancer; associated with Mycobacterium leprae it produces myomas and cysts. Women do have a prostate; it is behind the vagina. More than 100 viral types related to this condition are known.

entities/parainfluenza/description.text: Parainfluenza viruses are a group of paramyxoviruses about 100-200 nanometers in size. They normally produce frequent respiratory infections of variable severity. Upper respiratory tract infections are the most frequent infections produced by parainfluenza viruses; they occur both as primary infection and as reinfection, in childhood but above all in adults. They include sinusitis, rhinitis, pharyngitis, bronchitis or combinations of all of them (rhinosinusitis, rhinopharyngitis...) and febrile processes without an anatomical location. They correspond to the typical common cold or respiratory chill and are usually infections with a good prognosis, of mild severity, that resolve spontaneously after about eight days.

entities/paralisis-cerebral/description.text: Cerebral palsy (CP) is a permanent, nonprogressive disorder that affects the patient's psychomotor function. It is a group of disorders of psychomotor development that cause a limitation of the person's activity, attributed to problems in the brain development of the fetus or child. The psychomotor disorders of cerebral palsy are often accompanied by sensory, cognitive, communication and perception problems and, on some occasions, by behavioral disorders. The brain lesions of CP occur from the fetal period up to the age of 3 years. Brain damage after the age of 3 years and into adulthood can manifest as CP, but, by definition, these lesions are not CP. Cerebral palsy is a term that groups together a number of different conditions. It must be borne in mind that no two people with cerebral palsy have the same characteristics or the same diagnosis. Cerebral palsy is divided into four types, which describe the mobility problems they present. This division reflects the area of the brain that is damaged. The four classifications are: spastic (rigidity and shortening of muscles), athetoid (slow, uncontrolled, involuntary movements), ataxic (lack of coordination in the movement of body parts) and mixed (combinations of the above).

entities/paralisis-de-la-mirada/descript.text: In conjugate gaze palsy, the two eyes cannot move in the same direction (from side to side, up or down) at the same time. Conjugate gaze palsy most frequently affects horizontal gaze (looking to one side). Upward gaze is affected less frequently, and downward gaze even less. People notice that they cannot look in certain directions.

entities/paralisis-facial/description.text: Facial paralysis is dysfunction in the area of cranial nerve VII (facial nerve) that results in the inability to control the facial muscles on the side of the affected nerve. It occurs when a person is no longer able to move some or any of the muscles on one side of the face.

entities/paralisis/description.text: Paralysis is the loss of muscle function in parts of the body. It occurs when something goes wrong in the transmission of messages between the brain and the muscles. Paralysis can be total or partial. It can occur on one or both sides of the body. It can also occur in only one place or spread. Paralysis of the lower half of the body, affecting both legs, is called paraplegia. Paralysis affecting the arms and legs is quadriplegia. Most cases of paralysis are due to strokes or injuries, such as spinal cord injuries or a broken neck. Other causes of paralysis include: nerve diseases, such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis; autoimmune diseases, such as Guillain–Barré syndrome; and Bell's palsy, which affects the muscles of the face.

entities/paramixovirus/description.text: They can produce itching, irritation and dryness of the sexual organs. Paramyxoviruses are members of the Paramyxoviridae virus family, which have a single-stranded, negative-sense RNA genome as their nucleic acid.
