Vertebrates serve as natural hosts; there are no known plants that serve as vectors. There are currently 49 species in this family, divided into 7 genera. Members of this virus family are responsible for various human diseases, such as measles and mumps; two of the viruses are known to cause pneumonia in humans: respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and parainfluenza virus. Parainfluenza virus also causes bronchitis and croup, especially in children. Paramyxoviruses are also responsible for a variety of diseases in other animal species, for example canine distemper virus (dogs), phocine distemper virus (seals), cetacean morbillivirus (dolphins and porpoises), Newcastle disease virus (birds) and rinderpest virus (cattle).

entities/paranoia/description.text: Paranoia is a mental health condition in which a person has a prolonged pattern of distrust and suspicion of others but does not have a full psychotic disorder such as schizophrenia. People with paranoid personality disorder are highly suspicious of others and as a result drastically limit their social life. They frequently feel they are in danger and look for evidence to support their suspicions. People with this disorder have difficulty seeing that their distrust is out of proportion to their surroundings.

entities/pares-craneales/description.text: It is located on the upper cartilage of the ear, above the auditory canal. It corrects problems of intoxication and regulates the functions of the cranial nerves, nervous tics and severe headaches. This pair supports dysfunctions of the cranial nerves left by neurological pathologies that damage them, as in the case of facial paralysis, cerebrovascular accidents, traumatic brain injuries and, in general, those injuries or pathologies that impair the function of the cranial nerves. The cranial pairs, also called cranial nerves, are twelve pairs of nerves that arise directly from the brain or at the level of the brainstem and are distributed through the foramina at the base of the skull to the head, neck, thorax and abdomen. The cranial nerves are the following: 1) Olfactory nerve: transmits olfactory impulses. 2) Optic nerve: transmits visual information to the brain. 3) Oculomotor nerve (or common ocular motor nerve): innervates the muscles that perform most eye movements. 4) Trochlear nerve (or pathetic nerve): innervates the muscle that depresses, laterally rotates (around the optic axis) and internally rotates the eyeball. 5) Trigeminal nerve: perceives sensory information from the face and innervates the muscles of mastication. 6) Abducens nerve (or external ocular motor nerve): innervates the muscle that abducts the eyeball. 7) Facial nerve: Carries motor innervation to the muscles responsible for facial expression, the posterior belly of the digastric muscle and the stapedius; receives taste impulses from the anterior two thirds of the tongue and provides secretomotor innervation to the salivary glands (except the parotid) and the lacrimal gland; it runs through the internal auditory canal to the facial canal and exits through the stylomastoid foramen. 8) Vestibulocochlear nerve (or auditory nerve): Perception of sound, rotation and gravity (essential for balance and movement). The vestibular branch carries impulses to coordinate balance and the cochlear branch carries auditory impulses. 9) Glossopharyngeal nerve: Receives taste impulses from the posterior third of the tongue, provides secretomotor innervation to the parotid gland and motor innervation to the stylopharyngeus muscle and the styloglossus muscle. It also relays some information to the brain from the palatine tonsils. This information goes to the opposite thalamus and some nuclei of the hypothalamus. 10) Vagus nerve (or pneumogastric nerve): Provides innervation to most of the laryngeal muscles and all the pharyngeal muscles, except the stylopharyngeus (innervated by the glossopharyngeal); carries parasympathetic fibers to the vicinity of all the abdominal viscera located below the splenic flexure; and receives the sense of taste from the epiglottis. It controls the muscles that help articulate sounds in the soft palate. Symptoms of damage include dysphagia and velopharyngeal insufficiency. 11) Accessory nerve (or cranial accessory nerve or spinal accessory nerve): Controls the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles; it overlaps with functions of the vagus. Symptoms of damage include inability to shrug the shoulders and weakness of head movements. 12) Hypoglossal nerve: provides motor innervation to the muscles of the tongue (except the palatoglossus muscle, which is innervated by the vagus nerve, and the styloglossus muscle, which is innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve) and other lingual muscles. Important in swallowing (bolus formation) and the articulation of sounds. Proposed nerves: 0) Cranial nerve zero: recent research indicates that it may have a role in the detection of pheromones. It joins the olfactory system in human embryos.

entities/parestesia/description.text: Paresthesia is a condition in which a part of the body, usually a foot or a hand, begins to tingle and goes numb. This sensation can occur either temporarily or chronically. In most cases it is a short-term condition caused by pressure on a nerve, and the tingling sensation subsides within minutes. The tingling sensation occurs without any warning, is usually painless and is generally described as numbness or itching. When someone experiences paresthesia on a regular basis, it could indicate a more significant problem in the body. Frequent cases may be symptoms that the neurons in the brain are not working correctly because they are not properly transmitting signals to the brain. In other cases, nerve problems may be related to diabetes, malnutrition, thyroid problems or other underlying medical problems. In addition to problems with neuronal function, chronic cases of paresthesia can also be associated with damage to the nerves themselves. Some possible causes of nerve damage are Lyme disease, multiple sclerosis or a brain tumor.

entities/parkinson/description.text: Parkinson's disease is a chronic neurodegenerative disorder that leads to progressive disability, produced as a consequence of the destruction of the pigmented neurons of the substantia nigra of the brain. It is a movement disorder that also triggers alterations in cognitive function, in the expression of emotions and in autonomic function. A neurotransmitter is a chemical substance released from a nerve ending that interacts with a specific receptor to produce different physiological responses. They are made from amino acids, and vitamins and minerals are also required. Dopamine is a chemical messenger responsible for transmitting signals between the substantia nigra of the brain and the corpus striatum to produce smooth, purposeful movements. The loss of dopamine produces abnormal patterns of nerve activation within the brain that cause impaired movement; patients lose dopamine-producing cells in the substantia nigra. The medicinal plants that support the treatment of Parkinson's disease are the following: sage (Salvia officinalis), green tea (Thea sinensis) and Ojo de Gallina herb (Galphimia glauca).

entities/parvovirus/description.text: Parvovirus is the common name applied to all viruses of the family Parvoviridae. It is the main cause of female infertility; the second is chickenpox. One tube becomes positive and the other negative; the positive one rejects the semen (sperm), whose charge is positive, and the negative one rejects the ovum, whose charge is negative. This prevents fertilization.

entities/pasteurella/description.text: Pasteurella is a genus of Gram-negative bacteria, very small and coccobacillary in shape, although they tend to be somewhat pleomorphic. These microorganisms are nonmotile, aerobic or facultatively anaerobic, catalase-positive, oxidase-positive, encapsulated, non-spore-forming and indole-positive; some species are hemolytic. Pasteurella generally does not cause disease and is a natural part of the bacterial flora of the nose and mouth. When an infection occurs, the following symptoms may appear: swelling, cellulitis and bloody discharge at the wound site. Infections can progress to nearby joints, where they can cause inflammation and arthritis. When it affects the descending colon, it prevents proteins from being absorbed and, consequently, muscle mass is lost.

entities/patogenos-bucales-reservorio/de.text: Universal reservoir. Problems of pathogens lodged in teeth. If we divide the mouth into 4, two upper parts and two lower parts, each part contains the following teeth: 1) Incisors: 2 teeth: central incisor and lateral incisor; they are shovel-shaped and their function is to cut food. 2) Canine: 1 tooth, commonly called the eyetooth (fang); its function is to tear food. 3) Premolars: 2 teeth; they take part in both tearing and grinding food; they are slightly smaller than the molars. 4) Molars: 3 teeth, commonly called back teeth; their function is to chew and grind food. The last molar is known as the wisdom tooth. The lower teeth are lodged in the mandible or lower jaw (bone); the upper teeth are lodged in the maxilla or upper jaw (bone).

entities/paty/description.text: Pair related to extrauterine pregnancy. Paty de la Garza was the first person who helped Dr. Goiz teach the courses in Monterrey, followed by Sofía and later the IUTT.

entities/perdida-de-peso-involuntaria/de.text: Involuntary weight loss is a decrease in body weight when one is not trying to lose weight. Many people gain or put on weight. Involuntary weight loss is the loss of 5 kilograms or 5% of one's normal body weight over 6 to 12 months or less without knowing the reason. Weight loss is normally accompanied by weakness and a tendency to tire. It generally occurs in response to an insufficient intake of calories relative to the person's metabolic needs and takes place at the expense of adipose tissue (fat) stores. In more severe cases, atrophy of muscle mass and dryness of the skin are also observed.

entities/pereza/description.text: People who avoid doing any activity whose benefit is not immediate are called idle, lazy, slothful, loafers, sluggards, procrastinators or negligent. The causes of having this tendency can be varied, from poor nutrition and illness to simply that the activities they perform are not beneficial to them. In the case of human beings, the brain is very large and consumes a great deal of energy (20 % of the total the body needs), whether it is used or not. Not using it means a waste of energy. To avoid this, an unpleasant sensation, boredom, keeps the brain from remaining inactive, and a pleasant one, curiosity, moves the individual to seek some kind of interesting activity, even if there is no immediate need. The activities do not have to be purely mental; any activity that involves the brain will do, from reading to playing sports.

entities/perforacion-intestinal/descript.text: An intestinal perforation is a rupture through all the layers of the small intestine. This perforation can be a complication in which the intestinal contents are released into the peritoneal cavity, producing peritonitis. The intestinal contents may also be released into neighboring organs such as the pancreas, in the case of perforation of an ulcer on the posterior wall of the duodenum, producing penetration into the pancreas. A patient with an intestinal perforation presents with abdominal pain as the main symptom. This pain can be significant, so the patient should be asked about the characteristics of the pain, such as its course, intensity and onset, and depending on its location and radiation, one can begin to determine which organ(s) are involved.

entities/pericarditis-infecciosa/contagi.text: Infectious pericarditis is normally caused by a viral infection; less frequently it can be caused by a bacterial infection and rarely by a fungal infection.

entities/pericarditis-infecciosa/descrip.text: Pericarditis is a condition in which the sac-like covering around the heart (pericardium) becomes inflamed. There is usually chest pain that may be felt in the neck, shoulder, back or abdomen; it frequently increases with deep breathing and when lying flat; it may increase with coughing and swallowing.

entities/periodontitis/contagion.text: Having high levels of the bacterium Treponema denticola in the mouth is considered one of the main etiological agents of periodontitis. Also caused by the bacterium Veillonella.

entities/periodontitis/description.text: Periodontitis is a disease that may initially present with gingivitis and then proceed to loss of collagen attachment, gingival recession and bone loss if not treated, leaving the tooth without bony support. The loss of that support means the irreparable loss of the tooth itself. Periodontitis is the main cause of tooth loss in adults. Plaque and tartar accumulate at the base of the teeth; the inflammation resulting from this accumulation causes pockets to form between the gum and the teeth, which fill with tartar and plaque. The inflammation of the soft tissue traps the plaque in the pocket. Continued inflammation leads to damage of the tissues and bone around the tooth. Because plaque contains bacteria, infection is likely to occur, and a dental abscess may also develop. This also increases the rate of bone destruction. Some of the symptoms that occur are the following: bad breath, gums that are bright red or reddish-purple, gums that look shiny, gums that bleed easily (blood on the toothbrush, even when brushing gently), gums that may be tender to the touch (but otherwise do not hurt), loose teeth, swollen gums.

entities/peritonitis/description.text: Peritonitis is an inflammation of the peritoneum, the serous membrane that lines part of the abdominal cavity and the viscera. Peritonitis may be localized or generalized in the peritoneum and may result from infection (often due to rupture of a hollow organ, as can occur in abdominal trauma or appendicitis) or from a non-infectious process. Acute peritonitis usually manifests with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, fever, hypotension, tachycardia and thirst. Peritonitis also has to do with the appendix: when it becomes inflamed it bursts, releasing bacteria throughout the body. Peritonitis can cause dehydration in the patient and lead to multiple organ or multisystem failure, which results in death in most cases.

entities/pesimismo/description.text: Pessimism is a state of mind and a philosophical doctrine holding that we live in the worst of all possible worlds, a world where pain is perpetual and our destiny is to try to obtain what we will never have. Pessimism denies the progress of civilization and of human nature. From the psychological point of view, it constitutes one of the most notable traits or symptoms of the disease known as depression.

entities/peste/description.text: Yersinia pestis causes a bronchitis-type laryngeal cough. In women: vaginal discharge; in men: azoospermia (an organic disorder in which the man has no measurable level of sperm in his semen; it is associated with very low levels of fertility). In humans, Yersinia pestis produces pneumonic plague (infection of the lungs), bubonic plague (infection of the lymph nodes) and also septicemic plague (infection of the blood). Yersinia pestis is an infectious agent that has been directly responsible for more human deaths than any other infectious disease. Bubonic plague: this is the most common type of infection. Once the bacterial cells have been introduced into a human by a flea bite, they travel through the bloodstream to the lymph nodes, where they generate small swellings called buboes, which are filled with bacterial particles. The viscous capsule surrounding Yersinia pestis cells prevents them from being phagocytosed by macrophages. Within a short time, the peripheral lymph nodes are invaded by secondary buboes, until they rupture and the cells pass back into the bloodstream, but now in much greater numbers, which causes generalized septicemia. In this state, multiple hemorrhages occur that give rise to black spots on the skin, gangrenous processes at the distal ends of the extremities, severe pain in the lymph nodes, prostration, shock and delirium. If the plague is not treated before the septicemic stage, death ensues within 3-5 days. Pneumonic plague: this type of infection occurs when Yersinia pestis cells are inhaled directly, or reach the lungs during bubonic plague. The infection usually runs its course without symptoms until the last two days of the infective process, during which large amounts of bloody sputum are expelled. In the absence of treatment, death ensues in 2-3 days. Septicemic plague: this infection involves a rapid dispersal of Yersinia pestis throughout the body via the bloodstream, without time for buboes to form. Death usually ensues within one day, so there is usually no time for it to be diagnosed before autopsy.

entities/peyronie/description.text: Peyronie's disease, also called induratio penis plastica or IPP, is a disease of unknown cause, characterized by the formation of a fibrous band in the tunica albuginea of the corpora cavernosa of the penis that causes deviation or curvature of the penis during erection. Depending on the extent of the fibrous band, the process may make penetration impossible or make erection painful. The most common presenting symptoms are penile deformity and pain during erection, as well as erectile dysfunction. Pain appears during the inflammatory phase of the disease; it is generally mild and occurs during erection. The curvature of the penis may be toward its dorsal, ventral or lateral side, producing shortening of the penis.

entities/picaduras-de-insectos/descripti.text: Insect bites and stings can cause an immediate skin reaction. Fire ant bites and bee, wasp and hornet stings are generally painful. Mosquito, flea and mite bites are more likely to cause itching than pain. In most cases, bites and stings can easily be treated at home; however, some people have severe allergic reactions. This is a potentially fatal allergic reaction called anaphylaxis that requires urgent medical attention. Severe reactions can affect the entire body and can occur very quickly, often within a few minutes. If left untreated, these severe reactions can quickly become fatal. Some spider bites, such as those of the black widow or the brown recluse, are also serious and can be fatal. Most spider bites, however, are harmless. The Adrenal gland - Adrenal gland pair helps reduce inflammation and eliminate any toxin produced by insect bites.

entities/picornavirus/description.text: Picornaviridae is a family of viruses infectious to animals. The picornaviruses include important pathogens of humans and animals. The diseases they cause are varied, such as the common cold, poliomyelitis and chronic infections in livestock. Two main categories are the Enteroviruses and the Rhinoviruses. Enteroviruses infect the enteric tract, while Rhinoviruses mainly infect the nose and throat. The former replicate at 37 °C, while the latter grow best at 33 °C, since this is the lower temperature of the nose. Enteroviruses are stable under acidic conditions and are therefore able to survive exposure to gastric acid. In contrast, Rhinoviruses are acid-labile and for this reason are confined to the nose and throat.

entities/pie-de-atleta/description.text: Athlete's foot is a fungal infection of the feet, and its medical name is tinea pedis. Besides the toes, it can also occur on the heels, the palms of the hands and between the fingers. Athlete's foot is the most common type of tinea fungal infection. The fungus thrives in warm, moist areas. The risk of getting this condition increases if you: wear closed shoes (especially if they are plastic-lined), keep your feet wet for long periods, sweat a lot, or develop a minor injury to the nails or skin. Athlete's foot is contagious and can be spread by direct contact or by contact with items such as shoes, socks and swimming pool or shower surfaces. The most common symptom is cracked, flaking, peeling skin between the toes or on the sides of the foot. Other symptoms may include: red, itchy skin, burning or stinging, and blisters that ooze or crust. If the fungus spreads to the nails, they may become discolored, thickened and even crumble. Athlete's foot can occur at the same time as other fungal skin infections such as dermatophytosis and tinea cruris.

entities/pigmentacion-de-la-piel/descrip.text: Pigmentation means coloration. Skin coloration disorders affect the color of the skin. Skin cells give it its color by producing a substance called melanin. When these cells are damaged or become diseased, melanin production is affected. Some pigmentation disorders affect only certain areas of the skin; others affect the whole body. If the body produces too much melanin, the skin darkens. Pregnancy, Addison's disease and sun exposure can darken the skin. If the body produces too little melanin, the skin becomes lighter. Vitiligo is a condition that causes patches of light skin. Albinism is a genetic condition that affects all of a person's skin. Infections, blisters and burns can be other causes of lighter areas of skin.

entities/pitiriasis-versicolor/descripti.text: The fungus Malassezia furfur is part of the normal flora of people's skin and is the cause of dandruff and of an infectious, non-contagious skin disease called pityriasis versicolor. Pityriasis versicolor (also called tinea versicolor) is an infectious, cutaneous, superficial, chronic disease characterized by patches on the skin (hypo- or hyperpigmented macules) and is usually asymptomatic.

entities/plasmodium-falciparum/contagion.text: Blood transfusion. Pregnant mother to fetus. Bite of various species of infected mosquitoes of the genus Anopheles. As is known, only the females of this mosquito feed on blood in order to mature their eggs; the males do not bite and cannot transmit diseases, since they feed only on nectar and plant juices. The infected female Anopheles carries Plasmodium in her salivary glands.

entities/plasmodium-falciparum/descripti.text: Plasmodium falciparum is a parasite, one of the species of the genus Plasmodium that causes paludism or malaria in humans. It transmits the most dangerous form of malaria, with the highest rates of complications and mortality, producing 80% of all malaria infections and 90% of deaths from the disease. It is the only one capable of producing cerebral malaria. It causes death by coma and anemia.

entities/plasmodium-vivax/contagion.text: Blood transfusion. Pregnant mother to fetus. Bite of various species of infected mosquitoes of the genus Anopheles. As is known, only the females of this mosquito feed on blood in order to mature their eggs; the males do not bite and cannot transmit diseases, since they feed only on nectar and plant juices. The infected female Anopheles carries Plasmodium in her salivary glands.

entities/plasmodium-vivax/description.text: Plasmodium vivax is a parasite, one of the species of the genus Plasmodium that cause paludism, also called malaria. The symptoms are highly varied, beginning with high fevers, chills, flu-like symptoms, sweating, anemia and headache. In addition, there may be nausea, vomiting, cough, bloody stools, muscle aches, nausea, jaundice, blood coagulation defects, shock, kidney or liver failure, central nervous system disorders, seizures and coma. After infection, the parasites (called sporozoites) migrate through the bloodstream to the liver, where they mature and produce another form, the merozoites. The parasites enter the bloodstream and infect the red blood cells. The parasites multiply inside the cells, which rupture after 48 to 72 hours, infecting more red blood cells. The first symptoms usually appear 10 days to 4 weeks after infection, although they can appear as early as 8 days or as late as 1 year afterward. The symptoms occur in cycles of 48 to 72 hours. Both kidneys should be scanned.

entities/pleuritis-viral/description.text: Viral pleuritis. Breathing becomes difficult. Inflammation of the parietal pleura (the covering over the inner surface of the rib cage) and of the visceral pleura (the covering of the lungs), generally as a consequence of pneumonia. Because these membranes are in contact with the infected lungs, they tend to become inflamed, giving rise to a sharp pain similar to a stab wound, which intensifies on deep inspiration or coughing. It is rare and occurs in outbreaks. It simulates pneumonia or bronchitis with fever.

entities/pleuritis/description.text: Pleuritis, also known as pleurisy, is a disease consisting of inflammation of the parietal pleura (the lining over the inner surface of the rib cage) and of the visceral pleura (the lining of the lungs), usually as a consequence of pneumonia. As these membranes are in contact with the infected lungs, they tend to become inflamed, giving rise to a sharp pain similar to a stab wound, pain that intensifies on deep inspiration or coughing. The main symptom of pleuritis is chest pain. This pain often occurs when inhaling or exhaling deeply or when coughing. Some people feel the pain in the shoulder. Deep breathing, coughing and chest movement make the pain worse. Pleuritis can cause fluid to accumulate inside the chest cavity, which can make breathing difficult and cause a bluish discoloration of the skin (cyanosis), cough, difficulty breathing and rapid breathing (tachypnea).

entities/pneumocystis-carini/contagion.text: It is an opportunistic infection caused by a fungus that lodges in people with a compromised immune system, especially those who have received chemotherapy, AIDS treatments and immunosuppressants.

entities/pneumocystis-carini/description.text: Pneumocystis jirovecii, also known as Pneumocystis carinii or Pneumocystis pneumonia, is a pathogenic, opportunistic, extracellular fungus that parasitizes the human respiratory tree. Acute respiratory syndrome. It is a form of pneumonia. It produces fever, chronic cough, phlegm, shortness of breath, weight loss, chronic bronchitis, night sweats. It manifests in the lung.

entities/pneumocystis-jirovecii/contagio.text: It is an opportunistic infection caused by a fungus that lodges in people with a compromised immune system, especially those who have received chemotherapy, AIDS treatments and immunosuppressants.

entities/pneumocystis-jirovecii/descript.text: Pneumocystis jirovecii, also known as Pneumocystis carinii or Pneumocystis pneumonia, is a pathogenic, opportunistic, extracellular fungus that parasitizes the human respiratory tree. Acute respiratory syndrome. It is a form of pneumonia. It produces fever, chronic cough, phlegm, shortness of breath, weight loss, chronic bronchitis, night sweats. It manifests in the lung.

entities/polifagia/contagion.text: Among the diseases that trigger polyphagia are bulimia, hyperthyroidism, hypoglycemia, the intake of certain drugs, the action of some muscle relaxants associated with anesthesia (phenobarbital), premenstrual syndrome or the cessation of menstruation, among others. It is also one of the main symptoms of diabetes mellitus.

entities/poliglobulia/description.text: Polycythemia, also known as plethora, erythrocytosis or polyglobulia, is a disorder in which the hematocrit increases, that is, the proportion of red blood cells per blood volume, due to an increase in the number of erythrocytes or a decrease in blood plasma. It is the opposite of anemia, which occurs when there is a shortage of red blood cells or hemoglobin in the circulation. It corrects the excess of red blood cells in the blood. It corrects hematic (blood) alterations, mainly of hemoglobin and leukocytes, whose levels are above or below the standard mean. With these pairs, anemia problems that are not corrected by providing iron are also corrected. The classic complaints consist of marked headache, poor concentration, decreased hearing, pain in the feet and hands, generalized reddening of the skin, very reddened ocular conjunctivae, fatigue, dizziness; blood pressure tends to rise, and in more advanced stages it leads to heart failure. Polyglobulia causes an increase in the thickness or density of the blood, which causes the blood to stop perfusing some areas of the body, above all those where the caliber of the veins is very small.

entities/polineuritis/description.text: The term neuritis is used in medicine to describe inflammation of a nerve, which may result in pain, increased sensitivity, lack of sensation or a tingling sensation (paresthesia) in the affected area of the body. By extension, the word neuritis is used when the function of a peripheral nerve is affected even if there is no inflammation. If a single nerve is affected, the situation is described as mononeuritis, and when several are affected it is called polyneuritis. According to the time over which the disease develops, it is classified as acute when it sets in over a few days, subacute when it sets in over weeks or a few months, and chronic when it takes years to set in.

entities/polioma-virus/description.text: Polyomaviridae is a family of viruses containing a single genus, Polyomavirus, which infects animals and humans. Some of its symptoms are: appetite disturbances, anorexia, sleep and balance disturbances. Psychological disturbances.

entities/poliomielitis/description.text: Poliomyelitis is an infectious disease, also known by the abbreviated name polio, that mainly affects the nervous system. The disease is produced by the poliovirus. It is called infantile because the people who contract the disease are mainly children. It is transmitted from person to person through respiratory secretions or by the fecal-oral route. Most polio infections are asymptomatic. In only 1% of cases does the virus enter the central nervous system (CNS) via the bloodstream. Within the CNS, the poliovirus preferentially infects and destroys motor neurons, which causes muscle weakness and acute flaccid paralysis. Poliomyelitis is a highly infectious disease, but it is fought with vaccination. The disease affects the central nervous system. In its acute form it causes inflammation of the motor neurons of the spinal cord and brain and leads to paralysis, muscle atrophy and very often deformity. In the worst cases it can cause permanent paralysis or death when the diaphragm becomes paralyzed.

entities/poliovirus/description.text: Poliovirus is a virus belonging to the genus Enterovirus, of the family Picornaviridae. It is the causative agent of poliomyelitis in humans. It affects the nervous system. It affects the spinal cord and produces atrophy. Nerve disorders, may be unilateral. Paralysis. In only 1 % of cases does the virus enter the central nervous system (CNS) via the bloodstream. Within the CNS, poliovirus preferentially infects and destroys motor neurons. This destruction of neurons causes muscle weakness and acute flaccid paralysis. In its acute form it causes inflammation of the motor neurons of the spinal cord and brain and leads to paralysis, muscle atrophy and very often deformity. In the worst cases it can cause permanent paralysis or death when the diaphragm becomes paralyzed.

entities/polipos-nasales/description.text: Nasal polyposis or nasal polyps are masses that affect the inside of the nose (and the paranasal sinuses) due to the growth of benign tumors that obstruct breathing. It is a special form of sinusitis (called "polypoid sinusitis"). The most common symptoms are: difficulty breathing through the nose (mouth breathing, snoring), altered or absent sense of smell (anosmia), nasal voice or permanent nasal congestion, excessive nasal mucus.

entities/poliuria/description.text: Polyuria is a medical symptom consisting of the passage of a greater volume of urine than expected. It is an excessive urinary output. The most frequent causes are: increased fluid intake, abuse of alcohol or stimulant beverages containing caffeine, theine, etc., excess solutes (salt, glucose, etc.), use of drugs, consumption of infusions (tea, mate, etc.), certain diseases, psychogenic (nonorganic) causes, and a sensation of excessive cold. It is defined as a volume greater than 3 liters (3,000 ml.) in 24 hours for adults, and greater than 2-2.5 liters in 24 hours for children. The amount of urine excreted depends on the body's fluid and electrolyte balance. Excess fluid or the need to eliminate an excess of dissolved substances can lead to an increase in the amount of urine produced by the kidneys. It also depends on the filtering capacity of the kidney: when there is kidney failure, the tubules may be unable to reabsorb the filtered blood, which leads to an increase in the amount of urine formed. It should not be confused with pollakiuria, which is a situation of increased urinary frequency (the number of times one urinates per day) regardless of the volume of urine excreted.

entities/prada/description.text: Pair related to the virus reservoir in the gallbladder (Hepatitis & HIV). This pair was named in honor of Dr. Juan Manuel Prada, who has played an important role in research on biomagnetic pairs, both in certifying their existence and in assessing their depolarization.

entities/preeclampsia/description.text: Pre-eclampsia is a medical complication of pregnancy; it is associated with pregnancy-induced hypertension and with elevated levels of protein in the urine (proteinuria). Because pre-eclampsia refers to a clinical picture or set of symptoms, rather than a specific causal factor, it has been established that there may be several etiologies for the disorder. There may be a component in the placenta that causes endothelial dysfunction in the maternal blood vessels of susceptible women. Although the most notable sign of the disease is elevated blood pressure, it can lead to eclampsia (seizures or coma during pregnancy), with damage to the maternal endothelium, kidneys and liver. The only treatment is delivery, with induction of labor or cesarean section being the most common procedures. It can appear up to six weeks postpartum. It is the most common and dangerous complication of pregnancy, so it must be diagnosed and treated quickly, since in severe cases it endangers the life of the fetus and the mother.

entities/priones-reservorio/description.text: Prion diseases. It attacks the central nervous system. Neurodegenerative diseases. It affects skin and hair. Example: mad cow disease. A prion is an infectious particle formed by a protein called prion protein, which produces transmissible degenerative neurological diseases such as scrapie, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and bovine spongiform encephalopathy. Unlike the rest of the infectious agents (viruses, bacteria, fungi etc...), which contain nucleic acids (DNA, RNA, or both), a prion is composed only of amino acids and has no genetic material. The word prion is an English acronym derived from the words protein and infection. When a prion enters a healthy organism, it acts on the normal form of the same type of protein existing in the organism, modifying it and converting it into a prion. These newly formed prions can go on to convert more proteins, causing a chain reaction that produces large quantities of the prion protein.

entities/prostatitis/description.text: Prostatitis is an inflammation of the prostate gland. The prostatic tissue becomes inflamed. It comprises a group of syndromes, diseases and functional disorders affecting the prostate or the perineal area. It usually appears in young adults or middle-aged men. It is the most frequent urinary infection in men between the second and fourth decades of life. This problem can be caused by a bacterial infection. Acute prostatitis begins rapidly, whereas chronic prostatitis lasts 3 months or more. Continuous irritation of the prostate that is not caused by bacteria is called chronic abacterial prostatitis. Any bacterium that can cause a urinary infection can produce acute bacterial prostatitis. Sexually transmitted infections can cause prostatitis. These include chlamydia and gonorrhea.

entities/proteus-mirabilis/description.text: Proteus mirabilis is a gram-negative, facultatively anaerobic bacillus; it shows agglutination and motility and produces high levels of urease, which hydrolyzes urea to ammonia, making the urine more alkaline. As alkalinity rises, crystals of struvite, calcium carbonate and/or apatite may form. This bacterium can be found in stones and, hidden there, can restart an infection after antibiotic treatment. It produces pain on breathing, and pleural, pulmonary and diaphragmatic manifestations. Inflammation of the area separating the two lungs. Mediastinitis with laryngeal, pulmonary and bronchial symptoms; it gives a false AIDS when combined with another virus; it traps the thymus both anatomically and functionally; it causes immunodeficiency. It produces irritation, infection and degeneration of the cauda equina, infertility, and muscular problems in movements and joints of the lower limb.

entities/proteus-vulgaris/description.text: Proteus vulgaris is a Gram-negative, facultatively anaerobic, rod-shaped bacterium that inhabits the intestinal tract; it can also be isolated from soil, water and fecal matter. It is an opportunistic pathogen in humans, causing urinary tract infections, wound infections and liver abscesses.

entities/pseudomona-aeruginosa/descripti.text: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a species of Gram-negative, aerobic bacteria with unipolar motility. It is an opportunistic pathogen of immunocompromised individuals; it infects the lungs and airways, the urinary tract and tissues (wounds), and also causes other forms of sepsis (generalized infections in the body). It can cause pneumonia, digestive problems, cough and asthma. It is believed to give rise to metastases. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a rod-shaped, flagellated bacterium that produces fluorescent pigments whose colors can range from red to black. It is a very widespread bacterium and can be found in water, soil, animals or plants, since its nutritional requirements are minimal, although the diseases produced by this bacterium are associated with its preference for moist environments. In humans it can be found in the moistest areas of the body, such as the armpits, the ears and the area around the anus. It is very uncommon for Pseudomonas aeruginosa to cause disorders in healthy people. Disease arises as a result of alterations in the host's normal defenses. This may involve the loss of the protection provided by the mucous membranes or the skin. Its minimal nutritional requirements, adaptability and relative resistance to antibiotics allow this bacterium to survive near its host.

entities/psicosis/description.text: Psychosis is a generic term used in psychiatry and psychoanalysis to refer to a mental state described as a split from, or loss of contact with, reality. People who suffer from it are called psychotic. The term "psychotic" is often confused with the term psychopath, a personality disorder with no relation whatsoever to psychosis. People who experience psychosis may have hallucinations or delusions and may exhibit changes in their personality and disorganized thinking. These symptoms may be accompanied by unusual or strange behavior, as well as difficulty interacting socially and inability to carry out activities of daily living.

entities/psoriasis/description.text: Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease of autoimmune origin that produces thickened, inflamed, scaly lesions, with wide clinical and evolutionary variability. It is not contagious, although it can be hereditary, and men are more likely to inherit it than women. It can affect any part of the skin, frequently the areas of the elbows, knees, scalp, abdomen and back. It is not uncommon for it to involve the nails. This is known as nail psoriasis. The nails may be the only affected area at the onset of psoriasis. It sometimes produces complications such as psoriatic arthritis.

entities/pterigion/description.text: Pterygium is an abnormal growth, due to inflammation, of conjunctival tissue (the thin, transparent tissue covering the outer surface of the eye), which tends to extend from the white of the eye toward the corneal tissue (the anterior, transparent surface of the eye). This abnormal tissue becomes inflamed due to lack of lubrication (lack of tears), sun exposure, wind or other irritants. Those who suffer from it have the sensation of a foreign body in the eye, and the eye has a congested appearance (red eye).

entities/quemadura/description.text: A burn is a type of injury to the skin or other tissues that can be caused by various causes. Less serious burns are produced by contact with flames, hot liquids, hot surfaces and other sources of high temperatures, or by contact with elements at extremely low temperatures. There are also chemical burns and electrical burns. The immediate first-aid treatment for mild burns consists of running room-temperature water over the affected area, to try to normalize the temperature of the burned tissues and remove contaminants. It is preferable for the water to flow over the affected part rather than immersing it, always taking care not to use cold water because of the possibility of generating a thermal reaction that would separate the upper layers of the skin, making healing difficult. Burns can be categorized into three groups: first, second and third degree. First-degree burns are limited to the superficial layer of the skin, the epidermis; they may be called erythema or epidermal burns. This type of burn is generally caused by prolonged exposure to the sun or instantaneous exposure to another form of heat (an iron, hot liquids). Second-degree burns are divided into superficial and deep. Superficial burns involve the first layer and part of the second layer of the skin. There is no damage to the deeper layers, nor to the sweat glands or the oil-producing glands. There is pain and the presence of phlyctenae or blisters. Deep burns involve damage to the middle layer and to the sweat glands or the oil-producing glands. There may be skin loss and charring. A third-degree burn penetrates the entire thickness of the skin, including nerve endings, blood vessels, lymphatics, etc. The pilosebaceous follicles and sweat glands are destroyed, and the capacity for regeneration is compromised. This type of burn does not hurt to the touch, because the nerve endings were destroyed by the thermal source.

entities/quistes-en-pulmon/description.text: A cyst is a closed sac with its own membrane that develops abnormally in a cavity or structure of the body. Cysts occur as a result of an error in embryonic development during pregnancy. However, they sometimes appear spontaneously with no apparent cause. Cysts can be dangerous, often because of the negative effects they can have on nearby tissues. They can contain air, fluids or semisolid material. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a chronic, fatal disease characterized by a progressive decline in lung function. The term pulmonary fibrosis refers to scarring of the lung tissue and is the cause of worsening dyspnea (shortness of breath). Fibrosis is normally associated with a poor prognosis. The term “idiopathic” is used because the cause of pulmonary fibrosis is still unknown. IPF normally affects adults between 50 and 70 years of age, particularly those with a history of smoking, and more men than women. IPF belongs to a large group of more than 200 lung diseases called interstitial lung diseases (ILDs), which are characterized by mainly affecting the pulmonary interstitium, the tissue between the pulmonary alveoli. However, these diseases frequently affect not only the interstitium but also the alveolar space, the peripheral airways and the blood vessels. The lung tissue of those affected by IPF shows a characteristic histopathological pattern known as usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP). UIP is therefore the pathological counterpart of IPF.

entities/quistes-ovaricos/description.text: Polycystic ovary syndrome, also called Stein-Leventhal syndrome, is a complex and heterogeneous endocrine disease characterized by menstrual cycle disorders, hyperandrogenism and ovaries with multiple cysts. It is one of the most frequent hormonal imbalances, affecting between 6 and 20% of women of reproductive age, depending on the diagnostic criteria used. A cyst is a closed sac with its own membrane that develops abnormally in a cavity or structure of the body. Cysts arise as a result of an error in embryonic development during pregnancy. However, they sometimes appear spontaneously without apparent cause. Cysts can be dangerous, often because of the negative effects they can have on nearby tissues. They may contain air, fluid or semisolid material. Each month, during the menstrual cycle, a follicle (where the egg is developing) grows in the ovary. In most months, an egg is released from this follicle, which is called ovulation. If the follicle fails to open and release an egg, the fluid remains inside the follicle and forms a cyst, which is called a follicular cyst. Another type of cyst, called a corpus luteum cyst, occurs after an egg has been released from a follicle. This type of cyst often contains a small amount of blood. Ovarian cysts are more common during the reproductive years, from puberty to menopause. The condition is less common after menopause. Taking fertility drugs can cause a condition in which multiple large cysts form on the ovaries, which is called ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome. Cysts usually disappear after a woman's period or after a pregnancy. Ovarian cysts often cause no symptoms.

entities/quito/description.text: Pair related to Parkinson's disease. Quito means vertical sun. This pair was named in honor of this city, where the tremors caused by disease were calmed by welcoming Dr. Goiz's healing system with open arms.

entities/rabia-reservorio/contagion.text: Rabies is transmitted through a bite or direct contact of mucous membranes or wounds with the saliva of an infected animal. Bats, dogs, cats, mongooses, foxes, ferrets, raccoons and wolves.

entities/rabia/contagion.text: Rabies is transmitted through a bite or direct contact of mucous membranes or wounds with the saliva of an infected animal. Bats, dogs, cats, mongooses, foxes, ferrets, raccoons and wolves.

entities/rabia/description.text: Rabies is an acute, infectious viral zoonotic disease. It is caused by the rabies virus, which belongs to the family Rhabdoviridae; the virus attacks the central nervous system, producing an encephalitis with a lethality close to 100 %. The rabies virus is spread across the entire planet and attacks mammals, both domestic and wild, including humans. It is found in the saliva and secretions of infected animals and is inoculated into humans when infected animals attack them and cause a bite wound. In addition, the virus can also be transmitted when an individual who has a cut in the skin (the virus's entry route) comes into contact with the salivary secretions of an infected animal. People infected with rabies show hyperactivity, anxiety, depression, delirium, feelings of violence, urges to attack, paralysis, pharyngeal spasms (fear of water), laryngeal symptoms, otitis (inflammation of the ear and/or its tissues and parts), chronic sinusitis (also called rhinosinusitis, an inflammatory response of the mucosa of the nose and paranasal sinuses), asthma, central nervous system problems, aggressiveness, alterations of the thyroid, parathyroid and parotid, and chronic cystitis (acute or chronic inflammation of the urinary bladder, with or without infection). It is recommended to throw away the toothbrush, since it is a focus of infection. Propensity to cysts in the left breast (women). The “Pancreas - Peripancreatic region – Pancreas - Peripancreatic region” pair concerns the envelope of the pancreas; the magnets are placed vertically. One must ask in which part of the pancreas the magnets should be placed (head, body, tail, tip). The negative pole is placed at the top and the positive pole at the bottom.

entities/radiculopatia-de-nervios-cervic.text: The term radiculopathy refers to the loss or reduction of the sensory or motor function of a nerve root, which is distributed over the area where a dorsal root or nerve of the spinal cord is located. Radiculopathy commonly has effects on certain specific parts of the human body, such as the arms, neck, lower back and lower limbs. Radicular pain begins at the level of the spine. It may in turn be aggravated by coughing, sneezing, contraction of the abdominal muscles, or simply by sitting down or standing up. The pain tends to increase in those postures in which the nerves or roots are stretched.

entities/radiculopatia-de-nervios-sacros.text: The term radiculopathy refers to the loss or reduction of the sensory or motor function of a nerve root, which is distributed over the area where a dorsal root or nerve of the spinal cord is located. Radiculopathy commonly has effects on certain specific parts of the human body, such as the arms, neck, lower back and lower limbs. Radicular pain begins at the level of the spine. It may in turn be aggravated by coughing, sneezing, contraction of the abdominal muscles, or simply by sitting down or standing up. The pain tends to increase in those postures in which the nerves or roots are stretched.

For the Paravertebral-Paravertebral pair, the magnets are placed horizontally on both sides of the spine, where the pain is felt. The negative pole is placed on the right side of the body and the positive pole on the left side. If the pain is generalized, up to 6 pairs of magnets can be placed along the spinal column.

entities/ramses/description.text: Pair related to heavy metal poisoning and to medication poisoning or iatrogenesis. Ramsés was a boy from Acapulco who had hyperactivity. He was temporarily cured, but on eating seafood again he was poisoned again. He died during a burst of hyperactivity, run over by a vehicle.

entities/reflujo-gastrico/description.text: The word reflux means to go against a flow, in this case the normal flow of food. When swallowed, food passes from the mouth to the throat (pharynx), then to the esophagus and then to the stomach. In the stomach, food is mixed with the gastric juices, which among other things are composed of acid (which is necessary for digesting proteins). This acid does not damage the stomach because the organ produces a mucous substance that protects it from the action of hydrochloric acid; however, this protective mucus is not produced by the esophagus, the pharynx or the mouth. If food and stomach acid return to the esophagus, they will produce irritation and burns. When the esophagus is constantly irritated by stomach acid, the symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux appear: heartburn (pyrosis), chronic cough (lasting more than one month), shortness of breath (due to bronchospasm), difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) and, in the most serious cases, pain on swallowing (odynophagia) or chest pain that can spread to the neck and jaw; this pain is due to inflammation of the esophagus (esophagitis) and can easily be mistaken for a heart attack. Early diagnosis of this disease is important, because of the high associated risk of developing esophageal cancer if timely treatment is not received, as well as an increased risk of developing head and neck cancers and lung cancer.

entities/resentimiento/description.text: Resentment or rancor is an unease, bitterness or grievance left by an offensive remark or action that can last a long time and reappear when the offense is remembered. The type of feeling it causes can range from a slight temporary annoyance to a deep distress that can make relations with the offender difficult or impossible.

entities/resequedad-en-mucosas/descripti.text: Extreme dryness of the mucous membranes: ocular, nasal, oral. A mucosa is a layer formed by epithelium and the underlying loose connective tissue (lamina propria) that lines the inner walls of the organs that are in contact with the exterior of the body. It is usually associated with numerous mucus-secreting glands. In general, mucosae have protective, secretory and absorptive functions, and they house highly developed and specialized immunological subsystems. They are soft, moist organic tissues (like that of the inside of the mouth) that line the interior of the digestive organs (oral cavity, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, colon and rectum), the respiratory organs (nasal mucosa, trachea and bronchi), the urological organs (urethra, bladder, ureters) and the female genital organs (part of the vulva and vagina).

entities/resfriado-comun/contagion.text: The common cold is mainly caused by rhinovirus. Transmission occurs through contact with the secretions of the infected person or inhalation of their saliva droplets.

entities/resfriado-comun/description.text: The common cold, also known as a cold, catarrh or head cold, is a frequent viral infectious disease of the upper respiratory tract that affects the nose, paranasal sinuses, pharynx and larynx. It is caused mainly by rhinovirus, is self-limiting and can affect people of all ages. Symptoms appear one to two days after infection. Symptoms generally include sore throat, rhinitis, rhinorrhea and general malaise; they reach their greatest intensity between the first and third day and last seven to ten days, although they can occasionally persist for up to three weeks. Fever occurs more frequently in children. As age increases, the incidence of the common cold decreases. The common cold is a type of upper respiratory infection different from flu, a more serious viral infection of the respiratory tract that is distinguished by being a generalized illness, with more intense symptoms, especially in the airways, which often become complicated at the level of the bronchi or lungs. Likewise, flu can affect, simultaneously or successively, the brain, the meninges, the heart, the digestive tract and the musculature. Nevertheless, many people confuse the two terms.

entities/resistencia-a-la-insulina/descr.text: Insulin resistance, also known as insulinic resistance or insulin-resistance, is a condition in which the tissues show a diminished response in taking up circulating glucose under the action of insulin; especially the liver, skeletal muscle, adipose tissue and brain. This alteration, together with deficient insulin production by the pancreas, can lead after some time to the development of type 2 diabetes mellitus.

entities/retencion-de-liquidos/descripti.text: Fluid retention, or dropsy, is the accumulation of clear fluid in the tissues or cavities of the body. It is not an independent disease but a clinical sign that accompanies various diseases of the heart, kidneys and digestive system. These diseases have a close cause-and-effect relationship with fluid retention. This accumulation occurs in the peritoneum, which lies in the abdomen, although it also appears in the ankles, wrists, arms and neck. This symptom is the result of a deficiency in the digestive functions or in the excretory functions of the kidneys or skin of the person who has it. If the amount of retained fluid is large, disturbances in the functioning of the heart and lungs occur because of the pressure acting on these organs. When water retention occurs in the abdomen it is called dropsy or ascites; when the accumulation of fluid occurs in the feet and legs it is called edema, which is characterized by a typical swelling, although without giving rise to pain of any kind or altering the usual color of the skin. When the affected area is pressed with a finger, characteristic marks called pits persist for several minutes. The causes of edema and dropsy are the same: circulatory disorders, diseases of the heart, kidneys and liver, vitamin deficiencies and malfunction of the thyroid.

entities/retinopatia/description.text: Retinopathy is a generic term used in medicine to refer to any non-inflammatory disease affecting the retina, that is, the sheet of light-sensitive tissue found inside the eye. Retinopathy is therefore not a single disease; rather, this name designates a group of different conditions, each with specific characteristics. The most common retinopathies are diabetic retinopathy, which is a complication of diabetes; hypertensive retinopathy, a complication of arterial hypertension; and retinitis pigmentosa, which is a disease of genetic origin. All of them can produce considerable deterioration of visual capacity in their advanced stages.

entities/retinosis-pigmentaria/descripti.text: Retinitis pigmentosa is not a single disease, but a group of chronic eye diseases of genetic origin and degenerative character grouped under this name. It is characterized by progressive degeneration of the light-sensitive structure of the eye, the retina, which gradually loses the main cells that form it, the cones and rods. Its main symptoms are a slow but progressive decrease in visual acuity that in the early stages predominantly affects night vision and the peripheral field, while central vision is nevertheless preserved.

entities/reumatismo/description.text: Rheumatism, whether monoarticular (a single joint) or polyarticular (many joints). Presents joints in an acute inflammatory process. Helps reduce inflammation in the joint. Isolated, noninfectious joint problem. The word rheumatism is a term applied imprecisely to all diseases responsible for pain or inflammation of the joints or of structures located near them, such as tendons and ligaments. These diseases take different forms: chronic inflammatory rheumatism, acute arthritis, osteoarthritis due to joint degeneration (caused by aging), tendinitis, deposition of crystals in the joints, and post-traumatic joint pain, among others. Rheumatism affects patients of all ages and is not solely a prerogative of aging. Chronic inflammatory rheumatisms are the most disabling, and their course is often characterized by joint stiffness or deformity. Osteoarthritis, however, corresponds to wear of the joints that cannot be cured by treatment. When placing the magnets on the “Inguinal (ilioinguinal) nerve” – “Joint” pair, if the right hemibody shortens, the negative pole is placed on the inguinal nerve and the positive pole on the joint that resonates with it: wrist, elbow, shoulder, hip, knee, foot. If the right hemibody lengthens, the poles are placed the other way around.

entities/rhinovirus/contagion.text: There are two routes of transmission: through aerosols containing droplets from the respiratory tract and through contaminated surfaces, including person-to-person contact.

entities/rhinovirus/description.text: Rhinovirus is a genus of viruses of the family Picornaviridae; they are the most common pathogens in humans and are the causative agents of the common cold. There are more than 110 serotypes of rhinovirus capable of causing symptoms. Symptoms include pharyngitis, rhinitis, nasal congestion, sneezing and cough, sometimes accompanied by myalgia, fatigue, general malaise, headache, muscle weakness or loss of appetite. Fever and extreme fatigue are more common in influenza. Children may have six to twelve colds a year. There are more than 200 types of virus that cause the common cold.

entities/rickettsia/contagion.text: Rickettsiae normally live in mites, ticks, fleas and lice (domestic animals) and can be transmitted to humans through the bites of these bloodsucking agents.

entities/rickettsia/description.text: Rickettsiae are small bacteria of the phylum Proteobacteria. Most of the described species can live only in endosymbiosis with other cells. They normally produce pain and weakness in the feet and joints. Some diseases they cause are classic typhus (transmitted by lice), murine typhus (by fleas) and Rocky Mountain spotted fever (by ticks). The combination of the "Calcaneus - Calcaneus" and "Wrist - Wrist" pairs produces Alzheimer's disease.

entities/rinitis-alergica/description.text: Rhinitis is an inflammation of the mucous lining of the nose, clinically characterized by one or more symptoms: rhinorrhea, sneezing, nasal pruritus (itching), nasal congestion, postnasal drainage (discharge). According to its course it is classified as: 1) Acute rhinitis or coryza (colloquially a head cold, nasal cold or catarrh): that which lasts less than six months. 2) Chronic rhinitis: that which persists for more than 6 months. According to its cause it is classified as: 1) Allergic rhinitis: subclassified as seasonal or perennial. 2) Non-allergic rhinitis. 3) Atrophic rhinitis: caused by reduction of the inferior turbinates, which causes inflammation of the mucosa due to the passage of air, since the inferior turbinates serve to humidify, filter and sense the passage of air through the nose. Some of the symptoms in patients with rhinitis are the following: nasal itching, production of watery, liquid mucus, and frequent sneezing. If the physician examines the inside of the nasal passages, he or she will see that the mucosa of the turbinates is reddened, inflamed or has a very characteristic purplish coloration. The inflammation produces redness in the throat. The patient also usually has congested eyes that sting and water profusely. Since the entire nasal mucosa is congested, the patient cannot breathe freely and easily, so it is not surprising that the mucosa of the maxillary and frontal sinuses is also congested. This may favor sinusitis, a very common condition in these patients, which causes them frequent headaches, dizziness, general malaise and, depending on the person, changes in temperament and irritability. Allergic rhinitis also manifests with frequent sneezing, clear, watery nasal discharge and constant tearing, all of these symptoms especially in the mornings; this reduces people's daily activities and causes discomfort that is commonly mistaken for a simple cold, the difference being that a cold is accompanied by fever and high temperatures and does not last beyond one or two weeks. It sometimes causes diarrhea. It can also cause poisoning by toxoids, which are toxic substances that remain in the nasal septum as sequelae of chronic infections. Allergy is an immune reaction of the body to a substance that is generally harmless to the host, manifested by characteristic signs and symptoms when the host is exposed to it (by inhalation, ingestion or skin contact). For a long time allergy was considered equivalent to hypersensitivity (an older term) and was therefore erroneously regarded as an exaggerated immune reaction to a substance. But allergy is the clinical expression of the body's normal immune response mechanisms against potential invaders; the error lies not in the type of response or its intensity but in the target, which poses no threat. The final consequence of this error of the immune system is disease of the host, caused by the collateral effects suffered by the tissues wherever the immune system tries to defend itself against that harmless substance. The clinical manifestations of this disease are diverse, since they depend on the causative substance and the organ affected. At present, more than one third of the world's population has some disease of allergic origin.
