entities/roberta/description.text: Pair related to false pregnancy. Roberta is an Italian woman who paid all of Dr. Goiz's expenses so that he could go to Italy to give the first biomagnetism course. She translated both the course and the written material into Italian.

entities/roseola/description.text: Roseola, or exanthem subitum, is a childhood disease, especially of children under two years of age, whose external manifestations are usually limited to a transient eruption or "exanthem" that appears after three days of fever.

entities/rotavirus/contagion.text: Fecal-oral route. Through hands, dirty surfaces and objects. It can also be transmitted through the respiratory system. It affects other animals, being a pathogen for livestock.

entities/rotavirus/description.text: Rotavirus is a virus that causes severe diarrhea. It can also cause vomiting, fever and dehydration. It is the main cause of diarrhea among infants and young children. A large number of children are infected with rotavirus before the age of 5; however, with each new infection the immune system is strengthened and the infection becomes milder. In adults it is very uncommon. Children with this virus very easily infect other children and, on some occasions, adults. Once a child acquires the virus, about two days will pass before they become ill. The vomiting and diarrhea can last between three and eight days. It causes pelvic disorders. It infects and damages the cells lining the small intestine and causes gastroenteritis.

entities/rubeola/description.text: Rubella is an infectious disease caused by the rubella virus, an RNA virus belonging to the genus Rubivirus of the family Togaviridae. It is an exanthematous infectious disease. It can affect the fetus in pregnant mothers. It produces headache and general malaise and is highly aggressive. It can affect the macula of the eye. Only when contracted by the mother during pregnancy does it pose a serious threat to the fetus. It is characterized by a skin rash, swelling of the glands and, especially in adults, joint pain. The skin rash generally lasts about three days and may be accompanied by a slight fever. Up to half of affected people have no symptoms at all.

entities/salmonella-typhi/description.text: Salmonella is a bacterial genus belonging to the family Enterobacteriaceae, made up of intracellular, facultatively anaerobic gram-negative bacilli with peritrichous flagella. It produces the disease Salmonella typhus, or typhoid. It can also cause back pain (thoracolumbar), digestive disorders, diarrhea (avoid dehydration) and diabetes. In the incubation period, which lasts 10 to 15 days, there are disturbances of the general condition, a bacteremic phase with fever that rises progressively until it reaches 39-40 °C, at which point it is sustained, headache, stupor, rose spots on the abdomen, swelling of the nasal mucosa, coated (toasted) tongue, ulcers on the palate and, sometimes, hepatosplenomegaly and diarrhea. The disease may progress to recovery in 2 weeks or be prolonged with focal localizations from the fifth week on. Without appropriate treatment, serious complications may occur, such as intestinal hemorrhage and perforation, and septic shock. A certain degree of immunity develops which, although it does not protect against reinfections, makes them milder when they occur.

entities/sarampion/contagion.text: Virus of the paramyxovirus family (not to be confused with the genus Paramyxoviridae, to which the mumps and parainfluenza viruses belong) of the genus Morbillivirus. Transmission of the measles virus occurs by direct contact or by infected droplets from a sick person, who remains infectious from three to five days before the appearance of the rash until four days afterward. The virus penetrates the epithelial cells of the mucosa of the upper respiratory tract, such as the oropharynx or, less frequently, the conjunctiva of the eyes. There are many causes of conjunctivitis, but the most common is viruses.

entities/sarampion/description.text: Measles is an exanthematous infectious disease, like rubella or chickenpox, that is fairly frequent, especially in children, caused by a virus, specifically of the Paramyxoviridae family, genus Morbillivirus. It is characterized by typical red spots on the skin (eczemas) (exanthem) as well as fever and a weakened general state. In some complicated cases, measles causes inflammation of the lungs and brain that threatens the patient's life. The incubation period of measles usually lasts 4-12 days, during which there are no symptoms. Infected people remain contagious from the appearance of the first symptoms until 3-5 days after the appearance of the rash. The rash and fever gradually disappear between the seventh and tenth day, with the last traces of the rash generally disappearing by 14 days, with noticeable desquamation. In a child the disease is transient; in an adult it manifests with bleeding in the upper digestive tract. It can cause ulcers.

entities/sarcoidosis/description.text: Sarcoidosis, or Besnier-Boeck disease, is a systemic granulomatous disease of autoimmune character that affects all human populations and ethnic groups, mainly adults between 20 and 40 years of age. Its causes are unknown. Symptoms may appear suddenly, but usually manifest gradually. The course of the disease is variable and can range from asymptomatic to chronic (in 5% of cases), and may lead to death (in only 1% of the cases in which it becomes chronic). The disease can manifest in any organ of the body, most frequently in the lung and intrathoracic lymph nodes. Ocular, cutaneous and hepatic manifestations are also frequent.

entities/sarcoma-de-kaposi/description.text: Kaposi's sarcoma is a malignant tumor of the lymphatic endothelium caused by Kaposi's sarcoma virus or human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8). Its signs are bluish-red lesions, flat or raised and irregular in shape, bleeding from gastrointestinal lesions, difficulty breathing from pulmonary lesions and blood-stained sputum, also from pulmonary lesions. In patients with AIDS, the cancer can develop rapidly and can also involve the skin, lungs, digestive tract and other organs. In people with AIDS, Kaposi's sarcoma is caused by an interaction between HIV, a weakened immune system and human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8). Kaposi's sarcoma has been linked to the spread of HIV and HHV-8 through sexual activity.

entities/sarcoptes-scabiei/contagion.text: Animal hair. Domestic animals. The disease is easily transmissible by direct contact or through fomites (garments, clothing, sheets, towels). In some cases it can be acquired through contact with infected animals, especially dogs (Sarcoptes scabiei var. canis) and cats.

entities/sarcoptes-scabiei/description.text: Scabies. It is confused with psoriasis (a chronic inflammatory skin disease that produces thickened, inflamed, scaly lesions, frequently appearing on the elbows, knees, scalp, abdomen and back). Scabies is a skin disease caused by the parasitic mite Sarcoptes scabiei, commonly called the itch mite. It is an ectoparasitosis of worldwide distribution in all races. It causes dermatitis-type skin problems. Cause of alopecia areata (hair falls out in patches).

entities/sarna/contagion.text: Sarcoptes scabiei parasite. Animal hair. Domestic animals. The disease is easily transmissible by direct contact or through fomites (garments, clothing, sheets, towels). In some cases it can be acquired through contact with infected animals, especially dogs (Sarcoptes scabiei var. canis) and cats.

entities/sarna/description.text: Scabies. It is confused with psoriasis (a chronic inflammatory skin disease that produces thickened, inflamed, scaly lesions, frequently appearing on the elbows, knees, scalp, abdomen and back). Scabies is a skin disease caused by the parasitic mite Sarcoptes scabiei, commonly called the itch mite. It is an ectoparasitosis of worldwide distribution in all races. It causes dermatitis-type skin problems. Cause of alopecia areata (hair falls out in patches).

entities/sars/description.text: Severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) is a serious form of pneumonia caused by a virus that was first identified in 2003. Infection with the SARS virus causes acute respiratory distress (severe breathing difficulty) and sometimes death.

entities/saturnismo/description.text: Chronic dulling of consciousness. Saturnism, plumbism or "plombemianota" is the name given to the poisoning produced by lead (Pb) when it enters the human body. It is so called because, in antiquity, alchemists called this chemical element "Saturn." Waterborne saturnism is the form produced through ingested water, since lead, a highly malleable, non-corroding mineral, imparts no taste to water or food. Lead is the first known metal and the one most widely studied for its environmental risk. Saturnism causes anemia, because lead in the blood blocks hemoglobin synthesis and alters the transport of oxygen in the blood and to the other organs of the body. Lead is a neurotoxic heavy metal that, when present in the blood, circulates throughout the body, causing irreversible neurological damage when it reaches the brain. The first symptoms of lead encephalopathy consist of lethargy, vomiting, irritability, anorexia and vertigo, followed by ataxia (lack of coordination in the movement of body parts) and a decreased level of consciousness, which in the most severe cases can progress to coma and death. Recovery is accompanied by sequelae such as epilepsy, intellectual disability, optic neuropathy and blindness. It causes attention-deficit disorder, fatigue, and an irritable or dulled temperament.

entities/schistosoma/description.text: Schistosoma is a genus of parasitic flatworms of the class Trematoda, commonly called bilharzia. Among all flatworms, they cause the most important human infection, known as schistosomiasis, a parasitic disease characterized by continuous fever accompanied by cough, diarrhea, abdominal pain and fatigue. Some other conditions caused by this bacterium are described below. Skin problems: hypersensitivity, urticaria and/or dermatitis. Granulomas: the immune system's reaction to eggs deposited in the tissues produces granulomas, which are immune coverings (cellular and fibrotic) around the egg that become scarring; these granulomas can occur in any organ of the body; this pathology produces the so-called Katayama fever, with periportal fibrosis, portal hypertension and occasionally embolisms produced by cerebral or spinal granulomas. Bladder problems: hematuria, calcifications, squamous cell carcinoma, bladder cancer. Cardiopulmonary system problems: rupture of the pulmonary alveoli and capillaries, pneumonitis and Löffler syndrome; granulomatous lesions in the lung produce, in chronic cases, occlusions and arteritis in the pulmonary circulation, which produces hypertrophy of the right ventricle of the heart called cor pulmonale; the initial stages of the disease present with a dry, persistent cough. Intestinal problems: diarrhea with or without dysentery, abdominal pain in the right hypochondrium and/or epigastrium, tenderness on cecal palpation and poor general condition.

entities/septicemia/description.text: Septicemia or sepsis is a syndrome of potentially fatal physiological, pathological and biochemical abnormalities associated with an infection. These abnormalities are secondary to an unbalanced immune response to the infection, which ends up damaging the body's own tissues and organs and leading to multiorgan dysfunction. Systemic inflammatory response syndrome is associated with sepsis but is not an absolute cause of it, since sepsis involves the activation of both proinflammatory and anti-inflammatory responses.

entities/serenidad/description.text: Serenity is the attitude of people who respond to any event or situation without being carried away by destabilizing feelings or emotions. A serene person is a peaceful person, at peace with their surroundings, with others and with themselves. Serenity allows us to accept ourselves and our own feelings.

entities/serratia-fonticola/description.text: Serratia fonticola is a gram-negative, facultatively anaerobic bacterium of the Enterobacteriaceae family, genus Serratia. This bacterium has been isolated from water and soil; its presence has also been detected in infected wounds and in the upper respiratory tract of humans, as well as in the digestive tract of birds and on the skin of reptiles. It can exceptionally cause disease in humans. Serratia fonticola is an opportunistic germ that can only cause disease in certain unusual circumstances. In 1989 the first case of human involvement was described, corresponding to a patient who suffered an abscess in a leg after a femur fracture that underwent surgery; it has also been shown that it can colonize vascular leg ulcers and cause infections of animal-bite wounds. The germ is usually resistant to various antibiotics. It causes sepsis, which is a potentially fatal syndrome of physiological, pathological and biochemical abnormalities associated with an infection.

entities/serratia-marcescens/description.text: Serratia marcescens is a gram-negative bacillus of the Enterobacteriaceae family. It can be dangerous to humans, since it is sometimes pathogenic, as a cause of nosocomial and urinary infections. It is a motile bacillus that can grow at temperatures ranging from 3.5-40 °C, at pH levels varying between 5 and 9. The environment in which it predominates is humid conditions, which is why it can be found growing in bathrooms and sewers, although it can be eliminated by applying bleach and other disinfectants. Serratia marcescens can cause conjunctivitis, keratitis and infections of wounds, kidneys and urinary tract, as well as respiratory infections, meningitis and endocarditis. This bacterium especially affects hospitalized patients and patients whose immunity is reduced by systemic diseases or immunosuppressive medical treatments. Producer of red pigment.

entities/shigella/description.text: Shigella is a genus of Gram-negative, nonmotile, non-spore-forming bacteria incapable of fermenting lactose. They can cause diarrhea in living beings. Its most common symptoms are diarrhea, fever, nausea, vomiting, stomach cramps and other intestinal manifestations. The stools may contain blood, mucus or pus. Shigella causes dysentery, resulting in destruction of the epithelial cells of the intestinal mucosa at the level of the cecum and rectum.

entities/sida/description.text: Human immunodeficiency virus infection and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (HIV/AIDS) are a spectrum of diseases caused by infection with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). After the initial infection, a person may notice no symptoms at all, or may experience a brief period of influenza-like illness. This is typically followed by a prolonged period without symptoms. As the infection progresses, it interferes more with the immune system, increasing the risk of common infections such as tuberculosis, as well as other opportunistic infections and tumors that rarely affect people with an intact (unharmed, undamaged) immune system. These late symptoms of infection are known as AIDS, a stage that is often also associated with weight loss. HIV is spread mainly through unprotected sex (including anal and oral sex), transfusions of contaminated blood, hypodermic needles, and from mother to child during pregnancy, delivery or breastfeeding. Some body fluids, such as saliva and tears, do not transmit HIV. Prevention methods include safe sex, needle-exchange programs, treatment of those infected, and circumcision. Infection of the baby can often be prevented by giving antiretroviral medication to both mother and child. Without treatment, the average survival time after infection is 11 years.

entities/sifilis/description.text: Syphilis is an infectious disease with a chronic course, transmitted mainly through sexual contact and produced by the spirochete Treponema pallidum. Treponema pallidum can survive in a human host for several decades. During the first stage of the disease, painless papules appear at the inoculation site (the mouth, penis, vagina or anus) and quickly ulcerate, becoming a circular or oval sore with a reddish border resembling an open wound; this is called a chancre. The second stage may appear half a year after the chancre disappears and lasts three to six months, causing painless pinkish welts called "syphilitic clavi" on the palms of the hands and soles of the feet (which can sometimes appear in other sites such as the chest, face or back), fever, sore throat and joint pain, weight loss, hair loss, headaches and lack of appetite. In the third phase (also called the final phase), between one and twenty years after the onset of the infection, syphilis reawakens to attack the nervous system or some organ directly. In this phase the most serious problems occur, and it can lead to death. Some of the problems are: eye disorders, heart disease, brain lesions, spinal cord lesions, loss of coordination of the limbs, syphilitic or luetic aneurysm, syphilitic gumma or syphiloma, etc. Treated in time, the disease leaves no sequelae. If not treated in time, it can cause: skin ulcerations, circulatory problems, blindness, paralysis, dementia, neurological disorders and death.

entities/sincitial-respiratorio/descript.text: Critical neuroses. Respiratory problems. Human respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) causes respiratory tract infection in patients of all ages. It is the major cause of respiratory tract infections during infancy and childhood. In temperate climates it is an annual epidemic during the winter months. In tropical climates, infection is more common in the rainy season. Natural infection with RSV does not induce immunity, and people can become reinfected. In most cases, RSV produces only minor symptoms, indistinguishable from a common cold or minor illnesses. For some children, however, RSV can cause bronchiolitis, producing a severe respiratory condition requiring hospitalization and, very rarely, death. This occurs mostly in patients with immune problems or in premature babies. Treatment based on hydration and oxygenation is recommended until the disease completes its cycle.

entities/sincope-o-desmayo/description.text: Syncope, or fainting, is a sudden loss of consciousness and postural tone, of brief duration, with spontaneous recovery, without the need for resuscitation maneuvers. Presyncope is the sensation of dimming of consciousness without actually losing it. This concept should not be confused with lipothymia, since the latter is a swoon without loss of consciousness. The loss of consciousness can be short or long. It can have various causes: blows, shock, lack of oxygen or simply poor nutrition. Before fainting, spots of light, blurred vision and, sometimes, the feeling that a long time has passed appear. A faint is the temporary loss of consciousness as a result of decreased blood flow to the brain. The episode is brief (lasting less than a couple of minutes) and is followed by rapid and complete recovery. Affected people may complain of dizziness or vertigo before the faint occurs. The more prolonged and deeper state of loss of consciousness is often called coma.

entities/sindrome-de-cola-de-caballo/con.text: A common cause is a ruptured spinal disc. A spinal disc is a semi-soft mass of tissue that rests between the bones of the spine. These bones are known as vertebrae. The discs act as the shock absorbers of the spine. When a disc ruptures and protrudes into the spinal canal, it can press against the group of nerves, causing CES.

entities/sindrome-de-cola-de-caballo/des.text: Cauda equina syndrome occurs when the nerve roots at the base of the spinal column are compressed. Known as the cauda equina, this group of nerves governs sensation and function of the bladder, intestines, sexual organs and legs.

entities/sindrome-de-colon-irritable/des.text: Irritable bowel syndrome, also called irritable colon, spastic colon, functional colitis or intestinal neurosis, is a chronic functional digestive disease of unknown origin. It is a fairly frequent set of functional bowel disorders; the main symptoms are diarrhea and constipation.

entities/sindrome-de-cushing/description.text: Cushing's syndrome, also known as hypercortisolism, is a disease caused by an increase in the hormone cortisol. This excess cortisol can be caused by various factors. The most common, affecting 60-70 % of patients, is a pituitary adenoma; this form of the syndrome is specifically known as Cushing's disease. Other causes of Cushing's syndrome are tumors or abnormalities of the adrenal glands, chronic use of glucocorticoids, or production of ACTH by tumors that do not normally produce it (ectopic ACTH secretion). ACTH is the hormone, produced by the pituitary gland, that stimulates the adrenal glands to produce cortisol. This syndrome presents a clinical picture resulting from chronic excess of circulating cortisol. Patients may present one or more of the following symptoms: central obesity with a protruding abdomen and thin limbs, moon face (round and red), arterial hypertension (among the mechanisms causing hypertension in these patients is the sodium retention produced by corticosteroids), back pain and headache, acne, hirsutism (excess hair), erectile dysfunction, amenorrhea (absence of menstruation), thirst, increased urination (urine), buffalo hump (an accumulation of fat between the shoulders), unintentional weight gain, muscle weakness (especially in the pelvic girdle, which makes it difficult to get up from a chair without help), wine-red striae, frequent bruising due to capillary fragility, diabetes, easy fatigability, lack of libido, irritability, low self-esteem, depression, anxiety, psychosis. Mental disorders appear in 50% of patients with Cushing's syndrome. The most frequent manifestations are depression and insomnia.

entities/sindrome-de-guillain-barre/desc.text: Guillain–Barré syndrome is also known as inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy or acute post-infectious polyneuritis. It is an autoimmune neurological disorder in which the body's immune system attacks a part of the peripheral nervous system, the myelin, which is the insulating layer that covers the nerves. When this happens, the nerves cannot send signals effectively; the muscles lose their ability to respond to commands from the brain, and the brain receives fewer sensory signals from the rest of the body. The result is an inability to feel heat, pain and other sensations, as well as progressive paralysis of various muscles of the body. Some of the symptoms that may occur include paralysis and weakness of the limbs and of the respiratory muscles, dizziness, fatigue, and neuritis, which is a generic term denoting inflammation of a nerve or general inflammation of the peripheral nervous system. The symptoms of neuritis can be pain, paresthesia (abnormal sensation of the senses or of general sensibility, experienced as pins-and-needles pricking, tingling, numbness and/or deadness), paresis (partial absence of voluntary movement, partial or mild paralysis, muscle weakness), hypoesthesia (reduction or partial loss of sensation, or numbness), anesthesia (blocked sensation), paralysis, and weakening and disappearance of reflexes.

entities/sindrome-de-meniere/description.text: Problems of vertical balance and stuttering. Horizontal balance is controlled in the middle ear; its dysfunction causes dizziness or vertigo and is known as Ménière's syndrome. Positional balance is controlled in the cerebellum; its dysfunction causes cerebellar ataxia. Vertical balance is regulated in the anterior pole of the brain. Hearing problems. Ménière's syndrome is a disease affecting the inner ear, caused by an increase of endolymph in the labyrinth or by inflammation of the labyrinth, characterized mainly by vertigo, which usually manifests accompanied by acouphenes or tinnitus (ringing in the ears) and hearing loss (hypoacusis), the acouphenes or tinnitus and the hearing loss preceding the vertigo. Vertiginous attacks almost always appear in sudden episodes that can last hours or days and recur periodically. The hearing loss fluctuates and, over the years, progresses to irreversible hearing loss or deafness.

entities/sindrome-de-shock-toxico/descri.text: Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is an uncommon disorder caused by a bacterial toxin. It has fatal consequences and can recur in those who survive. Different bacteria are possible causes, depending on the case. Among the most common are Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes. The first cases of toxic shock syndrome described affected women who were using tampons during their menstrual periods. However, today fewer than half of cases are associated with tampon use. Toxic shock syndrome can also occur with skin infections, burns and after surgery. The condition can also affect children, postmenopausal women and men. Symptoms include: confusion, diarrhea, general malaise, headaches, high fever, chills, low blood pressure, muscle aches, nausea, vomiting, organ failure (usually the kidneys and liver), redness of the eyes, mouth and throat, seizures, and a generalized red rash resembling sunburn.

entities/sindrome-de-sjogren/description.text: Sjögren's syndrome is a systemic autoimmune disease characterized by mainly affecting the exocrine glands, which leads to the appearance of dryness. The exocrine glands are responsible for producing fluids such as saliva, tears, the mucous secretions of the larynx and trachea and vaginal secretions, fluids that hydrate, lubricate and soften the parts of the body that are in contact with the outside through the mucous membranes. It is also a rheumatic disease, which produces pain and swelling in the joints. It is named in honor of the Swedish scientist Henrik Sjögren. Sjögren's syndrome is included among the autoimmune diseases because the body's immune system, which is responsible for defending it against external aggressions, reacts for unknown reasons against its own organism; thus the so-called "autoantibodies" are produced, along with damage to these glands, mainly the lacrimal and salivary glands. It is also considered a systemic disease, which means that, in addition to the symptoms of dryness, the disease can affect any organ of the body and produce a wide variety of symptoms. It is a chronic disease that progresses very slowly over time; for this reason, there can be a period of up to 10 years between the onset of symptoms and the diagnosis of the disease.

entities/sindrome-del-tunel-carpiano/des.text: The carpal tunnel is a narrow passageway of ligaments and bones at the base of the hand that contains nerves and tendons. Sometimes, thickening of irritated tendons or other swollen structures narrows the tunnel and causes compression of the nerves. Symptoms usually begin gradually. As they worsen, holding objects can become difficult. Carpal tunnel syndrome is a peripheral neuropathy that occurs when the median nerve, which runs from the forearm to the hand, is pressed or trapped inside the carpal tunnel at the level of the wrist. Symptoms generally manifest as sensations of heat, cramping or numbness in the palm of the hand and the fingers, especially the thumb and the middle and index fingers. In some patients the fingers feel swollen and useless despite there being no apparent swelling. Symptoms often appear first in one or both hands during the night.

entities/sindrome-down/description.text: Down syndrome is a genetic disorder caused by the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21 (or a part of it), instead of the usual two, which is why it is also called trisomy 21. It is characterized by the presence of a variable degree of cognitive disability and peculiar physical features that give it a recognizable appearance. It is named after John Langdon Down, who was the first to describe this genetic alteration in 1866.

entities/sindrome-metabolico/description.text: Metabolic syndrome (also known as syndrome X, plurimetabolic syndrome, insulin resistance syndrome or Reaven syndrome) is a set of physiological, biochemical, clinical and metabolic factors that entail an increased risk of developing cardiovascular disease or type 2 diabetes mellitus and dying from it. These factors can be summarized as insulin resistance, excess abdominal fat, atherogenic dyslipidemia, endothelial dysfunction, genetic susceptibility, arterial hypertension, a hypercoagulable state and chronic stress. The underlying causes of this syndrome are related to access, in developed and developing countries, to an excess of calories, sugar, fats, salt, labor-saving technology and passive entertainment. As for the age profile of candidates for metabolic syndrome, it has been falling dramatically. Whereas previously one spoke of patients around 50 years of age, now the risk group is around 35 years of age, because from very early stages of life people adopt poor eating habits and get little physical exercise. This syndrome is therefore a consequence of poor lifestyle habits, for example the consumption of carbonated or sugary drinks, and excess simple carbohydrates and fats.

entities/sindrome-uremico/description.text: Uremic syndrome, also called uremia, is a set of cerebral, respiratory, circulatory, digestive and other symptoms produced by the accumulation in the blood of toxic products that, in a normal general state, are eliminated by the kidney and that are retained due to a disorder of renal function. The main cause of uremic syndrome is renal failure, although there may also be other less frequent causes: high-protein diet, increased catabolism, gastrointestinal bleeding, drug use, bladder rupture, dehydration, chronic pyelonephritis (kidney infection).

entities/sinusitis-alergica/description.text: Sinusitis, or rhinosinusitis, is an inflammatory response of the mucosa of the nose and the paranasal sinuses that may be due to an infection by bacterial, viral or fungal agents; or to an allergic condition; or to a combination of these factors. It is characterized by rhinorrhea (nasal discharge), nasal obstruction and facial pain; there may be hyposmia (partial reduction of the sense of smell) or anosmia (loss of the sense of smell), cough, fever, fatigue, dental pain, halitosis (bad breath) and otic (ear) discomfort. It is generally preceded by rhinitis, which is why the term rhinosinusitis is preferred. According to the duration of the disease, it can be classified as acute if it lasts less than four weeks, subacute if it lasts from four to twelve weeks, and a chronic form with more than twelve weeks of disease. Allergy is an immune reaction of the body to a substance that is generally harmless to the host, manifested by characteristic signs and symptoms when the host is exposed to it (by inhalation, ingestion or skin contact). For a long time allergy was considered equivalent to hypersensitivity (an older term) and was therefore erroneously regarded as an exaggerated immune reaction to a substance. But allergy is the clinical expression of the body's normal immune response mechanisms against potential invaders; the error lies not in the type of response or its intensity but in the target, which poses no threat. The final consequence of this error of the immune system is disease of the host, caused by the collateral effects suffered by the tissues wherever the immune system tries to defend itself against that harmless substance. The clinical manifestations of this disease are diverse, since they depend on the causative substance and the organ affected. At present, more than one third of the world's population has some disease of allergic origin.

entities/sinusitis/description.text: Sinusitis, or rhinosinusitis, is an inflammatory response of the mucosa of the nose and paranasal sinuses that may be due to infection by bacterial, viral or fungal agents; or an allergic condition; or a combination of these factors. It is characterized by rhinorrhea (nasal discharge), nasal obstruction and facial pain; there may be hyposmia (partial reduction of the sense of smell) or anosmia (loss of the sense of smell), cough, fever, fatigue, dental pain, halitosis (bad breath) and otic (ear) discomfort. It is generally preceded by rhinitis, which is why the term rhinosinusitis is preferred. According to the duration of the disease it can be classified as acute if it lasts less than four weeks, subacute if its duration is four to twelve weeks, and a chronic form with more than twelve weeks of disease.

entities/sistema-endocrino/description.text: The endocrine system, also called the system of internal-secretion glands, is the set of organs and tissues of the body that secrete a type of substance called hormones, which are released into the bloodstream and regulate some of the body's functions. It is a signaling system that bears some similarities to the nervous system, but instead of using electrical impulses at a distance, it works exclusively by means of substances (chemical signals) that are released into the blood. Hormones regulate many functions in organisms, including, among others, growth rate, tissue function, metabolism, the development and functioning of the sexual organs, and some aspects of behavior. The endocrine system acts as a cellular communication network that responds to stimuli by releasing hormones. Some organs that form part of the endocrine system are the following: hypothalamus, pineal gland, pituitary gland, thyroid, stomach, duodenum, liver, pancreas, kidney, adrenal glands, testicles, ovaries, placenta, uterus, parathyroids, skin and others.

entities/sistema-inmune/description.text: It improves the quality and production of white blood cells and raises lymphocytes (lymphocytes are lymphatic cells; they are made by lymphoid cells present in the bone marrow and later migrate to lymphoid organs such as the thymus, lymph nodes and spleen; they constitute 99 % of lymphatic cells; they are a type of leukocyte (white blood cell) that is part of the immune system, rank high in that system and react against foreign materials). It improves immune competence in patients with immune incompetence or immunodeficiency, who therefore have alterations in the production of lymphocytes and leukocytes.

entities/soberbia/description.text: Haughtiness or pride is a feeling of valuing oneself above others. It is a feeling of superiority that leads one to boast of one's own qualities or ideas and to belittle those of others.

entities/sobrepeso-por-mala-absorcion/de.text: Malabsorption or malabsorption syndrome is understood as a digestive disorder caused by difficulty assimilating, absorbing or digesting the nutrients present in food along the gastrointestinal tract. Malabsorption may be due to different types of diseases and may involve one or multiple nutrients, depending on the abnormality. It is generally associated with difficulty absorbing nutrients in the small intestine. It usually gives rise to diarrhea, gas, abdominal distension, weight loss, malnutrition, anemia, etc. It may also happen that the body does not metabolize food properly, causing overweight.

entities/sordera/description.text: Deafness is the difficulty or impossibility of using the sense of hearing due to a partial (hypoacusis) or total (cophosis) loss of hearing capacity; it can be unilateral or bilateral. Thus, a deaf person will be unable to hear or will have problems hearing. It can be a hereditary trait or the consequence of a disease, trauma, long-term exposure to noise, or medications aggressive to the auditory nerve.

entities/staphylococcus-albus/contagion.text: Hospitals. Dialysis. People with catheters or surgical implants. The ability to form biofilms on plastic devices is an important factor in transmission.

entities/staphylococcus-albus/descriptio.text: Staphylococcus albus, also known as Staphylococcus epidermis, is a bacterial species of the genus Staphylococcus, consisting of gram-positive cocci arranged in clusters. It is coagulase-negative and thermonuclease-negative, although this sometimes varies, and it is frequently found on the skin of humans and animals and on mucous membranes. Staphylococcus epidermis is part of the human bacterial flora, generally located on the skin; however, people with compromised immune systems can develop infections due to this bacterium. Because of contamination, S. epidermidis is probably the most common species found in laboratory tests. The bacteria have an outer polysaccharide layer that adheres firmly to plastic and causes biofilms that grow on plastic devices placed inside the body; this occurs most commonly with intravenous catheters and medical prostheses. Infection can also occur in patients undergoing dialysis or in anyone with an implanted plastic device that may have been contaminated. Some conditions related to Staphylococcus albus are the following: catheter infections, prosthetic implant infection, wound infection, cystitis (inflammation of the urinary bladder), septicemia (or sepsis, commonly known as systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), which is produced by the presence of pathogens in the bloodstream due to a focus of infection), endocarditis ((inflammation of the endocardium, that is, an inflammatory process localized in the inner lining of the heart chambers and valves), endophthalmitis (also known as panophthalmitis, an inflammation generally of infectious origin that affects all the internal structures of the eye). For the "Greater omentum – Greater omentum" pair, 4 magnets surrounding the navel may be required.

entities/staphylococcus-aureus-coagulasa.text: Staphylococcus aureus, known as golden staphylococcus, is a facultatively anaerobic, Gram-positive bacterium that produces coagulase and catalase and is nonmotile and non-spore-forming. It is widely distributed throughout the world, and it is estimated that one in every three people is colonized, though not infected, by it. Coagulase is a protein produced by various microorganisms that enables the conversion of fibrinogen into fibrin. Coagulase reacts with prothrombin in the blood. The resulting complex is called staphylothrombin, and it allows the protease enzyme to convert fibrinogen into fibrin. This causes the blood to clot. Staphylococcus aureus can produce a wide range of diseases, ranging from relatively benign skin and mucosal infections, such as folliculitis, furunculosis or conjunctivitis, to life-threatening diseases such as cellulitis, deep abscesses, osteomyelitis, meningitis, sepsis, endocarditis or pneumonia. Main cause of diabetes mellitus and appendicitis. Causes intolerance to gluten and other foods. It can affect the gastrointestinal tract, either through the physical presence of Staphylococcus aureus or through ingestion of the staphylococcal enterotoxin secreted by the bacterium. Gastroesophageal reflux. Problems in the larynx, trachea and pleura. At present, this microorganism is the main cause of nosocomial infections. This situation is favored by the fact that this species inhabits both the mucous membranes and the skin of humans, which allows it to enter the patient's bloodstream through surgical wounds by direct or indirect contact with health personnel, with a contaminated object or even with another patient.

Staphylococcus aureus, known as golden staphylococcus or golden staph, is a facultatively anaerobic, gram-positive, coagulase- and catalase-producing bacterium that is nonmotile and non-spore-forming. It is widely distributed throughout the world, and it is estimated that one in every three people is colonized, though not infected, by it. The resulting complex is called staphylothrombin, and it allows the protease enzyme to convert fibrinogen into fibrin. This causes the blood to clot.
