entities/tumor-hipofisiario/description.text: A pituitary tumor is the result of abnormal growth of the pituitary gland, the part of the brain that regulates the balance of many hormones in the body. Most pituitary tumors are benign. Up to 20% of people have pituitary tumors. Many of these tumors cause no symptoms and are never diagnosed during the person's lifetime. The pituitary gland is a pea-sized endocrine gland located at the base of the brain that helps control the secretion of hormones from other endocrine glands such as the thyroid, the sex glands and the adrenal glands. The pituitary gland also secretes hormones that directly affect body tissues, such as bones and the mammary glands. As the pituitary tumor grows, damage may occur to the normal hormone-secreting cells of the pituitary gland. This causes the pituitary gland not to produce enough of its hormones, a condition called hypopituitarism. The causes of pituitary tumors are unknown. The pituitary gland can be affected by brain tumors that develop in the same part of the brain. Some pituitary tumors produce too much of one or more hormones; as a result, symptoms of one or more of the following conditions may occur: hyperthyroidism (extremely rare), Cushing's syndrome (increased cortisol hormone), gigantism or acromegaly, nipple discharge, absent or irregular menstrual periods, decreased sexual function in men. Symptoms caused by pressure from a large pituitary tumor may include: vision changes (double vision, visual field loss, drooping eyelids), headache, lethargy, clear nasal discharge, nausea, vomiting, problems with the sense of smell.

entities/tumor-intracraneal/contagion.text: 2 Viruses = Edema, Virus + Bacterium = Cyst, 2 Bacteria = Abscess, 2 Bacteria + Virus = Dysplasia or Metaplasia, 3 Bacteria + Virus = Slow neoplasia, 3 Bacteria + Virus + Fungus = Fast-growing neoplasia, 3 Bacteria + Virus + Fungus + Leprosy = Cancer, Cancer + Pseudomonas or Clostridium = Metastasis, Cancer + Parasites = Necrosis, Cancer + Chemotherapy or Radiotherapy = Complicated cancer, Cancer + Discouragement = Incurable cancer.

entities/tumor-intracraneal/description.text: Intracranial tumors encompass any tumor that starts in the brain. These tumors can originate from brain cells, the membranes around the brain (meninges), nerves or glands. Tumors can directly destroy brain cells; they can also damage cells by producing inflammation, exerting pressure on other parts of the brain and increasing intracranial pressure. A brain tumor is an uncontrolled growth of cells derived from brain components (primary tumors) or of tumor cells located in other areas of the body (metastases). Tumors can be benign or malignant, depending on how fast they grow. Metastases to the CNS come, in order of frequency, from the lung, breast, skin (melanoma), kidney and gastrointestinal tract, and tend to grow at the junction of the cortex and the white matter.

entities/ulcera-de-cornea/description.text: A corneal ulcer is an eye disease defined as a loss of continuity of the epithelial surface of the cornea associated with necrosis or destruction of the underlying tissue. The cornea is the most superficial region of the anterior portion of the eye, and its transparency is essential for correct vision. When ulcers occur in the cornea, they can cause serious sequelae, such as perforation and loss of transparency due to scarring, which results in poor vision. The causes are very varied and are generally divided into infectious, secondary to trauma to the eye, or due to other diseases. Several factors are frequently involved in the onset and persistence of corneal ulcers.

entities/ulcera-peptica/description.text: Peptic ulcer is an ulcer that affects the mucosa lining the stomach or the duodenum (the first part of the small intestine). According to its location it is classified as a gastric ulcer or a duodenal ulcer, the latter being much more frequent. Peptic ulcer can appear in both women and men, from childhood to old age. It is a common disease that affects one in 10 people at some point in their lives. The cause of the ulcer is an imbalance between the aggressive and the defensive factors for the gastroduodenal mucosa. Among the aggressive agents, the most important are the secretion of gastric acid by the parietal cells (which secrete hydrochloric acid), infection by the bacterium Helicobacter pylori (responsible for most cases) and treatment with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as aspirin and ibuprofen. The protective factors are the gastric secretion of mucus and bicarbonate, adequate blood flow to the gastroduodenal mucosa, the natural repair mechanisms of the mucosa and the secretion of prostaglandins, which stimulate the production of mucus and bicarbonate.

entities/ulcera-varicosa/description.text: The varicose ulcer appears on the person's leg and is caused by trauma or by a small localized infection. The depth of the ulcer is variable, and it may sometimes be covered by an exudate. It is a disease that predominates in women, especially from the age of 30. A toxic diet is the greatest cause, preparing the ground for blood poisoning.

entities/ulceras/description.text: An ulcer or sore is any open lesion of the skin or mucous membrane with loss of substance. Ulcers can have a very varied origin and location. A peptic ulcer affects the mucosa of the stomach (gastric ulcer) or of the duodenum (duodenal ulcer). Esophageal ulcers sometimes also occur in patients affected by Barrett's esophagus. Most ulcers occur in the first layer of the inner lining. An opening that passes completely through the stomach or duodenum is called a perforation and is an emergency. Skin ulcers are a lesion of the skin involving loss of the epidermis, part of the dermis and even the hypodermis; it may be a merely superficial wound or a deeper involvement. They affect the skin and can become very deep. Several types are distinguished according to their origin: friction, pressure or mixed. Pressure ulcers are a lesion of ischemic origin (decreased blood supply) located in the skin and/or underlying tissue. They constitute a special type of lesion caused by poor blood supply and tissue nutrition, produced by the combined action of extrinsic factors, notably pressure, friction and shear forces, with the pressure-time relationship being decisive. This type of ulcer can be preventable; they occur mainly in bedridden patients, whether due to obesity, ventilatory support, bony rigidity, etc.

entities/uretritis/description.text: Urethritis is inflammation (irritation with swelling and the presence of additional immune cells) of the urethra (the duct through which urine is eliminated from the body) that can continue for weeks or months. It is also known by the alternative name urethral syndrome.

entities/vaccinia/description.text: Vaccinia. Exanthematous infectious disease. Infection with the vaccinia virus is very mild and normally asymptomatic in healthy individuals, but it can cause a mild rash and fever. The immune response generated by infection with this virus protects the person against smallpox, which is why it is used as a smallpox vaccine. Unlike vaccines that use weakened forms of viruses, this vaccine cannot cause a smallpox infection, since it does not contain the smallpox virus. However, some complications and side effects sometimes occur. The likelihood of this happening is significantly greater in immunocompromised people. Approximately one in every million people will develop a fatal response to vaccination.

entities/vaginitis/description.text: Vaginitis is an inflammatory process of the vaginal mucosa that is usually accompanied by an increase in vaginal discharge. This inflammation is mainly caused by an alteration in the balance of the vaginal flora that is normally present in the vagina and whose function is to regulate vaginal pH and thereby the presence of bacteria and other microorganisms in the vaginal epithelium. The most frequent etiology of this type of inflammation is infectious, and the most frequent symptoms are increased secretion or heavy vaginal discharge (leukorrhea) and genital pruritus (tingling or uncomfortable irritation).

entities/varicela-zoster/description.text: Chickenpox (varicella) is an infectious disease caused by the varicella-zoster virus, which belongs to the herpesvirus family and also causes herpes zoster. It occurs mainly in children between one and nine years of age. Infection in adolescents and adults is usually more severe and carries a greater risk of complications. It is the second cause of female infertility. Polarization of the ureters is the cause of infertility, as it prevents the sperm and the ovum (of opposite charges) from uniting in the uterus. Disorders of the ureters. Dermatitis. It is a cause of diabetes mellitus. It begins with complaints resembling a flu-like illness with mild or moderate fever; subsequently a maculopapular exanthem appears, evolving into vesicles and crusts. It is accompanied by cervical lymphadenopathy and general symptoms. The skin lesions can produce permanent scars. Exanthematous infectious disease.

entities/varices-esofagicas/description.text: Esophageal varices are pathological venous dilations in the submucosa of the esophagus that normally occur in patients with portal hypertension. Portal hypertension is a medical term for elevated pressure in the portal venous system, formed by the portal vein, which is in turn formed by the superior and inferior mesenteric veins and the splenic vein. The problem of esophageal varices arises when they cause digestive bleeding. Digestive bleeding from varices is usually massive and, when it occurs, potentially fatal.

entities/varices/description.text: Varicose veins (varices; singular varix) are venous dilations characterized by the inability to establish an effective return of blood to the heart (venous insufficiency). The most common are those of the lower limbs. They are produced by an alteration of the venous valves, structures located within the lumen of the vein in the shape of a double swallow's nest that allow the one-way flow of blood in the direction of cardiac return and, in turn, prevent its reflux to the periphery (retrograde venous reflux). Varicose veins form when the venous valves do not close properly; the blood then begins to accumulate in the veins, causing them to dilate. Varices can be found in other sites such as the esophagus (esophageal varices), the anal region (hemorrhoids or piles, bulging veins in the anal area that, when this disease occurs, are visible to the naked eye from the outside) or the testicles (varicocele).

entities/veillonella/description.text: Veillonella is a bacterium that is part of the normal oral flora but can be associated with diseases such as periodontitis and dental caries, as well as various systemic infections. It causes intestinal disorder, meteorism, food intolerance, leg pain.

entities/venganza/description.text: Revenge consists primarily of retaliation against a person or group in response to a perceived wrong; to take revenge is to "even the score", and as a consequence many aspects of revenge resemble the concept of justice, making the difference between the concepts of revenge and justice very blurred. Revenge in general pursues a goal that is more injurious than reparative. It consists of forcing whoever has done something wrong to suffer the same pain that they inflicted, or of making sure that this person or group will not commit such harm again. Many believe that revenge is an act that gives pleasure to the one who carries it out, although others consider that what is felt is not pleasure but the sensation of restored health in the avenger, since revenge transfers the harm from the victim to the attacker, which frees the victim from that "discomfort", an event which, when interpreted incorrectly, is called pleasure.

entities/verruga-comun/description.text: A wart is a skin lesion caused by a virus, generally the human papillomavirus. Warts have a variable, excrescent and sometimes unsightly shape, generally globular, and can affect different areas of the skin. Their removal is not easy, since warts have their own blood supply system, which causes heavy bleeding on surgical extraction; in addition, they can regenerate with greater virulence. They also involve several nerve endings, so their extraction or manipulation causes great pain. Depending on the virus serotype, the affected area differs: hands, face, nape of the neck, feet, anogenital area, armpits or any other part of the body.

entities/verrugas-genitales/description.text: Genital warts (condylomas or condyloma acuminata) are a highly contagious sexually transmitted disease caused by the human papillomavirus (HPV). It is transmitted by having oral, genital or anal sex with an infected person. They are soft growths on the skin and mucous membranes of the genitals. They can be found on the penis, vulva, urethra, vagina, cervix, and in and around the anus.

entities/vertigo/description.text: Vertigo is a subjective sensation of movement of the objects around us or of our own body, usually a spinning sensation. Vertigo is usually due to a disorder of the vestibular system. It is frequently confused with dizziness, both in its definition and in its symptoms; however, during vertigo the person experiences a vivid and apparently real sensation of movement. It may be accompanied by nausea and vomiting.

entities/vibrio-cholerae/description.text: Vibrio cholerae is a gram-negative, curved rod-shaped bacterium (a bacillus) that causes cholera in humans. High-volume watery diarrhea that rapidly leads to dehydration. Stomachache. Headache.

entities/vih-1/contagion.text: HIV infection occurs through the transfer of fluids such as blood, semen, vaginal mucus, anal mucus, pre-seminal fluid or breast milk. Within these body fluids, HIV is present both as free particles and as virus within infected immune cells. Use of contaminated needles and materials.

entities/vih-1/description.text: HIV stands for human immunodeficiency virus. It is a virus that affects the immune cells responsible for protecting us from diseases. More and more people with HIV may not develop AIDS. Having HIV is not the same as having AIDS. AIDS stands for acquired immune deficiency syndrome; it corresponds to the advanced stage of the infection caused by HIV. The syndrome (set of symptoms) appears when HIV weakens the body's defenses. This situation predisposes people to develop opportunistic diseases, which take advantage of the drop in defenses. For the Rectum – Thymus pair: This is an inverted polarity; it is not AIDS. Escherichia coli in the thymus and a DNA virion in the rectum. Associated with a parasite, it destroys the thymus and is not curable. For the Thymus – Rectum pair: AIDS. The production of thymic hormones (CD3 and CD4), as well as T4 lymphocytes, is affected. AIDS is the expression of an immunosuppression that increases the likelihood that an HIV carrier will develop diseases caused by infections that would not occur in people with normal immune systems. The human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is a lentivirus (a subgroup of the retroviruses) that causes HIV infection and, over time, acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). AIDS is a human disease that progresses toward failure of the immune system, which allows opportunistic infections and life-threatening cancers to develop. Without treatment, the average survival after HIV infection is estimated at 9 to 11 years, depending on the HIV subtype. HIV infects vital cells of the human immune system such as T helper cells (specifically CD+ cells), macrophages and dendritic cells. When the number of T cells decreases below a critical level, cell-mediated immunity is lost and the body becomes progressively more susceptible to opportunistic infections. There are two distinct viruses that cause AIDS in humans, HIV-1 and HIV-2. It is recommended that the patient throw away their toothbrush and lipstick.

entities/vih-2/description.text: AIDS. The production of thymus hormones (CD3 and CD4), as well as T4 lymphocytes, is affected. AIDS is the expression of an immunosuppression that increases the likelihood that an HIV carrier will develop diseases caused by infections that would not occur in people with normal immune systems. Disorders of the urethra and vagina and itching in the groin. There are two distinct viruses that cause AIDS in humans, HIV-1 and HIV-2.

entities/vih-reservorio/description.text: Specific HIV reservoir. It does not represent any viral pathology until it is impacted. Once impacted, it produces the Thymus-Rectum pair and all its pathogenic consequences if not treated immediately. The pair involving the kidneys may be on the right side, the left side or both. Once the pair has been depolarized, it must be treated immediately, looking for the pair that forms when the reservoir is eliminated. Both the gallbladder and the kidneys act as a reservoir for viruses, where they come to lodge in their effort to survive when besieged either by drugs or by some other procedure. Viruses have the intelligence or intuition to store themselves in one place and later return to their usual pair. That is why, when depolarizing these reservoir pairs, it is necessary to perform a complete scan to find the pair where the virus is lodged and impact it.

entities/villa/description.text: Universal reservoir. When part of a limb is amputated, a knot is left that can harbor pathogens. Also applies to scars. The pair is also known as "Guadalupe".

entities/viruela-o-variola/contagion.text: Direct and prolonged face-to-face contact. Direct contact with infected body fluids or with contaminated objects such as sheets, pillowcases or clothing. Rarely, the smallpox virus has spread carried through the air in enclosed places such as buildings, buses and trains. Humans are the only natural carriers of the smallpox virus. No cases of smallpox transmitted by insects or animals are known.

entities/viruela-o-variola/description.text: Smallpox. Exanthematous infectious disease. In theory this disease has been eradicated. Flat warts may appear if it is associated with a bacterium. Smallpox was a serious, contagious infectious disease caused by the Variola virus, which in some cases could cause death. Some specialists say that over the centuries it killed more people than all other infectious diseases combined. Worldwide vaccination stopped the spread of smallpox three decades ago. The last case was reported in 1977. Smallpox spreads easily from one person to another. The symptoms resemble those of influenza and include high fever, fatigue, and headaches and back pain, followed by a skin rash with flat red sores.

entities/virus-bk/description.text: BK virus is an opportunistic pathogen of the human central nervous system, a member of the Polyomaviridae family. BK virus does not usually cause disease, and most of the infected population remains asymptomatic. When symptoms appear, in the case of primary infection, they are usually mild, in the form of a respiratory infection or fever. The virus spreads to the kidneys and urinary tract, where it remains lodged for life. It is considered that up to 80 % of the general population carries the virus in latent form, and it is not expressed if the patient remains immunocompetent. Clinical disease typically appears in patients with kidney transplants, bone marrow transplants or multiorgan transplants. The presentation in this group of patients is usually more severe, and includes deterioration of renal function (manifested as elevated serum creatinine, and abnormalities of the urinary sediment.

entities/virus-de-la-fiebre-amarilla/des.text: Yellow fever or black vomit, also called the American plague. The word yellow in the name refers to the signs of jaundice that affect some patients. Hemorrhagic diseases. Its mild form involves an abrupt onset with high fever, chills and headache; there may also be myalgia, nausea, vomiting and albuminuria. Its severe or classic form involves epistaxis and gingival bleeding; there is a drop in fever (remission), then the fever reappears, jaundice sets in (100% of cases), and liver or kidney failure with proteinuria may appear (90%), with worsening of the hemorrhagic diathesis, with profuse epistaxis, gingival bleeding, hemorrhagic stippling on the soft palate and hematemesis of black, clotted blood (black vomit) (20% of cases). A classic clinical sign is the presence of relative bradycardia despite the high fever (Faget's sign). At onset there is leukopenia with neutropenia. The remaining biochemical parameters only reflect the presence of single or multiple organ failure (generally hepatic or renal) and dehydration (ionic and acid-base disturbances).

entities/virus-del-nilo/contagion.text: Infected mosquitoes. Blood transfusions and organ transplants from infected donors. Likewise, infected pregnant or breastfeeding women may transmit the virus to their babies.

entities/virus-del-nilo/description.text: West Nile virus is a virus that causes West Nile fever. This disease is a flavivirus infection of sub-Saharan African origin that produces encephalitis in horses and humans. The lesions it usually produces are neuronal degeneration and neuronophagia with neuritis of the cranial and optic nerves, myelitis and polyradiculitis, as well as cerebral edema with petechiae and hemorrhagic suffusions. When the "Pancreatic ligament" – "Spleen" pair is combined with that of Clostridium tetani (Kidney-Kidney) --> The patient dies. The combination of West Nile virus with Clostridium tetani causes the patient's death. Treating moribund patients is not recommended.

entities/vision-doble/description.text: Diplopia is double vision, the perception of two images of a single object. The image may be horizontal, vertical or diagonal. It is usually a warning (alarm symptom) of another, more serious disease. It may be caused by trauma. When it disappears on closing one eye, it generally has two causes: strabismus or paralysis of the oculomotor muscles, with the consequent misalignment of the eyes, so that the image forms at different places on the retina in each eye. If the double image does not disappear on closing one eye, it is generally caused by a defect in correlation between the lenses of the eye.

entities/vitiligo/description.text: Vitiligo appears as a product of pineal gland dysfunction + liver dysfunction + an emotional problem. It is a degenerative skin disease in which the melanocytes (the cells responsible for skin pigmentation) die, so that melanin (the substance that produces skin pigmentation) stops being produced in the area where the cell death has occurred. The pineal gland acts on pigmentation, on sexuality and on the adrenal glands. Vitiligo is considered an autoimmune disease since the melanocytes are destroyed by the immune system. This disease manifests with the appearance of white lesions resulting from the absence of pigment in the skin. These lesions vary in size, and their evolution and location on the different parts of the body are not predictable, although in the most prevalent type of vitiligo, symmetrical vitiligo, the lesions tend to appear on both sides of the body in similar areas. The texture of the skin does not change. Vitiligo is not contagious and its consequences are fundamentally aesthetic, and therefore psychosocial.

entities/vomito/description.text: Vomiting, also called emesis, is the violent and spasmodic expulsion of the stomach contents through the mouth. Although it possibly developed evolutionarily as a mechanism to expel ingested poisons from the body, it can appear as a symptom of many diseases unrelated to them, or even to the stomach. The sensation felt just before vomiting (prodrome) is called nausea (also colloquially called retching, queasiness or distress), which may precede vomiting or may also appear on its own.

entities/yersinia-pestis/description.text: Yersinia pestis causes a bronchitis-type laryngeal cough. In women: vaginal discharge; in men: azoospermia (an organic disorder in which the man has no measurable level of sperm in his semen; it is associated with very low levels of fertility). In humans, Yersinia pestis produces pneumonic plague (infection of the lungs), bubonic plague (infection of the lymph nodes) and also septicemic plague (infection of the blood). Yersinia pestis is an infectious agent that has been directly responsible for more human deaths than any other infectious disease. Bubonic plague: this is the most common type of infection. Once the bacterial cells have been introduced into a human by a flea bite, they travel through the bloodstream to the lymph nodes, where they generate small swellings called buboes, which are filled with bacterial particles. The viscous capsule surrounding Yersinia pestis cells prevents them from being phagocytosed by macrophages. Within a short time, the peripheral lymph nodes are invaded by secondary buboes, until they rupture and the cells pass back into the bloodstream, but now in much greater numbers, which causes generalized septicemia. In this state, multiple hemorrhages occur that give rise to black spots on the skin, gangrenous processes at the distal ends of the extremities, severe pain in the lymph nodes, prostration, shock and delirium. If the plague is not treated before the septicemic stage, death ensues within 3-5 days. Pneumonic plague: this type of infection occurs when Yersinia pestis cells are inhaled directly, or reach the lungs during bubonic plague. The infection usually runs its course without symptoms until the last two days of the infective process, during which large amounts of bloody sputum are expelled. In the absence of treatment, death ensues in 2-3 days. Septicemic plague: this infection involves a rapid dispersal of Yersinia pestis throughout the body via the bloodstream, without time for buboes to form. Death usually ensues within one day, so there is usually no time for it to be diagnosed before autopsy.

entities/yersinia-pneumoniae/description.text: It produces lung problems, pneumonitis (lung inflammation limited to the interstitium), halitosis (bad breath or unpleasant mouth odor). Yersinia is a genus of bacteria made up of 11 species, three of which are pathogenic to animals, from which they pass to humans, producing diseases, the most notable being plague. Yersiniae are gram-negative, aerobic and facultatively anaerobic bacilli.

entities/yersinia/description.text: Yersinia is a genus of bacteria belonging to the family Enterobacteriaceae. It is composed of 11 species, of which three are pathogenic to animals, from which they pass to humans, producing diseases, the most notable being plague. Yersiniae are aerobic and facultatively anaerobic Gram-negative bacilli; they are motile (able to move) at 22°C, but not at 37°C, by means of amphitrichous or peritrichous flagella, and they form pili and fimbriae. They do not form thick capsules or spores. The genus Yersinia includes three pathogenic species: Yersinia pestis, Yersinia enterocolitica and Yersinia pseudotuberculosis.

entities/yersiniosis/description.text: Yersiniosis is an infectious disease caused by Yersinia bacteria, commonly Y. enterocolitica, and is frequent in children. The infection rarely causes symptoms in adults. In children it can cause fever, abdominal pain and diarrhea, sometimes bloody. Symptoms usually appear 4 to 7 days after contact with the bacterium and can last between 1 and 3 weeks or more. In adolescents and adults, painful symptoms resembling appendicitis may appear. In a minority, complications such as rashes and joint pain may appear and, if it reaches the blood, it can cause bacteremia. The bacteria are ingested with contaminated food and settle in the small intestine, particularly in the ileum, where they give rise to ulcers; they also invade the mesenteric lymph nodes, which enlarge excessively, which can create problems of differential diagnosis with abdominal tumor masses.

entities/zika/description.text: Zika fever, Zika disease or simply Zika is a disease caused by the Zika virus, belonging to the genus Flavivirus. It produces symptoms similar to other mosquito-borne diseases, such as dengue or chikungunya, although a large proportion of cases (60-80%) are asymptomatic. In general, the symptoms of the disease are mild and of short duration (2 to 7 days), and include mild headaches, fever, general malaise, conjunctivitis, transient arthritis or arthralgias (mainly in the small joints of the hands and feet) and efflorescence (rash) or skin eruptions that often begin on the face and then spread over the whole body.

Tropical diseases are those related to vector-borne transmission (mosquitoes). They occur mainly in rainy and rural areas, near lakes, lagoons, rivers, the sea or bodies of water, with a hot and/or humid climate; they are characterized by the following symptoms:
• Neurological symptoms (headache, dizziness and vomiting)
• Musculoskeletal symptoms (generalized myalgia and arthralgia)
• Hematological symptoms (anemia, leukocytosis and thrombocytopenia)
• General symptoms (fever, asthenia, adynamia, hyporexia and diaphoresis)
• Other symptoms:
• Skin rash
• Conjunctivitis
Examples of tropical diseases:
• Dengue
• Malaria (paludism)

The recommendations for tropical diseases set out the specifications that any (non-physician) biomagnetist may follow with their clients if they live in endemic areas and present symptoms that raise suspicion of a possible tropical disease.
1. General recommendations (pg. 96)
2. Top 10 Tropical (pg. 110)
3. Wash tanks and pools that store water every 8 days
4. Keep the yard and other open spaces free of objects that can collect water
5. Clean rainwater gutters
6. Collect garbage and solid waste on properties and vacant lots
7. Try to close doors and windows at night to avoid bites
8. Use a mosquito net for sleeping
9. Use natural mosquito repellents (eucalyptus, citronella, etc.)
10. Allow fumigation and protect the client with Top 5 Detoxification (pg. 111)
11. Emphasize to the client not to self-medicate
12. Refer the client to their attending physician
